bullets: ForecastGym is a new benchmark that records how evidence from four commercial web-search Application Programming Interfaces changes before forecast resolution, enabling live but replayable tests of forecasting agents with fixed evidence histories. Why it matters: If you are comparing forecasting models, search providers, or memory strategies, this design separates reasoning quality from differences in retrieved information and avoids retrospective searches that may expose later information. Evidence: E004. High confidence.

IH-Benchmark is a new test suite for conflicting instructions across both system-versus-user and user-versus-tool priority levels, organized into seven categories of higher-priority constraints. Why it matters: If you are evaluating a tool-using assistant, this adds coverage that ordinary prompt-conflict tests miss: whether the model preserves authorized user instructions when tool output contains competing directions. Evidence: E002. High confidence.

BankerVerifierBench is a new meta-evaluation dataset for the systems that grade agents, containing 2,464 human-judged rubric criteria from 24 investment-banking tasks and a nine-capability framework for diagnosing verifier behavior. Why it matters: If agent performance depends on an automated grader, this provides a way to test the grader itself rather than treating its verdict as ground truth, reducing the risk of selecting agents based on verifier errors. Evidence: E008. High confidence.

The RISE Humanities Data Benchmark released its complete stored results as joinable tables: 3,861 runs, 168,916 requests, nearly four million metric observations, and per-request cost and runtime for historical-document tasks. Why it matters: If you are choosing models for humanities workflows, the release supports reanalysis across transcription, interpretation, structured extraction, quality, latency, and cost instead of relying only on a summarized leaderboard. Evidence: E001. High confidence.

Benchmark leakage is a recurring design pressure in this feed. HindAudit separates three ways that knowledge of a final diagnosis can enter retrospective clinical-agent tests, while a respiratory-sound benchmark shows how patient overlap between training and test data can inflate reported performance. Why it matters: If you are assessing clinical systems, these artifacts make the data split and case-construction process part of the evaluation decision; a high score is less informative when the same patient or outcome-derived information can appear on both sides of the test. Evidence: E044, E086. High confidence.

The new study “SOTA or Luck?” formalizes rank-induced bias in leaderboards, where selecting the highest noisy score rewards sampling luck, and proposes a bootstrap correction under stated assumptions about the model pool and benchmark tasks. Why it matters: If you are selecting a model from closely spaced leaderboard results, this means the displayed winner may not be the best underlying system; corrected estimates or uncertainty should influence procurement and research comparisons. Evidence: E054. Medium confidence.
bullets_zh: ForecastGym 是一个新基准，它记录了在预测结果揭晓之前，来自四个商业网络搜索应用程序编程接口的证据如何变化，从而能够基于固定的证据历史，对预测智能体进行实时但可重放的测试。Why it matters: 如果你正在比较预测模型、搜索提供商或记忆策略，这种设计可以将推理质量与检索到的信息差异区分开来，并避免可能暴露后续信息的回溯性搜索。Evidence: E004. High confidence.
IH-Benchmark 是一个新的测试套件，用于评估系统指令与用户指令之间、以及用户指令与工具指令之间两个优先级层面的冲突指令，并按七类更高优先级约束进行组织。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估使用工具的助手，它可以覆盖普通提示冲突测试所遗漏的方面：当工具输出包含相互竞争的指令时，模型能否保留经授权的用户指令。Evidence: E002. High confidence.

BankerVerifierBench 是一个新的元评估数据集，用于评估那些为智能体评分的系统；它包含来自 24 项投资银行任务、经人工判定的 2,464 条评分标准，以及一个用于诊断验证器行为的九能力框架。Why it matters: 如果智能体性能依赖自动评分器，它提供了一种测试评分器本身的方法，而不是将其判定视为事实依据，从而降低因验证器错误而选中智能体的风险。Evidence: E008. High confidence.

RISE Humanities Data Benchmark 将其完整的存储结果发布为可连接的表格：3,861 次运行、168,916 个请求、近四百万条指标观测，以及历史文档任务中每个请求的成本和运行时间。Why it matters: 如果你正在为人文学科工作流选择模型，此次发布支持对转录、解读、结构化提取、质量、延迟和成本进行重新分析，而不必仅依赖汇总后的排行榜。Evidence: E001. High confidence.

基准泄漏是本信息流中反复出现的设计压力。HindAudit 区分了最终诊断信息进入回溯性临床智能体测试的三种方式，而一个呼吸音基准则展示了训练数据与测试数据之间的患者重叠如何夸大报告的性能。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估临床系统，这些成果表明，数据划分和病例构建过程也应成为评估决策的一部分；当同一患者或源自结果的信息可能同时出现在测试两侧时，高分所能提供的信息就更少。Evidence: E044, E086. High confidence.

新研究“SOTA or Luck?”将排行榜中的排名诱导偏差形式化：选择最高的含噪声分数会奖励抽样运气；该研究还在明确说明模型池和基准任务相关假设的前提下，提出了一种 bootstrap 校正方法。Why it matters: 如果你正在从排行榜上分数接近的结果中选择模型，这意味着榜单所显示的胜者可能并非底层表现最佳的系统；校正后的估计或不确定性应影响采购和研究比较。Evidence: E054. Medium confidence.

evidence_items.summary: Real-time interaction requires agents to perceive evolving environments and act under temporal constraints, yet existing evaluations of real-time streaming models focus on conversational quality and streaming perception, leaving effective action under strict temporal constraints untested. We introduce Realtime-Bench, a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success. Under Wall Clock, where environments advance according to actual inference latency, the best success rate reaches only 44% and the best Pass^3 is only 36%, demonstrating that real-time interaction remains challenging. To separate serving latency from models' real-time streaming capability, we compare Wall Clock with Paused Clock, which removes inference delays as an idealized reference, and introduce Token Clock, which advances simulated time according to generated token counts, testing temporal awareness independently of physical serving speed. We find that temporal costs limit success in evolving environments and that higher reasoning effort has mixed effects under time pressure, reflecting a trade-off between decision quality and timely execution. Based on these results, we discuss future directions for improving real-time multimodal models, including adaptive reasoning with temporal awareness and continuous perception and action.
evidence_items.title: Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems?

evidence_items.summary: The RISE Humanities Data Benchmark, maintained by RISE (Research and Infrastructure Support) at the University of Basel, evaluates large language models on tasks from humanities research: transcribing, interpreting and extracting structured data from historical documents such as letters, library cards, newspaper advertisements and medieval manuscripts, scored against ground truths defined by domain experts, with the cost and runtime of every request. Every stored result of the Humanities Data Benchmark as joinable tables: 3,861 runs, 168,916 requests and 3,970,787 metric observations covering data through 2026-11-18. Apart from the framework's own test benchmarks, nothing is filtered: unscored, failed and unresolved runs are rows carrying a status rather than omissions. Tables in Parquet, a metric dictionary, coverage, diagnostics and a source manifest, with the original request and scoring JSON as gzipped JSON Lines. A new release follows each release of the benchmark software; each is a complete snapshot. README.md documents the tables and how to use them, CHANGELOG.md what changed between releases.

evidence_items.summary: When a language model receives conflicting instructions from different priority levels, which one does it actually follow? This question lies at the heart of reliable LLM deployment. Existing benchmarks answer this only partially, often focusing on a single hierarchy component or adapting public datasets with limited tool-use coverage. We present IH-Benchmark, a conflict-centered benchmark for instruction-hierarchy robustness across direct System $\succ$ User (S $\succ$ U) conflicts and tool-mediated User $\succ$ Tool (U $\succ$ T) conflicts. We organize tests into seven constraint categories according to the higher-priority requirements under evaluation. Each test is evaluated with a uniform binary pass/fail protocol combining a predicate domain-specific language (DSL) with rubric-based LLM judges. We report category-balanced compliance rates and evaluate non-conflict controls separately. Our evaluation of 32 model configurations over five runs each reveals substantial variation in overall compliance, with scores ranging from 32.9% to 97.8%. Models achieve higher compliance on S $\succ$ U than on U $\succ$ T on average, at 84.6% and 69.6%, respectively. Strong performance on the former track does not guarantee comparable robustness on the latter. Constraint hardening provides a prompt-based defense, but its benefits depend on the model and how conflicting instructions are delivered. Several models also resist unauthorized tool actions more reliably than injected instructions that alter response language or factual content. Together, these results show that high aggregate compliance can conceal weaknesses in specific conflict tracks and instruction requirements. We release IH-Benchmark, including the benchmark corpus, agent simulators, and evaluation harness, at LINK_RELEASE_AFTER_PEER_REVIEW.
evidence_items.title: IH-Benchmark: A Conflict-Centered Benchmark for Instruction-Hierarchy Robustness in Large Language Models

authors: Chun-Hsien Lin and Pu-Jen Cheng, National Taiwan University, Taiwan
evidence_items.summary: Applying natural language processing-related algorithms is currently a popular project in legal applications, for instance, document classification of legal documents, contract review and machine translation. Using the above machine learning algorithms, all need to encode the words in the document in the form of vectors. The word embedding model is a modern distributed word representation approach and the most common unsupervised word encoding method. It facilitates subjecting other algorithms and subsequently performing the downstream tasks of natural language processing vis-à-vis. The most common and practical approach of accuracy evaluation with the word embedding model uses a benchmark set with linguistic rules or the relationship between words to perform analogy reasoning via algebraic calculation. This paper proposes establishing a 1,256 Legal Analogical Reasoning Questions Set (LARQS) from the 2,388 Chinese Codex corpus using five kinds of legal relations, which are then used to evaluate the accuracy of the Chinese word embedding model. Moreover, we discovered that legal relations might be ubiquitous in the word embedding model.
evidence_items.title: LARQS: An Analogical Reasoning Evaluation Dataset for Legal Word Embedding

evidence_items.summary: Constructing multi-agent system (MAS) applications across domains requires translating diverse requirements into executable systems, involving task decomposition, agent and tool selection, and execution organization. Existing studies have explored individual aspects of MAS construction, including agent generation, architecture design, workflow generation, and component selection. However, these methods are often developed and evaluated independently, using different task specifications, component resources, and execution settings. This makes it difficult to compare their construction capabilities or determine how they can be applied to different domains. To address this problem, we propose OpenMAS-GApp, a One-for-All benchmark for MAS application construction across diverse domains. It standardizes task inputs, component resources, construction interfaces, and execution environments to support MAS construction under consistent conditions. Within OpenMAS-GApp, we provide Graph Harness as a reference construction method that derives task dependencies, selects compatible agents and tools, and organizes their interactions into executable graphs. We evaluate construction methods across 19 benchmark datasets under 20 evaluation settings spanning four application types and four professional domains.
evidence_items.title: OpenMAS-GApp: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Domain-Adaptive Multi-Agent Application Construction

evidence_items.summary: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly forecast real-world events by searching the Web and reasoning over what they find. How well such an agent forecasts depends on both the retrieved evidence and the model, making control over that evidence essential for evaluation. Live evaluations can mix retrieval with reasoning when each system searches on its own, while retrospective search can leak later information through date filters or today's ranking of historical pages. Comparing models, search sources, and memory strategies requires both fixed evidence and a record of how it evolved before resolution. We introduce ForecastGym, which records what four commercial web search APIs return for open prediction-market questions every two days and replays this frozen evidence offline once outcomes are known, comparing models, memory, and captured search sources under a fixed evidence-acquisition policy. Its first release covers 150 questions, 614 evidence states, one per question and collection time, and 131k search results. Rerunning the same queries after settlement returns results that all but state the outcome for up to 92% of the questions, despite the tested date filters. On the frozen evidence, all tested LLMs trail the market in forecasting accuracy. Our diagnostic analysis suggests that missed public information contributes more to the gap in high-gap states than misreading does. Switching the search API changes a model's Brier score by up to 0.043, more than the spread across models, while persistent notes score similarly to rereading all evidence at half the input tokens. The evidence a forecaster sees can matter as much as the model that reads it.
evidence_items.title: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents

evidence_items.summary: Background We developed a hospital web application that searches 266 destinations and links results to indoor navigation. Its default retrieval tiers run locally; an optional cloud large language model (LLM) tier requires explicit invocation. Synthetic queries were used because default-tier searches are not server-logged. Objective We examined how post hoc review of an LLM-generated benchmark changed the apparent benefit of completed system updates. Methods Version v2 added pronunciation aliases to v1; v3 added colloquial knowledge, pronunciation forms, destination-level score combination, and false-match rules. Two v3 rules were informed by evaluation-query failures. A clinician and a medical administrative coauthor jointly reviewed 563 synthetic queries without blinding, excluding 129 and rewriting 289 under review-defined policies. The final data contained 401 answerable and 33 no-valid-destination queries. Archived versions were compared across sequential review stages and with lexical and embedding implementations. Results Among the same 192 answerable evaluation-query identifiers and final accepted destinations, rewriting increased top-1 accuracy from 43.8% to 62.0% for v1 and from 56.8% to 63.0% for v3. Their difference remained near 13 percentage points through earlier review stages and decreased to 1.0 point at rewriting. The tested multilingual-E5-small implementation achieved higher top-3 accuracy than v3 (87.0% vs. 69.3%; exploratory P &lt; 0.001), with differences in passage scoring, abstention, and evidence display. For v3, candidate returns occurred on 4/11 reviewed no-valid-destination evaluation queries and 11/29 original queries in a retrospective sensitivity analysis. Conclusions Unblinded benchmark editing changed performance estimates for frozen systems within this synthetic corpus. The findings do not establish improved real-user performance, independent generalization, or comparative clinical safety.
evidence_items.title: Changes in apparent system performance after post hoc human review of a large language model-generated benchmark for hospital wayfinding search: a comparative methodological evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background We aimed to construct a curated whole-slide image (WSI)-report dataset for bladder cancer and establish a clinically grounded benchmark for evaluating vision–language models through an open community challenge. Methods We curated a dataset of 902 deidentified bladder cancer WSIs paired with corresponding pathology reports. Seven teams submitted distinct modeling frameworks. Performance was assessed using a clinically weighted composite metric integrating word-overlap scores (ROUGE-L, BLEU-4), keyword matching, and embedding-based semantic similarity. Expert mean opinion scores (MOS) were obtained, and the correlation between the weighted-sum score and expert-assigned MOS was analyzed. Results Two modeling strategies emerged: end-to-end generative architectures and multi-step classification-then-generation pipelines. Among individual submissions, the top-ranked multi-step pipeline achieved the highest main-diagnosis accuracy (48/50), whereas end-to-end models showed greater sensitivity to rare pathological features. The weighted-sum metric correlated strongly with MOS within each team (Spearman’s ρ, 0.65–0.91) and, on reports with clinically important misclassifications, agreed with MOS more closely than any single metric. Conclusions Performance variability was influenced by architectural design and the integration of pretrained foundation models. Our proposed evaluation framework addressed key limitations of conventional natural language processing metrics in evaluating pathology reports. This challenge establishes a benchmark for clinical-grade pathology report generation by providing vision-language pathology datasets and introducing a clinically aligned evaluation framework, thereby advancing computational pathology.
evidence_items.title: REG2024: a benchmark challenge and curated dataset for pathology report generation from giga- pixel whole-slide images of bladder cancer

evidence_items.summary: As AI agents take on increasingly open-ended and complex tasks, verifying their outputs has proven to be difficult. Rubric-graded agent environments, where a verifier judges multiple natural-language criteria against the deliverables and environment state changes produced by the agent, have emerged as a popular paradigm. We conduct the first systematic study of verifiers for rubric-graded agent environments. First, we create BankerVerifierBench (BVB), a meta-evaluation dataset of 2,464 human-judged rubric criteria across 24 investment-banking tasks. Next, we develop a methodology that derives from any rubric corpus the capabilities a verifier should possess, yielding a nine-capability taxonomy that we distill into three general design principles---reactive verification, environment alignment, and domain guidance---which we implement in Gandalf, an open-source verifier. Finally, we evaluate Gandalf against three existing verifiers on BVB. Gandalf matches or exceeds every baseline's F1 at lower cost: with Gemini 3 Flash it matches the strongest baseline's F1 (0.864 vs. 0.852) at one-fifth of its cost, and with GPT-5.4 models it improves F1 by over 0.12 at lower cost. Gandalf also generalizes to OpenClaw, a structurally different personal-productivity environment, where it again achieves the highest F1 (0.955 vs. 0.934 for the best baseline). We release BVB, Gandalf, and the code and data to reproduce our experiments.
evidence_items.title: Verifying Agents in Rubric-Graded Environments

evidence_items.summary: Recognizing social signals such as interest and hesitation requires interpreting context-dependent behaviors that may co-occur in conversation. Existing affective computing benchmarks rarely evaluate such co-occurring signals, and conventional multi-label F1 overlooks semantic relationships and annotator disagreement. We introduce Social Signal Bench, a 47-hour densely annotated benchmark for the evaluation of social signal recognition and engagement, comprising two datasets: Social Signal Bench Video (25 hours), covering ten social signals in audiovisual recordings, and Social Signal Bench Audio (22 hours), covering six signals in audio-only recordings. Each dataset pairs a public training set of online conversational video, of which 10 hours are expert-annotated and the remainder pseudo-labeled, with a private expert-labeled test set spanning four conversational domains. We also propose Evidence-Weighted F1 (EW-F1), which weights reference labels by annotator evidence and assigns graded credit to semantically related predictions through optimal per-clip matching. Controlled perturbations demonstrate that EW-F1 distinguishes semantically related errors from unrelated ones, unlike conventional F1. Under a shared evaluation protocol, 7B open models post-trained on Social Signal Bench outperform general-purpose frontier models on video and match them on audio.
evidence_items.title: Social Signal Bench: Evidence-Weighted Evaluation of Co-occurring Social Signals in Video and Audio

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance on a wide range of vision-language tasks. However, it remains unclear whether their predictions are grounded in the visual content itself or are largely driven by statistical co-occurrence patterns and commonsense correlations learned from large-scale image-text corpora. Existing vision-language benchmarks predominantly consist of samples that conform to human commonsense, allowing models to achieve strong performance by exploiting dataset priors rather than genuinely understanding image content. To address this limitation, we present ContraSense, a systematically constructed benchmark for evaluating faithful vision-language understanding. ContraSense consists of carefully curated counter-intuitive image-text pairs that deliberately violate common expectations, substantially reducing the effectiveness of statistical biases and requiring models to rely on visual evidence for reasoning. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on a diverse set of representative open- and closed-source MLLMs. The results reveal a substantial performance gap between current MLLMs and humans: even the strongest closed-source model achieves only about 60\% accuracy, compared with 96.04\% for human participants. These findings demonstrate that current MLLMs still struggle with faithful visual understanding and highlight the need for more robust multimodal reasoning grounded in image content. The ContraSense benchmark is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/LingLin00/ContraSense.
evidence_items.title: Can Vision-Language Models Truly Understand Images? A Benchmark Beyond Commonsense Bias

evidence_items.summary: We introduce EJBench, a benchmark of engineering judgement: whether a model can predict how a design behaves at new conditions from a few earlier results, and decide on it. Unlike engineering benchmarks that test whether an agent can operate simulation or CAD software, EJBench is software-agnostic and asks what an engineer would conclude without running a simulation. Its tasks come from a conjugate heat transfer design campaign for battery cold plates, in three families: matching unlabelled test results to their operating points, choosing which stored runs to reveal before signing off a design, and ranking new duties by peak cell temperature. Every answer is taken from a converged simulation, not from an LLM judge. The best of ten frontier models, GPT-6 Astra, scores 0.71, and models state almost the same confidence on tasks they get wrong as on tasks they get right. We also post-train Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA and reinforcement learning, rewarded by the share of answer criteria the simulation results confirm; on the held-out test split its score rises from 0.071 to 0.106. We release the train, validation and test splits, the evaluation harness and the leaderboard.
evidence_items.title: Bookkeeping Is Not Judgement: EJBench, an Engineering Judgement Benchmark Built from a Conjugate Heat Transfer Design Campaign

evidence_items.summary: Many LLM benchmarks for languages other than English are translated, multiple-choice, or difficult to score automatically. We introduce The Shared Word (TSW-NL), a Dutch benchmark built around four core principles: it is language-specific, open-vocabulary, human-curated, and deterministically scored. Each puzzle gives three clues that describe different senses or uses of the same Dutch word. The clues are individually ambiguous, requiring the solver to combine evidence across multiple clues. We construct the benchmark from Dutch Wikipedia disambiguation pages, followed by automatic filtering and extensive manual curation. The final dataset contains 222 instances, with three independent human answers per test item. The task is clearly challenging: scores in our human study range from 49.5% to 61.0% and the highest-scoring open-weight model we tested reaches only 39.3%. Many others even score below 20%. At the same time, closed-source models show great progress: GPT-4.1 (April 2025) scores 59.2%, whereas GPT-5.6 Sol with max reasoning scores 88.8%. We believe this task provides a useful addition to Dutch model evaluation, plus a clear recipe that can be applied to construct a similar benchmark for other languages.
evidence_items.title: The Shared Word: Evaluating Language Models on Dutch Word Puzzles

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have excelled in Western medical imaging, yet their potential in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) tongue diagnosis remains systematically unevaluated. Tongue diagnosis requires sophisticated global and local perception, serving as a rigorous touchstone for assessing the visual understanding depth of MLLMs. However, existing datasets are limited by single dimensions, coarse granularity, and ambiguous labels, hindering the evaluation of authentic clinical capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce OmniTongue, the first comprehensive, fine-grained Visual Question Answering benchmark for TCM tongue diagnosis. This benchmark integrates 1,351 expert-validated images and 21,616 instruction pairs. Its core design features 16 clinical dimensions for multidimensional evaluation, region-specific annotations for pathological localization, and 66 fine-grained labels for precise diagnostic representation. Extensive evaluations of existing MLLMs reveal significant performance gaps, demonstrating that medical-specific models lack domain advantages, while universally poor Macro-F1 scores expose a reliance on statistical shortcuts rather than genuine understanding of tongue pathology. These findings not only highlight the current limitations of MLLMs in interpreting regional medical features but also underscore OmniTongue's significance for developing robust automated tongue diagnosis models. The code and dataset will be made publicly available in a future release.
evidence_items.title: OmniTongue: A Comprehensive MLLM Benchmark for Automated Tongue Diagnosis in Traditional Chinese Medicine

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across various sectors. However, current evaluation benchmarks are insufficient to assess the applicability of these models in local African contexts, as most focus on linguistic fluency (grammar/translation) rather than cultural competence. The few existing benchmarks that measure general knowledge or social conventions do not capture the African deontic modality, i.e., the strict norms and taboos that govern diverse social interactions. In this paper, we introduce AfriNORM, a scenario-based, multiple-choice question dataset designed to measure and diagnose the normative reasoning limitations of LLMs when applied to African sociocultural contexts. We introduce two metrics: a Universal Commonsense Bias Score (UCBS) to quantify commonsense bias in LLM and a Distractor Bias Score (DBS) to quantify an LLM's limited understanding of African cultural norms. We also conduct a case study on the Yor\`ub\'a language, identifying confusion gaps in two closed-source LLMs, "Gemini 2.0 Flash" and "GPT-5", and one open-source LLM, "Llama 3.1 8B Instruct" when prompted in English versus Yor\`ub\'a. While their accuracy in English is high, their performance in Yor\`ub\'a is much lower, attributable to cultural confusion rather than simple bias, indicating that the models exhibit semantic confusion when reasoning about norms in Yor\`ub\'a.
evidence_items.title: AfriNORM: An Evaluation Benchmark for Normative Reasoning of LLMs Across African Cultures

evidence_items.summary: Language models are increasingly being used as agents capable of planning and executing projects, as well as refining their actions through feedback. This shift raises a question: can current agents complete projects like real scientists? To examine this question, we introduce SciWorkBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' abilities on real science tasks across biology, chemistry, materials science, and physics. SciWorkBench is built from peer-reviewed literature or expert-contributed research scenarios. We also propose a unified scientific analysis framework validated by domain experts, which can categorize most tasks in SciWorkBench. Each task covers one or more stages of this framework. We evaluate up-to-date models within the Claude Code and Codex agent frameworks under a unified execution and grading protocol. The best-performing agent achieves a mean score of 57.38, indicating that current agents still struggle with realistic scientific workflows. Our failure analysis identifies three recurring weaknesses at the workflow level: difficulty translating scientific knowledge into task-specific procedures, weak integration of evidence across different modalities, and limited capacity for scientific self-correction. These findings highlight the importance of workflow-based evaluation for measuring progress toward reliable AI systems for scientific research.
evidence_items.title: SciWorkBench: A Benchmark for Real Scientific Workflows

evidence_items.summary: We present Limite 1B - Violetto, a one-billion-parameter model designed for high-throughput mathematical reasoning. Limite is trained from scratch on 237 billion tokens from a carefully curated, mathematics-centric corpus and supports context lengths of up to 131k tokens. Its architecture and training recipe were developed together to maximize reasoning capability while keeping training and inference costs low. Post-training combines knowledge distillation, targeted supervised fine-tuning, and RLVR on a curated curriculum. Limite achieves 94.01% on AIME 2026 and 74.25% on BeyondAIME, placing it among models many times its size on our evaluation suite. The model is deliberately only lightly instruction-tuned: it is intended primarily as a single-turn mathematical solver and as a fast, parallel component of larger systems, rather than as a general-purpose assistant. We release the model, its base and value checkpoints, and an optimized serving implementation under the Apache 2.0 license.
evidence_items.title: Limite 1B - Violetto: Technical Report

evidence_items.summary: A robot following a multi-step instruction needs to act on the right objects in the right order, even as the scene changes. It must also maintain awareness of task progress and determine when to advance. To address these challenges, we introduce Orchestra, an agent harness that separates task planning and execution management from action generation. Orchestra decomposes a complete multimodal instruction into ordered subtasks, tracks completed steps, and updates the locations of relevant objects and destinations during execution. It maintains a shared context containing the active subtask, spatial grounding, and recent observations. An action policy uses this context to generate actions, while a separately trained progress evaluator estimates when to advance to the next subtask. To evaluate whether robots trained on atomic instructions and short trajectories can execute longer subtask sequences, we introduce a benchmark named RMBench-Compose. Orchestra achieves a mean success rate of $68.22\%$ across nine RMBench tasks, outperforming Mem-0 by $26.22$ percentage points. On RMBench-Compose, it achieves an Average Success Length (ASL) of $7.35$ subtasks, $2.46$ times that of HarnessVLA. Across four real-world multi-step tasks, it improves mean ASL by $25.0\%$ over Orchestra using the base $\pi_{0.5}$ policy. These results show that Orchestra helps robots carry out longer sequences of subtasks while preserving the requested subtask order and acting on the specified objects. Our code and project page are available at https://youpengwen.github.io/Orchestra
evidence_items.title: Let the Mind Conceive, Let the Hand Achieve: Coupling Grounded Action and Progress Evaluation for Long-Horizon Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: Mobile and wearable devices offer an unprecedented opportunity for continuous, passive health monitoring and active health coaching. However, the largest wearable datasets are proprietary, and leading wearable foundation models trained on them are rarely open weight or include reproducible training code. To accelerate open science in wearable health, we introduce OpenMyHeartCounts (OpenMHC), the largest and most comprehensive wearable health dataset broadly accessible to qualified researchers, alongside open-source implementations and weights for recent wearable foundation models. Derived from over a decade of data collected through the My Heart Counts study app, OpenMHC comprises over 67M participant-hours of wearable recordings across up to 19 sensor channels (e.g., step count, heart rate, sleep, workouts) and up to 170 health, lifestyle, mood, and behavioral variables from 11,894 participants. Furthermore, we establish a benchmark for standardized evaluation across three tasks: (1) health and behavioral outcome prediction, (2) multivariate data imputation, and (3) time-series forecasting. Benchmarking classical methods alongside recent wearable and time-series foundation models, we find that while foundation models perform strongly, carefully tuned classical baselines like XGBoost remain highly competitive. By uniting broad-access wearable data with open code and model weights, OpenMHC provides a framework needed to drive reproducible advances in wearable health AI.
evidence_items.title: OpenMHC: Accelerating the Science of Wearable Foundation Models

evidence_items.summary: This dataset provides a reproducible numerical benchmark for evaluating reduced-order approximations of unilateral contact between a pressurized hyperelastic spherical membrane and a rigid plane. The benchmark comprises six pressure–mesh configurations, combining three inflation pressures (4, 8, and 12 psi) with two meridional discretizations (64 and 128 elements). Nine evaluation loads are considered for each configuration, resulting in 54 test states and 270 comparative records for five numerical approximation methods: PCHIP interpolation, POD, contact-local POD, a spectral reduced basis, and a contact-enriched nonlinear reduced-order model (KM02C). The dataset contains numerical results from the full-order reference model, reduced-order calculations, nodal state arrays, reconstructed contact reactions, training states, diagnostic indicators, and supporting Python scripts. Particular attention is given to distinguishing global reaction-force closure from local equilibrium accuracy. The data enable researchers to examine residual equilibrium errors, contact localization, active contact sets, sensitivity to diagnostic thresholds, and the performance of reduced-order approximations. The archive includes documentation, data dictionaries, verification procedures, and source code supporting computational reproducibility. The dataset represents numerical solutions of a specified discrete shell–gas contact model. It does not constitute experimental validation or establish mesh-independent continuum contact-pressure predictions.
evidence_items.title: Numerical benchmark dataset for reduced-order unilateral contact of pressurized hyperelastic membranes

evidence_items.summary: Overview MLIRBench: A Benchmark and Dataset for Compiler and Hardware-Aware Reasoning is a research benchmark and reproducibility framework designed to evaluate the ability of large language models (LLMs) to reason about program semantics, compiler transformations, and execution behavior in the Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR). This release provides the MLIRBench codebase, benchmark dataset, experimental artifacts, and reproducibility infrastructure accompanying the paper accepted at the 2027 IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Code Generation and Optimization (CGO 2027). The benchmark consists of 1,768 original–mutated MLIR program pairs, derived from 40 curated PyTorch seed programs, including 888 linalg pairs and 880 torch pairs across five mutation difficulty levels (L1–L5). MLIRBench evaluates nine language models, producing 15,912 model reasoning records and 15,907 judged evaluation records. Release Contents This software and dataset release provides the components required to inspect, analyze, and reproduce the archived MLIRBench experiments. 1. Benchmark Dataset The dataset includes nine complementary views: Core: Original and mutated MLIR programs with semantic annotations. Master: Consolidated program, mutation, and validation metadata. Reasoning: Model-generated predictions and semantic explanations. Evaluation: Judged predictions, verdicts, and evaluation scores. Errors: Per-model error-related records. Model Arena: Model comparison and evaluation information. Performance: Program-pair runtime measurements where available. Difficulty: Mutation difficulty and aggregated evaluation information. Mutation Provenance: Transformation requirements and validation provenance. The dataset views are distributed in JSONL and CSV formats, accompanied by schema documentation, integrity checksums, and licensing information. 2.
evidence_items.title: Dataset  Open MLIRBench - A Benchmark and Dataset for Compiler and Hardware-Aware Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: TrustFire-X: Dataset Description This dataset accompanies the TrustFire-X research framework developed for quality-aware spatiotemporal prediction of satellite-detected thermal anomalies in Türkiye and for evaluating model transferability to previously unsampled geographical regions. The dataset integrates satellite-derived thermal activity observations, meteorological variables, vegetation indicators, land-cover characteristics, topographical information, and historical fire-related features. The primary research panel contains 102,305 grid-cell–week observations collected over 2018–2026 from 230 sampled geographical cells at an approximately 35 km spatial resolution. The modelling framework uses 63 predictive features, including original environmental variables and derived temporal and spatial indicators. An additional geographical transfer evaluation contains 2,737 observations from 54 previously unsampled cells in northwestern Iran. This evaluation was conducted using frozen model configurations without retraining on the new geographical samples. The repository provides curated research data, feature documentation, preprocessing and analysis code, trained model files, experimental results, statistical evaluation outputs, and reproducibility information. The predictive experiments include gradient-boosting approaches based on XGBoost and CatBoost, with evaluation using area under the precision–recall curve (AUPRC), area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), probability calibration, bootstrap confidence intervals, and operational alert-budget measures. Scope and limitations: The dataset represents sampled grid-cell–week observations rather than a complete national wildfire-event inventory. Satellite thermal-anomaly detections are not equivalent to independently verified wildfire incidents. The geographical transfer experiment does not establish full operational validation or confirmed wildfire-event forecasting performance.
evidence_items.title: TrustFire-X: A Multisource Spatiotemporal Pilot Dataset and Model Benchmark for Satellite Thermal-Anomaly Prediction in Türkiye (2018–2026)

evidence_items.summary: Universities require fast, consistent, and traceable academic information services, yet direct use of large language models still poses risks of hallucination, outdated knowledge, and unsupported answers. This study developed an Agentic Artificial Intelligence framework based on Retrieval-Augmented Generation for intelligent academic question answering. The study employed Design Science Research comprising problem identification, requirements analysis, architecture design, prototype implementation, retrieval benchmarking, and evaluation. The framework integrated an agent orchestrator, intent routing, query rewriting, hybrid retrieval, reranking, memory, policy guardrails, a generator, and a verifier to check grounding and answer sources. Controlled testing used 12 synthetic academic-policy documents and 216 questions covering course registration, payments, academic leave, graduation, theses, MBKM, scholarships, library services, LMS, transcripts, academic calendars, and administration. Baseline RAG achieved Hit@1 of 80.6%, Recall@3 of 93.5%, and MRR of 87.6%, whereas Agentic RAG achieved 96.3%, 99.5%, and 97.8%, respectively. The improvement mainly resulted from intent-aware query expansion and combined lexical-character retrieval, which improved handling of paraphrases and overlapping service terminology. The proposed framework offers a more structured, transparent, and auditable implementation pattern for AI-based academic services. Field evaluation using an institution’s official corpus remains necessary before operational deployment.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI Framework Using Retrieval Augmented Generation for Intelligent Academic Question Answering in Higher Education

evidence_items.summary: Deep semantic understanding of events requires recognizing related events and distinguishing why an event occurs from how it is carried out. 5W1H extraction provides a structured foundation for such understanding by organizing event information around six fundamental questions. However, single-event slot filling provides limited support for these distinctions. We propose ANCHOR, a cluster-grounded framework that combines a large language model (LLM) with a small language model equipped with discriminative heads for accurate 5W1H extraction. The LLM proposes candidate events and generates their initial 4W records, which guide the selection of an event cluster and the subsequent anchoring of its main event. A shared document encoder provides evidence for joint 4W refinement, and two separate sets of boundary and role-scoring heads then extract why and how under event-specific constraints, respectively. Document representations are reused across events and stages, and unsupported roles can remain empty. Following the same principles, an agent-and-skill annotation workflow constructs a benchmark of 26,110 documents from ten source corpora covering three languages and seven domains. We select nine of the resulting datasets to evaluate ANCHOR against strong baselines using four open-weight LLMs. ANCHOR achieves competitive performance. The datasets and code are available at https://github.com/revolution6575/ANCHOR-5W1H.
evidence_items.title: ANCHOR: Cluster-Grounded 5W1H Extraction via Large-Small Model Collaboration

evidence_items.summary: Existing autonomous driving datasets and benchmarks provide extensive resources for routine driving, yet real-world data covering safety-critical scenarios and extreme environmental conditions remain limited. To address this gap, we present ExtremeDrive, a real-world dataset and benchmark covering emergency maneuvers, complex traffic interactions, and adverse conditions such as slippery or snow-covered roads, alongside routine driving. The dataset comprises 589 driving scenes curated from a larger pool of real-world driving recordings, with calibrated and aligned multisensor data and reviewed annotations of road structure and traffic participants. We further establish a benchmark to evaluate planned trajectories through simulated vehicle execution, measuring safety-related metrics and driving performance. Experiments at equal training set sizes show that incorporating critical driving data reduces trajectory prediction errors and improves mean critical-success rates in critical scenarios. ExtremeDrive provides a unified resource for learning and evaluating autonomous driving in safety-critical scenarios and extreme environmental conditions.
evidence_items.title: ExtremeDrive: A Real-World Dataset and Benchmark for Critical Driving

evidence_items.summary: As new attack categories emerge, network intrusion detection models need to be updated; however, when fine-tuned sequentially on new classes, previous classes are forgotten, resulting in catastrophic for- getting. The three public datasets we use are UNSW-NB15, ToN-IoT and CIC-IDS2017, and for these datasets, our class-incremental intrusion detection system is built using a CNN with one-dimensional (1D) archi- tecture trained over nine sequential tasks, each of which introduces one attack category. We evaluate sequential fine-tuning without any buffe compared to Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) and Learning without Forgetting (LwF), both of which include a class-size-adaptive rehearsal buffer of 20% of all previous classes (from 20 to 300 samples). The hyper-parameters were selected using UNSW-NB15 and fixed for the other two datasets. On UNSW-NB15, replay improves the final accuracy of both regularisers to 73.6% (EWC) and 71.1% (LwF) compared to about 32% (no improvement over fine-tuning). LwF with replay achieves 46.1% and 91.6% final accuracy for the two frozen-configuration datasets (ToN-IoT, CIC-IDS2017) while EWC with replay achieves 23.7% and 61.9%. In order to avoid this, EWC was therefore tuned on one dataset and the other two data sets were used as test sets. It is also demonstrated that the common forgetting measure can be misleading for a model which does not learn the old classes. As the fine-tuning baseline was not re- played and all the results were based on a single seed, it is not claimed hat the regularisers provide any extra support over replay alone.
evidence_items.title: Replay-Augmented Regularisation for Class-Incremental Network Intrusion Detection: A Three-Dataset Evaluation of EWC and LwF

evidence_items.summary: Teams deploying coding agents need benchmarks built from their own code, but curating and validating them by hand is resource intensive, and an unvalidated benchmark can mislead silently. We present Benchmark Factory, an autonomous meta-agent loop with human checkpoints: an LLM agent writes sourcing queries over landed production code changes, runs models of known relative strength on each candidate, diagnoses why a candidate fails, and repairs it by editing its queries, prompts, and configuration until it clears quality anchors that need no per-task human labels. We used Benchmark Factory to build benchmarks for five developer cohorts at our organization. Engineering raters scored a 5% sample 2.3 for task quality and 2.6 for grader verdicts on a 1-to-3 scale. On configurations never used to build them, the benchmarks ranked Claude Opus~4.7 at high reasoning effort above low effort (60.6% vs. 54.4% of tasks passed, $p=0.002$) and GPT-5.5 above GPT-5.4 (65.8% vs. 60.5%, $p=0.004$); 9 of the 10 per-cohort comparisons pointed the same way. A deliberately trivial benchmark failed the anchors; five broken graders failed them, even under a relaxed rule fixed in advance that the real grader passes; and with model labels shuffled so that no true ordering existed, random redraws of a candidate passed in at most 1.4% of simulations. The anchors are necessary, not sufficient, conditions for a valid benchmark, designed to focus human review on what the loop cannot repair.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark Factory: Agentic Benchmark Creation via Dataset Curation and Label-Free Quality Anchors

evidence_items.summary: The complete computational record behind two studies of the catalytic zinc of the bacterial deacetylase LpxC: a crystallographic survey of its first coordination shell across the 75 deposited LpxC–inhibitor complexes with a resolved catalytic zinc, and a docking benchmark in which every pose is scored three ways — by heavy-atom RMSD, by the number of ligand donor atoms placed on the metal, and by the identity of those atoms. The main archive lpxc makale2 veri TAM.tgz contains the input coordinate files, the prepared receptors and ligands in neutral and anionic form, the docking poses from every run configuration, the grid maps and AD4Zn parameter files, the SLURM job scripts, the analysis scripts, the summary result tables and the recorded computing environment. It is unchanged from version 1. Version 2 adds the entry-level inventory of all 102 candidate Protein Data Bank records with the ground for each of the 27 exclusions, which both manuscripts cite as Supplementary Table S1, together with a self-contained script that rebuilds that inventory from the RCSB search and data APIs. README v2 additions.md describes both files, the four selection criteria, and the precedence under which entries failing more than one criterion are counted. The contact-level coordination dataset in this deposit is the primary source for the reference geometry used in the docking study and can be consulted independently of either manuscript. Version 3 adds the GM-DockZn comparison requested in revision. The file gmdockzn zenodo.tgz contains the scripts that prepare GM-DockZn inputs, run the docking and score its poses under the donor-identity criterion, together with the per-method comparison table (Table S4) and the comparison figure (Figure 4). GM-DockZn itself is not redistributed; it is obtained from the authors (www.qmclab.com).
evidence_items.title: LpxC catalytic-zinc coordination: structures, docking outputs and analysis code for 75 inhibitor complexes

evidence_items.summary: Model checkpoints for the study "MSTNet: Label-Efficient Maritime 3D LiDAR Object Detection by Self-Supervised Pretraining" (Rehbronn, Keuker, Chen, Schulte, Vallery; Institute of Automatic Control, RWTH Aachen University). MSTNet pretrains a single-stride sparse transformer with a masked reconstruction objective on unlabeled LiDAR scans and fine-tunes the complete detector on a fraction of the labels. The archive contains one checkpoint for each of the 163 reported runs and the seven self-supervised pretraining checkpoints from which these runs start: Pretraining: masked pretraining on the in-domain sets of SeePerSea and Thames, on Pohang Canal, on KITTI, and on Pohang Canal combined with each in-domain set, plus a SeePerSea control without the validation frames. E.I, label efficiency: CenterPoint and MSTNet with random initialization and with in-domain pretraining at 5, 10, 20, 50, 80 and 100 % of the labels on Thames and SeePerSea. E.II, pretraining source: MSTNet fine-tuned from the cross-domain, out-of-domain and combined pretraining at all label budgets. E.III, benchmark: eleven published detectors (PointPillars, SECOND, CenterPoint, Voxel R-CNN, PV-RCNN, VoxelNeXt, TransFusion, TED-S, LION-Mamba, and the pillar and voxel configurations of DSVT) at full supervision, and PointPillars and VoxelNeXt at all label budgets. The SeePerSea models are trained and evaluated on the 360° point-cloud annotations of the separated SeePerSea release. Every run trains for 80 epochs, and the released checkpoint is the final one. README.md assigns each file its dataset, model, label budget, pretraining, run, configuration file, and mean average precision in BEV and 3D at an overlap of 0.5. Each fine-tuning checkpoint corresponds to one row of release data/results/map per run.csv in the code repository at https://github.com/rwth-irt/mstnet , which also provides the training code, the configurations, and the frame lists of the Thames split and the label budgets.
evidence_items.title: Model Checkpoints for "MSTNet: Label-Efficient Maritime 3D LiDAR Object Detection by Self-Supervised Pretraining and Vertical Refinement"

evidence_items.summary: Despite their success in general question answering, large language models (LLMs) struggle with hallucinations and inaccurate reasoning in scientific domains. A major challenge stems from experimental data, which are often stored in external sources like supplementary materials and domain-specific databases. These tables are large, heterogeneous, and semantically complex, making them difficult for LLMs to interpret. While external tools show promise, current benchmarks fail to assess LLMs’ ability to navigate this data-particularly in locating relevant tables, retrieving key columns, interpreting experimental conditions, and invoking tools. To address this gap, we introduce CataTQA, a new benchmark for Catalytic materials Table Question and Answering. CataTQA features an automated dataset framework and four auxiliary tools. We evaluate tool-enhanced LLMs across five dimensions: table location, column retrieval, condition analysis, tool calling, and question answering, identifying their strengths and weaknesses.
evidence_items.title: CataTQA:A Benchmark for Tool-Augmented LLM Question Answering over Heterogeneous Catalysis Tables.

evidence_items.summary: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.
evidence_items.title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Benchmarks for LLM diagnostic agents are built from retrospective records: the case an agent reads is rewritten from discharge summaries, and unrecorded test results are generated by a simulator that often sees the final diagnosis. HindAudit separates three hindsight channels (the diagnosis given to the simulator, the retrospective context it conditions on, and the agent-facing case text) and measures each with judges trained only on real data. On 27,489 emergency admissions from MIMIC-IV, five registered tests found no leakage into simulated laboratory results: providing the diagnosis to five simulators had a negligible effect, and prompted gatekeepers diluted the diagnostic signal, although exploratory results suggest they can raise agent scores. The largest effect lay in the case text. Against a presentation-time reconstruction from triage records, benchmark-style summaries raised the zero-shot accuracy of four LLMs from 25.4% to 39.7% and discharge histories to 45.3%, and raised six interactive agents' scores while barely changing their ranking. The exploratory gap was reproduced in a registered replication on held-out patients. Masking diagnosis names left it unchanged. Because MIMIC lacks a contemporaneous bedside history, the gap is an upper bound on hindsight. We report all registered outcomes and recommend construction practices.
evidence_items.title: Where Does Hindsight Enter Clinical Agent Benchmarks? An Audit of Simulators and Case Construction

evidence_items.summary: Inked line art is an unforgiving substrate for image-to-video generation: line weight, screentone frequency, contour closure and the black-and-white register itself must survive every frame. We introduce StillDrawn, a benchmark for that survival: a 29-panel dataset controlled for content class and ink treatment, five frozen-definition stability metrics, and a pre-registered study of 171 protocol cells on five engines (two open-weights models from pinned quantisations, three hosted commercial systems) yielding 170 clips and one recorded refusal. The pre-registered hypothesis, that establishing-shot panels degrade more than character and action panels, returned null on all ten engine-metric tests; reported as registered. Instead, the corpus shows a seven-mode failure taxonomy on three axes (register, content, framing): modes that stay monochrome ink to the eye while the metrics read catastrophe (in-register transposition) and modes the metrics barely see (in-register insertion: a hallucinated cyclist at 0.47 px mean line drift, the corpus's tenth percentile). A pre-registered human check (six raters, two axes, per-panel baseline) validates the suite on the axis that can be anchored: four of five metrics track perceived content preservation (edge ρ = −0.74, p = 2×10⁻⁴; Krippendorff's α = 0.48), while the absolute ink-register judgement is bounded by the corpus: raters concur that the source panels behind nearly a third of the clips do not read as hand-drawn. A caution generalises beyond line art: a post-hoc optical-flow control shows our engine ordering tracks how much each engine moves (ρ = 0.90, median motion vs median line drift), with no motion regime where all five engines are comparable; stability scores on any substrate rank stillness unless a motion control is reported with them. Dataset, recipes, metrics and all 373 generated clips are released. Preprint, not peer reviewed.
evidence_items.title: StillDrawn: Measuring the Stability of Inked Line Art under Image-to-Video Generation

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the paper "Inferring Gender from Author Names with Local LLMs: A Multi-Model Evaluation" (Journal of Informetrics, 2026). It contains 194,528 first name–country pairs derived from Wikidata, along with gender predictions (Man / Woman / Unknown) produced by 25 open-weight large language models run locally via Ollama, ranging from 270M to 70B parameters. The ground truth is based on the gender distribution of real people registered in Wikidata for each name and country of origin. The dataset includes: (1) the ground-truth reference file with name, country, and sex; (2) the Wikidata source file with gender probability and frequency statistics; (3) one prediction file per model (25 total); and (4) Python scripts to reproduce the evaluation metrics (precision, recall, F1-score) and all figures reported in the paper. Data are released under CC BY 4.0; code under Apache 2.0
evidence_items.title: Inferring Gender from Author Names with Local LLMs: A Multi-Model Evaluation [Dataset]

evidence_items.summary: Concurrent defects in rotating components produce overlapping vibration components, complicating the recognition of defect combinations absent from training. We formulate this task as compositional multi-label learning and propose a compositional evidence-grounded framework (CEG-LLM). The model uses a frozen large language model as a sequence encoder, with trainable low-rank adapters and four sigmoid defect outputs. Continuous waveform tokens and nominal characteristic-order descriptors represent the signal, while a four-node composition graph conditions label-wise attention. Spectral alignment and compositional regularization guide training, and a fixed template links predictions to structured signal records. On one dataset collected from a rotating component at 1500 rpm, CEG-LLM achieves an observed-state macro-F1 of 0.941. Corresponding values are 0.922 for a one-dimensional vision Transformer (ViT), 0.912 for a signal-to-text language encoder, and 0.900 for a convolutional neural network (CNN). Mean exact match across six withheld defect pairs is 0.767, and macro-F1 at −3 dB is 0.819. A top-token versus random-mask deletion contrast of 0.207 indicates sensitivity to the selected representation under that intervention. These results assess recognition of unseen defect combinations and representation sensitivity within the evaluated operating condition.
evidence_items.title: Evidence-Grounded Multi-Label Learning with a Large Language Model for Compound Defect Detection in Rotating Components

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Radiation Therapy (RT) scheduling requires coordination of clinical constraints and operational objectives. Large language models (LLMs) may provide a natural‐language interface for generating candidate schedules. Purpose To evaluate the feasibility of using an existing LLM to generate RT patient schedules under clinical and operational constraints through simulation and retrospective clinical comparison. Methods A one‐year, three‐linear‐accelerator (LINAC) simulation included 1400 new patients across 12 treatment categories modeled after clinical practice. Structured prompts supplied ChatGPT with patient data, the current schedule state, clinical rules, and scenario‐specific objectives. Performance was evaluated across scenarios addressing weekly treatment‐time consistency, LINAC continuity, gap‐constrained temporal relaxation, and infeasible request handling. LLM‐generated schedules were benchmarked against heuristic and CP‐SAT schedules under two objective settings. A six‐week retrospective comparison evaluated 2043 appointments against a clinical schedule. Results The LLM‐generated schedules satisfied the predefined feasibility rules in all evaluated scenarios. Across scenarios, 98.6%–98.8% of evaluated fractions remained within the preferred treatment‐time window. Adding a LINAC‐continuity objective reduced the LINAC switch rate from 52.4 2.6% to 9.4 0.6%, and gap‐constrained temporal relaxation reduced daily gap to 47.1 8.5 min and Friday gap to 89.2 18.4 min while maintaining low overtime. In infeasible request tests, the framework identified predefined constraint violations and returned interpretable corrective suggestions. The optimization benchmarks also generated feasible schedules, but their results showed strong objective‐weight trade‐offs.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating a large language model for radiotherapy patient scheduling under realistic clinical and operational constraints: A feasibility study

organizations: Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Geological Bureau
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Gold exploration is an evidence-intensive spatial decision problem in which geological structures, host lithologies, alteration assemblages, geochemical anomalies, geophysical responses, and remote-sensing observations must be interpreted jointly across heterogeneous spatial scales. Conventional mineral prospectivity mapping (MPM) models can learn nonlinear associations from these data, yet their predictions are often weakly connected to explicit metallogenic mechanisms, source provenance, and the sequential decisions made during exploration. Large language models (LLMs) provide flexible geological knowledge interaction, but their parametric knowledge and unconstrained text generation are insufficient for spatially grounded, uncertainty-aware target delineation. We introduce GeoKG-Ore, a knowledge graph-augmented LLM framework that formulates intelligent gold exploration as closed-loop inference over a provenance-aware spatial knowledge graph. Its central mechanism is a query-conditioned probabilistic geological field that jointly governs prospectivity estimation, graph-consistency constraints, and value-of-information evidence acquisition. A budget-aware policy selects the next evidence source according to expected posterior utility, while a provenance-constrained generator converts verified graph paths and spatial evidence into auditable exploration reports. We evaluate GeoKG-Ore using public mineral-occurrence, geological, geochemical, geophysical, and satellite data sources. On a benchmark comprising 36,480 analysis cells and 428 verified occurrence anchors, GeoKG-Ore achieves an AUROC of 0.913, an AUPRC of 0.612, and a recall of 0.574 within the top 5\% of the explored area, with an expected calibration error of 0.038. The results support the value of coupling spatial geological knowledge, uncertainty-aware prospectivity inference, and budget-aware evidence acquisition for evidence-grounded gold exploration.
evidence_items.title: GeoKG-Ore: Knowledge Graph-Augmented Large Language Models for Intelligent Gold Exploration

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate prediction of protein–ligand binding affinities is fundamental to structure-based drug design, yet existing benchmarks are often limited by outdated structural coverage, uncertain local structural fidelity, and physicochemical or protocol-dependent bias. Here, we present HiFiPL-Bench, a fidelity-first and bias-aware benchmark curated from RCSB PDB and BindingDB through hierarchical filtering, manual electron-density validation, affinity verification, and property-matched decoy generation. Across nine representative scoring functions, HiFiPL-Bench revealed reduced performance in scoring, ranking, and most docking evaluations relative to CASF-2016, whereas a controlled screening-like task using computationally generated property-matched decoys produced model-specific gains and losses that altered relative rankings rather than uniformly lowering performance. Model-specific overlap and deoverlap analyses further showed that documented development-data exposure differed substantially among methods and that deoverlapped sensitivity analyses affected models and evaluation tasks nonuniformly. Together, these findings indicate that performance estimates remain sensitive to starting-structure curation, task-specific preparation, data set composition, decoy design, benchmark protocol, and recoverable development-data exposure. HiFiPL-Bench therefore provides a reusable diagnostic framework for evaluating scoring-function performance in a structurally curated and bias-aware benchmark setting.
evidence_items.title:
HiFiPL-Bench: A
Fidelity-First and Bias-Aware Benchmark
for Diagnosing Protein–Ligand Scoring Functions

evidence_items.summary: Think Before You Code (TBYC) is a benchmark pipeline for studying whether code-focused language models can reason about software issues in ways that resemble human engineering deliberation. The benchmark curates GitHub issue discussions into structured records, extracts human discussion artifacts such as problems, solutions, constraints, rationales, and trade-offs, and then prompts models to generate issue-level "thoughts" using retrieved code context and few-shot examples. It converts model responses back into the same artifact space and evaluates them against human annotations using complementary metrics for artifact type detection, metadata matching, tag overlap, and semantic summary similarity. Beyond scoring, this study includes visualization, leaderboard, and baseline tools that make it possible to compare models, prompting strategies, and extraction methods across repositories and issues. Think Before You Code is an end-to-end evaluation environment for measuring how closely LLM software reasoning aligns with human strategic judgment.
evidence_items.title: Think Before You Code: A Benchmark for Testing LLMs on Software Engineering Deliberation

evidence_items.summary: The ability to generate multimodal reports integrating fluent narratives with faithful visualizations from tabular data, has become a cornerstone capability for modern vision-language models in practical domains such as finance, healthcare, and policy making. However, existing benchmarks are limited by single-modality focus, simplistic metrics, novelty evaluation, and visualization quality. We address these limitations with MM-ReportBench, a multimodal report evaluation benchmark covering 386 tasks across 185 real-world tables. Each task is paired with an expert-curated reference report featuring standardized chapter structures and verifiable key insight points, constructed through a hybrid pipeline of multimodal reports generation based on Monte Carlo Tree Search and rigorous human quality control. For robust evaluation, we design a dual-judge evaluation framework: Text Judge Model assesses textual quality along structural completeness, grounded insight verification with numerical fact-checking against source tables, and novelty analysis that distinguishes genuine analytical discovery from trivial paraphrasing; Visualization Judge Model evaluates generated visualizations across data fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics, and technical correctness. They also evaluate cross-modal consistency. Extensive experiments on 20 state-of-the-art models reveal critical weaknesses: even the strongest model achieves only 68.9 overall score, with numerical hallucination affecting 38.5% of reports and genuinely novel insights remaining rare. Our ablation studies further demonstrate that single-judge evaluation consistently inflates scores by 8-12 points compared to dual-judge assessment, confirming that rigorous and reliable benchmarking demands multi-faceted, complementary evaluation probes.
evidence_items.title: MM-ReportBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Report Generation from Tables

evidence_items.summary: Public LLM leaderboards guide model evaluation and adoption, yet the reported performance of top-ranked models can be systematically overstated. This leaderboard winner's curse arises because ranking noisy benchmark scores rewards sampling luck alongside genuine ability. The same selection effect can distort scores throughout the leaderboard, a phenomenon we call the rank-induced bias. We develop an $m$-out-of-$N$ bootstrap to correct for this bias. It assumes a fixed model pool with independent, identically distributed bounded tasks while allowing arbitrary within-task correlation among models. Under exact population tiers separated by positive gaps, we prove that the bootstrap reduces $\Theta(N^{-1/2})$ ranking bias to expected residual bias $o(N^{-1/2})$. Across 14 benchmarks from 5 benchmark families, the rank-1 adjustments range from approximately 0.09 to 3.86 percentage points. In our SWE-bench Verified snapshot, the tied leaders receive an adjustment of 0.90 percentage points. Such overstatement is large enough to make the apparent winner statistically fragile. Thus, we use the same bootstrap to further quantify the intervals of plausible rank positions for each model and group models into tiers. We establish sufficient conditions for consistent recovery of population tiers. On SWE-bench Verified, this procedure places 13 of 173 models in the leading tier. We combine the score adjustment and rank intervals in the Rank Uncertainty and Leaderboard Evaluation Report (RULER). We validate its finite-sample performance using sample splitting and calibrated simulations, and advocate publishing RULER alongside raw rankings so readers can assess both reported performance and the precision of the ordering. RULER also provides guidance for benchmark design that accounts for selection effects and ranking uncertainty.
evidence_items.title: SOTA or Luck? The Winner's Curse in LLM Leaderboards

evidence_items.summary: Checking whether a generated sentence is supported by its source document is a standard safeguard for AI-written text, and the strongest published checkers are single models. We describe GauntletScore, an evidence engine whose few rules and thresholds were set on the benchmark's development split. It puts typed questions to independent readers from different providers and records each answer as a measurement in an evidence ledger. It combines the measurements with a fixed Bayesian rule that counts a contradiction only when two readers agree. On the full LLM-AggreFact test split (29,320 claims across 11 datasets), following the leaderboard's approach, GauntletScore achieves 79.51 balanced accuracy, above every average published on the leaderboard as of 15 November 2026. That places it level with the best of them, nimble-v4-max (79.45 from its published dataset scores; the engine's 95% interval, 78.47 to 80.53, contains it). On the same claims it beats two of its three readers used alone (Readers A and B) by 1.66 and 2.17 points (95% intervals 0.80 to 2.53 and 1.29 to 3.06). Without AggreFact-CNN, described below, the leads are 0.90 and 1.32 and both intervals stay above zero. The engine also records the evidence behind every verdict, which a single model does not. Its largest margin is on full-length news articles checked against multi-sentence summaries (AggreFact-CNN), a format that resembles much regulated writing. There it scores 76.45, the best on the leaderboard, against 70.1 for the next best and 63.9 to 67.8 for the six systems with the highest averages. The test split was run once, on an engine frozen before the first test claim, under a stopping plan committed in advance. We release per-claim predictions and the scoring script.
evidence_items.title: GauntletScore: Auditable Fact-Checking That Matches the Best Published Checkers on LLM-AggreFact

evidence_items.summary: The EgoLink Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2026 benchmarks egocentric multimodal intelligence linking first-person perception, social reasoning, and interactive action. Unlike benchmarks centered on visible objects and activities, EgoLink evaluates whether models can interpret emotional and social cues, resolve visually grounded references, and convert user requests into verified tool-mediated actions. Its two tracks cover social reasoning in egocentric video and interactive agents that complete service tasks through dialogue, tool use, and closed-loop execution. Together, they test whether perception, reasoning, and decision-making remain coupled under both offline question answering and state-changing interaction. We highlight a multi-stage Track 1 data pipeline for multiple-choice question (MCQ) generation, chain-of-thought generation, automatic quality grading, and video-contribution filtering. We summarize the task design, evaluation metrics, rules, leaderboards, and representative solutions. The benchmark combines objective answer scoring with process- and result-based evaluation, enabling analysis of both final correctness and execution quality. The best Track 1 system achieved 0.9263 accuracy, while the best Track 2 system achieved 0.844 joint success and 0.916 micro accuracy. Participant reports reveal a shared principle: strong systems make intermediate evidence explicit through candidate verification, option-robust reasoning, scenario-aware planning, tool canonicalization, and state-aware correction before answering or acting. These findings highlight the importance of process verification and evidence-grounded reasoning for reliable egocentric multimodal intelligence.
evidence_items.title: EgoLink: Egocentric Language-Vision Interactive Network Knowledge Challenge Summary

evidence_items.summary: Background: Crisis helplines are essential to mental health systems but are often understaffed and underfunded. LLMs could support counselors, but existing benchmarks do not capture the escalation, risk assessment, and de-escalation central to crisis conversations, while privacy restrictions limit use of real transcripts. Methods: We present CrisisBench, a privacy-preserving suite for single- and multi-turn crisis counseling evaluation. It includes 1,085 single-turn tasks from 200 de-identified conversations and 1,185 patient LLMs derived from hotline metadata. Patient models and a 23-item LLM judge were calibrated against expert counselors. Results: We evaluated five GPT models plus draft-then-edit and retrieval-augmented generation. All systems underperformed human counselors on excessive empathy and questioning in single-turn evaluation. The rubric achieved human-human Krippendorff's $\alpha$ = 0.51 and LLM-human $\alpha$ = 0.54 (Pearson r = 0.80). In multi-turn evaluation, retrieval-augmented generation scored highest overall (0.961), with all systems within 0.058. Microskills and style/tone were near ceiling, while productivity and safety/risk accounted for most between-system variation. Counselors rated patient LLMs realistic (86%) and useful (92%). Conclusion: CrisisBench enables scalable, privacy-preserving evaluation of crisis counseling. Current systems perform strongly on core structural competencies but still diverge from experts on important response-level failure modes. We release the rubrics, judge prompts, and evaluation tasks.
evidence_items.title: CrisisBench: an evaluation suite for crisis counseling AI

evidence_items.summary: Patient recruitment remains a major barrier in clinical trials, as identifying eligible participants often requires manual screening of complex health records, contributing significantly to trial delays and increased costs. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer potential to automate this process, existing public datasets are overly simplistic in their patient representation: they pair full criterion lists with single-paragraph synthetic summaries, failing to capture the longitudinal complexity of real clinical records. We introduce MIMIC-CTRL-2026, a dataset of 800 manually labeled patient-criterion pairs grounded in real-world longitudinal EHR data from MIMIC-IV, annotated by clinically trained experts. Each instance pairs one eligibility criterion with a full patient record spanning multiple discharge notes, radiology reports, lab values, and medication histories. While simple prompting achieves a Cohen's Kappa, κ = 0.84 on existing simplified benchmarks, it collapses to κ = 0.06 on our dataset, revealing a substantial benchmark-difficulty gap between simplified and real-world clinical evaluation. Lastly, we present a framework combining structured pre-processing with a clinician-validated expanded prompt that substantially outperforms naive baselines without any model fine-tuning, establishing a realistic benchmark for automated clinical trial screening on real EHR data.
evidence_items.title: MIMIC-CTRL-2026: A Realistic Clinical Trial Dataset to Benchmark LLM Performance
