evidence_items.summary: Medium-chain dehydrogenases/reductases are highly versatile oxidoreductases with broad industrial relevance but complex structure-function relationships that continue to challenge catalytic performance prediction. A Benchmark for Medium-Chain Dehydrogenases (MCDBench) is introduced as a rigorously curated benchmark dataset comprising 792 enzyme-substrate-cofactor combinations, including experimentally validated inactive cases obtained under standardized conditions. MCDBench spans 36 chemically diverse alcohol substrates, representative MDR subclasses, and multiple cofactor types, enabling systematic evaluation of model generalization. Benchmarking four representative activity-prediction models (DLKcat, UniKP, TurNuP, and CataPro) shows that correlations with experimental activities remain modest under standardized conditions, and that distinguishing active from inactive catalytic space remains a practical challenge across enzyme classes and substrate types. Analysis points to a positive-data skew inherited from widely used biochemical databases and the relative scarcity of validated negative samples as key factors shaping this behavior. By providing a standardized benchmark that integrates experimentally validated negative cases, MCDBench offers a unified experimental and computational framework to help the field measure and further improve the discrimination of active and inactive catalytic space for biocatalyst design.
evidence_items.title: Precision in Predicting Catalytic Performance of Medium Chain Dehydrogenase: A Benchmark Data Set and Comparative Metrics

organizations: School of Electronic and Computer Engineering, Peking University Shenzhen Graduate School
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Language models are revolutionizing the biochemistry domain, assisting scientists in drug design and chemical synthesis with high efficiency. Yet current approaches struggle between small language models prone to hallucination and limited knowledge retention, and large cloud-based language models plagued by privacy risks and high inference costs. To bridge this gap, we introduce ChemCRAFT, a novel framework leveraging agentic reinforcement learning to decouple chemical reasoning from knowledge storage. Instead of forcing the model to memorize vast chemical data, our approach empowers the language model to interact with a sandbox for precise information retrieval. This externalization of knowledge allows a locally deployable small model to achieve superior performance while being highly token-efficient compared to traditional multi-agent systems. To enable small language models for agent-calling ability, we build an agentic trajectory construction pipeline and a comprehensive chemical-agent sandbox. Based on sandbox interactions, we constructed ChemToolDataset, the first large-scale chemical tool trajectory dataset. Simultaneously, we propose SMILES-GRPO to build a dense chemical reward function, promoting the model's ability to call chemical agents. Evaluations across diverse aspects of drug design show that ChemCRAFT outperforms current cloud-based LLMs in molecular structure analysis, molecular optimization, and synthesis pathway prediction, demonstrating that scientific reasoning is not solely an emergent ability of model scale, but a learnable policy of tool orchestration. Furthermore, assessments in real-world drug optimization scenarios, including fentanyl analog optimization and pro-inflammatory GSTO1 inhibitors optimization, reveal that ChemCRAFT generates optimization trajectories mirroring human experts, confirming its reliability as a scientific assistant.
evidence_items.title: Agentic reinforcement learning empowers next-generation chemical language models for molecular design and synthesis

evidence_items.summary: This reproducibility package supports the study “Wearable Stress Models Across Sessions and Exercise Conditions: A Cross-Dataset Evaluation with Same-Session Controls.” The study developed wearable stress classification models using the WESAD dataset and externally evaluated them using the Wearable Device Dataset from Induced Stress and Structured Exercise Sessions, PhysioNet version 1.0.1. The package contains the analysis scripts, locked study protocols, Protocol Amendment v1.1, source manifests, integrity records, model settings, aggregate results, and analysis-freeze outputs used to produce the reported findings. It covers the 20-second primary analysis, the 30-second sensitivity analysis, external stress-versus-rest transport qualification, cross-session affective and exercise evaluation, same-session exercise-minus-final-rest comparisons, internally derived operating points, protocol-version checks, and self-report alignment analyses. The original WESAD and PhysioNet datasets are not included or redistributed. Users must obtain the datasets from their respective official sources and comply with their original terms of use. The package contains no newly collected participant data and no directly identifying information. The package is intended to support transparent inspection and computational reproduction of the study procedures and aggregate results. Differences in software versions, operating systems, or access to the original third-party datasets may affect exact execution details. Version v3 includes an additional audit package containing scripts and aggregate results for the original 70-feature diagnostics, participant-level and exercise-stage error analysis, and AUROC transport-gate sensitivity at 0.60, 0.65, 0.70, and 0.75. The supplement uses the existing study outputs without changing the trained models, evaluation protocol, or source datasets. Original WESAD and PhysioNet recordings are not redistributed.
evidence_items.title: Reproducibility Package for "Wearable Stress Models Across Sessions and Exercise Conditions: A Cross-Dataset Evaluation with Same-Session Controls"

evidence_items.summary: The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) combines clinical physiological data with cyber-system information, creating challenges in determining whether an abnormal reading reflects a genuine physiological event, a device fault, or a cyber-attack within the expected physiological range. Answering this requires counterfactual ground truth, which no existing dataset provides. We present IoMT-SecAlarmBench, a semi-synthetic benchmark that injects controlled integrity attacks into genuine coupled ECG+PPG recordings using a structured experimental design combining four attack morphologies, four severity levels, two physiological plausibility conditions, and replay attacks. Each injected window retains its cause, attack subtype, and the clean signal that would have been observed without the attack. We evaluate six detectors from five method families using threshold-independent measures and a matched false-alarm budget. Results show no method consistently detects the most difficult cases: replay attacks and low-amplitude transient spikes remain close to chance-level performance across detectors. Results also reveal a trade-off between detecting attacks and distinguishing them from sensor faults: the best-performing detector on hard cases flags fault/artifact windows at 5.3 times its false-alarm rate on normal data. Three-way classification performs poorly for genuine physiological events, and a leakage audit of a dual-modality network dataset indicates previously reported IoMT intrusion-detection performance is partly driven by identifying information. Benchmark, generation code, preprocessing, evaluation tools, and datasheet are released.
evidence_items.title: IoMT-SecAlarmBench: A Semi-Synthetic Counterfactual Benchmark for Integrity Attacks in IoMT

evidence_items.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are often deployed as embodied controllers for robotics, yet it remains unclear how well they can explore an environment, maintain an internal map, and ground safety-critical decisions in long-horizon sequential trajectories. In this work, we introduce EMRD, an evaluation framework that decouples spatial reasoning into four stages: Explore (what the agent observes), Map (what it records and where), Remember (what it retains), and Decide (whether its final choice is justified), scored across 18 stage-specific metrics. We use EMRD to evaluate eleven open- and closed-weight VLMs across 16 buildings under nominal conditions and three environmental stresses (darkness, smoke, and motion noise), where an embodied VLM explores unknown rooms, maps observed objects, and selects the safest gathering place. Open-weight models leave rooms unvisited in 95% of episodes and detect at most 51% of objects; closed-weight models explore more, though with an external memory (notepad), two of the three stop prematurely. Without external memory, most VLMs keep fewer of the objects they saw, especially in larger buildings. The start limits which rooms are explored, and open-weight models started in different rooms agree on the final room not significantly more often than chance. Moreover, these choices are biased by semantic priors: swapping a room's label is often enough to change the final choice. Finally, motion noise increases object position error (by 12-60% for closed-weight models), strong darkness lowers map recall by 28-31 percentage points, and dense smoke reduces seen objects by 25-39 points, while the choice among the rooms entered does not change significantly.
evidence_items.title: Explore, Map, Remember, Decide: A Benchmark for VLM Readiness in Safety-Critical Scenarios

evidence_items.summary: Third-party API routers have become a common layer that unifies access across increasingly diverse LLM providers. In coding-agent workflows, high-autonomy operation is widely adopted because it reduces interaction overhead. As a result, a third-party API router, which sits between the agent and the upstream provider, inevitably occupies the trusted path. It can inspect and modify every request and response, yet no mechanism verifies alignment between the provider's output and the repository-level actions ultimately executed by the agent. Consequently, client-side permission mechanisms may become ineffective in practice. Whether this control gap produces real, hard-to-detect effects on software development tasks remains empirically unmeasured. In this paper, we conduct an empirical study of router-side injection in coding agents, examining four intervention levels of increasing subtlety: Response Substitution (L1), Response Append (L2), LLM-Polished Injection (L3), and LLM-Polished with Distribution Alignment Injection (L4). Moreover, we develop SIDEL, a framework for trace recording, replay, injection, and defense evaluation, with a curated dataset of 400 samples. We evaluate four representative coding agents, and further evaluate whitelist-based execution control and LLM review. Router-side intervention substantially alters repository-level actions and remains difficult for existing client-side safeguards to detect. Without additional mitigations, all evaluated agents achieved a defense success rate of 0 percent across all injection levels. Client-side mitigations and reactive reviews improve resistance but do not fully restore end-to-end control, motivating provider-side output-integrity guarantees. Our code is available at https://github.com/Riyasushin/SIDEL.
evidence_items.title: Where Is the Cost of Third-Party API Routers in Agentic Software Development?

evidence_items.summary: Multi-subject reference-based image generation requires jointly preserving multiple human identities, binding per-person objects and fashion items, and respecting a specified background scene, a regime where current diffusion models remain brittle. Existing benchmarks evaluate only one axis at a time and none jointly captures multi-identity composition with human-object interaction, background grounding, and spatial plausibility. We introduce CogCanvas, a benchmark of 1,952 curated reference images spanning 100 celebrity identities, 115 distinctive objects and fashion items, and 29 real-world background scenes including landmarks, from which we construct 1,361 compositional prompts covering 2-5 person group sizes. The curation pipeline combines DINOv2-based deduplication, two-stage aesthetic filtering, and automated derivation of structured interaction and position graphs that serve as ground-truth supervision. CogCanvas supports three tasks, reference-based multi-human-object generation (primary), text-to-image compositional generation, and reference retrieval, under a unified six-axis evaluation protocol. We introduce two metrics tailored to the multi-reference setting: BG-Sim, which scores background fidelity on SAM 3-masked regions via DINOv3 feature similarity, and Attr-VQA, which uses a multimodal LLM to verify per-subject attribute binding and inter-person interactions against the structured graphs. Benchmarking five SOTA methods reveals that every model degrades substantially as group size grows from 2 to 5, with near-complete failure on object/fashion binding beyond three subjects.
evidence_items.title: CogCanvas: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multi-Subject Reference-Based Image Generation

evidence_items.summary: Evaluation of software engineering (SWE) agents is dominated by a binary signal: whether the final patch passes the tests. This outcome-only view treats a principled solution and a chaotic trial-and-error process as equivalent. We show that this equivalence is empirically false. We evaluate 2,614 OpenHands trajectories from eight model backends on 60 SWE-bench Verified tasks. Of these, 47 have enough passing trajectories to construct task-level process references, yielding a 1,815-trajectory evaluation subset. Among passing trajectories in this subset, 10.7% exhibit behavior we call a Lucky Pass: regression cycles, blind retries, missing verification, or temporally disordered exploration, implementation, and verification. We introduce AgentLens, a framework for process-level assessment of SWE-agent trajectories, and release AgentLens-Bench, a dataset of 1,815 trajectories annotated with quality scores, waste signals, divergence points, and 47 task-level Prefix Tree Acceptor (PTA) references. AgentLens builds PTA references by merging multiple passing solutions for the same task, and uses a context-sensitive intent labeler to assign actions to Exploration, Implementation, Verification, or Orchestration based on trajectory history rather than tool identity alone. On AgentLens-Bench, the quality score separates passing trajectories into Lucky, Solid, and Ideal tiers and further decomposes Lucky Passes into five recurring mechanisms. Across the eight model backends, Lucky rates range from 0.5% to 23.2%, and some models move by as many as five rank positions when ranked by quality score instead of pass rate. We publicly release AgentLens-Bench and the AgentLens SDK at https://github.com/agentlens-framework/agentlens, with a project page at https://agentlens-framework.github.io/agentlens/.
evidence_items.title: AgentLens: Revealing The Lucky Pass Problem in SWE-Agent Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Traffic Sign Recognition (TSR) is a core perception capability for autonomous driving, where robustness to cross-region variation, long-tailed categories, and semantic ambiguity is essential for reliable real-world deployment. Despite steady progress in recognition accuracy, existing traffic sign datasets and benchmarks offer limited diagnostic insight into how different modeling paradigms behave under these practical challenges. We present TS-1M, a large-scale and globally diverse traffic sign dataset comprising over one million real-world images across 454 standardized categories, together with a diagnostic benchmark designed to analyze model capability boundaries. Beyond standard train-test evaluation, we provide a suite of challenge-oriented settings, including cross-region recognition, rare-class identification, low-clarity robustness, and semantic text understanding, enabling systematic and fine-grained assessment of modern TSR models. Using TS-1M, we conduct a unified benchmark across three representative learning paradigms: classical supervised models, self-supervised pretrained models, and multimodal vision-language models (VLMs). Our analysis reveals consistent paradigm-dependent behaviors, showing that semantic alignment is a key factor for cross-region generalization and rare-category recognition, while purely visual models remain sensitive to appearance shift and data imbalance. Finally, we validate the practical relevance of TS-1M through real-scene autonomous driving experiments, where traffic sign recognition is integrated with semantic reasoning and spatial localization to support map-level decision constraints. Overall, TS-1M establishes a reference-level diagnostic benchmark for TSR and provides principled insights into robust and semantic-aware traffic sign perception. Project page: https://guoyangzhao.github.io/projects/ts1m.
evidence_items.title: Traffic Sign Recognition in Autonomous Driving: Dataset, Benchmark, and Field Experiment

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents are increasingly important in security, yet leading systems are typically closed-source and cloud-hosted, limiting reproducibility and their use with sensitive data. This creates a need for small, local models that can perform security tasks under strict resource constraints, though effective methods for developing them remain underexplored. In this paper, we address this gap by proposing a two-stage post-training recipe that turns a small local language model into a security agent. To this end, we focus on Linux privilege escalation as a representative setting to systematically study the training of local models, as the task is automatically verifiable and requires multi-step interactive reasoning. Using an experimental setup that mitigates benchmark leakage, we post-train a small 4B model in two stages: supervised fine-tuning on traces from procedural privilege-escalation environments, followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. On a held-out benchmark of 12 Linux privilege-escalation scenarios, supervised fine-tuning nearly doubles the baseline success rate under a tight budget of 20 interaction rounds, and subsequent reinforcement learning improves our model, PrivEsc-LLM 4B, to 93.3% success, ahead of all other evaluated models that fit a single consumer GPU. At the same time, its expected inference cost per successful escalation is more than 80x lower than that of Claude Opus 4.7. Our findings show that small local models can be adapted to complex security tasks. We document the challenges involved and offer guidance for transferring this recipe to other settings.
evidence_items.title: Towards Reliable Local Security Agents: Verifiable Post-Training for Linux Privilege Escalation

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) perform well on video benchmarks, yet many video questions can be answered from a single frame or from language priors, which leaves open whether these models perceive how an event unfolds in time. We introduce \rtqa, a benchmark for atomic temporal event understanding built on time-reversed question pairs: each video is accompanied by its reversal, and each question is asked on both videos with identical text and options but different correct answers, so that a deterministic model that ignores the order of the frames cannot answer both. \rtqa{} comprises 8,420 questions of five types on 1,278 videos, 639 videos and their reversals. The questions are derived from event annotations that a proposer model writes, a reviewer model checks and human annotators verify, and three subsets target fast evaluation (\rtqatiny), questions that are hard to answer from the first and last frames (\rtqacore) and two consecutive events (\rtqacomp). All 20 evaluated models are less accurate on reversed videos. On \rtqafull, proprietary models answer both questions of 90.6--94.4\% of the pairs and the strongest open-source model of 66.8\%; on \rtqacore, the proprietary models drop to 55.6--64.5\%, and shuffling the frames reduces the paired accuracy of the tested open-source models to 3.4--7.4\%. We further build \rtqatrain{} with the same pipeline, without human verification, and train three open-source MLLMs on it with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (DAPO) under matched settings: both raise paired accuracy on \rtqafull, SFT by 20.7--27.4 points and DAPO by 5.9--22.9 points. For Qwen3.5-9B-Thinking, the training data also help on two other temporal benchmarks: SFT and DAPO raise the Vinoground text score by 5.8 and 3.8 points, respectively, and DAPO raises the TVBench macro accuracy by 4.6 points.
evidence_items.title: RTime-QA: A Benchmark for Atomic Temporal Event Understanding in Multimodal Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: The dataset contains metadata for 194,322 individual publications used in the article “Sipilä, Matilda, et al. ‘Question Answering models for information extraction from perovskite materials science literature.’ Communications Materials 6.1 (2025): 260.” The publications are grouped according to their data source. For articles retrieved through the CORE API and arXiv API that did not have a DOI, the corresponding CORE or arXiv identifier is provided instead. The metadata file contains five columns: DOI (or an alternative identifier for articles without a DOI), PUBLISHER, YEAR, TITLE, and JOURNAL. The PUBLISHER column indicates the source from which the publication was obtained (e.g., Elsevier or arXiv). The YEAR column specifies the publication year, TITLE contains the article title, and JOURNAL identifies the journal in which the article was published. The metadata were extracted from the publications themselves; therefore, some records may lack one or more metadata fields. The zipped folder QA for MS-main.zip contains the code used in the article. The code is also available in the GitLab repository .
evidence_items.title: Publication identifiers of the perovskite dataset and the QA code

evidence_items.summary: Enabling large language models (LLMs) to autonomously conduct training and improve target models is an important foundation for recursive self-improvement (RSI). As LLMs expand their role from being trained to conducting training, their model-training capability warrants dedicated study and systematic development. To this end, we construct RSI-Prime, a dataset for improving model-training capability, comprising 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories. To help LLMs learn to make high-quality experimental decisions from training practice, we perform fine-grained decision identification and quality annotation, then apply decision-level loss masking to exclude supervision on low-quality behavior. Experiments with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench, a benchmark for autonomous post-training, show that training on RSI-Prime yields a 31.95% relative improvement in overall performance over the original GLM-5.3, highlighting a path toward future RSI systems in which models autonomously sustain their own advancement.
evidence_items.title: RSI-Prime: Training Models to Train Models

evidence_items.summary: Detecting multiple reflection symmetries in 3D shapes requires aggregating geometric evidence over a large space of candidate planes, making traditional voting approaches computationally expensive. We introduce the Fourier Accelerated Symmetry Transform (FAST), a training-free framework that combines geometric pair voting with efficient spectral computation. Exploiting the fact that global reflection planes pass through the shape centroid, we reduce the search to plane orientations, while geometric consistency filtering and independent witnesses suppress unreliable pair hypotheses. Our key insight is to represent these votes as a signal over plane orientations and efficiently compute a continuous, smoothed symmetry field in the spherical-harmonic domain. Specifically, we exploit the Funk-Hecke theorem, the spherical counterpart of the Fourier convolution theorem for rotationally symmetric kernels, to transform Gaussian smoothing into multiplication of harmonic coefficients. This enables efficient field evaluation, from which symmetry candidates are extracted, refined, and geometrically verified. Across two benchmarks, including a new benchmark of highly symmetric shapes, FAST achieves the highest clean multi-plane detection $F_1$ scores among evaluated methods (0.861 and 0.947), with GPU inference below 4 ms per shape: over $100\times$ faster than the next-fastest evaluated multi-plane GPU baseline. FAST also demonstrates strong robustness to geometric noise and competitive single-plane detection, achieving 94.9% success on clean single-plane shapes.
evidence_items.title: Propose & Verify: Fast Reflection Symmetry Detection via Harmonic Fields

evidence_items.summary: Clinical care is a closed loop: clinicians observe partial evidence, infer the patient's state, and intervene, and each intervention determines what is observed next. This makes clinical decision making a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), in which a belief over a latent patient state must be updated from irregular, multimodal, and incomplete records. Yet most deep clinical models predict from a single snapshot or from coarsely aggregated history, while POMDP-based clinical methods need hand-specified discrete state spaces and transition models that real electronic health records cannot supply. We introduce OICycle (Observe, Infer, and Intervene Cycle), which learns a stochastic belief state directly from retrospective trajectories. At every episode, a learned recurrent operator fuses a sample of the previous belief with the new multimodal observations and the intervention that produced them. The resulting Gaussian belief is trained to predict clinicians' next interventions, the time to the next episode, and next-episode mortality. To enable reproducible evaluation, we release a benchmark derived from MIMIC-IV, MIMIC-IV-Note, and MIMIC-CXR that organizes 72,075 hospital admissions (5.4M laboratory, microbiology, radiology, prescription, and note records) into temporally ordered therapeutic--diagnostic episodes. Compared with an otherwise identical history-free model, OICycle improves next-intervention adaptive recall from 0.253 to 0.347, time-to-next-episode macro-F1 from 0.293 to 0.351, and next-episode mortality macro-F1 from 0.585 to 0.649. Analysis shows that the learned belief encodes intervention type and trajectory position and evolves smoothly across episodes, and that the benefit of history is concentrated in interventions whose ordering depends on prior findings.
evidence_items.title: OICycle: Observe, Infer, and Intervene Cycle for Belief-State Learning in Longitudinal Clinical Decision Making

evidence_items.summary: Evaluation readings of document-level relation extraction (DocRE) systems depend jointly on the model and the evaluation contract: gold version, scoring function, threshold. Rankings reverse across contracts, yet no existing method determines which comparisons survive the reversal. We address this gap with contract-explicit evaluation: a preregistered five-step protocol (Declare, Measure, Scope, Certify, Hedge), operationalizing the classical concordance decomposition of Kendall's rank correlation, that scopes certifiable regions and delivers distribution-free census certificates across two ecosystems. In the DocRE audit (44 training runs of one in-house architecture family), the scoring dimension scopes to a census certificate (three flagged instances, Clopper--Pearson upper bound 0.146); the confirmatory record includes registered negatives, and the audit prices its own simplification finding---the calibration dial's entire margin is one withdrawn commit. In an LLM-judge census (17 judges, 49,938 battles), 12.25% of leaderboard comparisons require hedging at the pre-declared split criterion (bound 0.124; panel-robust 0.143), with an exploratory two-tier reading certifying 69% at a bound \le 0.072 and a validity decomposition against released human labels (65% of contested battles are judge error, not ambiguity). The cross-model certificate is withdrawn on real confidence scores; the failure spectrum maps the boundary. The protocol, map, ledger, and per-instance artifacts are released.
evidence_items.title: Contract-Explicit Evaluation: From Auditing Learned Readers to Scoped Certificates

evidence_items.summary: Executing an idea often changes how promising it looks, so the next step in autonomous research should rest on results, not on proposals. After each round of experiments, the system must decide whether to refine the best solution or start a new direction, which solution to build from, and what goal to set. We call this the between-round decision. Existing systems wrap it in machinery such as rules, scores, search trees, and schedules; where an LLM makes it, what the LLM needs to read is left open. We ask whether an LLM can make this decision from accumulated evidence, without a search structure around it, and how much of that evidence it needs to read. We present BRED (Between-Round Evidence-based Decision), an LLM-based controller that maintains the best verified solution so far (the Champion) and a log of past rounds, and makes one decision per round. On three widely used research-agent benchmark tasks, BRED improves on the task baselines by 4.80% in MAE on ETTh1 (to 0.4172) and by 3.44 and 3.43 points of accuracy on SST-2 (to 95.07%) and CIFAR-100 (to 84.63%), ahead of the published results. When the controller does not read the accumulated evidence, the same loop gains less: with no history it reaches 0.4299 on ETTh1 and 83.71% on CIFAR-100, whereas the full controller's MAE is 2.95% lower and its accuracy 0.92 points higher. On a new task, speech-based depression detection under a leakage-free protocol, it reaches a macro-F1 of 0.6164 on seeds held out from selection, 5.5 points above its baseline and 4.0 above the strongest published system. Code is available at https://github.com/learninginvision/BRED.
evidence_items.title: The Between-Round Decision in Autonomous Research: An LLM Controller That Reads the Whole Trajectory

evidence_items.summary: Amodal perception enables humans to perceive entire objects even when parts are occluded, a remarkable cognitive skill that artificial intelligence struggles to replicate. Recent diffusion-based methods have extended amodal completion from images to videos, yet they lack auxiliary priors to guide the reconstruction of heavily occluded content and to maintain temporal consistency over long sequences. We present REVEAL (REconstructing VidEo Amodal content via Language and flow guidance), a unified diffusion-based framework that integrates complementary motion and semantic priors for video amodal completion. A user-provided text query serves a dual role: it drives open-vocabulary video segmentation to obtain visible masks, and it provides semantic guidance for texture reconstruction. For amodal segmentation, we introduce optical flow guidance: by warping visible masks from previous frames to the current frame, the flow-warped mask propagates visible content into occluded regions and approximates the object's current shape, providing a strong shape prior even under simultaneous deformation and occlusion. For texture completion, text guidance constrains the reconstruction of occluded appearance while providing a stable semantic reference that helps maintain visual coherence throughout the reconstruction. We also contribute LAVAT, a new benchmark featuring long video sequences paired with text descriptions, enabling evaluation of text-guided video amodal completion under heavy occlusion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that REVEAL achieves state-of-the-art performance on existing benchmarks while maintaining high-quality temporal consistency over extended sequences. The project page is available at: https://uark-aicv.github.io/REVEAL/.
evidence_items.title: REVEAL: Reconstructing Video Amodal Content via Language and Flow Guidance

evidence_items.summary: We propose a self-configuring framework that extends the nnU-Net workflow to both segmentation and classification in 3D medical imaging. Building on nnU-Net's self-configuring method, the framework reuses representations learned by a segmentation model for image-level classification. Its encoder features and predicted segmentation probabilities are used by a lightweight classifier. Two information-sharing strategies are investigated. In the frozen-backbone branch, features are augmented with region-of-interest information, predicted foreground volume, and segmentation confidence. In the adaptation branch, the final encoder stage is partially fine-tuned for classification, with an auxiliary segmentation loss to preserve segmentation-related information. Additional five-fold experiments showed that more complex configurations did not consistently improve classification performance. On the public validation leaderboard, our selected framework achieved an Overall score of 0.8056. In the official FLARE 2026 Task 2 final evaluation, our framework ranked first overall, achieving the highest DSC, NSD, and AUROC across all four testing tasks, including two hidden testing tasks. Local inference measurements also remained below the challenge limits of $60 \mathrm{s}$ per case and $4 \mathrm{GB}$ GPU memory. These results demonstrate the practical value of reusing segmentation representations for classification while maintaining a simple and efficient framework.
evidence_items.title: Leveraging Segmentation Representations for Efficient Classification: A Self-Configuring Framework Based on nnU-Net

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning benchmarks. However, existing evaluations typically provide all patient information upfront and assess only the final diagnosis or rationale. This setup ignores the need to acquire diagnostic evidence incrementally from incomplete information in real-world diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we introduce DiagTrace, a source-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can reconstruct the documented diagnostic trajectory through interactive information seeking. Each benchmark instance is built from a PubMed Central case report and includes an initial presentation, an event bank, a clinical course, and diagnostic references. DiagTrace contains 510 cases across eight specialties, with 225 used to evaluate four LLMs on clinical-course alignment, interaction quality, and efficiency. Results reveal trade-offs in coverage, source-consistent ordering, and turn use.
evidence_items.title: DiagTrace: An Interactive Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making

evidence_items.summary: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. Each sensor stream may have different network and compute requirements depending on its type and data volume. However, current wireless systems typically allocate resources at the device level, leading to contention among co-located sensor streams, where bulk data transfers may starve latency-critical telemetry. To this end, this paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL). SL provides deterministic, medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within a single user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN). Using agentic coding techniques, SL is implemented in two O-RAN-compliant packages, reducing development time by 400 times (2 h 40 min [OCUDU] vs. 6.5 weeks [OAI]), 228-fold fewer human prompts (4 vs. 913), and less than half the tokens (0.64B vs. 1.43B). An associated end-to-end framework, SLED, is implemented to establish per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. Over-the-air wireless experiments demonstrate that while conventional network slicing causes critical delays to increase more than 2,300-fold under high traffic load, SLED maintains stable latency. Scaling evaluations on the two RAN stacks show that throughput remains within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations even as the number of sensor slices increases. The results demonstrate that SLED preserves latency-critical telemetry while effectively utilizing resources across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter.
evidence_items.title: SLED: Sensor SLicing from Edge to Datacenter

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for knowledge-intensive and safety-critical applications in nuclear engineering. However, existing nuclear-domain benchmarks provide limited content coverage or focus primarily on answer accuracy without systematically evaluating the quality of the underlying reasoning. This study introduces NEBench R1, a reasoning-oriented benchmark comprising 7,546 unique multiple-choice questions extracted from U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) reactor operator licensing examinations covering 18 nuclear facilities. Each question is classified according to the NRC Knowledge and Abilities catalogs and accompanied by an official explanation serving as a reference for reasoning evaluation. Six LLMs were evaluated, with overall accuracy ranging from 34.0% to 73.9% across three distinct performance tiers. To assess reasoning quality, an LLM-based judge evaluated correctly answered responses using a multidimensional rubric. Although responses generally demonstrated strong problem comprehension, they scored lower in factual and procedural accuracy and distractor analysis, indicating that correct answers were not necessarily supported by technically sound justifications. Response clarity was also weakly indicative of technical quality. Furthermore, longer reasoning traces were associated with lower accuracy in both frontier reasoning models, suggesting that reasoning length may reflect question difficulty rather than improved problem-solving performance. Reasoning-token consumption may therefore provide an additional signal for identifying potentially unreliable responses. NEBench R1 establishes a benchmark for evaluating both answer accuracy and reasoning quality, providing a foundation for assessing the domain competence and reliability of LLMs in nuclear engineering.
evidence_items.title: NEBench R1: a Reasoning Benchmark for Evaluating Nuclear Domain Competence in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel in vision-language tasks; yet, whether they maintain consistent understanding of information-rich visuals (InfoVis) when the surface language changes remains unclear. To quantify this capability, we introduce MInfoVisQA, a parallel benchmark with 8,960 QA configurations derived from 128 seed instances across 24 languages. We construct seed-matched, language-parallel visuals and QA pairs by disentangling numerical-structural data from text and programmatically synchronizing translated labels. We evaluate 25 MLLMs under two settings: Language-Aligned QA (LQA, matching visual-text languages) and Cross-Language QA (XQA, fixed QA language with varying visual languages). The results show that aggregate accuracy masks substantial robustness gaps: two models with comparable mean LQA accuracy (80.4\%) exhibit performance spreads of 7.8 and 20.3 percentage points across languages. Moreover, all 25 models score lower with non-English visuals under fixed English QA, underscoring the need for cross-language sensitivity metrics.
evidence_items.title: MInfoVisQA: A Multilingual Benchmark for Information-Rich Visual Question Answering

evidence_items.summary: We introduce TableVista, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating foundation models in multimodal table reasoning under visual and structural complexity. TableVista consists of 3,000 high-quality table reasoning problems, where each instance is expanded into 10 distinct visual variants through our multi-style rendering and transformation pipeline. This process encompasses diverse scenario styles, robustness perturbations, and vision-only configurations, culminating in 30,000 multimodal samples for a multi-dimensional evaluation. We conduct an extensive evaluation of 29 state-of-the-art open-source and proprietary foundation models on TableVista. Through comprehensive quantitative and qualitative analysis, we find that while evaluated models remain largely stable across diverse rendering styles, they exhibit pronounced performance degradation on complex structural layouts and vision-only settings, revealing that current models struggle to maintain reasoning consistency when structural complexity combines with visually integrated presentations. These findings highlight critical gaps in current multimodal capabilities, providing insights for advancing more robust and reliable table understanding models.
evidence_items.title: TableVista: Benchmarking Multimodal Table Reasoning under Visual and Structural Complexity

All numerical examples are synthetic. No clinical or volitional-entanglement claim is established. F096 · Physical Feasibility of Volition-Related Quantum Entanglement Hypotheses at the Limit F097 · Nonlocal Neural Correlations and Common-Cause Exclusion at the Limit F098 · Entanglement Witnesses and Identifiability in Neural Measurements at the Limit F099 · Distant Volitional Synchrony Claims and Information-Leakage Blinding at the Limit F100 · Quantum Entanglement Versus Classical Correlation in Volitional Research at the Limit   Scientific position and cultural inheritance Five evidence identities F096 asks whether a specified physical joint state and measurement path are even feasible. F097 compares neural associations against common-cause alternatives. F098 requires a physically defined witness; F099 investigates concealed-target identification; F100 tests classical predictive residuals. These outputs have different units and logical meanings. A likelihood ratio does not have the interpretation of an operator expectation or an accuracy contrast. A negative result at one necessary link cannot be paid for by a high score elsewhere. The family is integrated by traceable interfaces, not by a civilization index. Entanglement is a property of specified subsystems A nonseparable density operator is not defined by a narrative about connectedness. The tensor partition, physical preparation and observation operators establish the question. Classical mixtures can produce striking correlations. Begin with reference qubits in a controlled bench or simulation; verify independent preparation and record losses, phase, basis, source identity and uncertainty. Do not extrapolate a verified laboratory entangled state to neural tissue without an independently validated transduction and state model. Bell tests and the locality boundary The CHSH inequality constrains a class of local hidden-variable models under specified assumptions. Hensen and colleagues used independently controlled electron spins in diamond; this is not a demonstration in human brains. The experiment must specify the settings, admissible trials, event ordering and outcome distribution. Analyze the actual four setting-conditioned correlations, not an ordinary Pearson coefficient from two EEG traces. Even a valid Bell violation does not provide controllable faster-than-light signalling. Ordinary correlation deserves the strongest defense A shared environment, clock, stimulus schedule or physiological rhythm can create cross-site association. F097 makes this ordinary explanation a serious predictive model rather than a weak nuisance adjustment. Measure independent reference channels, precommit preprocessing, retain dyad-level units and fit common-driver alternatives on training records only. A residual unexplained by measured covariates is uncertainty, not a unique indication of nonlocal causation. An operator is not a metaphor F098 starts from a concrete witness, such as the Bell-projector witness W=I/2-P. Negative expectation certifies entanglement for a trusted two-qubit measurement with established assumptions. The blueprint leaves the witness units unspecified. This edition uses a dimensionless normalized operator and requires an explicit mapping for any physical readout; no EEG amplitude is silently promoted to that operator. A witness can miss some entangled states. Failure of a particular witness is not universal separability unless the chosen test is complete for that state family. Independent settings and trial accounting Detection loss, setting prediction and memory across trials can bias certification. A physically valid source is not sufficient if the statistical experiment changes which events count. Publish setting-conditioned counts and all registered event statuses. Check calibration and confidence intervals on reference systems, and choose sequential inference consistent with the design. A failed trial-accounting audit vetoes a strong physical attribution even if the plotted statistic looks impressive. Distance is not isolation Distant volitional synchrony is a behavioral claim until a physical mechanism has independently been identified. A target bit could travel through an ordinary sensory, digital or procedural channel. Seal responses before target disclosure; separate target generation from local event timing and audit ordinary pathways using dummy records rather than participant data. Bound ordinary leakage, and publish uncertainty or abstain when isolation cannot be certified. Qigong and Xianggong as cultural inheritance Qigong and Xianggong may motivate research questions about breath, movement, attention, expectation and reported experience. Their descriptive vocabulary need not be erased to pursue an experiment. Where a consented nonclinical practice protocol is later proposed, preserve participant reports and compare independently scheduled or matched sham contexts. Odor, breathing and instruction are ordinary variables. No traditional concept is assumed to be a quantum state, a force or a mechanism of information transfer. Daoist humility and the discipline of refusal Relational change and restraint can inspire a method that leaves room for uncertainty. They are philosophical analogies rather than derivations of Bell inequalities. A decision ledger records the distinction between a measured result, an unresolved alternative, a failed calibration and a claim withdrawn after an adversarial test. A cultural idea can retain its poetry even when a particular proposed physical interpretation fails. A classical competitor is a positive research object F100 allows dynamic latent-factor models, nonlinear common causes and ordinary sensors to explain the evidence. A residual measures the adequacy of one specified model on a specified dataset. Use matched acquisition and fitting resources, a frozen scoring rule, held-out dyads and proper uncertainty. Compare prediction and calibration, not rhetoric. The benchmark can favor the classical model without implying that quantum mechanics is false.

evidence_items.summary: Batch job schedulers run the nightly file transfers, scripts and database loads of many organisations, and their administrators spend much of their time on routine repairs: a rotated password, a broken key permission, a held lock, a full disk, a wrong date pattern in a file name. I present SchedOps-Bench, a live benchmark in which a language-model agent acts as the scheduler administrator in a Docker lab with a real scheduler (JS7), two Linux agent hosts, an SFTP server and a PostgreSQL database. Each scenario really breaks the site, gives the agent a ticket that does not name the root cause, and judges the episode only by the end state read from the servers, with separate verdicts for partial, false green and harmful outcomes. The benchmark has 165 scenarios in six sets, each validated in both directions. I also present Vardiya, an open harness that aims to help small and mid-sized models adapt to this work, and compare three rungs: a bare model (zero by construction), a tool-equipped model with only the access layer, and Usta, the same model inside the full harness. The main measured gain is access: with tools, a light hosted model solves 15 of 15 development episodes. The harness adds step efficiency (8.3 against 14.1 steps on average) and, with a weaker model on the hidden test set, 11 of 27 against 8 of 26 correct with 1 against 4 harmful outcomes, a difference that is not statistically significant. With a small local model (qwen3:14b) on the development set, which the harness was tuned on, the harness removed all harmful outcomes (0 against 10 of 16) and raised correct episodes from 3 to 9. On the hard tier there is no correctness gain: on the 17-scenario hard hidden test set both arms are correct in 0 episodes. I release the lab, scenarios, harness, raw episode evidence and analysis scripts under Apache 2.0, and I present the hard tier as an open challenge.
evidence_items.title: SchedOps-Bench and Vardiya: a live benchmark and an open harness for language-model agents in batch job scheduler operations

evidence_items.summary: Journeyman grades how an agent worked, not whether it passed. It drops an agent into eight small simulated jobs — diagnose a crashed service, assay an alloy at a bench, walk a fogged maze, pick up a night shift from a note that lies — and scores the walk on ten axes: did it keep hitting a wall that had already answered, did it stop when the work's object was served or when the budget ran out, could it name what it could not reach and price it, did it repeat a planted false story as fact. Nothing touches real files; every world is simulated and seed-rebuilt, so a claimed exit never reached is caught by arithmetic. What is unusual is not the grading — it is who is allowed to grade. Calibrating an LLM judge before trusting it is standard advice; almost nobody ships the labels to do it with. Three things follow from taking it literally. The calibration set is inside the package: 82 cases across seven axes, labelled by a three-family council in a blind round and an anonymous evidence-quoted second round, distilled from real agent records rather than synthetic vignettes. A judge that has not passed it cannot score — journeyman qualify grants or refuses a badge, and an unqualified run is stamped NOT COMPARABLE. And the judges that failed are published by name, beside the ones that passed. Two scoring layers, and the boundary between them is enforced. Facts are counted programmatically from the record; the questions no counter can answer go to a pluggable judge, one call per rubric item, with the verdict echoed from a fixed label set. Moving a judgement into a deterministic counter to save a call is a standing prohibition, not a preference. The record of being wrong is shipped with it. The first calibration set taught a lesson that the second retracted: under the earlier questions no judge outside one family read one axis at threshold, and that looked like a finding about judging skill. Under the revised definition every judge screened passes it.
evidence_items.title: Journeyman: a process-quality benchmark for LLM agents

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Calibration and scope choices determine what set-theoretic estimands represent, yet applied studies often treat them as neutral preprocessing. We benchmark the recovery and false-detection behaviour of Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA) and fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) using a public-service measurement framework motivated by five rural services in Vietnam. The evaluation uses 456,000 synthetic datasets from 456 scenarios with 1,000 replications each. Scenarios vary sample size, measurement error, condition correlation, cellwise missingness, outcome resolution, missingness mechanism and two data-generating processes: a two-condition gate and a substitutive non-gate. Across the 432-scenario missing-completely-at-random factorial, fsQCA calibrated with substantive 2/3/4 anchors recovered the programmed gate in 0.749 of replications and falsely detected the pair in 0.015 of non-gate replications. Raw-score NCA yielded rates of 0.673 and 0.087, respectively. NCA applied to 2/3/4 fuzzy memberships was conservative (0.049 recovery), whereas percentile-calibrated fsQCA was less specific (0.519 recovery; 0.162 false detection). In matched scenarios, increasing sample size improved semantic-anchor fsQCA recovery but reduced raw NCA recovery as observations filled the ceiling region. These results show that calibration anchors and NCA scope definitions are part of the estimand. Applied studies should preregister external anchors, report scope and algorithmic non-results, and test recovery against a plausible counterfactual data-generating process. The benchmark evaluates analytical workflows; it does not estimate how Vietnamese residents assess public services.
evidence_items.title: Calibration and Configurational Recovery in NCA and fsQCA: A Monte Carlo Benchmark for Public-Service Research in Vietnam

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), is increasingly applied in civil and structural engineering for disaster assessment, structural analysis, and engineering decision support. However, the extent to which current VLMs possess the reasoning capabilities required for reliable engineering judgments remains unclear. In this work, we introduce CivilBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs in civil engineering and disaster-related scenarios. CivilBench covers three major task families: Sequential Reasoning, Image-based Structural Understanding, and Open-world Understanding, encompassing numerical reasoning, structural damage assessment, risk inference, causal analysis, and repair planning. The benchmark is constructed through a systematic pipeline of domain-specific data collection, engineering-oriented captioning, expert annotation, question design, and quality verification. Evaluation of representative state-of-the-art VLMs reveals substantial limitations in domain-specific reasoning, with Sequential Reasoning emerging as a major bottleneck, particularly when models must infer numerical relationships from sparse structured observations. Further experiments show that numerical priors and external knowledge can alleviate these limitations, although their effectiveness depends on the model's ability to reliably interpret and use the available evidence. CivilBench provides a capability-oriented testbed for identifying reasoning limitations and evaluating progress toward reliable AI-assisted engineering decision-making. The benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/traceuryuan/CivilBench.
evidence_items.title: CivilBench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Multimodal Information Integration in Civil Engineering

evidence_items.summary: Process Reward Models (PRMs) are widely used for step-level evaluation of multi-step reasoning in large language models, but existing methods are often limited by weak historical dependency modeling and insufficient global awareness. They typically fail to leverage prior step evaluations for coherent judgment and lack visibility into subsequent reasoning, leading to suboptimal assessment of intermediate steps. To address this issue, we propose the Global Perspective Process Reward Model (GPRM), which jointly models the problem, previous reasoning steps and their evaluations, the current step, and future steps to enable history-aware and globally informed process evaluation. We further introduce a structured evaluation framework along four dimensions---look back, look ahead, self-check, and goal alignment---to assess prior consistency, future plausibility, step validity, and task alignment. Based on this framework, we construct datasets for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (GRPO). Experiments show that, despite using less training data and smaller model sizes, GPRM outperforms strong baseline models by 7.8 and 5.4 points on PRMBench and ProcessBench, respectively. GPRM also generalizes well across tasks, surpassing the GPT-4.1 baseline on Agent Error Bench, improving strong baselines by around 4 points under test-time scaling (TTS), and achieving competitive performance on PPE.
evidence_items.title: GPRM: Global Perspective Process Reward Model

evidence_items.summary: Quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising approach to time series prediction. While quantum reservoir computing has been widely explored for this setting, variational quantum models tailored to sequential data remain comparatively understudied, largely because they are difficult to train. In this work, we present a rigorous benchmark of variational quantum recurrent neural networks (QRNNs) on time series prediction tasks, focusing on two key capabilities: memory and nonlinear processing. We introduce a task-driven methodology that quantifies model capacity, enabling an intuitive and fair comparison across architectures, including classical recurrent baselines. We evaluate the proposed framework on two generic benchmark tasks and on a synthetic dataset describing a chaotic system. Overall, the quantum models achieve performance comparable to their classical counterparts, but classical models scale better with the memory size within the range studied. Notably, one QRNN variant shows higher average capacity on the task designed to jointly probe memory and nonlinear capacity. Moreover, our results show that quantum models offer better capacity when we are able to find a good parameter initialization. However, the increasing sensitivity to initialization leads to a lower probability of finding good solutions as the model size increases. These results provide a principled starting point for designing richer quantum recurrent architectures and for assessing where they may offer practical benefits.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking memory and nonlinear processing capacity of quantum recurrent neural networks for time series prediction

evidence_items.summary: We present K2-Horizon, a fleet of six fully open language models, from a 0.9B dense model to a 375B-A23B MoE, built for general-purpose reasoning and agentic work across math and science, software engineering, deep research, office automation, and beyond. The models lead or are competitive with strong open models of their size on agentic and coding benchmarks. On the modeling side, to strengthen reasoning, we introduce Mixture-of-Value Attention (MoVA), applying MoE to attention value projections, and softplus attention gating, a more flexible, theoretically motivated gate. Our 36B-A4B model uses both and nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data, with one-seventh the active parameters. We also introduce Uno, lossless diffusion adapters that speed up decoding by up to 2.2x without a separate draft model. Our release follows the LLM360 definition of open source for transparency and reproducibility: the full development history, including intermediate checkpoints from every training stage, pre-training data, training logs, and all training, evaluation, and infrastructure code, notably our production-scale xLLM framework for dense and MoE training and the RL360 reinforcement-learning stack. Beyond the data itself, we release and document in detail every pipeline that built it, the part of model development that open releases most rarely disclose. These pipelines produced roughly 10T synthetic pre-training tokens, showing that synthetic data can be a major ingredient of pre-training at scale. Four of the models share one 22T-token pre-training corpus and recipe, revealing consistent scaling behavior and enabling controlled studies of scale and sparsity. All artifacts are available at https://ifm.ai/k2/
evidence_items.title: K2-Horizon: A Frontier Fleet of Open Source Language Models

evidence_items.summary: In windows environment PowerShell becomes an integral part who’s responsible for system automation, management and configuration tasks. It is very flexible and helps in performing all the operations, which makes it more popular among developers and users. Yet, this flexibility is also the reason for being targeted for criminal activities by implanting PowerShell scripts in the form of File less malware as it doesn’t leave any trace in memory. So detecting these scripts before execution is the best way to counter the filmless attacks. For that, an authentic and reliable dataset with advanced Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models was required with the most useful feature sets for better detection. This paper implemented a generalized workflow to create a reliable dataset by collecting PowerShell scripts from different repositories and cleaning the obfuscated script by implementing a deobfuscation technique. Then evaluated them with a well-known antivirus (AV) platform, Virus Total, to label those scripts. The extracted meaningful features from those clean and labelled scripts are passed as inputs to ML models for evaluation of those models. Among defined models, Trigonometric Functional Link Artificial Neural Network (TFLANN) performed outstandingly with an accuracy of 97.68%. The proposed reliable dataset offers effective support to future research in PowerShell-based file less malware detection and can be used to create more effective machine learning-based cybersecurity mechanisms.
evidence_items.title: Generation and Evaluation of Reliable Dataset for PowerShell Based Fileless Malware Detection: A Machine Learning Approach

evidence_items.summary: Mid- to long-term supply chain risk management requires proactively identifying how disruptions such as natural disasters and geopolitical risks may affect the network and preparing countermeasures in advance. In practice, such planning integrates knowledge from multiple disciplines and stakeholders and evolves through iterative scenario exploration rather than one-shot analysis. While recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can detect causal relations, most approaches are noninteractive and do not reflect how users iteratively introduce novel factors during planning. This limits practical exploratory analysis and hinders alignment between diverse domain expertise and model structure in dynamic supply chain contexts. This study introduces an interactive decision-support framework for causal inference using LLMs that supports transdisciplinary risk analysis. Users propose new factors and specify their placement within the current causal narrative, enabling incremental incorporation of knowledge from different domains. The framework updates causal relationships while enforcing structural consistency constraints and supports repeated edits to explore relationships and compare scenarios. We demonstrate the framework on a supply-chain-motivated case and evaluate it on benchmark causal datasets against representative baselines. Results indicate that the framework preserves coherence and interpretability while enabling transparent and repeatable model updates, providing a practical foundation for transdisciplinary engineering decision-making under uncertainty.
evidence_items.title: Interactive Causal Inference with Large Language Models for Supply Chain Risk Management

evidence_items.summary: Network intrusion detection plays a crucial role in cybersecurity, aiding in the detection of malicious traffic and the ability to distinguish between attacks and normal network traffic. This paper compares a Transformer-based model for network intrusion detection on the NSL-KDD benchmark dataset with a binary classification approach. The architecture proposed uses a 41-input-feature projection to 64 dimensions, followed by two Transformer encoder blocks with 4 attention heads processing the 64-dimensional features. The confusion matrix for the resulting model on the evaluation set of 30,000 records is 98.72% accuracy, 98.56% precision, 98.78% recall, and 98.67% F1-score. The false-positive and false-negative rate are 1.34% and 1.22%, respectively. When compared with conventional classifiers, the reported accuracy of the Transformer is lower than the accuracy of XGBoost (99.44%) and Random Forest (99.31%) while being superior to the reported accuracy of the multilayer perceptron (98.56%) and close to the reported accuracy of Gradient Boosting (98.80%). These findings demonstrate that the evaluated Transformer model can achieve a high classification performance on the selected NSL-KDD records, although it does not outperform all conventional classifiers. The study provides a benchmark-based assessment of the model and highlights the importance of consistent evaluation procedures when comparing intrusion detection approaches. Further research may investigate feature-tokenized Transformer architectures and evaluate their performance on datasets representing industrial control system networks.
evidence_items.title: Transformer-Based Intrusion Detection on the NSL-KDD Benchmark: A Performance Assessment Against Conventional Classifiers

evidence_items.summary: Sindhi is a low-resource Indo-Aryan language written mainly in an extended Perso-Arabic script. Several Sindhi tokenizers have been released on public model hubs, but they have not been compared with one another on shared data. We train SentencePiece Unigram tokenizers with byte fallback at four vocabulary sizes (32k to 150k) on about 1.10 million Sindhi sentences and a smaller, repeated Urdu, Persian and Arabic slice, from four public sources, and compare them with fourteen existing tokenizers on four evaluation sets: FLORES+, Sindhi Wikipedia, a news-derived sentiment corpus, and a contemporary news corpus. The metrics are fertility, single-token retention, UNK rate, byte-fallback rate, and round-trip character loss. At 64k, our tokenizer averages 1.147 tokens per word, against 1.208 for the best existing tokenizer and 1.512 for XLM-RoBERTa, and keeps 88.6% of words as single tokens. On fertility, single-token retention and UNK rate it is best or tied for best in all four evaluation sets at 64k and above; at 32k it trails one baseline on FLORES+. Margins over the best Sindhi-adapted baselines are small (0.002 fertility on FLORES+ at 64k), and we report no significance tests. A round-trip check finds no character loss for our tokenizer and silent character deletion (up to 0.85% of characters) in two existing ones; seven others lose less than 0.1%. We evaluate intrinsic metrics only, so effects on downstream tasks remain untested. Code and tokenizer files are public (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23962474).
evidence_items.title: A Corpus‑Driven SentencePiece Unigram Tokenizer for Sindhi: Design and Benchmark Against Fourteen Existing Tokenizers

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning models of groundwater levels are usually reported with a single accuracy score, yet that score depends on how data are split and on what a trivial predictor achieves. We assembled an analysis-ready dataset of more than 90,000 monthly depth-to-water observations from 644 monitoring wells across continental Chile (1982–2021), paired with 37 environmental and location predictors. Using a fixed modeling pipeline, we evaluated three tree-based learners under five train–test splitting designs (one random, two that withhold whole wells or regions, and two that withhold later records) and compared each with applicable baselines on the same test data. The best random-split model achieved R2 = 0.91, but a lookup of each well’s mean performed nearly as well, while temporal interpolation at the same well performed better. At withheld wells, the best learner roughly matched interpolation from neighboring wells; when whole regions were withheld, all learners had negative mean R2. Under a common calendar split, carrying forward each well’s last observation outperformed every learner at every evaluated horizon, although the learners’ R2 exceeded 0.8. Shuffled cross-validation also substantially understated chronological test error. These results show that a high accuracy score can reflect recognition of monitored wells rather than useful prediction at new locations or later times. Herein, we release the dataset, split assignments, predictions, and code as an open benchmark for evaluating groundwater models against validation designs and baselines matched to their intended use. Those results will help water managers judge when groundwater predictions are reliable enough to inform decisions.
evidence_items.title: Matching Validation Design to the Prediction Task in Groundwater Machine Learning: An Open National Benchmark for Chile

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Molecular simulation workflows based on the GFN family of semiempirical methods (GFN1‐xTB, GFN2‐xTB, GFN0‐xTB, and GFN‐FF) are benchmarked as geometry engines against the original BP86/def2‐SVP DFT level of theory of the Harvard Clean Energy Project (CEP) database for high‐throughput organic photovoltaic (OPV) molecule screening. Two representative datasets are evaluated: a 73‐molecule subset of the CEP database of extended ‐conjugated systems and a 56‐molecule subset of the QM9 database of small organic molecules, selected via variance‐based Neyman allocation from stratified and clustered chemical spaces. Structural fidelity is assessed through heavy‐atom RMSD, radius of gyration, equilibrium rotational constants, bond lengths, and bond angles, and topological consistency via the VF2 graph isomorphism algorithm. GFN1‐xTB and GFN2‐xTB achieve the highest structural fidelity for both datasets, with mean hRMSD values of 0.765 and 0.771 Å for CEP and bond length MADs of 0.018 and 0.021 Å, respectively. GFN2‐xTB achieves the best angle accuracy (MAD = 0.70°) among all methods. VF2 topological failure rates are minimal for CEP (1.4% for both GFN1/2‐xTB workflows) but substantial for QM9 with GFN0‐xTB (26.8%) and GFN‐FF (16.1%), indicating that self‐consistent‐charge methods (GFN1/2‐xTB) provide substantially higher topological reliability than non‐self‐consistent methods for chemically diverse molecular spaces. Meanwhile, GFN‐FF provides the largest computational speedup (up to ∼177× relative to BP86/def2‐SVP) with an empirical ‐like apparent scaling over the sampled molecular size range. Sensitivity analyses across solvation environments, basis sets (def2‐SVP vs. def2‐TZVP), and DFT levels of theory (BP86/def2‐SVP vs. B3LYP/6‐31G(2df,p) for QM9) confirm that method rankings are preserved in all cases (rank correlation ρ > 0.98), validating the primary benchmark as robust for relative method comparison.
