evidence_items.summary: Automated diagnostic report generation lies at the core of clinical diagnosis and can alleviate clinician shortages. Existing diagnostic report generation methods have two major limitations: they rely on unimodal inputs (e.g., images), ignoring textual biomarkers like medical history, and lack proactive dialogue capabilities to elicit personalized clinical information. To address those issues, we propose a ProActive Multimodal Agentic (PAMA) system, which performs a comprehensive disease analysis by examining biomarkers in diverse sources, including multi-view medical images, medical histories, and diagnostic conversations. Built upon a knowledge graph and recommendation-based dialogue architecture, PAMA actively initiates adaptive, multi-turn conversations with patients, which is integrated with visual data for robust and reliable report generation. Specifically, PAMA actively generates adaptive multi-turn questions to collect clinically relevant background information and then fuses the resulting dialogue context with visual representations for robust diagnostic report generation. We validate our approach on two real-world benchmark datasets, MIMIC-CXR and IU-X-ray, through extensive quantitative evaluations and comparisons with state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, we conduct user studies to assess the realism and clinical quality of the generated reports. Finally, we present real-world case studies to examine the performance of our system across diverse scenarios, demonstrating its robustness on scalability, complexity, and data variability.
evidence_items.title: Diagnostic Report Generation via a ProActive Multimodal Agentic System

evidence_items.summary: Pixel art is widely used in games and digital content creation, requiring readable forms, coherent spatial relationships, and harmonious colors under limited resolution and palette constraints. Language models show growing promise in visual creation, yet their pixel art creation capabilities lack systematic evaluation. We introduce PixelBench, formalizing text-to-image generation and instruction-guided editing for pixel art and providing a benchmark for these tasks. We further present a creation environment in which language model agents invoke drawing tools through code to generate and edit pixel art. We assess the quality of generated artwork through human evaluation and employ a multimodal large language model as a judge, validating the agreement between its automated assessments and human preferences. We compare language models and configurations across diverse subjects and canvas sizes. In our experiments, GPT-6 Astra achieves both the highest average judge score and the best average human rank, highlighting the potential of general-purpose language models for pixel art creation. We release the tasks, all artworks, the human rankings, and the judge protocol.
evidence_items.title: PixelBench: Evaluating Language Models for Pixel-Art Creation

evidence_items.summary: Assessing large language models for linguistic annotation requires task-specific evaluation under documented conditions. We present dhAIBench, a Python benchmarking and annotation tool with a web interface for exploring and sharing results. It records prompts, configurations and predictions, enabling comparisons of annotation quality, confidence calibration, repeatability and estimated cost. We demonstrate the framework and the associated methodology through 293 runs of 48 models on nine linguistic annotation tasks spanning morphology, syntax, semantics, discourse-pragmatics, spelling normalization and learner-language correction. Models achieve high agreement with reference annotations on several tasks, including those on non-standardized, historical varieties as well as requiring contextual interpretation. The results support evaluating models against specific linguistic tasks, rather than relying on general rankings. To this end, we make the current and future benchmarks publicly available at dhaibench.silent3.ff.cuni.cz.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Linguistic Annotation

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong multimodal capabilities across scientific and biomedical domains, yet their ability to understand electroencephalography (EEG) signals remains unclear. We introduce EEGProbe, a signal-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether general-purpose VLMs can extract and reason from minimally processed, channel-wise EEG without task-specific feature engineering or EEG-specific adaptation. EEGProbe contains 620 EEG-centered questions across 13 subtasks and three capability categories: EEG Signal Classification, EEG Cross-modal Alignment, and EEG Neurophysiological Reasoning. To reduce shortcut-based answering, EEGProbe preserves the temporal structure of the recordings where possible, minimizes benchmark-induced processing, and applies signal-necessity testing followed by expert verification. We evaluate 11 representative open- and closed-source VLMs under a unified zero-shot protocol. The strongest model, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves an overall score of only 41.63\%, with cross-modal EEG alignment emerging as a major bottleneck. We further examine model behavior from a neurophysiological perspective and analyze how temporal, spectral, spatial, and physiological EEG structure relates to model successes and failures. Inference-time neurophysiological guidance can reshape model predictions by helping models recognize the neurophysiological patterns present in the input and connect them with relevant neurological knowledge, narrowing the gap between general multimodal competence and EEG understanding. EEGProbe provides a testbed for current VLMs and a basis for developing future multimodal models that can interpret EEG evidence more reliably. The EEGProbe benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/2122ZHU/EEGProbe.
evidence_items.title: EEGProbe: Do Vision-Language Models Really Understand EEG? A Benchmark for Signal-Grounded EEG Signals Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for industrial tasks, yet few benchmarks evaluate their mastery of industrial knowledge across different types of cognitive demand. We introduce IndustrialKnowEval (IndKnow), a benchmark for industrial knowledge and engineering question answering. It contains 43,282 samples covering 21 task types across seven industrial sectors, including aerospace, electric power, and metallurgy, organized into four levels of cognitive demand: memory, comprehension, reasoning, and engineering application. Enterprise-based domain specialists and experienced researchers participate in all stages of dataset construction and quality control. We conduct a series of experiments on 18 representative LLMs, with domain experts deeply involved in the evaluation. Building upon IndKnow, we propose the Industrial Cognitive Capability Gap (ICCG) metric to characterize the performance differential between foundational industrial knowledge and higher-order reasoning and application, and we analyze it alongside absolute performance to provide a more complete view of model capabilities. We anticipate that IndustrialKnowEval will support the benchmarking of LLMs in industrial scenarios and promote the development of robust industrial intelligence. Code is available at: https://github.com/J4cksonLee/IndKnow
evidence_items.title: IndustrialKnowEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multi-Level Industrial Knowledge in LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Object re-identification (Re-ID) benchmarks remain predominantly confined to single-category evaluations, limiting the development of unified systems capable of operating across diverse object types. This paper presents VisDrone-ReID, a unified multi-category Re-ID benchmark derived from the VisDrone2019-MOT dataset through a principled conversion pipeline. The pipeline resolves structural incompatibilities between multi-object tracking annotations and Re-ID evaluation requirements, addressing sequence-scoped identity collision, temporal redundancy, and the absence of a principled identity-level train/test split. The resulting benchmark comprises 9,516 identities and 150,016 images across ten object categories - pedestrian, people, bicycle, car, van, truck, tricycle, awning-tricycle, bus, and motor, sourced from 80 unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) sequences captured across urban environments. A leave-one-out (LOO) evaluation protocol is adopted to provide a comprehensive assessment. Baseline experiments across four representative Re-ID models spanning CNN and transformer architectures establish the first systematic performance reference on this benchmark. Results reveal a consistent Rank-1 to mAP gap across all models, suggesting that VisDrone-ReID presents a genuine retrieval challenge beyond nearest-neighbour matching. Per-category analysis identifies pedestrian as the most challenging category and reveals that vision-language pretraining provides a measurable advantage on semantically distinctive categories. VisDrone-ReID provides a consistent platform for studying multi-category object re-identification under the scale variation, viewpoint challenges, and category diversity characteristic of real-world surveillance scenarios.
evidence_items.title: VisDrone-ReID: A Unified Multi-Category Object Re-Identification Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics. Its wo-scale architecture integrates theorem formalization and proof formalization agents, empowered by structured proof decomposition, parallel verification, accumulated proof experience, and selective semantic review. Leveraging our collaborations with theoretical computer science (TCS) researchers, we focus our evaluation on TCS, a particularly demanding domain characterized by intricate quantification, complex dependencies, and stringent semantic requirements. Against direct generation and general-purpose coding harnesses, including Codex CLI and Claude Code, Turing Agent achieves approximately 57-62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused subset of RLMEval, using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Notably, Turing Agent, built on DeepSeek, successfully completes the formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks from OpenAI's October 2026 collection. One particularly challenging TCS problem required about a hundred formally verified auxiliary claims. Moreover, by actively exploring and refining the formalization process, Turing Agent can uncover simpler alternative proofs, expose unnecessary dependencies in original proofs, and generate reusable mathematical knowledge as a byproduct of verification.
evidence_items.title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to build interactive honeypots, yet existing evaluations mainly assess isolated command outputs and cannot determine whether a system remains believable when later commands depend on earlier results. We present ReconPotBench, a multi-round benchmark for Linux reconnaissance honeypots. It contains 1{,}032 three-round reconnaissance interactions across eight reconnaissance categories, with reference outputs collected from a real Linux environment. Under a unified testing protocol, we compare Cowrie, open-source LLMs, and closed-source LLMs along three dimensions: round-level authenticity, cross-round contextual consistency, and hacker-oriented reconnaissance value. Results show that multi-round evaluation exposes failures hidden by single-round testing, as authenticity declines with interaction depth and both open-source and closed-source LLMs struggle to maintain coherent state across rounds. LLM-based honeypots nevertheless outperform Cowrie in authenticity and reconnaissance value, while Cowrie remains more consistent because of its rigid templated behavior. Category-level analysis further shows that tasks requiring systems to preserve network relationships across rounds are harder than tasks centered on explicit entities such as ports. ReconPotBench enables reproducible evaluation of LLM honeypots across authenticity, entity consistency, and hacker-perspective utility in dependent multi-round interactions. The dataset is available at: https://github.com/qianli-wang/ReconPotBench
evidence_items.title: ReconPotBench: Evaluating LLM Honeypots in Multi-Round Linux Reconnaissance

evidence_items.summary: Memory systems address the challenge of context loss in Large Language Models during prolonged interactions. However, as an essential tool for warm companionship and personalized services, the effectiveness of memory systems in processing affective information remains underexamined. To bridge this gap, we propose an emotion-enhanced memory evaluation benchmark to assess the performance of mainstream and state-of-the-art memory systems in integrating and harnessing emotional information. First, we design a benchmark called \textbf{MemEmo} to assess the affective reasoning and tracking capabilities of memory systems across four dimensions: emotional information extraction, emotional memory updating, emotional memory question-answering, and emotional conflict detection. Second, we construct the \textbf{H}uman-\textbf{L}ike \textbf{M}emory \textbf{E}motion (\textbf{HLME}) dataset to provide an empirical foundation for scrutinizing memory systems. Finally, We evaluate five representative memory systems on the HLME dataset, reporting 11 performance metrics across four dimensions. Experimental results reveal that aggregating scores for all tested memory systems is up to 45\%, far below 100\% scale, exposing a profound disparity between memory system and affective intelligence.
evidence_items.title: MemEmo: Evaluating Emotion in Memory Systems

evidence_items.summary: Expert interface evaluation is costly and typically applies only one or two analytic frameworks. We present Iris, a system that dispatches ten framework-grounded large-language-model (LLM) evaluator agents in parallel, spanning usability heuristics, accessibility, design theory, cognitive load, behavioural design, and ability-based design, over an evidence bundle enriched with rendered HTML, interactive CSS pseudo-class rules, and keyboard-focus screenshots captured from a live browser session. Findings are returned at criterion level for practitioner review; Iris is positioned as decision support within a human–agent workflow, not as a replacement for expert judgment. A controlled sensitivity study shows composite scores respond monotonically to targeted design changes (11.9 → 80.4 across four page versions), and a temperature analysis identifies deterministic sampling as necessary for reproducible scoring. We describe the system, what current evidence does and does not establish, and an ongoing validation programme comprising an expert-annotated benchmark, tool and monolithic-prompt baselines, and a controlled practitioner study.
evidence_items.title: Iris: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Framework-Grounded, Human-in-the-Loop HCI Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: While the ability of video generation models to accurately depict scientific phenomena has received growing attention, determining whether these models genuinely understand the underlying principles remains a critical challenge. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate video samples in isolation, making it difficult to expose models that simply fit superficial visual priors. In scientific experiments, a small change in one condition produces a markedly different outcome even when the rest of the setup remains fixed. Capitalizing on this sensitivity, we introduce SciWorldBench, a benchmark comprising paired scientific experiments. Each pair varies a single condition in an otherwise fixed setup, yielding two mutually exclusive expected outcomes. Each generation prompt specifies the condition but omits the expected outcome. We evaluate ten text-and-image-to-video (TI2V) models using an independent vision-language model (VLM) that assesses each video without access to the condition text or the label identifying the correct outcome. A pair is scored as correct only when both videos depict their respective scientifically correct outcomes. Across all ten models, we find that the two videos in an experimental pair frequently depict the same outcome even though the conditions require different results. This recurring failure suggests that current video world models struggle to apply the underlying scientific principles reliably during generation. We will publicly release the benchmark dataset and open-source the evaluation code.
evidence_items.title: SciWorldBench: Do Video World Models Really Understand Scientific Experiments?

evidence_items.summary: Visual grounding benchmarks usually do not consider the contextual uncertainty of real-world scenarios. In this study, we construct a novel benchmark, the Japanese evaluation for Ambiguous visual Grounding with Dialogue (JAG-D) dataset. It consists of human-robot conversational multimodal interactions covering different types of ambiguity, arising from visual and linguistic categories. We evaluate the capabilities of different state-of-the-art Visual Language Models (VLMs) for ambiguity recognition and resolution. We compare dialogue context grounding performance for visual and linguistic ambiguity resolution. Our experiments show that VLMs can substantially improve the resolution of linguistic ambiguity, especially Japanese zero anaphora, by using dialogue context. We further conduct a comparative analysis to understand whether grounding improvements arise from the semantic content of the dialogue or from its conversational structure.
evidence_items.title: Seeing Isn't Resolving: Visual and Linguistic Disambiguation with Conversational Grounding

evidence_items.summary: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models often synthesize policy-violating content, necessitating robust safeguards and rigorous evaluation frameworks. However, current approaches remain largely monolithic in both execution and evaluation, limited to coarse-grained categorization within broad unsafe concepts. Such approaches fail to account for the specific constituent factors of a violation, resulting in weak learning signals and allowing model collapse to bypass safety checks. To overcome these limitations, we propose Example-Based Spatial Guidance (EBSG), a training-free method that utilizes user-editable exemplar packs to provide granular spatial guidance for precise concept steering. Unlike existing methods that coarsely steer the entire image away from a broad concept, EBSG decomposes these categories into specific sub-concepts via exemplar text-image pairs, providing explicit, localized steering signals for more robust safety control. Furthermore, we introduce a vision language model (VLM)-based evaluation protocol that provides a fine-grained assessment, avoiding the pitfall of conventional binary evaluators that permit model collapse to bypass safety checks. Empirically, EBSG achieves state-of-the-art erasure performance across diverse safety datasets and concept categories, spanning four nudity benchmarks, seven I2P harmful-concept slices, and four MJA metaphor categories, while supporting multi-concept removal and transferring to a modern backbone, SD3.
evidence_items.title: Example-Based Spatial Guidance for Training-Free Concept Erasure in Diffusion Models

evidence_items.summary: Benchmarks judge language-model agents mainly by whether they reach the correct final state, not by how they got there. Endpoint scoring cannot separate an agent that retrieved exactly the evidence a decision required from one that read most of the environment, nor an agent that never located the evidence from one that stopped a single action short. Settling this needs a reference cost, and authored solutions establish only that a task is solvable, not that no shorter route exists. We present DetourBench, which constrains the environment until that minimum is computable. Each task is a finite, partially observable transition system with unit-cost accesses whose resources become globally addressable after discovery. Exhaustive search yields the full-information minimum action count $L_0$ with a replayable witness; from graph-recoverable terminal states it also yields exact residual work $R_T$, which separates an episode that stopped one access short from one that wandered, while an irreversible wrong commitment is recorded as having no finite residual distance rather than assigned one. Success, attainment, residual progress, and normalized detour are reported separately. Across 375 scored episodes --- five model endpoints, 25 integrated tasks, three repeats --- success ranges from 58.7% to 96.0% while conditional attainment ranges from 0.803 to 0.890 and orders the models differently. Among recoverable failures, residual work separates near-complete trajectories from costly incompletion and from irreversible commitment. We open-source the instances, oracle witnesses, and evaluation harness at https://github.com/DatagridsAI/DetourBench.
evidence_items.title: DetourBench: Trajectory-Level Evaluation of Interactive Agents with Exact Minimum-Action Bounds

evidence_items.summary: Tamarin-based formal verification of security protocols requires expert-authored multiset rewriting rules and temporal-logic lemmas. Translating a natural-language protocol description into a complete formal model with an LLM is hard because syntactic, reachability, and property-level errors compound across the multi-step modeling process, and a single agent that both authors and self-evaluates cannot reliably localize them. We present MASTA, a multi-agent system that addresses these difficulties through three innovations. First, an operational--evaluative role decomposition assigns rule modeling to an Architect, property modeling to an Auditor, and pure dispatch to a dedicated Arbiter that holds no authoring duties. Second, the Arbiter implements a Tamarin-anchored scheduler that dispatches the next agent based on the latest verifier verdict and routes problem-tagged fixes through a modification list, with a six-class problem taxonomy and an LLM deduplication check preventing routing deadlock. Third, we construct a benchmark of 10 protocols paired with 139 mutation variants and five fine-grained metrics that jointly assess model correctness ($M_1$--$M_3$) and completeness ($M_4$--$M_5$). On this benchmark, MASTA on Qwen 3.5-plus improves over OpenCode on the same backbone by up to $+0.27$ on individual metrics and ranks first on both the correctness and completeness averages, surpassing Codex (GPT-5.5) and Claude Code (Opus 4.7) despite using a weaker LLM. Ablations on five protocols confirm that removing the Arbiter collapses property and verification scores to zero.
evidence_items.title: MASTA: A Feedback-Scheduled Multi-Agent System for End-to-End Tamarin Modeling and Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Zero-shot monocular metric depth models are evaluated by averaging metric and scale-aligned scores across datasets. Averages cannot show how many images still have severely wrong metric depth, whether depth is under- or overestimated, or whether different models fail on the same images. We propose an evaluation built on per-image results: the failure rate (metric $\delta_1$<0.5); scale-aligned metrics for structure, and the bias, dispersion and absolute error of the alignment scale for scale; and a cross-model comparison that separates shared from model-specific failures. We apply it to 11 recent architectures with and without ground-truth intrinsics (18 model evaluations) on the 7 everyday-scene benchmarks (4,406 images) used by MoGe-2. Metric depth estimation is not solved in everyday scenes, and the remaining difficulty is mainly scale: the best of the 18 evaluations still has a failure rate of 7.7% (datasets weighted equally); pooled over all failures, 78.8% have intact structure, and after scale correction 98.3% no longer fail. Images failed by at least 6 architectures make up 7.3% of the data, concentrated on HAMMER and DIODE; even when selected only by architectures of other families, they hold 34% to 40% of the error of the top 6 models, against 14% to 18% for as many random images from the same datasets. Adding objects reduces the scale error of most models; ground-truth intrinsics and, in most families, larger models reduce the failures but do not remove them. We recommend reporting failure rates, structure and scale separately, and results stratified by how many models fail. We will release the code, the per-image results with shared-failure labels, and two diagnostic sets built from TUM RGB-D.
evidence_items.title: What the Averages Hide: Monocular Metric Depth Models Still Fail in Everyday Scenes, Mostly on Scale

evidence_items.summary: AI is increasingly used for cybersecurity tasks such as intrusion and malware detection, in enterprise, industrial, vehicular and mobile networks. Its effectiveness depends on data: models need representative network traffic, both to be trained and to be evaluated realistically. Public datasets of cybersecurity network traffic, however, are scattered across laboratory pages, repositories and aggregators, and are continuously released, corrected and withdrawn: 92 of the 234 datasets we catalog were released in 2023 or later. At this pace, surveys that list them are outdated soon after publication, since they describe the field only as it was when they were written. We present the Cybersecurity dataset observatory, a public and continuously updated catalog of cybersecurity datasets based on network traffic. New datasets are added as they are found or submitted, every record is periodically re-checked against its original source, to which it links rather than hosting the data, and every change is recorded in a public change log. This paper documents the first release: we define a traffic-centered scope and a seven-axis taxonomy, and review 234 datasets (204 original captures and 30 derivatives) across 14 domains. The review shows a field that grows quickly but unevenly, where 91 datasets distribute only processed records, a few laboratories produce a large share of the data, and UAV, wireless and V2X networks have little public evidence, while 5G has few real captures. We then relate the catalog to common uses in AI research, outline a procedure for selecting datasets, and discuss benchmark pitfalls and open gaps.
evidence_items.title: The Cybersecurity Dataset Observatory: Which Data for AI in Cybersecurity?

evidence_items.summary: Internet of Things (IoT) technology has substantially reshaped smart home automation and security through intelligent monitoring, control, and remote management of residential spaces. This paper reports a systematic literature review (SLR) on IoT-based smart home automation and security systems following the PRISMA framework, guided by four explicit research questions on communication technologies, AI/cloud/edge adoption, security and privacy, and research trends. Searches of IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, ScienceDirect, Scopus, and Google Scholar identified 142 records, of which 32 studies met the inclusion criteria after a four-stage PRISMA screening process; two pre-2021 foundational studies were retained under an explicit foundational exception rule, and two preprints on emerging topics were retained under a peer-review exception rule. These exceptions were pre-specified and are reported transparently as potential sources of selection bias. The review examines key technologies reported in the corpus, including ESP32/NodeMCU microcontrollers, the MQTT protocol, artificial intelligence and machine learning, cloud and edge computing, blockchain-based security, and voice-controlled automation, and reports how frequently each appears in the 32 included studies rather than claiming market-wide adoption. Based on this literature, IoT-based smart homes are reported to offer real-time monitoring, intelligent appliance automation, intrusion detection, emergency alerts, remote access, and energy efficiency relative to traditional automation systems, while cybersecurity risks, limited interoperability with standards such as Matter and Thread, privacy gaps, and scalability constraints remain open challenges. Because the included studies report heterogeneous, non-comparable outcome metrics, no quantitative meta-analysis was performed; this and other methodological limitations—corpus size, database coverage, and single-reviewer screening with second-author verification—are reported explicitly. Prioritized future research directions include standards-aligned interoperability research, standardized evaluation benchmarks, explainable AI, Zero Trust and lightweight security for resource-constrained devices, and LLM-assisted automation. This review is intended as a structured, transparently limited synthesis of the current literature and identified research gaps, rather than a comprehensive benchmark of the field.
evidence_items.title: A systematic literature review on IoT-based smart home automation and security systems

evidence_items.summary: MegNIST is a benchmark dataset for developing and evaluating machine learning methods for inner speech decoding from magnetoencephalography (MEG). The dataset comprises 12,000 trials of a single participant imagining speaking the digits zero through nine, recorded across four sessions. Each trial contains 306-channel MEG recordings sampled at 250 Hz, preprocessed using signal space separation, filtering, and downsampling. Data are provided as pre-defined training (10,000 trials), validation (1,000 trials), and test (1,000 trials) splits, with entire experimental runs assigned to each split to preserve temporal independence. The dataset is available in both BIDS format for neuroimaging analysis and as serialised tensors for machine learning workflows. Baseline classification results demonstrate that imagined digits can be decoded significantly above chance. Standardised splits, validated baselines, example code, and a PyTorch-compatible loader in the pnpl Python library enable straightforward integration with machine learning frameworks, lowering barriers for researchers to rapidly develop and benchmark inner speech decoding methods for non-invasive brain-computer interfaces.
evidence_items.title: MegNIST, A Benchmark for Non-Invasive Inner Speech Decoding

evidence_items.summary: Transmitting semantically structured embedding vectors over digital channels is costly in bit rate, while conven- tional vector quantization approaches face limitations in scalabil- ity, encoding complexity, and index assignment. This paper inves- tigates binary hashing techniques from the information retrieval literature as semantic indexing strategies for general-purpose networks. We study random Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) along with Principal Component Analysis (PCA)-, Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA)-, and ITQ (Iterative Quantization)- based variants in a semantic communication pipeline over a Binary Symmetric Channel. Embeddings are compressed into binary codes, reconstructed through Hamming retrieval from a shared table, and evaluated on downstream classification. Ex- periments on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) and the Banking77 dataset show that data-dependent hashing improves upon random LSH, while ITQ refinement increases robustness to channel noise. Among the evaluated methods, CCA- ITQ achieves the best classification accuracy across the tested channel conditions. These results indicate that binary hashing is an efficient and scalable alternative to quantization-based embedding compression for semantic communications.
evidence_items.title: Leveraging Binary Hashing for Scalable Index Assignment in Semantic Communications

evidence_items.summary: We developed CAE-Bench, a benchmark to evaluate AI agents on Computer-Aided Engineering (CAE) solver development. A CAE solver is more than a PDE solver; it must be able to generalize across various inputs, such as different boundary conditions, geometries, and material properties. CAE-Bench evaluates the generalizability of AI-developed CAE solvers by providing the same task, such as a heat transfer problem, multiple cases, with each case specifying an input. The AI agent develops a solver for a fixed task using only a few public cases, and the resulting solver is then tested on held-out cases, i.e., cases it has never seen before. We evaluate 12 models across a range of reasoning settings on 80 computational tasks. Our experiments show that even if a solver developed by an AI agent performs well on the public cases, it may even get 0 score on held-out cases. For tasks such as fluid dynamics problems, even the solver developed by GPT-6 Astra performs poorly on held-out cases. A data format and an SDK for task registration are provided, so the researcher can use the benchmark on their own infrastructure. We hope that CAE-Bench will help the community to develop AI agents that can develop reusable CAE solvers that generalize to various inputs.
evidence_items.title: CAE-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Reusable CAE Solver Development

evidence_items.summary: CMI-9905 is the benchmark dataset accompanying the manuscript "NSWSSC: multi-channel chaos game representation with dual-branch CNN for circRNA-miRNA interaction prediction" (Scientific Reports, under revision). Experimentally validated circRNA-miRNA interactions were curated from CircBank and CircR2Cancer; the corresponding sequences were retrieved from CircBank and miRBase. Contents: 9,905 positive interaction pairs covering 2,346 circRNAs and 962 miRNAs; an equal number of randomly paired negative samples (19,810 pairs in total); and 311,484 site-level candidate target site (CTS) samples obtained by seed-based fuzzy matching of the miRNA extended seed region (positions 2-10, up to 2 mismatches) against circRNA sequences with a 40-nt flanking window, giving a positive-to-negative ratio of approximately 3.72:1. Train/validation/test CSV splits and leakage-controlled, pair-grouped five-fold cross-validation tensors (precomputed Chaos Game Representation matrices at k = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, stored as NumPy .npz) are included. File structure: database/ contains the sequence tables (circSequence 9905.csv, miSequence 9905.csv), positive/negative Train/Validation/Test splits, GraRep node-behaviour features, FastText embeddings and two helper scripts. database/CMI-9905-Full/ holds a self-contained copy of the core CSV tables. database/precomputed/cv/ holds all data.npz and all data k{2,3,4,5,7}.npz CGR tensors. Companion records: the NSWSSC source code is deposited as a separate Zenodo software record. Cross-links will be completed with the final DOIs after publication.

evidence_items.summary: We construct confidence intervals for linear functionals $θ(F m)=\int h\,dF m$ of the empirical law $F m$ of success probabilities $p 1,\dots,p m$, from independent counts $c i\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p i)$, as for a language model run $n$ times per problem. Coverage is at least $1-α$ for every $n$, $m$ and fixed $(p i)$, simultaneously for all bounded $h$. The variance-adaptive (VA) region tests each candidate mixing law with the conditional variance of the tail counts it implies. This variance is linear in the law, so the region is a linear program, and cell envelopes keep it valid off-grid. Regions calibrated for iid sampling target a super-population law and are conservative for $θ(F m)$. With all $n$ tail counts, fixed $n$, continuous $h$ and a grid refined as $m\to\infty$, the identification part of VA's width is first-order worst-case optimal, as for any localization with the same index set. Under a rule fixed before the main comparator runs, VA was narrower than a two-stage plug-in band at every $n$ (median width ratio 0.60 at $n=128$), but not than the asymptotic, pointwise AMARI interval at $n=128$; on real rollout pools it was wider than both pointwise and Bonferroni-adjusted AMARI at $n\le128$. For $P(p>0)$ and pass@$k$ with $k\gg n$ the data support only lower bounds.
evidence_items.title: Variance-adaptive confidence regions for fixed-benchmark binomial mixtures, with application to LLM evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) trading agents now trade stocks for their users, and benchmarks rank models by their agents' returns. Yet a single run's return says little about skill. In our study, two runs of the same model that differed only in the random seed ended 5.2 points apart on average, so telling skill from luck takes many backtests across markets, models and seeds. However, live arenas trade each day only once, and backtests either use the few months after a model's training cutoff or run on years the model may remember, often with news joined to prices by calendar date. In this paper, we present rta-bench-1, a backtest over three US markets (a rally, a bear market and a crash). It shows each headline only after its publication minute, plays each period blind and named, and checks every run for look-ahead. It also splits each return into factor exposure and alpha and scores every decision against random choices of the same day and sector. In 91 runs of six models from four vendors, no alpha was significant, market and style exposure accounted for a median 78% of the return, and the decisions did no better than random stocks of the same sector. The agents bought the stocks with the most positive news, yet in ablations they earned as much without their headlines. Still, the agents carried out rules reliably, since a single cash rule in the prompt cut a GPT-based agent's share in stocks by 30.3 points in all six pairs. Builders should therefore supply the edge themselves and report exposures and alpha, and benchmarks should replay news by publication time.
evidence_items.title: LLM Trading Agents Earn Beta, Not Alpha: A Look-Ahead-Free Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: This repository provides supporting computational materials for the study entitled “Beyond Muscle Contraction: Transcriptomic and Structural Insights into Skeletal Muscle Responses Following Competitive Football.” The study integrates paired skeletal muscle RNA-sequencing data from nine football players (GSE337399), Reactome pathway analysis, systematic gene-removal sensitivity testing, experimental protein structural characterization, and independent transcriptomic assessment using GSE43856. The analyses identified significant downregulation of MYH1 and an exploratory mixed-direction transcriptional response involving the Reactome pathway Regulation of CDH11 function . Exhaustive analysis of 165 three-gene removal combinations identified ADAM33, AMOT, and JUP as the combination producing the greatest attenuation of the pathway signal. Structural analyses examined experimentally determined protein complexes (PDB: 3IFQ, 3L6X, and 7NND), including interfacial residue contacts and buried solvent-accessible surface areas. Independent evaluation of an external exercise cohort did not consistently reproduce the complete three-gene transcriptional pattern. The repository is intended to support transparency, reproducibility, and independent evaluation of the computational results. The original transcriptomic datasets and protein structures remain accessible through their respective public repositories.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Muscle Contraction: Transcriptomic and Structural Insights into Skeletal Muscle Responses Following Competitive Football

evidence_items.summary: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) enables a single student to absorb the skills of several domain teachers by learning from its own generated responses. We present Multimodal Model Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation Reasoner (M3OPD-Reasoner), a fully open recipe for post-training vision-language models (VLMs) over three reasoning domains: image STEM, image perception, and video. We curate two datasets, M3OPD-SFT-1.35M for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and M3OPD-RL-193K for reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards. On these data, we compare post-training recipes that start from Qwen3.5-9B: training one model on the mixed data of all domains (MixSFT and MixRL), and training one teacher per domain with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), directly or after an SFT warm-up, and distilling the teachers into one student with MOPD. We evaluate on 21 image STEM, image perception, and video reasoning benchmarks after we decontaminate the training data against them. The comparison establishes MOPD of teachers trained with GSPO directly from Qwen3.5-9B as the best recipe: the student closely matches each teacher on its own domain and is on average above the mixed-training baselines on the same prompts. Since MOPD already merges the domain capabilities that MixRL would otherwise have to learn, its student is a stronger starting point for RL, and we ask whether the same data can carry the model further from there: we add MixRL on top of the MOPD student, on the same prompts and with the same settings, which, to our knowledge, no prior VLM recipe has studied. The same prompts still improve the MOPD student, with no collapse, and give our main model, M3OPD-Reasoner-9B. MOPD and MixRL can therefore work as consecutive stages that get more out of the same data. We release all data, the training code, and the checkpoints of every stage.
evidence_items.title: M3OPD-Reasoner: An Open Recipe for Post-Training Multimodal Reasoning with Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation

evidence_items.summary: Higson and Prodan's universal Chern Hamiltonians are closed-surface models built from the simplicial boundary operator and Poincaré duality. We treat the boundary and interface classes obtained from finite surfaces with boundary by doubling the surface and jamming the reflected copy. For every finite triangulated oriented surface with boundary we construct an intrinsic Poincaré–Lefschetz Hamiltonian, compare it with the original-side compression of the doubled closed Hamiltonian, identify the discrepancy as boundary-collar supported, and prove Schur-complement estimates for finite-\(M\) jamming. Along families with negligible collar dimension these estimates identify the normalized bulk spectral limits of the intrinsic, compressed, and jammed models. The main Roe-algebra theorem identifies the doubled-and-jammed interface class in \(K 1(C^ (Y\subset X))\) with \(\partial Y(E +(\pi(P \pm)))\), using the Higson–Prodan closed universal-model theorem \cite{HigsonProdanUniversalPRL,HigsonProdanUniversalArxiv} for the closed-bulk gap and Chern value; this \(K 1\)-class identity is unconditional modulo HP. The integer interface winding \(\pm1\) is proved internally in the periodic triangular Toeplitz case via the \(K 1\)-to-\(\mathbb Z\) Toeplitz extension, and is stated as a conditional corollary for general partitions, conditional on the existence of an integer-valued Chern-jump pairing for the interface ideal. The periodic triangular Bloch class is a fully internal benchmark: its closed-bulk gap, Chern signs, and straight Toeplitz winding are proved in the paper. \medskip\noindent Dependency categorization (sharp framing). The results split into three buckets according to which external theorems each one uses. (A) Fully internal: the finite-dimensional boundary theory and Schur-complement estimates, the internal bulk spectral equivalence, and the periodic triangular benchmark (gap, Chern signs, and integer Toeplitz winding for the straight periodic interface).
evidence_items.title: Boundary and Interface Classes for Universal Chern Hamiltonians via Doubling and Jamming

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Many studies on automated respiratory sound classification report near-perfect accuracy. In most of these studies, respiratory cycles are split randomly into training and test sets, so cycles of the same patient can be found in both sets. This patient-level data leakage makes the reported results higher than the real performance. In this study, we show this problem on the ICBHI 2017 dataset and build a leakage-free benchmark. Methods: We compare TabPFN-3, a pretrained tabular foundation model that predicts by in-context learning without task-specific gradient updates, with eight standard machine learning classifiers in a three-stage framework. Results: When the cycle-level split was replaced by a patient-level split (a stratified five-fold split repeated three times, 15 test folds, with every class present in every test fold), the accuracy of TabPFN-3 decreased from 0.9943 to 0.8722, the macro-F1 from 0.9807 to 0.5010 and the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) from 0.9805 to 0.5788. Nadeau–Bengio-corrected t-tests with Holm adjustment over the 15 folds showed that TabPFN-3 had a significantly higher MCC than all eight baselines. SHAP analysis showed that the first MFCC coefficient, the spectral bandwidth and the RMS energy contributed most to the predictions. We also distilled TabPFN-3 into small student models. The best student, a small transformer (276.3 KB), reached an MCC of 0.5140; its MCC difference from the teacher was not significant after Holm correction, but an equivalence test did not show equivalence and its macro-F1 was significantly lower. A shallow distilled decision tree gave readable rules, mainly for COPD and healthy recordings. Conclusions: Performance on several minority diseases remains low, so the models are not ready for clinical use, and the results should be seen as a realistic baseline for future work.
evidence_items.title: Exposing Patient-Level Data Leakage in Respiratory Sound Classification: A Leakage-Free Benchmark Leveraging Transformer-Based TabPFN-3 and Knowledge Distillation

evidence_items.summary: Professional work involves under-specified assignments, where relevant information is spread across workplace applications and may conflict or change over time. To evaluate how well frontier agents can perform economically valuable work in such settings, we introduce ATLAS-Finance, a benchmark of 100 end-to-end investment-banking tasks across 13 simulated firms. As in real banking workflows, agents must search email, chat, calendars, notes, and files to identify requirements, gather information, reconcile conflicts/updates, and then build complex financial models. Tasks were developed by experienced bankers based on their real deal work and take them 15-30 hours to complete. Agent deliverables are evaluated with expert-authored rubrics (median: 124.5 criteria) covering financial rationale and results, spreadsheet construction, completeness, and formatting. Despite completing substantial portions of the requested work, current agents rarely produce correct deliverables. Across today's frontier models, the best ones (Claude Opus and Fable) pass fewer than 11% of tasks.
evidence_items.title: ATLAS-Finance: Benchmarking AI Agents in Realistic Banking Environments

evidence_items.summary: Text-to-image (T2I) safety evaluation typically assigns each prompt or image a single culture-blind harm label, so content that is harmful only within a particular culture can pass as benign. We introduce CultureCraft, an agentic framework that constructs T2I prompts that appear benign under a general-purpose rubric yet carry a latent harmful meaning in a target culture, and use it to build CuRSE-Bench: 10,709 culture-specific prompts and 2,648 culture-general controls over six regions and ten harm axes, each drawn from a predefined knowledge base of documented harm vectors and traceable to at least two independent sources. Scoring every prompt under six region persona judges and a paired culture-blind judge, we find that the culture-blind judge under-rates culture-specific latent harm while matching the persona judges on the controls. Each persona judge, in turn, chiefly decodes its own region's latent harm under our instrument: a selective cultural blind spot that persists in deployed moderators.
evidence_items.title: CuRSE-Bench: A Benchmark for Probing Cultural Blind Spots in Text-to-Image Safety Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly used for medical guidance, but women's health remains under-evaluated in benchmark design. We present the Women's Health Benchmark (WHBench), a targeted evaluation suite of 47 expert-crafted scenarios across 10 women's health topics, designed to expose clinically meaningful failure modes including outdated guidelines, unsafe omissions, dosing errors, and equity-related blind spots. We evaluate 22 models using a 23-criterion rubric spanning clinical accuracy, completeness, safety, communication quality, instruction following, equity, uncertainty handling, and guideline adherence, with safety-weighted penalties and server-side score recalculation. Across 3,102 attempted responses (3,100 scored), no model mean performance exceeds 75 percent; the best model reaches 72.1 percent. Even top models show low fully correct rates and substantial variation in harm rates. Inter-rater reliability is moderate at the response label level but high for model ranking, supporting WHBench utility for comparative system evaluation while highlighting the need for expert oversight in clinical deployment. WHBench provides a public, failure-mode-aware benchmark to track safer and more equitable progress in womens health AI.
evidence_items.title: WHBench: Evaluating Frontier LLMs with Expert-in-the-Loop Validation on Women's Health Topics

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The rapid expansion of data center infrastructure, accelerated by the growing computational demands of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), has led to an unprecedented increase in electricity consumption. As AI developers race to deploy GenAI products, time-to-market pressure drives continuous model training that demands baseload power, often from high-CO 2 emissions sources like natural gas and coal instead of intermittent renewables like wind and solar. Carbon-aware strategies that shift model training in real time to periods or locations with cleaner power on the margin have emerged as a near-term decarbonization lever, but the relative effectiveness of temporal flexibility (pausing model training during high-carbon hours) versus spatial flexibility (migrating workloads to cleaner grid regions) remains poorly understood under real-world constraints. This study evaluates these strategies using 2025 marginal operating CO 2 emissions rate (MOER) data from WattTime across 43 subregions spanning four US grid operators: California Independent System Operator (CAISO), Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), Midcontinent Independent System Operator, and Pennsylvania–Jersey–Maryland (PJM). Using Meta’s LLaMA 3.1 model family as representative workloads, we simulate four scenarios: business-as-usual, reflecting a carbon-informed siting choice with no real-time operational flexibility (S1, BAU); temporal flexibility with varying pause thresholds (S2); ideal spatial flexibility (S3); and spatial flexibility incorporating migration overhead (S4). We find that effective strategies are grid-dependent. In grids with high subregional MOER heterogeneity, spatial flexibility dominates: ERCOT achieves up to 36% emissions reduction via intraday alternation between wind-rich and solar-heavy zones, and the inter-ISO configuration achieves 67.3% reduction, with CAISO and ERCOT absorbing over 80% of training hours.
evidence_items.title: Carbon-aware scheduling of large language model training across multiple US power grid operators: a marginal emissions analysis

evidence_items.summary: Aim: Artificial intelligence-based systems are increasingly used for recognizing and assessing skin lesions, yet studies focusing on pregnancy-specific dermatological findings are limited. This study aimed to compare the accuracy of artificial intelligence based large language models in diagnosing pregnancy related dermatological lesions, explaining their etiopathogenesis, and providing clinically appropriate treatment recommendations.Materials and Methods: In this observational study, ten pregnancy-specific dermatological lesions were evaluated using ChatGPT (version 5) and Google Gemini (version 2.5). Each case was presented with an image from Williams Obstetrics, 26th edition, and a standardized patient statement: “I am pregnant. I have a skin lesion like this. What is it, why does it occur, and what should I do for treatment?” Responses were blindly rated by obstetrics and gynecology and dermatology specialists for diagnostic accuracy, etiopathogenesis explanation, and treatment appropriateness, using a five-point Likert scale. Cohen’s kappa was used to assess inter-rater agreement; the Wilcoxon test compared the models; Spearman’s correlation examined score relationships. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.Results: ChatGPT outperformed Gemini in etiopathogenesis explanation (p = 0.002) and treatment recommendations (p = 0.002), with no significant difference in diagnostic accuracy (p = 0.336). ChatGPT generally provided more detailed, applicable responses, whereas Gemini often gave limited or purely directive information. Correlations between criteria were weak and statistically insignificant for both models.Conclusions: ChatGPT was superior to Gemini in etiopathogenesis and treatment recommendations but comparable in diagnostic accuracy. However, no artificial intelligence system can replace clinical evaluation by a physician.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Based Clinical Decision Support in Pregnancy Specific Dermatological Lesions

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for de novo small-molecule design, but the practical and translational utility of generated candidates depends on the configuration of the entire discovery workflow rather than on generative model architecture alone. This review adopts a workflow-based perspective on generative molecular design, tracing the process from existing molecular data sets, preprocessing and representation, to molecule generation, conditioning, candidate prioritization, evaluation, and iterative refinement. It examines how generative AI model families, constraints, and predictive oracles interact within this pipeline, and evaluates generated candidates using intrinsic metrics, computational assessments, and experimental and translational evidence. Active learning, computational and experimental feedback, and human expert input are further discussed as mechanisms for closed-loop refinement. Across these stages, we identify data construction and representation choices, oracle quality, evaluation protocols, and the availability of informative feedback as major determinants of how model performance should be interpreted and whether generated structures progress toward biologically and translationally meaningful candidates, with selected examples. In conclusion, reliable generative drug discovery requires coordinated design across the entire workflow rather than isolated advances in individual components.

Abstract Background To evaluate the clinical performance of a novel artificial intelligence (AI)-based image processing algorithm for two-dimensional angiographic imaging compared with its predecessor across multiple imaging modes, anatomic regions, and endovascular specialties. Materials and methods This retrospective, comparative, randomized, paired, and blinded multicenter reader study included anonymized images acquired during clinically indicated endovascular interventions at 11 institutions in the United States and Europe. A total of 553 image series from 182 patients representing 51 procedure types across interventional radiology, neurointervention, cardiology, and pediatric cardiology were processed using both the AI-based and predecessor image processing algorithms. Thirteen board-certified physicians independently evaluated paired images using five-point Likert scales for overall image quality, contrast of clinically relevant details, noise reduction, and confidence in assessing device and vessel details. The primary endpoint was non-inferiority of overall image quality. Secondary endpoints evaluated superiority across image quality metrics using a predefined hierarchical testing strategy. Results The AI-based image processing algorithm demonstrated non-inferior overall image quality in 98.9% of all evaluations (95% confidence interval [CI], 98%–100%), meeting the primary endpoint across all imaging modes, anatomic regions, and predefined subgroups. Superiority of the AI-based algorithm was demonstrated for overall image quality, contrast of clinically relevant details, noise reduction, and confidence in assessing device and vessel details across fluoroscopy, roadmap, overlay reference, and native acquisition imaging. Overall image quality superiority was not demonstrated for digital subtraction angiography, likely reflecting the intrinsically higher signal-to-noise characteristics of these acquisitions.
evidence_items.title: Clinical evaluation of a novel artificial intelligence-based image processing algorithm for two-dimensional angiography

organizations: School of Mechanical Engineering, Purdue University
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate diameter-at-breast-height (DBH) measurement is essential for forest inventory and ecological monitoring. This work evaluates two artificial intelligence-assisted smartphone frameworks: a text-prompt Segment Anything Model 3.1 (SAM3.1) that segments trunks from red–green–blue images, and a depth-guided MobileSAMv2 model that uses depth cues to generate geometry-based prompts. The resulting masks are integrated into a geometric pipeline for accurate and interpretable DBH estimation. Both methods were tested on 202 planted and 285 natural trees. In planted forests, both achieved high accuracy with no failures and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.0 cm. In natural forests, SAM3.1 remained robust (1.5 cm RMSE), while MobileSAMv2 failed in two cases and showed lower accuracy (1.9 cm excluding failures). Using all 487 images, MobileSAMv2 model inference averaged 1.3 s per image on an iPhone 15 Pro. SAM3.1 segmentation averaged 37.2 s per image on an Intel Core i7-1260P CPU, compared with 3.1 s on an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU and 0.8 s on an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB GPU through Google Colab. Overall, MobileSAMv2 supports direct on-device deployment, while SAM3.1 offers greater robustness in complex environments and benefits substantially from GPU acceleration.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted tree diameter-at-breast-height measurement

evidence_items.summary: Study on survey of post harvest pathogen, field and storage pests and diseases of three varieties of sugarcane found in Port Harcourt was carried out in the Department of Plant Science and Biotechnology and Rivers State Teaching and Research Farm, all in the Rivers State University. Three sugar cane varieties identified based on stem colour viz: Kasha Cane-B51415 (Dark green), Anancy-BJ6183 (Green) and Kava Rangi-B64.277 (Red stem) were collected from Port Harcourt. The cultural laboratory technique was used for the microbial study while the hand book of South African Sugarcane Research Institute was used for field pests and diseases identification. Microbial shelf-life evaluation further revealed the red variety to contain reduced bacterial (3.8 x106 , 3.5 x106 and 2.2x106 cfu/g) and fungal (0.7 x104 , 1.3 x104 and 1.3 x104 cfu/g) loads for months 1, 2 and 3 respectively than other varieties within the storage months. A total of three bacterial organisms (Bacillus sp, Pseudomonas sp, Staphylococcus sp) and three fungal organisms (Aspergillus niger, A. flavus, Yeast) were isolated within the months of storage. Four field pests were observed viz: locust, aphid, trash caterpillar and fall army worm. However, none was recorded on the red variety. Five field diseases were observed including streak, red rot, rust, leaf spot and smut. The green variety recorded lowest number of prevailing field diseases. Generally, the three varieties of sugar cane performed differently with respect to pest and diseases.
evidence_items.title: Microbial Contamination, Field Diseases and Pests of Three Sugarcane Varieties Found in Port Harcourt

evidence_items.summary: Nuclear segmentation across patient-derived organoids (PDOs) is complicated by differences in morphology, staining, image scale, and acquisition format. We present ARIPA, an automated human-in-the-loop (HITL) system that coordinates pre-trained segmentation tools through a vision-language model (VLM)-based agentic planning, verification, and refinement loop for hematoxylin and eosin images of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded PDOs. In contrast to existing tools, ARIPA does not require training and achieves good performance. Tissue-aware tiling and image-derived calibration initialize segmentation; optional expert corrections guide configuration search and light-weight object-level rules without retraining or fine-tuning the pre-trained segmentation networks. We evaluated initial ARIPA predictions on more than 50,000 nuclei from 19 images of breast, head and neck, and lung patient-derived cancer PDOs, where nuclear segmentation was challenging due to its 3D structure and variation in imaging layers and malignant cell morphology. Performance was evaluated on agent-selected models before expert feedback, after feedback from the initial runs excluding direct expert edits, and in comparison to a custom-trained HoVer-Net model previously published by our group. At a minimum polygon intersection over union (IoU) of 0.5, image-macro F1 was 0.8380 before feedback, 0.9849 after feedback, and 0.4713 for HoVer-Net. Mean area under the F1 score versus IoU curve was 0.8013, 0.9700, and 0.4317, respectively. The mean paired F1 increase after feedback was 0.1468, with increases in 17 out of the total 19 images and no changes in the remaining two. Ground truth nuclei annotations were created by expert review and editing of ARIPA's post-feedback outputs. In this cohort, ARIPA outperformed the custom-trained HoVer-Net, and its performance was improved further following expert-guided HITL refinement.
evidence_items.title: ARIPA: Agentic Reasoning for Image-based Pathology Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.
evidence_items.title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory

evidence_items.summary: Training coding agents for long-horizon tasks requires environments with verifiable feedback. Existing pipelines often follow a linear process that ends with validation, establishing usability but providing little guidance on improving training value. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) often requires model rollouts or model training followed by downstream evaluation, with costs and feedback delays amplified on long-horizon tasks. How can we use timely, reliable proxy signals to improve training value and synthesize environments at scale? We present RepoFactory, an automated pipeline that converts real repositories into verifiable environments where agents build complete projects from scratch given a language specification. Its Environment Evolution Loop optimizes a multiplicative objective combining validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope through proxy feedback. RepoFactory produces 10,159 environments across 17 software domains. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on these environments yields RepoHorizen-35B-A3B, which achieves gains of 22.6 percentage points on NL2Repo-Bench and 8.5 points on average across five benchmarks covering long-horizon coding and agentic tasks in real-world production settings, compared with 17.5 and 6.4 points without environment evolution. These results highlight the training value of RepoFactory environments and the additional gains from the Environment Evolution Loop.
evidence_items.title: From Repositories to Training Environments: Scaling Long-Horizon Coding Agents with Environment Evolution Loop

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Biomedical research is constrained by the time and domain expertise required to analyze increasingly large and complex datasets. Here we present OpenScientist, an open-source agentic AI co-scientist designed to address this gap by investigating scientist-defined queries and generating verifiable, data-grounded analyses. OpenScientist was evaluated by domain experts across five biomedical case studies, completing analyses in minutes that otherwise would take months of human time and expertise. It accurately quantified Alzheimer’s blood biomarker performance, generated a plasma proteomic survival model that predicted survival in a hidden-evaluation cohort, proposed a reproducible mechanism linking tau pathology to altered lysosomal acidification, generated multiple myeloma hypotheses validated in an external cohort with attenuated signal in randomized controls, and demonstrated concordance with an independent human analysis in a blinded, prespecified proteomic comparison. These results support the use of OpenScientist to assist biomedical data analysis in concert with human experts. To support research involving sensitive clinical datasets, OpenScientist can operate in a fully air-gapped environment using open-source models for inference. OpenScientist demonstrates that open, auditable, agentic AI can support real-world clinical research by researching the literature, generating hypotheses, executing analyses, and generating insights from complex datasets.
evidence_items.title: An open agentic AI co-scientist for clinical and biomedical discovery

evidence_items.summary: Supporting visual recovery and semantic interpretation within the same communication framework remains difficult when channel quality deteriorates. To address this issue, this paper proposes a large language model (LLM)-guided channel-aware semantic communication framework that jointly supports these two tasks through decoupled transmission streams. An LLM-based channel-aware encoder jointly processes image features and a textual prompt describing the current channel condition. This design allows the semantic representation to adapt to different signal-to-noise ratio levels while retaining an independent reconstruction pathway. A lightweight learnable masking mechanism is also incorporated to scramble the transmitted latent features. The ablation results indicate that this mechanism introduces only a limited impact on reconstruction performance. Evaluation under additive white Gaussian noise shows that the proposed design remains effective across the tested channel conditions. In particular, the framework achieves classification accuracies of 90.58% and 88.23% at 0 dB on the CIFAR-10 and Intel image classification datasets, respectively.
evidence_items.title: Large language model-guided channel-aware semantic communication

evidence_items.summary: Logical reasoning is a highly valued capability in language models. However, high-quality logical reasoning data remain scarce, while manual data creation is costly and time-consuming. We introduce Operations Research Aided Synthesis (ORAS), a solver-verified, two-layer incremental framework for synthesizing logic question-answering data. ORAS leverages operations research techniques to systematically generate high-quality datasets for evaluating large language models (LLMs) and, when used for training, improving their reasoning capabilities. ORAS’s pipeline integrates mathematical programming methods to generate question–answer pairs, and then employs a dual-phase approach: the first phase uses optimization algorithms to construct and evaluate the logic systems by solving the problem using a mathematical solver. The second phase translates the logic system to human-readable problems and generates answers according to the information from the mathematical solver. The fine-tuned model achieves a 22–33% (percentage point) improvement in accuracy on in-sample tests and a 4–22% (percentage point) improvement on similar out-of-sample tests.
evidence_items.title: Synthesis of Reliable Logic Question Answering Data for Large Language Model with the Aid of Operations Research Program

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Antifreeze proteins (AFPs) offer promising prospects as biocryoprotectants, yet their discovery remains a great challenge due to the lack of efficient large-scale screening tools. Here, we present a benchmark-optimized, multimodel computational pipeline that integrates property evaluation and structural assessment for high-throughput AFP identification. Through systematic benchmarking on independent testing data set, two optimal strategies were identified: the two-model-based Strategy 8 achieved the highest accuracy of 0.82, while the stricter four-model-based Strategy 18 attained the highest precision of 0.97, making it optimal for initial large-scale screening. Furthermore, this pipeline was applied to screen 153,359 Antarctic krill sequences and discovered 13 novel antifreeze peptides. Dynamic ice shaping assays revealed that four out of 13 peptides significantly inhibited ice crystal growth. Notably, Peptide 10 (SPHSWANTYQQCK) could inhibit ice growth and recrystallization. This study establishes a robust framework for large-scale AFP identification and provides a set of experimentally validated Antarctic krill peptides with strong potential as novel biobased cryoprotectants.
evidence_items.title:
Benchmark-Optimized Pipeline Identifies Experimentally
Validated Antifreeze Peptides in Antarctic Krill

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Introduction Physician assistant (PA) programs need practical ways to recognize early academic difficulty. Existing predictors, including admission metrics and later summative assessments, have mixed reliability or occur too late to support timely intervention. This study examined whether first-semester below-benchmark (below-BM) examinnation counts in foundational courses were associated with Physician Assistant National Certifying Examination (PANCE) outcomes. Methods This retrospective, observational study included graduates from five consecutive cohorts with first-attempt PANCE outcomes (N = 228). Below-benchmark counts were summed across Clinical Medicine, Patient Evaluation, and Anatomy exams. Associations between below-BM count and PANCE, Physician Assistant Clinical Knowledge Rating and Assessment Tool (PACKRAT ® ) 1, PACKRAT ® 2, and End of Curriculum (EOC) scores were examined. Below-BM counts were compared by PANCE outcome, and logistic regression examined the association with PANCE failure. Results Below-benchmark count was significantly and negatively correlated with PANCE (ρ = −0.529, P < .001), PACKRAT ® 1 (ρ = −0.491, P < .001), PACKRAT ® 2 (ρ = −0.518, P < .001), and EOC scores (ρ = −0.452, P < .001). Students who failed the PANCE had higher below-BM counts than students who passed (median 4, interquartile range [IQR] 4 vs. median 1, IQR 2; P < .001). Each additional below-BM score increased the odds of PANCE failure by 32% (odds ratio = 1.32, 95% confidence interval [1.07, 1.63], P = .009). Discussion First-semester below-BM count is a simple, early, and easy-to-monitor measure of academic risk that may help PA programs identify students who need support before high-stakes outcomes, including PANCE.
evidence_items.title: First-Semester Below-Benchmark Examination Performance as an Early Indicator of PANCE Risk
