evidence_items.summary: This study examines whether adding waveform-derived information-theoretic descriptors to Mel-spectrogram inputs offers a measurable benefit for five-class amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) dysarthria speech-status classification. The primary evidence is a study-specific, five-fold recording-level CNN comparison: Mel-only accuracy is 0.926±0.012, while historical fusion accuracy is 0.927±0.008. A distinct CNN fusion verification/reproduction run, with traced propagation of the Mel input and all 17 information-theoretic descriptors, reports accuracy of 0.927±0.010; it does not retrospectively verify the archived historical input tensors. Thus, the available comparisons show only a small numerical change, not a demonstrated general advantage of fusion. Complementary analyses include a direct participant-disjoint CNN comparison, a fixed-duration CNN comparison, and seed, duration, padding, and task-specific controls. In the participant-disjoint comparison, Mel-only and fusion achieve accuracies of 0.820 and 0.823, respectively, whereas under the fixed-duration condition they achieve 0.914 and 0.915. These distinct result series show similarly small numerical differences between Mel-only and fusion under the additional evaluation conditions. They do not establish a matched estimate of the effect of participant overlap or a statistically reliable advantage of feature fusion. Source-code auditing identifies discrepancies between an available implementation and the documented score-producing benchmark, without establishing that leakage occurred in the latter. Missing run-linked records, class imbalance, and the absence of external validation constrain conclusions to the evaluated speech-processing pipelines. Class 4 represents ALS without dysarthria, not early bulbar disease detection.
evidence_items.title: Speech-Based Dysarthria Severity Classification in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: A Controlled Deep Learning Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Post-quantum cryptography migration can depend on the readiness of shared trust, software, control, and recovery services. We evaluate GridPQC-Graph, a temporal relational estimator coupled to constrained migration planning, in a constructed energy-sector benchmark. Six public power-system cases supply physical topology; deterministic cyber-dependency fixtures, archived primitive timings, and a disclosed stochastic label generator supply the remaining evidence. The benchmark contains 769 assets, 5,242 directed relations, and 110,736 controlled trials. Fifty-three time-indexed features feed calibrated histogram gradient boosting. Training, calibration, unseen-topology testing, and later-epoch testing use disjoint rows. Across 20 seeds, the model attains average precision 0.8884 and Brier score 0.1178 on the held-out 300-bus case. Against a newly calibrated logistic comparator, the corresponding paired differences are 0.00415 and − 0.00244; the logistic comparator has lower expected calibration error. Relation-group substitution measures output sensitivity and local ranking stability, without identifying causal effects. A mixed-integer planner enforces maintenance, criticality, privileged-asset, and prerequisite constraints. Its ten-wave mean exposure retirement is 0.3210, with a consequence proxy of 15.895; readiness-first scheduling trades lower consequence for less retired exposure. Optimizer-matched comparisons separate scoring effects from solver choice. These findings establish conditional benchmark performance, not operational effectiveness, field-disruption probabilities, or safe deployment. Formal stochastic models offer complementary assurance when their transition assumptions and probability bounds are independently validated.
evidence_items.title: Explainable temporal relational learning for constraint-aware PQC migration in a constructed energy-sector benchmark

organizations: Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Electricity demand forecasting is harder on grids where supply often falls short, because load shedding changes how demand behaves. This study benchmarks one-hour-ahead forecasting on the national grid of Bangladesh from April 2015 to March 2026, a period in which load shedding rose from less than 1% of hours to 44% of hours in 2022 to 2025. Eleven models were compared under a single leak-free protocol: three naive baselines, two linear models, Random Forest, XGBoost and four deep learning architectures (PatchTST, iTransformer, CNN-BiLSTM and BiGRU). All were scored on the same 14,142 test hours from July 2024 to March 2026, 41% of which had load shedding. PatchTST was the most accurate model, with an RMSE of 203.8 MW and a MAPE of 1.26%. Its RMSE was 34% lower than that of a tuned XGBoost and 58% lower than persistence. Diebold-Mariano tests with autocorrelation-robust variance and paired block-bootstrap intervals confirmed that it was significantly better than every other model. The advantage came mainly from load-shedding hours, where the error of XGBoost rose by 36% while that of every deep learning model changed by about 5% or less. Integrated Gradients and TreeSHAP showed that the transformers used the full weekly demand cycle and the recent shedding history, whereas XGBoost could not predict demand above its training range. BatchNorm improved the transformers but not the recurrent models. Forecasting models for energy-constrained grids should therefore be evaluated separately for hours with and without load shedding.
evidence_items.title: Forecasting Electricity Demand Under Severe Load Shedding: An Explainable and Statistically Validated Deep Learning Benchmark

organizations: Department of Emergency, Shijingshan Teaching Hospital, Capital Medical University
evidence_items.summary: Background Biomarkers may show strong outcome associations without adding information to detailed electronic health record (EHR) models. We developed a reproducible benchmark separating association from incremental value for the lactate-to-albumin ratio (LAR) and troponin in older high-acuity patients, with the aim of locating where marker-specific information remains distinct after an information-rich baseline. Methods From 12,000 records in the official CinC 2012 Sets A, B, and C, we included 1,640 patients aged at least 65 years with computable LAR. First-48-h measurements from 37 raw variables produced a transparent 290-feature baseline. Baseline, LAR-augmented, missingness-aware troponin, integrated, and score-enhanced models used L2-regularized logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting. Set A supported development, Set B validation and recalibration, and Set C locked internal testing. Evaluation combined discrimination, calibration, paired bootstrap ablation, optimism correction, decision curves, permutation importance, and risk concentration. Results Mortality rose from 18.2% in the lowest LAR max quartile to 36.7% in the highest, with 2.60-fold higher odds of death. The association pointed in the same direction across four ICU categories (odds ratios per stratum-specific LAR interquartile range, 1.30–1.76). The score-enhanced random forest achieved the highest Set C AUROC (0.769; 95% CI: 0.729–0.809). Recalibration improved its Brier score from 0.200 to 0.170 and moved calibration-in-the-large from − 0.652 to 0.078, thereby reducing average overprediction. Paired-bootstrap intervals for LAR or troponin augmentation crossed zero, locating an information-saturation boundary after the 290-feature EHR baseline; decision-curve mean net benefits for baseline and LAR-augmented gradient boosting were 0.120 and 0.122. Troponin-tested patients had higher mortality than untested patients (31.6% vs. 23.6%).
evidence_items.title: Separating biomarker association from incremental EHR value: a reproducible LAR and troponin benchmark in older high-acuity patients

evidence_items.summary: Remote sensing (RS) image understanding has significantly advanced through deep learning and vision-language models, yet most approaches still operate mainly as prediction systems that return class labels with limited explanation of the semantic evidence supporting them. Attribute-based representations offer a more interpretable alternative, describing RS scenes in terms of visible objects, dominant colors and geometric patterns. However, these representations are typically used within offline datasets and benchmarking pipelines rather than in interactive systems that enable users to inspect, query and reuse semantic reasoning. This paper presents GeoRS-Agent, an agentic geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) framework for explainable and attribute-grounded RS scene understanding. A vision–language model reports 38 attributes, a deterministic classifier assigns one of 19 classes from class–attribute profiles, and a language model explains the decision citing only the evidence used; an agentic mode exposes these components as tools. On 301 test images, with Qwen2.5-VL 7B throughout, the pipeline reached 58.1% accuracy, against 71.1% with the class list in the prompt, 77.4% with the knowledge base also in the prompt, and 91.7% with reference attributes; with profiles estimated from the model’s own attributes it reached 75.1% in an exploratory analysis; its difference from the knowledge-in-prompt condition was not statistically significant, while the class decision remained inspectable. Explanations were always consistent with the evidence; tools improved knowledge and contrastive queries but not counterfactual ones.
evidence_items.title: GeoRS-Agent: An Agentic GeoAI Framework for Attribute-Grounded and Explainable Remote Sensing Scene Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Security operations capabilities are commonly distributed across security operations centres (SOCs), security information and event management (SIEM), vulnerability assessment and penetration testing (VAPT), security awareness training (SAT), secure software development life-cycle (SDLC) practices, continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) controls, and AI security testing. Although enterprise platforms increasingly integrate telemetry, detection, response, cloud and identity capabilities, evidence and workflows across these seven capability areas are not necessarily connected through a shared, auditable operating model. This paper proposes a Unified Agentic Security Operations Platform (UASP), a conceptual architecture for coordinating the seven capabilities through specialist agents, a shared telemetry and evidence substrate, risk-context orchestration, and policy-governed human oversight. The framework specifies six illustrative feedback loops, including VAPT findings informing development and pipeline controls, deployment provenance enriching SOC investigations, security incidents informing targeted awareness interventions, and AI security testing events becoming correlated SIEM/SOC telemetry. It distinguishes the operational roles of the SOC and SIEM, and of secure SDLC and CI/CD, while allowing them to be implemented through coordinated agents. The design uses the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) for event normalization and treats entity, temporal and provenance modelling as a complementary semantic layer. It also defines bounded autonomy, risk-graded approvals, and an evaluation agenda. The paper is a narrative conceptual synthesis of selected standards, research and public vendor materials; it does not report a deployed implementation, original empirical dataset, or measured performance results. Its contribution is therefore a structured architecture and a set of testable design propositions for subsequent implementation and evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Toward a Unified Agentic Security Operations Platform: A Conceptual Architecture for Cross-Domain Cybersecurity Integration

evidence_items.summary: Background: Increasing volumes of heterogeneous digital-health intelligence challenge conventional horizon-scanning methods and their ability to examine how technologies, clinical priorities and innovation pathways evolve over time. This study developed an agentic AI-assisted methodology for longitudinal digital-health horizon scanning. Methods: We analysed 123 NHS horizon scans conducted in 2015 and annually from 2019 to 2026, comprising 4,039 company-year profiles. Horizon-scan records were integrated with policy, clinical, funding and media evidence. Entity harmonisation, transformer-based semantic representations, TF-IDF analysis, machine learning and semantic clustering were used to characterise thematic evolution and estimate next-year corpus reappearance and future documented maturity. Performance was evaluated using nested company-grouped and rolling-origin validation, and candidate themes were contextualised through human-reviewed multi-agent synthesis. Results: The corpus shifted from enterprise, workforce and operational technologies towards condition-specific clinical applications, including oncology, women’s health, cardiovascular care, cognitive assessment, neurodevelopmental conditions and imaging artificial intelligence. Under nested company-grouped validation, XGBoost estimated next-year corpus reappearance with an F1 score of 0.67, ROC-AUC of 0.89 and average precision of 0.72. Extra Trees estimated future documented maturity with R2=0.40and RMSE =0.96, compared with R2=0.27and RMSE =1.05for direct carry-forward. Chronological performance was more variable across annual cohorts. Conclusions: The framework provides a structured and traceable approach for transforming historical horizon scans into longitudinal thematic intelligence, company-level estimates and candidate areas for further investigation. It is intended to augment expert-led horizon scanning rather than replace clinical, regulatory, procurement or commissioning judgement.
evidence_items.title: Mapping the Evolution of Digital Health Innovation Using an Agentic AI-Assisted Longitudinal Horizon-Scanning Methodology

evidence_items.summary: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) coding tools have the potential to democratise the development of teacher-facing learning analytics dashboards by enabling educators to generate complete applications from natural language specifications. In this study we evaluate Claude Code (Fable) and OpenAI Codex (GPT-5.5 High) across three dashboard specifications of increasing complexity using realistic educational datasets typically available to educators. Both AI systems successfully generated functional dashboards that accurately implemented the required visualisations and interactions. However, they also independently introduced additional analytical functionality, including student risk classifications and AI-generated insights, despite these features not being requested. These implicit inferences raise important concerns regarding transparency, bias and student data privacy, particularly where educators may be unaware of the analytical models or external AI services embedded within generated applications. The findings suggest that while agentic AI can significantly reduce the technical barriers for end user educators developing learning analytics tools, careful review of generated analytical logic and data flows is essential to support responsible and trustworthy use in educational settings.
evidence_items.title: Where did that student risk model come from? Hidden inference in agentic AI-generated teacher-facing dashboards

evidence_items.summary: Consolidation freight forwarders frequently face cargo-acceptance decisions in which available cargo exceeds container capacity, shipment groups must be preserved, priority customers require service protection, and actual cargo volume and weight may deviate from declared values. This study develops a robust, service-aware cargo-selection variant of the Container Loading Problem that integrates selected freight revenue, complete-shipment requirements, customer-priority penalties, and scenario-based robust volume and weight capacity constraints. A mixed-integer linear programming formulation is proposed and used to provide exact benchmark solutions for seven controlled instances. Six metaheuristic variants are then designed and evaluated across three algorithmic families: Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search, Adaptive Simulated Annealing, and Binary Particle Swarm Optimization, each compared with its baseline counterpart. The controlled benchmark results show that Adaptive BPSO achieved the smallest average gap to the MILP optimum, at 0.0071%, while LNS and ASA also produced competitive solutions. The results also show that adaptivity is beneficial but not uniformly dominant across algorithm families. In the real-case-derived experiment using anonymized export-shipment data from an Indonesian logistics provider, Adaptive BPSO reached the best-found reference in all tested runs, while Baseline BPSO provided a strong balance between solution quality and runtime. Robust capacity analysis further shows that the selected cargo plans remained feasible under all predefined volume and weight scenarios while maintaining high container utilization. The study contributes a robust service-aware formulation, exact benchmark evidence, adaptive metaheuristic designs, and practical insights for cargo-acceptance decision support in consolidation freight forwarding.
evidence_items.title: Adaptive metaheuristics for solving the container loading problem

evidence_items.summary: Co-speech gesture generation aims to synthesize natural gestures that are both temporally synchronized with speech and semantically consistent with the spoken content. Although recent methods can generate rhythmically plausible motions, they often rely heavily on acoustic prosody while underutilizing textual semantics, especially when semantic annotations are incomplete, noisy, or unavailable. Consequently, the generated gestures may follow speech rhythm while failing to express the intended semantics. To address this problem, we propose a reliability-aware semantic-rhythm control framework for co-speech gesture generation. We first learn a discrete motion prior that represents continuous gestures in a compact and structured motion-code space. We then introduce a dual-branch semantic contribution estimation mechanism consisting of a full multimodal branch and an audio-only branch. Their distributional discrepancy provides a model-based proxy for text-induced predictive influence, which is interpreted jointly with segment-level semantic relevance. Based on this estimate, a controllable semantic-rhythm objective selectively strengthens semantic guidance in content-relevant segments while limiting unnecessary semantic intervention in rhythm-dominant segments. Furthermore, we treat background noise as an acoustic reliability condition and introduce noise-conditioned feature modulation together with benefit-regularized latent perturbation to improve generation robustness under realistic acoustic environments. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a favorable balance among semantic expressiveness, rhythmic synchronization, motion diversity, and robustness, enabling reliable and controllable co-speech gesture generation.
evidence_items.title: When Semantics Matter: Reliability-Aware Semantic-Rhythm Control for Co-Speech Gesture Generation

evidence_items.summary: A key challenge in physics diagram understanding is correctly associating visual information with the physical entities, relations, and conditions it describes. Even when a value, symbol, or other local element is accurately recognized, assigning it to the wrong entity or scope can distort the underlying physical premise and lead to incorrect reasoning. To systematically study this challenge, we introduce \textbf{PhysAlign}, a benchmark designed to assess whether multimodal models correctly associate information recognized from physics diagrams with its intended physical role. By disentangling visual recognition from physical-role assignment through localized probes and controlled variants, PhysAlign isolates correspondence errors from recognition failures. It contains 3,341 human-validated probes spanning 986 physics problems, enabling systematic evaluation of visual recognition and physical-role correspondence at scale. We further introduce five complementary evaluation metrics, including CAcc, GAcc, and JAcc, which provide a comprehensive assessment of models' ability to recognize diagram content, establish correct physical correspondences, and solve the underlying physics problem. Across our evaluated multimodal models, PhysAlign reveals a consistent gap between local visual recognition and physical-role grounding. Even when the queried content is correctly recognized, the conditional correspondence error rate remains 13.8\% for GPT-6-Astra and rises to about 50.6\% for InternVL3.5-8B. These findings indicate that strong perception alone does not ensure reliable physical interpretation, exposing a distinct grounding bottleneck that is largely hidden by answer-level accuracy and highlighting the need for future models to better align recognized visual evidence with its physical meaning.
evidence_items.title: PhysAlign: A Benchmark for Evidence-Grounded Role Alignment in Multimodal Physics Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Physical video understanding requires more than naming an event correctly. A model can answer a question about pouring, sliding, or collision from textual regularities while still failing to localize the event in time or space. We introduce a grounded benchmark for physical video understanding that extends the what--when--where evaluation structure of V-STaR to four video sources, six physics domains, three prompt families (physics, vstar_like, and neutral_rstr), and four input conditions (original, shuffled, ablated, and frame-masked). The benchmark contains 1,560 base video clips from SSV2, YouCook2, HoloAssist, and Roundabout-TAU. Each clip is first converted into a shared grounded event record, and the three query families are derived from that record. Temporal and spatial targets are shared across prompt families, while the non-physics families use deterministic family-appropriate semantic a_what targets derived from the same record. Across models and prompt families, physics remains the strongest regime overall, vstar_like is the clearest non-physics semantic comparison, and neutral_rstr behaves as a harder templated control. Prompt-family robustness is selective rather than universal, perturbation gains cluster in weak original cases, and spatial grounding is the weakest across settings. These results suggest that video Q&A reasoning benchmarks shall report physically grounded, prompt-aware, and perturbation-aware diagnostics alongside aggregate accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Grounding Video Reasoning in Physical Signals

evidence_items.summary: Query-based 3D object detection methods using multi-view images often struggle to efficiently leverage dynamic multi-scale information, e.g., the relationship between the object features and the geometric of the queries are not sufficiently learned, directly exploring the multi-scale spatiotemporal features will pay too many costs. To address these challenges, we propose CAM3DNet, a novel sparse query-based framework which combines three new modules, composite query (CQ), adaptive self-attention (ASA), and multi-scale hybrid sampling (MSHS). First, the core idea in the CQ module is a multi-scale projection strategy to transform 2D queries into 3D space. Second, the ASA module learns the interactions between the spatiotemporal multi-scale queries. Third, the MSHS module uses the deformable attention mechanism to sample multi-scale object information by considering multi-scales queries, pyramid feature maps, and 2D-camera prior knowledge. The entire model employs a backbone network and a feature pyramid network (FPN) as the encoder, then introduces a YOLOX and a DepthNet as a ROI\_Head to produce CQ, and repeatedly utilizes ASA and MSHS as the decoder to gain detection features. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes, Waymo, and Argoverse benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our CAM3DNet, and most existing camera-based 3D object detection methods are outperformed. Besides, we make comprehensive ablation studies to check the individual effect of CQ, ASA, and MSHS, as well as their cost of space and computation complexity.
evidence_items.title: CAM3DNet: Comprehensively mining the multi-scale features for 3D Object Detection with Multi-View Cameras

evidence_items.summary: Negation is a fundamental linguistic operator, yet it remains inadequately modeled in vision-language generation systems. In this work, we present a formal treatment of linguistic negation in vision-language models by modeling it as a structured feasibility constraint on semantic guidance within diffusion dynamics. Rather than introducing heuristics or retraining model parameters, we reinterpret classifier-free guidance as defining a semantic update direction and enforce negation by projecting the update onto a convex constraint set derived from linguistic structure. This formulation provides a unified framework for handling diverse negation phenomena, including object absence, graded non-inversion semantics, multi-negation composition, and scope-sensitive disambiguation. Our approach is training-free, compatible with pretrained diffusion backbones, and defined on the classifier-free guidance update, which lets it operate over temporally evolving video trajectories. In addition, we introduce a structured negation-centric benchmark suite that isolates distinct linguistic failure modes in generative systems, to further research in this area. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves robust negation compliance while preserving visual fidelity and structural coherence, moving the treatment of linguistic negation in generative vision-language models beyond representation-level evaluation.
evidence_items.title: NEGATE: Constrained Semantic Guidance for Linguistic Negation in Text-to-Video Diffusion

evidence_items.summary: While large language models (LLMs) have captured global attention for their linguistic abilities, our work harnesses their power to overcome traditional barriers in querying Linked Data (LD) and Resource Description Framework (RDF) triplestores. This article presents an innovative framework that integrates LLMs into conversational user interfaces (UIs), enabling the dynamic generation of precise SPARQL queries without the necessity for constant retraining. Most conversational UI models struggle with adaptability as they require frequent retraining whenever datasets are updated or expanded. This limitation impedes their effectiveness as general-purpose extraction tools. To address this challenge, our approach 1 seamlessly incorporates LLMs into the conversational UI process, fostering a more sophisticated understanding and interpretation of user queries and enhancing overall responsiveness. By leveraging the advanced natural language processing capabilities of LLMs, our method improves RDF entity extraction in web systems that utilise conventional chatbots. Furthermore, it extends the functionality of these chatbots, allowing them to respond directly to queries based on the RDF schema while providing an assistive interface that deepens understanding of the dataset and its underlying domain. This facilitates the extraction of more meaningful information. By adopting this approach, interactions become more refined and context-sensitive, a crucial advancement for managing the intricate query structures commonly found in RDF datasets and Linked Open Data (LOD) endpoints. We have evaluated our approach in practical settings by assessing the tool’s ability to address complex queries and to answer general ecological queries, with the outputs evaluated by human experts. The results demonstrate a notable improvement in system expressiveness and response accuracy, showcasing the potential of LLMs to transform information retrieval.
evidence_items.title: Dialogue Meets Data: A Large Language Model Approach for Efficient Linked Data Retrieval

evidence_items.summary: Visual proxies decouple explicit world-state simulation from photorealistic video synthesis, offering a controllable interface for both offline clip creation and real-time interactive streaming. Yet a practical renderer must address two challenges. Upstream proxies vary from coarse layouts to fine articulated geometry depending on the interaction, and streaming inference must operate in a few causal steps without accumulating drift across self-generated history. We present Invoker-Render, pairing a bidirectional creation model with a causal four-step streaming model under a shared conditioning interface over structural proxies, an appearance reference, and language. Trained on an aligned approximately 200-hour multi-granularity corpus, Invoker-Render honors fine geometric constraints when supplied while synthesizing plausible local motion under coarse proxies, enabling runtime selection of input detail. To bridge bidirectional creation and real-time streaming without compounding step compression and rollout drift, we introduce Progressive Forcing (ProForcing). ProForcing first trains a causal predictor and distills it into a four-step renderer using histories derived from training videos. Training then shifts to continuous self-generated rollouts. A pipelined serving stack supports efficient streaming inference. Experiments show versatile control across proxy families, granularities, and camera paths, consistent gains over recent streaming baselines, and stable 30-minute racing rollouts that preserve scene and subject appearance.
evidence_items.title: Code World Model 2.0: Towards Infinite Controllable Video Generation

evidence_items.summary: State-of-the-art world models have been used to produce sequences of gameplay that accord with provided user-input actions. However, high quality, consistent gameplay generation often comes at the cost of inference speed, making real-time interactive play and ideation challenging. The substantial quantities of data used to train state-of-the-art models have also made custom training of these models appear impractical, limiting many of their potential uses in creative fields. In this work we demonstrate a major step towards efficient world models: achieving both fast high-quality inference, and improved data efficiency. This is done by replacing the next-token prediction paradigm with a two-stage discrete diffusion-based approach, introducing a lightweight refinement transformer which carries out iterative masked predictions. Building on an autoregressive world model capable of generating highly consistent and complex sequences over minutes (Kanervisto et al., 2025), we achieve substantial model speed-up (79x) with a modest quality trade-off. Additionally, we demonstrate that this model can be trained to reproduce high-quality, consistent gameplay using a dataset containing approximately one day (28 hours) of gameplay data. Our results demonstrate progress towards removing barriers to the use of world models in settings where real-time inference and data efficiency are essential.
evidence_items.title: Towards Data-Efficient, Real-Time World Models

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous avionics controllers must satisfy stringent real-time functional and performance require- ments even in the presence of run-time faults. In this paper, we analyze ROSACE, an open-source control engineering benchmark for flight control systems, focusing on its run-time resilience against faults such as sensor noise and sensor failures. We extend the benchmark with an FDIR (Fault Detection, Identification and Recovery) component based on Triple Modular Redundancy. Our approach builds upon COMPASTA, a tool for Model-Based Design developed on top of the TASTE tool by ESA. COMPASTA enables the modeling and injection of faults into a system's design. Moreover, it implements a simulation-based verification and validation workflow, automating the generation and execution of a set of test cases, based on a user-defined notion of coverage. Using COMPASTA, we construct a set of formal models, with faults and with FDIR, and we formally analyze their impact on the system properties. The analysis is based on the coupling of the formal models with the Simulink models used for the simulations.
evidence_items.title: Formal Analysis of a Fault-Tolerant Extension of the ROSACE Flight Controller

evidence_items.summary: Identity matching asks whether two records denote the same identity, yet the answer depends on the target granularity. Two records may match at the base level but not at the variant level: they share an underlying design while differing in attributes such as color or size. Final matching accuracy does not separately characterize the capabilities involved. To study this problem, we use e-commerce as a challenging real-world domain. We introduce PURE, a diagnostic benchmark for multi-granularity multimodal identity matching covering four capability dimensions: Perception, Understanding, Reasoning, and Evidence-grounded Judgment. The benchmark comprises 1,457 multiple-choice questions across 14 tasks, derived from real-world matching pairs and verified by two domain experts. Across ten recent MLLMs, overall scores range from 47.1% to 86.0%. Understanding receives the highest mean score and Judgment the lowest, with weaknesses in visual difference localization and variant-level rule judgment. Modality ablations show that models benefit from multimodal evidence but can incorrectly identify conflicts between matching records. In direct matching, most models recognize matching pairs more reliably than non-matching pairs at the base level, whereas the reverse holds at the variant level. PURE therefore reveals what aggregate matching accuracy hides: not only whether models judge a pair correctly, but where they struggle to interpret evidence and apply matching criteria.
evidence_items.title: PURE: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multi-Granularity Multimodal Identity Matching

evidence_items.summary: Safety is personal: the same action can be safe for one person but unsafe for another. Yet current guardrails judge content without considering who is affected. Using medication safety, we introduce \textit{patient-conditioned medication guarding}, which predicts a safety verdict and 17 risk categories from a patient profile and prescription. We release \textbf{MedGuardBench}, a drug-disjoint benchmark of 5{,}001 scenarios across 87 medications. We find that standard guardrails rely on surface cues, such as wording and profile presence, rather than patient facts. To address this, we develop \textit{personalized reasoning guardrails} with three components. \textbf{Personalized Reasoning Distillation} links risks to relevant patient fields. \textbf{Context Unrolling (CU)} makes models check each field themselves, reducing false alarms on most backbones; controls show that providing the check does not yield the same benefit. A \textbf{rule-based reward (guided GRPO)} improves unsafe recall and complex-risk detection, including allergies and adverse reactions, on some backbones, but increases false alarms on others. Our models outperform base models and matched no-profile controls in accuracy, while reducing false alarms relative to no-profile controls. Profile removal and swapping confirm that gains come from patient information, not fine-tuning alone.
evidence_items.title: MedGuardBench: A Patient-Oriented Benchmark for Personalized Guardrail Development

evidence_items.summary: Problem: When a party supports claims about a private dataset by disclosing a sample, auditors cannot tell whether it was drawn at random or"cherry-picked"to hide flaws in the rest of the data. Solution: The data holder commits to the hashes of every item in its dataset and registers the commitment with independent servers. Selection then waits on a decentralized randomness beacon: a network that jointly emits a fresh random value every few seconds, outside the control of the data holder and the auditors. The value emitted two beacon rounds after the commitment picks the sample. Each server returns a signed receipt, so anyone can later check that the revealed sample is exactly the one that value prescribes. Selection from the committed set stays unbiased as long as the beacon's threshold holds and one required server is honest, and a pre-agreed name, checked with the servers, stops repeated or abandoned draws. We call this protocol NoCherry. Applications: Any audit that spot-checks a private corpus: private AI benchmarks and held-out test sets, dataset quality claims, code and security audits, test-fairness review, vulnerability handling, and compliance sampling. Auditors need not trust the data holder to hand over a representative sample of the committed data, since the protocol proves it, and data holders need not expose their entire dataset.
evidence_items.title: Verifiable Random Sampling of Private Data Without a Trusted Single Party

evidence_items.summary: Safety benchmarks for computer-use agents (CUAs) place the harm either in the intent of the task or on a single screen: a malicious instruction, an injected command, a phishing page. An agent that checks the task and each screen in isolation can pass them, so they do not test whether it combines facts seen on different screens. Yet in delegated work, harm often arises exactly this way: a fact about a person on one screen, a fact about an item on another, and a legitimate task that binds them. We introduce SEAM (Safety Execution Across Multiple screens), a benchmark of such cross-screen compositional harm: 600 multi-step, cross-application OSWorld tasks in which the instruction and every single observation are benign and only their combination is harmful. Minimal-pair variants that differ in one place, scored from the server log rather than by an LLM judge, locate where an agent fails. General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents carry out the harm in up to 92% of runs, yet decline when the user states it in one sentence. Agents open the decisive pages, so exposure is not the primary bottleneck. Asked about those pages, they flag the harm, and with thinking they often write the conflict into their reasoning and confirm anyway. Safety recognition thus does not reliably translate into safe execution, and the translation depends on the information channel: the same warning stops agents far more often in the user's instruction than on screen. Proprietary models are markedly more cautious. We release SEAM with its generator and quality gates at https://yuxuan2003.github.io/SEAM/ .
evidence_items.title: SEAM: Computer-Use Agents Know the Harm Between Screens, and Commit It Anyway

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents make videos by writing and refining programs in a build--inspect--edit loop. A finished film costs a median of $2.85 in model calls and 11 minutes, over a third of that time in builds that block the agent. We find that much of this time is avoidable, for two reasons. First, 37.5% of the frames of a session's later films were drawn before, many shifted in time or inside an edited scene. Second, half of the builds stop at a check, where the agent needs only the verdict, but which builds stop is unknown until the checks finish. We present CodeReel, a training-free execution layer behind agents' existing commands. Exact frame reuse keys each frame by its drawing commands, regardless of its position in time, and reuses each frame whose key recurs. Blocking-aware scheduling runs the checks first and starts the render alongside them, at idle priority, unless the session's recent builds make a pass unlikely. Scheduling spends CPU to answer sooner and reuse returns it; exact keys let later versions use frames rendered for a failed one as the agent thinks. We introduce EditLoop, a benchmark of replayable agent sessions whose films are checked against renders from scratch. On it, CodeReel cuts the agent's wait by 36.3% against Rebuild, a warm pipeline with parallel rendering, and by 57.9% against Sequential, today's step-by-step pipeline. On time-shifting edits its reuse renders 43.9%, close to the 43.0% whose pixels are new, while Manim-style caching renders 99.8%. With real agents, the median wait per build is 0.62x Rebuild's in Claude Code, on topics never used in development, and 0.67x in Codex CLI. The gain holds for five models and two frameworks.
evidence_items.title: CodeReel: Accelerating Code-to-Video Agents with Exact Frame Reuse and Blocking-Aware Scheduling

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the paper “Seeing is Believing: The Case for Hardware-Centric Inefficiency Detection and Remediation,” published in the ACM Symposium on Cloud Computing (SoCC 2026). It provides the evaluation data for Unveil, a hardware-centric observability framework designed to detect, identify, and remediate silent performance inefficiencies in machine learning workloads. Unveil operates using host-visible telemetry without requiring guest-side instrumentation or modifications to applications and their software environments. The dataset covers controlled microbenchmarks and large language model (LLM) serving workloads, including experiments involving NUMA misplacement, interrupt locality issues, reduced transparent huge-page coverage, and GPU power throttling. It includes hardware telemetry traces, anomaly detection results, inefficiency fingerprints, performance measurements, and supporting data for reproducing the evaluation presented in the paper. The dataset is intended to facilitate reproducibility and further research into hardware-centric observability, online anomaly detection, inefficiency fingerprinting, and performance diagnosis in machine learning systems. A detailed description of the dataset structure, file formats, and correspondence to the paper's evaluation is provided in the accompanying README. Associated Publication Ziji Chen, Steven W. D. Chien, Peng Qian, and Noa Zilberman. 2026. Seeing is Believing: The Case for Hardware-Centric Inefficiency Detection and Remediation. ACM Symposium on Cloud Computing, Volume 2 (SoCC 2026). DOI: https://doi.org/10.1145/3828161.3857898

evidence_items.summary: Text simplification has been a long-standing research topic to make complex information more accessible to a wider audience, yet high-performance Large Language Model (LLM) fine-tuning remains computationally expensive. This research proposes a cost-effective alternative: a multi-agent framework utilizing Small Language Models (SLMs) to achieve high-fidelity simplification for educational knowledge management. Our methodology frames simplification as an iterative, multi-stage reasoning process rather than a single-step transformation. Specialized agents perform sequential semantic analysis, linguistic simplification, and factual verification to minimize information loss and ensure interpretability. To validate the framework, we applied the system to a scientific corpus regarding Robotic Mobile Fulfilment Systems (RMFS). Performance was evaluated using BERTScore, SARI, and Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level across three SLM backbones (Llama3.2 3B, Gemma3 4B, and Qwen3 4B). Results show that the multi-agent pipeline consistently outperforms zero-shot baselines in edit quality, with Qwen 3 achieving SARI of 51.82 while maintaining strong semantic fidelity (BERTScore up to 0.94). The contributions of this work are twofold: (1) a novel, iterative SLM-based multi-agent architecture for scientific text simplification; and (2) a domain-specific RMFS dataset featuring simplifications validated by both human expert and LLM judges with substantial inter-rater agreement (κ = 0.703).
evidence_items.title: Minimal Lossiness Agentic AI for Scientific Text Simplification Leveraging Multi-Agent SLMs for Effective Knowledge Transfer

evidence_items.summary: Large language models read Thai through subword tokens, without a word segmenter. Yet Thai treebanks, speech metrics and morphological resources are built on words, often at several granularities, and word boundaries resolve ambiguities that subword tokens leave open. LATTE (Lattice ATTentive Encoding) reads a text at several granularities at once, through a lattice of dictionary words, but it is a large GPU model. We distil it into LATTE-WordSeg-Lite, a CPU segmenter of 1.17M parameters that keeps the lattice as features. It outputs compounds, words and morphemes in one pass, and learns only from annotated data and text whose licences allow commercial use. To compare it with other tools, published Thai scores do not suffice, as they come from different files, splits and scorers. We therefore rebuild seven test sets from pinned sources and score twelve systems under one protocol. With the unit that fits each test set, LATTE-WordSeg-Lite scores above DeepCut on five sets, four of them from corpora that its teachers learnt from. Called line by line on one CPU thread, it runs 23 times as fast as DeepCut. We release the model, the benchmark scripts and all predictions.
evidence_items.title: LATTE-WordSeg-Lite: Multi-Granularity Thai Word Segmentation on a CPU, with a Reproducible Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: The same molecule can be expressed in multiple, syntactically distinct representations, yet it remains unclear whether large language models (LLMs) can recognize and relate these equivalent encodings. We introduce MolReps, a pipeline that generates 9,600 question-answer pairs across ten representations for conversion, normalization, and 2D structure recognition. Post-training on MolReps improves text-only and multimodal models, MolQwen3-4B-Instruct (MQ3-4B-I) and MolQwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (MQ3-VL-4B-I), from $4.01\%$ to $75.13\%$ and from $7.11\%$ to $73.14\%$ (InChIKey match) on the molecule-overlap test set, respectively. On the molecule-disjoint test set, post-training increased validity from $20.35\%$ to $58.12\%$ for MQ3-4B-I and from $17.19\%$ to $59.34\%$ for MQ3-VL-4B-I. However, InChIKey match remained low, decreasing from $3.86\%$ to $3.09\%$ and from $6.44\%$ to $2.29\%$, respectively. Furthermore, the resulting models achieve a relative $27.84\%$ improvement in average over their base model on MolRepBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating molecular property prediction. These results show the effectiveness of targeted post-training for enhancing molecular representation understanding and its potential to improve downstream molecular tasks.
evidence_items.title: MolReps: Taking SELFIES, Making SMILES, Teaching LLMs

evidence_items.summary: As artificial intelligence becomes deeply integrated into our daily lives, designing truly inclusive Human-Agent Interaction (HAI) is an urgent societal imperative. Historically, HAI research has been heavily skewed towards hearing-centric spoken dialogue systems, often marginalizing Deaf and hard-of-hearing users. The SignHAI 2026 workshop challenges this paradigm by shifting the research focus from isolated sign language recognition to dynamic, multimodal sign language dialogue. We emphasize the critical role of non-verbal conversational dynamics, specifically turn-taking, in facilitating seamless human-agent interactions. A core feature of this workshop is a “semi-competition” addressing the challenge of turn-taking prediction in Sign language dialogue, supported by the release of a newly annotated dataset built upon the Japanese sign language (JSL) corpus. Alongside the challenge track, a general track will explore broader topics in non-verbal behaviors in visual dialogue, and inclusive agent design. By bridging HAI researchers, multimodal AI experts, and the Deaf community, SignHAI 2026 aims to establish new technological baselines, provide crucial benchmark resources, and set a strategic roadmap for the next generation of inclusive multimodal dialogue foundation models.
evidence_items.title: SignHAI 2026: Moving Towards Inclusive Sign Language Dialogue and Turn-taking

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to interpret, generate, and mediate public-facing language, which makes their reliability especially consequential in politically sensitive settings. Although sentiment analysis is a common task in this area, affective meaning in social media discourse is often conveyed through culturally situated and pragmatically indirect cues that are not well captured by label-centric evaluation alone. In this paper, we evaluate the robustness of LLMs for sentiment analysis of Spanish political discourse from social media, with emphasis on culturally situated affective interpretation. We introduce a diagnostic protocol that combines three independent human annotation views into Gold and Ambiguous subsets, and extends the corpus with a Synthetic subset built from sentiment-flipped counterfactuals selected through model-conditioned perplexity and LLM-as-a-judge criteria. Using this framework, we compare proprietary and open-weight models under zero-shot and few-shot prompting, focusing on predictive robustness across human agreement conditions and counterfactual shift. Our results show that annotation ambiguity and counterfactual perturbation reveal failure modes that conventional evaluation on the original corpus tends to obscure. GPT-4.1-mini remains the most stable among the evaluated models, whereas the two smaller open-weight models degrade more markedly under synthetic perturbations, and few-shot prompting provides only limited gains. Overall, the paper contributes a reproducible protocol for robustness-oriented evaluation in political sentiment analysis, an empirical characterization of model behavior under ambiguity and sentiment-flipped counterfactuals, and a publicly available Spanish social media dataset with three-way human sentiment annotations.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Cultural Reasoning and Robustness in LLMs for Spanish Political Discourse

evidence_items.summary: Sensitive peptide identification is fundamental to protein characterization and novel protein discovery, for which de novo peptide sequencing (DNPS) from tandem mass spectra provides an important database-independent approach. Although deep learning has substantially advanced de novo sequencing, existing models are predominantly trained on high-confidence peptide-spectrum matches obtained through database search. This search-conditioned supervision excludes a large fraction of unidentified spectra, creating a distribution mismatch between the selectively labeled training data and the complete spectrum stream encountered at inference time, thereby limiting peptide identification performance. To address this challenge, we propose SemiNovo, a semi-supervised framework that learns jointly from identified and unlabeled spectra. SemiNovo first constructs DarkSpec, a large-scale quality-controlled corpus of unlabeled spectra collected from diverse public proteomics projects, thereby extending training beyond search-identified spectra and mitigating the resulting shift in DNPS supervision. It then combines stepwise mass-constrained autoregressive decoding with cumulative path confidence to derive reliable supervision from unlabeled spectra. Moreover, SemiNovo introduces head-wise chemical-evidence gating to improve spectral evidence aggregation under noisy and incomplete fragmentation. Experiments show that SemiNovo performs favorably against state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks. Code and dataset are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: SemiNovo: Learning Beyond Search-Identified Spectra for De Novo Peptide Sequencing

evidence_items.summary: Scientific machine learning has opened new avenues for solving parameterized partial differential equations (PDEs), enabling models to learn a family of PDEs and generalize to unseen instances. In this context, data-driven operator learning methods typically require large training datasets, while physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) suffer from difficult optimization and limited generalization, especially for nonlinear PDEs. We propose Newton-PINet, a physics-informed network enhanced by Newton linearization, offering an effective meta-learning framework for nonlinear PDEs. Newton-PINet (i) employs a physics-informed multilayer network with skip connections, where the output-layer weights are solved by least squares; (ii) adopts a two-stage learning strategy that first leverages gradient-based training to learn robust representations from the available training tasks, and then performs gradient-free fine-tuning on the output layer for fast task-specific generalization; and (iii) incorporates a Newton linearization method to speed up the least-squares iteration for nonlinear PDE problems. On a challenging nonlinear reaction-diffusion benchmark, Newton-PINet achieves up to three orders of magnitude lower relative error than recent neural solvers, while using 16x fewer training tasks and over an order of magnitude less training time (about 5 minutes versus several hours). This work advances the meta-learning of PINNs toward data-efficient, fast, and generalizable physics solvers. The code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/fycAIwj/Newton-PINet.
evidence_items.title: Newton-PINet: A fast physics-informed neural network with Newton linearization for meta-learning nonlinear PDEs

evidence_items.summary: Benchmark contamination is not new, but recent model releases show it in a sharper form. We use the term benchleaking for the case in which a benchmark's own test examples enter training data, so that a score reflects recall rather than capability. This differs from benchmaxxing, which optimizes toward a benchmark without seeing its test set. We document two escalations over the past month. First, in post-training, the traces have become explicit: recent audits show an agent stating hidden test requirements it was never given in 23% of its attempts, where its predecessor did so in none, and continuing to follow them after the task is changed to contradict them (Schaeffer and R\"auker, 2026; Lo and Lo, 2026). Second, the problem has reached pre-training. Using few-shot continuation on 20 benchmarks across four public base models, we find that some base models write out other test examples---complete questions, options, and answers---that appear nowhere in their input. For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers, against 9% and none for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. To quantify what a reported score owes to such examples, we define an Anti-Hack score: the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked wrong and the number of examples unchanged. Averaged over the suite, it costs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base 1.5 points and Hy3-preview-Base 1.3, against 5.0 for MiMo-V2.5-Base and 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base. Open base models are the foundation of much downstream research, so benchleaking now affects more than leaderboard rankings. We call for decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted scores to become standard practice.
evidence_items.title: Benchleaking Is Accelerating: Benchmark contamination has worsened sharply in the past month -- from post-training down to pre-training base models

evidence_items.summary: Fuel adulteration risks operational reliability in defence supply chains, yet chemically similar adulterants can escape routine quality testing. The review analyses separation detection methods of diesel adulteration, particularly kerosene blending, including methods of comparing laboratory benchmarks with portable separations, spectroscopy and sensor alternatives. Atmospheric distillation and gas chromatography simulated distillation explore the volatility distributions but are limited in providing adulterant identity. Detailed compositional information is a result of Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and two-dimensional gas chromatography; however, enhanced profiling does not necessarily establish improved adulteration detection. Similarly, microfabricated gas chromatography offers portable field screening, while infrared spectroscopy and electronic noses enable model-assisted assessments. Chemometrics, machine learning and distillation aid interpretation; contrarily performance relies on calibration coverage and validation conditions. The gap principle is an inadequate validation across independent fuel batches, authorised blends and operational environments. Priority future research focuses on laboratory benchmarking, assessments of uncertainty, false-negative reporting and realistic field trials. We propose rapid screening with laboratory separation methods to investigate samples, whilst checking their origin and handling procedures. Meeting fuel specifications does not guarantee a fuel is unadulterated, and differences in composition do not necessarily indicate deliberate tampering.
evidence_items.title: Separation-Based Detection of Fuel Adulteration in Defence Supply Chains: Benchmark Methods, Sensor Alternatives, and the Field-Deployment Gap

evidence_items.summary: This study compares mBERT and MuRIL for binary harmful-speech classification across three Hindi-English/Hinglish dataset settings: a Kaggle Hinglish hate subset, a code-mixed offensive-language dataset, and THAR targeted religious hate. Matched multi-seed experiments show that model performance varies substantially across datasets: mBERT performs better on some settings, while MuRIL performs better on THAR. Cross-dataset evaluation, TF-IDF baselines, and mixed-training experiments suggest that label definitions, platform, topic, and script mix materially affect model behavior. The results therefore do not support a universal claim that either mBERT or MuRIL is superior for Hinglish harmful-speech detection; instead, they highlight the importance of dataset choice and cross-dataset robustness when evaluating multilingual harmful-speech classifiers.

evidence_items.summary: Visual artifact tasks test agents' ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs. Evaluation across artifact families helps distinguish broadly applicable authoring capabilities from strengths confined to a particular medium. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Each task specifies authoring objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables. Existing benchmarks provide limited support for systematically evaluating how authoring choices suit different audiences, purposes, and media across artifact families. VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulfillment verifies explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Task-specific rating anchors instantiate shared criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in source materials and artifact inspection records. We evaluate nine model-harness configurations on all 211 tasks. Overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance accounting for 73.4% of the gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring configurations.
evidence_items.title: VisualArtifactSpec 1.0: Evaluating Visual Artifacts under Task Specifications

evidence_items.summary: Asynchronous reinforcement learning increases training throughput, but data from stale policies and numerical mismatch between training and inference can destabilize learning. To stabilize off-policy learning, score centering (SC) removes the effect of reward baselines on the expected update. Our gradient diagnostics show less extreme gradients with SC than with importance sampling (IS), but SC can still fail when the learner moves far from the behavior policy that generated the data. To limit this policy mismatch, we introduce Regularized Score Centering (RSC), which adds a reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty to encourage the learner's next-token distribution to stay close to the behavior policy's next-token distribution. RSC works with or without truncated importance sampling (TIS), which caps token importance weights. Our theoretical analysis supports this approach, showing that KL regularization improves convergence guarantees. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts models on mathematical reasoning and agentic tasks, including online shopping, tool use, games, and fully asynchronous software engineering. RSC with TIS substantially improves sample efficiency across all agentic benchmarks, attaining higher training rewards with the same number of sampled responses. In final evaluations, it achieves top performance across all six agentic tasks, improving by 14.3% on AppWorld and reaching 9.9 times the strongest baseline's score on BabyAI.
evidence_items.title: Regularized Score Centering

evidence_items.summary: Visual agents answer questions about ultra-high-resolution photos by zooming into the relevant regions. However, existing agents often answer from common sense instead of reading the evidence. Reinforcement learning (RL) on the final answer cannot correct this, because a guess earns the same reward as reading. We propose Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization (CrossRPO), which trains agents on contrast sets. A contrast set asks one question about several versions of an image that differ only in a small region with the evidence and have different answers, so only reading the evidence solves the whole set. CrossRPO rewards solving the whole set, and we prove that it does not reinforce a set answered from common sense. We build contrast sets for training (ViRA-Train) and evaluation (ViRA-Bench) by editing one small object in images of 21 to 120 megapixels, and we photograph further sets with real changes (ViRA-Bench-Real) to exclude editing traces. We train two Visual Reasoning Agents, ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B, with CrossRPO on only about 3,500 items of ViRA-Train each. CrossRPO achieves 63.3% set accuracy on ViRA-Bench at the maximum resolution, against 59.3% for GRPO. ViRA-9B is the most accurate open model of its size on all benchmarks, and ViRA-27B outperforms Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6-Luna, both at their highest thinking level, on most benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: ViRA: Toward Ultra-High-Resolution Visual Agents via Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Application optimization requires coding agents to discover useful changes and coordinate them across a complete program while preserving the required computation. We introduce Accelerate Bench, a benchmark of 32 CPU optimization tasks adapted from scientific applications and supercomputing competitions. Each task provides a working program and specifies the workload, correctness requirements, timing boundaries, and permitted edits, leaving agents to choose where and how to optimize. Public testing supports iterative development, and a separate verifier scores the final submission. On benchmark version 1.1, we evaluate 16 coding agents, each pairing a model with a harness. Their Score@1 ranges from 25.5% to 67.4%. Most of their programs are correct, and the size of the speedup separates them: the two leading agents are at least 2x faster on 22 or more of the 32 tasks, while the other fourteen reach 2x on 8 to 17 and leave 125 of their 412 correct outcomes below 1.25x. Controlled replays show why coordination across an application matters: identical source code runs between 0.29x and 2.12x depending only on build and runtime settings, and one code change is worth 1.01x or 6.4x depending on another. Accelerate Bench pairs executable workloads with agents' programs and trajectories to evaluate both their gains and the process behind them.
evidence_items.title: Accelerate Bench: Evaluating Agents for Application-Level Program Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) lets the model act on what it sees by invoking external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporating returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Answering: Learning to Speak First and Act in Streaming Video

evidence_items.summary: A coding agent working within a software organization must establish what to build, collaborate with colleagues, and verify what it delivers. We introduce SWE-CoWork, a benchmark comprising 101 development assignments across 101 real repositories, 11 programming languages, and 12 application domains. Each assignment places an agent in a simulated engineering organization with 26 colleagues who have distinct responsibilities, bounded knowledge, and controlled collaboration behavior. Starting from a brief handoff, agents must recover requirements distributed across colleagues and workplace records, reconcile conflicting evidence, and implement changes evaluated by private executable tests. We evaluate eleven models and find a substantial gap between partial implementation and complete task delivery. The two leading models satisfy approximately 63% of fail-to-pass (F2P) tests but complete fewer than 8% of assignments. Providing complete requirements upfront improves F2P by approximately 16 percentage points for Seed Evolving and GPT-6 Astra, yet leaves complete task success unchanged. Requirement-level trajectory analysis reveals failures throughout the delivery process: Claude-Opus-5.5 directs a mean of 93% of first questions about queried cards to their accountable owners across runs but obtains only 64% of colleague-held requirements. Deferred questions go unfollowed, implementations remain incomplete even after requirements are acquired, and 31% of requirements reported as completed fail their tests. These findings highlight sustained requirement tracking, from clarification through implementation, verification, and handoff, as a key challenge for reliable autonomous software engineering.
evidence_items.title: SWE-CoWork: Benchmarking Coding Agents as Digital Employees in Organizations

evidence_items.summary: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.
evidence_items.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs

evidence_items.summary: Harness optimization is often studied with a fixed policy model and benchmark. When either changes, the optimizer must decide which parts of an evolved harness to reuse or revise, but the harness alone may not explain why earlier edits were made or how they performed. In this work, we study Continual Recursive Self-Improvement (CRSI), a setting for continuing existing harness-optimization methods across compatible benchmarks or policy models. We propose Self-Improvement Memory (SIM) for the harness optimizer, rather than the task-solving policy. SIM groups edits by recurring harness problem and records their rationale, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation context. New attempts extend this history as optimization continues. In our experiments across four domains, SIM achieves higher final scores than harness-only and root-cause-only continuation in cross-dataset and pairwise cross-model comparisons. Across ten independent source runs in coding, paired continuations with SIM improve final scores by an average of 2.36 points over harness-only continuation (p=0.003).
evidence_items.title: Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement

evidence_items.summary: In many long-horizon settings, an agent's own choices create future constraints: committing finite capacity establishes future obligations and forecloses later opportunities. Sustaining performance therefore requires both keeping evolving plans feasible and comparing the value of resource allocations with the alternatives they displace. Recent benchmarks increasingly evaluate LLM agents in continuing operations, but give less attention to how agents keep their own commitments feasible while reassessing resource allocations as opportunities change. We introduce OutfitterBench, where agents manage an outdoor-equipment rental business for 200 days, purchasing from a 46-product catalog and handling roughly 1,100 reservation requests. Under a fixed capital ceiling, reservations and uncertain walk-in demand compete for reusable equipment whose availability changes over time. Experiments with seven frontier LLMs show that several agents underperform a simple rule-based baseline, while only the leading agent consistently surpasses it. Trajectory analysis shows that some agents apply known constraints inconsistently and make new decisions that conflict with existing commitments. Agents with more reliable fulfillment can still secure low returns from comparable commitments or delay resource reallocation. The leading agent better connects preparation with economic choices but also misses opportunities for more profitable asset use. These findings highlight limitations in sustaining coherent resource plans and reassessing their value over time. The benchmark code is publicly available at https://github.com/adminblackjack/OutfitterBench.
evidence_items.title: OutfitterBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Resource Allocation and Commitment Coordination

evidence_items.summary: As AI conference submissions grow rapidly, AI reviewers are being considered as an alternative. However, simply imitating human reviewing is problematic because reviewing serves multiple purposes, including evaluating papers' soundness, interestingness, and clarity, the last two of which are subjective. In this work, we focus solely on evaluating soundness, the most important and objective criterion, and define the learning objective as jointly maximizing (1) precision, based on the soundness and substantiveness of review points, and (2) recall, the coverage of high-quality reference review points. Under this problem formulation, we construct a quality-labeled review point dataset, PaperSound-23K, using 1K ICLR submissions and 23K human-written and LLM-generated review points. Using this dataset, we train an AI reviewer model, PaperCritic, through reinforcement learning with the F1 score of precision and recall as the reward. Our experiments show that PaperCritic outperforms frontier models and models trained with other AI reviewer training methods on an in-domain test set. Surprisingly, learning to review ICLR submissions also transfers to reviewing Nature-family papers and even to out-of-domain reviewing tasks (e.g., code review, legal contract review, and feedback on story writing).
evidence_items.title: PaperCritic: Training AI Reviewers to Assess the Soundness of Papers

evidence_items.summary: Electronic nose (eNose) technology offers a portable, non-invasive route for disease screening via exhaled breath analysis. However, progress in the field is hindered by the lack of systematic benchmarks that compare machine learning methods under realistic conditions, particularly sensor drift, a known but rarely quantified failure mode. Most existing studies rely on small, private datasets with inconsistent protocols, rendering results non-comparable and slowing progress. We introduce Breath-Dx, the first comprehensive benchmark of time series classification methods for breath-based disease screening. Our work leverages the Scent of Health (S-OH) dataset, the largest public clinical eNose collection to date, comprising 1,234 patients across nine diagnostic groups, each providing a 17-channel multivariate time series with explicit temporal train/test splits that account for sensor drift. We systematically evaluate 10 methods spanning four families: feature-based tabular learners, convolution-based models, graph-based, and time series architectures. All methods degrade significantly under temporal validation (0.05-0.12 AUC drop compared to random cross-validation), confirming that drift embeds a strong temporal signal. Under this realistic evaluation, the best methods achieve ROC AUC of 0.74-0.76 for some lung conditions, though others remain near chance. Recurrent architectures show the most consistent performance across diseases, while specialized time series methods achieve the highest peak results. Demographic confounders matter: breath signals provide independent diagnostic value for some conditions but add little beyond age for others. We release the S-OH dataset, all temporal splits, evaluation protocols, and code to enable reproducible research and accelerate progress in clinical breathomics.
evidence_items.title: Breath-Dx: A Time Series Classification Benchmark for Disease Screening with eNose

evidence_items.summary: Long-range Saharan dust transport affects radiation, clouds, and air quality, yet its vertical structure and entrainment into the boundary layer remain challenging to simulate. We investigate four contrasting dust events over southwestern Germany using ground-based lidar, sun-photometer and in situ aerosol measurements, satellite observations, backward trajectories, and ICON-ART simulations. The events represent diverse atmospheric conditions, including a six-day cloud-free 5 episode, a cloudy episode involving dust–cloud interactions, and an intense outbreak with aerosol optical depth approaching 1.4. A depolarization-based lidar method separated dust backscatter from contributions by other aerosols, enabling a like-forlike evaluation of the dust represented by ICON-ART and providing a useful approach for evaluating dust models in mixed aerosol layers. ICON-ART reproduced the large-scale transport and arrival of the dust layers, with mean differences of approximately 20 min in arrival time and 50 m in layer height. Daily re-initialization of the global simulations improved correlations 10 with observed near-surface particulate matter concentrations from 0.65–0.69 to 0.86–0.88 and better reproduced the timing and persistence of boundary-layer dust. The benefits of higher resolution (2 and 1 km) become more apparent when combined with model reinitialization. However, ICON-ART consistently overestimated particles of 0.5–2 μm and underestimated particles larger than 2 μm. These results demonstrate the complementary benefits of accurate meteorological initialization and convection-permitting resolution while identifying size-dependent emission, sedimentation, and deposition as priorities for 15 model development. By distinguishing errors in dust transport from those arising from aerosol size representation, this study provides an observation-constrained framework for evaluating and improving convection-permitting dust forecasts.
evidence_items.title: Dataset: Saharan dust transport and boundary layer entrainment over Western Europe: multi-instrument observations and convection-permitting model evaluation

evidence_items.summary: README Contextualization  This repository contains the anonymized dataset used in the data report entitled "Communication, education, and health for the sustainability of Brazil's National Health System: data report on the COVID-19 learning pathway of the AVASUS platform." The data report structures, describes, and makes publicly available records from the 24 courses that constitute the COVID-19 learning pathway of the Virtual Learning Environment of the Brazilian National Health System (AVASUS), a national technology-mediated education platform developed by the Laboratory for Technological Innovation in Health (LAIS) at the Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte (UFRN), in cooperation with Brazil's Ministry of Health. The dataset comprises 490,821 enrollments from 253,986 course participants, recorded between March 6, 2020, and December 31, 2025. Primary data were extracted from AVASUS and integrated with three official secondary sources: the National Register of Health Facilities (CNES), the Brazilian Classification of Occupations (CBO), and the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE). The repository is organized to support transparency, reproducibility, and reuse. All attributes that could identify course participants, or minimally enable their tracing, were removed.
