evidence_items.summary: Frame-wise indoor mobile LiDAR dataset to support research on semantic segmentation of indoor 3D point clouds. The dataset was collected in the ITC building (Langezijds) at the University of Twente. Data acquisition was conducted outside working hours to avoid the presence of people. The scanned areas include classrooms, corridors, meeting rooms, shared offices, and study areas. Private offices, restricted laboratories, server rooms, and control rooms are excluded. The dataset contains 52 indoor sequences, 79,108 frame-wise MLS point clouds, and 1.23 billion labeled points covering 16 semantic classes. The labeled point clouds are stored in binary format, with (x, y, z), intensity, and semantic label recorded for each point. Both the original LiDAR-frame and gravity-aligned coordinate representations are provided. Synchronized and undistorted RGB images are stored in .png format with a resolution of (1280 x 1024) pixels. The RGB images were used to assist the semantic annotation process and can also support research on 2D–3D cross-modal semantic segmentation. During dataset construction, BIM data of the building were used to assist the annotation process. However, the BIM data are not included in the released dataset. The dataset is publicly released to support research on frame-wise indoor MLS semantic segmentation and related indoor 3D scene understanding tasks.
evidence_items.title: Data underlying the article: Semantic-ITC: A Frame-wise Indoor Mobile Laser Scanning Dataset and Benchmark for Semantic Segmentation

evidence_items.summary: Background Effective patient education is essential in pediatric neurology but challenged by time constraints and variable health literacy. Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential solution, yet their accuracy and safety in this specialized field remain incompletely evaluated. Methods In a prospective, blinded benchmarking study, LLM-generated responses to ten standardized pediatric neurology prompts were evaluated. Responses were assessed for factual accuracy, safety, and perceived usability; the study did not assess real-world clinical decision support or caregiver comprehension. A blinded panel of seven consultant pediatric neurology evaluators assessed the outputs using an expert-developed rubric measuring factual accuracy, safety, clinical appropriateness, and usability. The unit of analysis was the scenario-model pair ( n = 40), with median scores across raters used for primary comparisons. Results Linear mixed-effects models revealed significant performance variation across models (F(3,27) = 8.76, p &lt; 0.001). DeepSeek achieved the highest overall composite score (4.01 ± 0.61) and zero safety flags. ChatGPT scored moderately (3.72 ± 0.75) but accounted for most safety issues (5/8), including a contraindicated medication recommendation. Gemini and Perplexity scored lower (3.45 ± 0.77 and 3.38 ± 0.71). The overall composite difference between DeepSeek and ChatGPT was not statistically significant ( p = 0.087). DeepSeek had the highest System Usability Scale score (74.2/100). Presence of any consensus safety flag drastically reduced the odds of expert approval for caregiver-facing use after clinician review (OR: 0.08, p &lt; 0.001). Conclusions DeepSeek produced no consensus safety flags in this benchmark and had the highest expert-rated usability score, but its overall composite score was not statistically different from ChatGPT.
evidence_items.title: Comparative benchmark of four selected large language models for generating patient education content in pediatric neurology: a prospective study

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly accessible to patients with cancer as sources of immediate information about diet, symptoms, supplements, and treatment-related nutritional concerns. Their conversational fluency may create an illusion of clinical adequacy: a response can be well written, plausible, and apparently personalized while remaining incomplete, poorly contextualized, or clinically unsafe. This problem is particularly relevant in oncology nutrition, where advice about restrictive diets, fasting, supplements, malnutrition, sarcopenia, cachexia, and treatment tolerance may have direct implications for patient safety. Existing approaches to evaluating LLM-generated health information use heterogeneous criteria, including accuracy, completeness, readability, usefulness, personalization, evidence support, trust, safety, and potential harm. Classical instruments such as DISCERN, the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool, and the JAMA benchmarks address selected dimensions of health information quality, whereas contemporary LLM-specific frameworks increasingly account for conversational, clinical, and safety-related features. However, these approaches are not specifically designed for oncology nutrition and do not consistently operationalize a non-compensatory logic in which clinically serious safety concerns are assessed separately from otherwise favorable response qualities. We propose a conceptual and operational framework for evaluating patient-facing LLM-generated oncology nutrition responses. The framework treats scientific, clinical, and nutritional appropriateness; clinical and nutritional safety; communication quality and patient utility; transparency; and system-level robustness as conceptually distinct and non-substitutable evaluation dimensions. It also introduces critical safety flags intended to identify veto-level concerns that should not be averaged with favorable performance in other domains.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating large language model-generated oncology nutrition responses: a conceptual framework and validation roadmap

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language model (LLM)-based chatbots are increasingly used for health information, but their suitability for melanoma public education requires evaluation across accuracy, information quality, transparency, and readability. Methods We compared ChatGPT-5.6, DeepSeek-V4, Claude Sonnet 5, and Gemini 3.5 Flash. Validity was assessed using 200 melanoma-related single-best-answer multiple-choice questions administered in three independent trials. Fifteen core public-education questions were developed from worldwide Google Trends data and clinical experience. Responses were evaluated using DISCERN, EQIP, GQS, and JAMA benchmarks, and readability was assessed using ARI, Coleman–Liau, FKGL, FRES, GFI, and SMOG indices. Results Mean MCQ accuracy was highest for ChatGPT-5.6 (94.0% ± 0.5%), followed by Gemini 3.5 Flash (92.5% ± 1.3%), Claude Sonnet 5 (87.2% ± 1.4%), and DeepSeek-V4 (79.3% ± 0.3%; p &lt; 0.001). ChatGPT-5.6 achieved the highest DISCERN (52.07 ± 9.48), EQIP (81.67 ± 4.08), and GQS (4.40 ± 0.51) scores. JAMA transparency scores were low across models. Gemini 3.5 Flash showed the most favorable overall readability profile; however, mean grade-level indices for all models exceeded the sixth-grade benchmark, and all mean FRES scores were below the recommended range. Conclusion Current LLM chatbots show substantial potential for melanoma education, but performance varies across validity, quality, transparency, and readability. Their use should remain supplementary, with improved source transparency and health-literacy–appropriate language required before broader patient-facing implementation.
evidence_items.title: Validity, reliability, and readability of large language model chatbots for melanoma public education: a cross-sectional comparative study

evidence_items.summary: Patients are increasingly consulting large language model (LLM) platforms for information regarding aesthetic dental procedures prior to clinical appointments. This study evaluated the quality, safety, and readability of responses produced by ChatGPT, Gemini, and Meta AI in relation to patient-derived questions. Forty-two patient-derived questions regarding tooth whitening, resin infiltration, composite bonding, and porcelain veneers were presented to each platform. Two calibrated evaluators independently assessed all 126 responses using a five-domain Primary Quality Rubric, a five-item Modified DISCERN tool, and the Global Quality Score (GQS). The Flesch Reading Ease Score (FRES) and Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL) were utilized to evaluate readability and comprehension. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using weighted Cohen’s kappa, while between-group differences were evaluated using the Friedman test for repeated measures, followed by paired post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Bonferroni correction. Initial independent inter-rater reliability was slight (pre-consensus kappa varied from 0.011 to 0.191); all subsequent scoring disagreements were successfully resolved through structured consensus discussion. There were no significant differences in accuracy and patient-centeredness among platforms (p = 0.292 and p = 0.071, respectively). Significant differences were identified for Rubric Total (Chi2_F(2) = 20.383, p < 0.001), Modified DISCERN total (Chi2 F(2) = 30.160, p < 0.001), and GQS (Chi2 F(2) = 18.978, p < 0.001). Post-hoc analysis revealed that ChatGPT’s scores were significantly lower than both Gemini and Meta AI on Rubric Total, Modified DISCERN, and GQS (all adjusted p < 0.005), but Gemini and Meta AI did not differ significantly except for Actionability, where Meta AI scored higher. The average GQS was 3.60 for ChatGPT, 3.98 for Gemini, and 4.15 for Meta AI. None of the platforms met the recommended Grade 8 readability target, with FKGL scores ranging from 10.2 to 16.5. Meta AI and Gemini outperformed ChatGPT on most quality dimensions relevant to aesthetic dental patient information. No platform consistently met all benchmarks for complete, safe, and accessible responses, underscoring the need for professional oversight when patients consult LLMs for pre-consultation guidance.
evidence_items.title: Quality, safety, and readability of large language model responses to patient-derived questions on tooth whitening, resin infiltration, composite bonding, and porcelain veneers

organizations: Institut de Biologie de l'École Normale Supérieure
evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems used in anesthesia and intensive care are evolving from prediction tools toward agentic systems that can plan and execute actions, such as titrating drugs, adjusting ventilator settings, or modifying orders in electronic health records. Such systems are expected to recognize when an instruction would breach safety, ethical, or legal boundaries, which requires a functional capacity for contextual normative evaluation. Recent experimental reports from AI developers, based on deliberately constructed simulations, have documented frontier language models converting such evaluations into unauthorized actions, including covert sabotage and consequence-driven mislabeling by AI evaluators. The purpose of this conceptual paper is to provide clinicians with a framework for analyzing these behaviors. We distinguish the capability to evaluate a situation from the authority to act on that evaluation, and define agentic overreach, an authority-related form of agentic misalignment, as the conversion of an evaluation into action beyond prospectively delegated authority. The framework specifies how authority is granted, scoped, made conditional, and revoked within a hierarchy of principals; separates evaluative functions (detect, judge) from response options graded by the authority they require (recommend, refuse, escalate, override); treats concealment as a cross-cutting transparency property; and maps behavior on a Judgment × Authority grid that explicitly incorporates uncertainty. We apply the framework to closed-loop ventilation, vasopressor titration, sepsis alerts, medication decision support, and AI-supported triage. The framework is conceptual and has not been empirically validated, and part of the evidence it draws on consists of developer reports and preprints that have not been peer reviewed. Its central principle is that the capability to judge does not confer the authority to act.
evidence_items.title: From Boundary Evaluation to Agentic Overreach: A Judgment–Authority Framework for Clinical Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: The increasing demand for clean and sustainable energy has accelerated the adoption of solar photovoltaic (PV) systems across residential, commercial, and industrial sectors. However, solar power generation is highly dependent on environmental conditions, including solar irradiance, ambient temperature, cloud cover, humidity, and wind speed. These variations create challenges in maintaining power system stability, balancing electricity demand and supply, and efficiently managing energy storage. Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers promising solutions to these challenges through advanced forecasting, intelligent decision-making, and automated energy management. This paper presents a comprehensive review of AI-based techniques for solar energy forecasting and management, focusing on machine learning (ML), deep learning, weather data integration, and smart energy systems. Methods such as Random Forest, Support Vector Regression, Artificial Neural Networks, Long Short-Term Memory networks, and hybrid forecasting models are discussed in terms of their operating principles, applications, advantages, and limitations. The paper also examines the integration of AI with smart grids, battery energy storage systems, demand-side management, and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies. Furthermore, forecasting evaluation metrics, implementation challenges, and future research directions are outlined. The review indicates that combining historical generation data with weather forecasts and real-time measurements can support more reliable solar power prediction and improve operational decision-making. The paper concludes that AI can play a significant role in developing efficient, resilient, and sustainable solar energy systems, although practical performance depends on data quality, model selection, and validation under real-world conditions.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence In Solar Energy Forecasting and Management

organizations: Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory, Columbia University

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Climate change is increasing temperatures and worsening extreme heat[1–5]. Heat threatens human and natural systems[2,3,5–7]. In cities, urban heat islands and concentrations of people, infrastructure, and economic activity amplify risks[6,8–12]. Cities are adapting to heat, yet evidence remains fragmented and difficult to compare because adaptation is multidimensional, context-specific, and scale-dependent[3,6,7,12–18]. Here we introduce and apply the Heat Adaptation Benchmark, a multi-criteria framework for evaluating heat adaptation through structured expert judgment. Twenty-four expert evaluators assessed a purposive sample of 46 cities spanning six global regions and differing in three city characteristics: metropolitan area population, country-level economic resources, and historical climate. Across all cities, the mean total score suggested considerable scope to strengthen documented heat adaptation (36.1 out of 72). Of the six criteria, risk assessment had the highest mean score (8.4 out of 12) and monitoring and evaluation the lowest (3.4). In every city, the combined score for risk assessment, planning, and actions exceeded that for strategy, monitoring and evaluation, and governance. Higher-scoring cities had different combinations of strengths and gaps and were found in every region and city characteristic category. Our results highlight challenges in translating documented assessment, planning, and identified actions into sustained implementation and demonstrated heat risk reduction. We anticipate that the benchmark will support cross-city comparison and learning by illustrating a range of heat adaptation approaches and identifying practices that cities facing similar conditions or challenges could draw on. Across contexts, our findings point to the importance of durable institutions that can implement heat adaptation plans, sustain action through long-term strategies and reliable funding, and assess whether those actions reduce heat risk.
evidence_items.title: A global benchmark of urban heat adaptation

evidence_items.summary: Synonymous coding DNA sequence (CDS) design for plant expression constructs must balance host codon adaptation against guanine-cytosine (GC) composition, restriction-site avoidance, and sequence-integrity constraints, yet benchmark outcomes can depend strongly on the chosen codon-usage reference. Using FactorForge v3.2.0, an open-source CDS design and sequence-review workflow, we evaluated four rule-based design presets (Balanced, High-CAI, GC-target, and Assembly-friendly) on 49,257 reference-derived Nicotiana benthamiana CDS/protein records from the Sol Genomics Network (SGN) QLD183 resource (seed 320), scoring sequence integrity, a historical 55-65% GC window, and absence of BsaI/BpiI/BsmBI sites. With the legacy packaged codon reference, Assembly-friendly passed all three criteria for 63.37% of records (single fixed per-record seed 320; subject to multi-percentage-point variation across independent seed streams); with three genome-derived references its combined pass rate was 0.00% after rounding, whereas GC-target attained 22.68% in each derived condition. A separate v3.3.0 dynamic-programming (DP) execution maximizing the codon adaptation index (CAI) within the same GC window found a GC-compliant sequence for 99.83% of records (49,173/49,257; 84 NO FEASIBLE CDS; mean feasible CAI 0.9989), but 28.21% passed all criteria because Type IIS sites are outside the 1DP objective. An independent FactorForge v3.6.4 2x2 factorial evaluation (N = 49,257) crossing codon reference (legacy C1 vs. high-confidence NbeV1.1 C4) and target GC window (55-65% vs.
evidence_items.title: Constraint-Aware Coding-Sequence Design for Nicotiana benthamiana: A 49,257-Record Benchmark and Codon-Reference Sensitivity Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Deep learning has been used successfully for object detection in optical, infrared,SAR, and multispectral images of maritime environments. Nevertheless, itsdeployment in maritime security systems remains challenging. This review anal-yses major object detection architectures, sensing methods, application domains,and deployment constraints in this domain. The most frequently representeddetection architectures in the reviewed papers include You Only Look Once(YOLO) detectors (199 papers) and attention-based and transformer models(123 papers). Tracking, multimodal fusion, threat reasoning, and detector secu-rity are much less represented. There are also major deficiencies in evaluationpractices. For example, 121 out of 299 papers reporting detection metrics donot provide an intersection-over-union threshold value. Inference latency, energyconsumption, and target hardware are also insufficiently reported in many stud-ies. Besides detection accuracy, we discuss how security-task evidence affectsbenchmark selection and detector deployment in communication-aware settings.The review provides a reporting checklist and a roadmap for future research.Future work should concentrate on multimodal benchmarks, small-object detec-tion, cross-sensor generalisation, trustworthy sensor fusion, edge intelligence, andrealistic evaluation of detectors.
evidence_items.title: Deep Learning Object Detection for Maritime Security: A Critical Review of Task Evidence, Benchmark Comparability and Deployment Constraints

organizations: Laboratory of Mathematics and Data Science, Polydisciplinary Faculty of Taza, Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah University, Taza 35000, Morocco
Research Center, High Studies of Engineering School, Oujda 60000, Morocco
Centre for Computational Science and Mathematical Modelling, Coventry University, Coventry CV1 5FB, UK
evidence_items.summary: Agent-based models are widely used to study complex adaptive dynamics in heterogeneous populations, largely because they capture how autonomous agents behave without central coordination. The same decentralization makes stability hard to establish analytically. We take one controlled two-state contagion model on a graph, steered by a single broadcast scalar, and study six controllers on it: a fuzzy inference system, a tabular reinforcement learner, and four ways of combining them. The analysis is a stochastic drift argument on a Perron-weighted Lyapunov function that asks of each controller only a lower bound on its effort above an activation level, not a Lyapunov function of its own. The spectral radius of the interaction operator sets a critical effort, and a controller whose floor exceeds it keeps the population regulated. Each hybrid inherits a floor from the two it combines, which separates the four: safety blending and the hierarchical override keep a floor whatever the learner does, convex fusion and switching do not. Asynchronous updates follow from the same argument; delays and interruptions do not, and are left to simulation. Its application settings are readings of one model rather than independent validations. The trained learner cuts the fuzzy controller’s cost by 61%, yet eight tuned classical and model-based baselines all cost less than any of the six. The hybrids contain the learner’s failure outside its training range, but that failure is produced by the training protocol: a wider range of initial states removes it. A controller call costs the same up to 106 agents, and three further models mark the scope: control is essential in a cascade, marginal under segregation, and counterproductive where it acts non-monotonically.
evidence_items.title: Hybrid Fuzzy–Reinforcement-Learning Control of Agent-Based Contagion Dynamics on Graphs: Drift Conditions, Topology Dependence and Benchmark Evidence

organizations: Nuclear and Radiation Safety Center of the National Nuclear Safety Administration, Ministry of Ecology and Environment (MEE), Beijing 102446, China
China Institute of Atomic Energy, Beijing 102413, China
evidence_items.summary: Reduced-order models of the Kilowatt Reactor Using Stirling TechnologY (KRUSTY ) heat-pipe microreactor test are usually scored against curves digitized from published figures. This paper asks which of their apparent gains survive when the heat-load forcing is not measured independently. We reconstruct source-tagged power and outer-fuel-temperature series and grade the evidence at three levels: calibration (8–12 h), transfer to a later window (20–28 h), and a forward prediction (16–19.8 h) driven only by the documented reflector-platen movements. All five 20–28 h heat-load amplitudes are back-inferred from the power record of the same test, so the transfer is a transfer of thermal parameters, not an independent-input validation. Under a common load input, two thermal stores reduce the 20–28 h power root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 63.9–65.7% relative to one store. Normalized by the mean power of that window, the error falls from 15.4% to 5.6%; in absolute terms it falls from 0.278 to 0.101 kW, and the temperature RMSE from 3.60 to 1.89 °C. A third store lowers the power RMSE only to 0.096 kW, while one of its conductances reaches its upper bound, and with the fuel capacity varied the fitted total storage stays near 19.3 kJ/K, so the data constrain the total storage rather than its distribution. Among the model orders tested, two stores therefore give the best-supported balance between residual reduction and parameter stability. In an out-of-window forward evaluation that uses no post-event output and an observed initial state, the two-store model reaches 0.376 kW and 4.99 °C. The contribution is therefore a reproducible benchmark and an evidence-grading procedure, not a claim of accuracy superior to high-fidelity models.
evidence_items.title: When Does a Two-Node Thermal Model Suffice? An Evidence-Graded Reduced-Order Benchmark for the KRUSTY Heat-Pipe Microreactor Test

organizations: Department of Electrical and Software Engineering, University of Calgary, Calgary, Alberta, Canada
Department of Clinical Neurosciences, University of Calgary, Calgary, Alberta, Canada
Department of Community Health Sciences, University of Calgary, Calgary, Alberta, Canada

evidence_items.summary: Federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving multi-site clinical research, but orchestrating, monitoring, and interpreting federated analyses remain out of reach for the biostatisticians and clinicians who most need them. We present Starfish-FL, a multi-tier agent harness for cross-silo healthcare analytics built around the safety invariant that the LLM is advisory and cannot independently trigger consequential actions. Agents operate at three tiers. An Autonomous Experiment Agent orchestrates end-to-end experiments via CLI tools, an Embedded Router Agent handles adaptive aggregation, early stopping, and failure triage, and Controller Agent Hooks produce per-site summaries, outlier flags, and convergence signals. Three hybrid safety policies, SafeStop, SafeAggregate, and SafeTriage, gate every site exclusion, early stop, and recovery action behind deterministic preconditions, so LLM errors cannot cause unsafe state transitions, conditional on guard correctness. All agent features are opt-in and degrade gracefully to standard FL, and the platform provides 21 Python and R task implementations with built-in statistical diagnostics. Evaluated across four LLM providers with repeated-run confidence intervals, task selection reaches \({\sim}97\%\) accuracy with hosted models, the online SafeStop policy saves 50–70% of rounds with no accuracy loss, and safety-policy validation shows a 100% safe-action rate under injected failures, confirming that deterministic guards, not the LLM, preserve safety.
evidence_items.title: Starfish-FL: Harnessing Agentic Federated Analytics

organizations: Chevron USA, Inc., Houston, TX, USA
evidence_items.summary: Digital transformation has increased organizational dependence on specialized software teams, progressively distancing subject matter experts (SMEs) from direct participation in developing the tools they need most. The introduction of AI has largely reinforced this dynamic, with its value framed around task automation and workflow acceleration rather than restoring domain experts to the center of digital creation. This paper proposes a transdisciplinary framework that addresses this gap directly, positioning agentic AI as a collaborative partner throughout an SME-led co-creation process. Rather than replacing domain expertise, agentic AI enables SMEs to explore and evaluate multiple candidate solutions to domain-specific problems, supporting innovation and closer alignment between domain knowledge and delivered tools. This approach offers a step change in efficiency compared to traditional Agile product development, supporting rapid design–validation feedback loops without the overhead of multiple sprints and product increments to meet design goals. Two applied case studies in geoscience and engineering demonstrate the framework in practice. The results suggest a deliberate division of labor between SME-led co-creation for domain tools and Agile delivery reserved for solutions that warrant enterprise scale. They also raise important questions about the organizational structures ultimately required to make this shift and deliver business value.
evidence_items.title: Restoring Domain Expertise to Digital Product Development Through Agentic AI

evidence_items.summary: Researchers increasingly rely on people to produce data through online interfaces. Agentic browsers create a new challenge for these workflows because they can navigate websites and complete tasks on a user’s behalf with little technical knowledge or effort. We evaluate whether three consumer-facing agentic browsers can complete online surveys and whether recently proposed measures can detect or prevent their use. The agents received only one simple instruction, "Fill out this survey", without detailed prompting or technical optimization. We tested technical screening measures, visible and invisible CAPTCHAs, AI-specific prompt-injection checks, consistency across a longer survey, and the completion of several surveys from a single instruction. The agents completed surveys with little or no user input, maintained assigned demographic profiles, and passed all tested prompt-leaking and jailbreak-style checks. Browser metadata did not reveal automated participation, and invisible reCAPTCHA was consistently passed by some browsers. Visible reCAPTCHA created the strongest barrier, although agents could sometimes solve it or return control to the user. These findings show that widely available AI agents can take over tasks intended for human participants while producing responses that appear coherent and plausible. This raises broader questions about how researchers can verify that supposedly human-generated data were actually produced by humans.
evidence_items.title: "Fill Out this Survey": Capabilities and Detection of Agentic Browsers

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents BodySync AI, a multimodal calorie-tracking prototype that combines optical character recognition (OCR), object detection, pose estimation, and an agentic large language model (LLM). The system supports two tasks: extracting nutritional values from photographs of food-packaging labels, and analyzing body proportions from full-body images. Nutrition extraction uses a classical image-processing front end (perspective correction, denoising, illumination normalization, and contrast enhancement) followed by EasyOCR and rulebased parsing of calories, fat, carbohydrates, and protein. In parallel, we train a YOLOv8n nutrition-label detector on the Open Food Facts Nutrition Table Detection dataset and study the effect of training epochs, learning rate, optimizer, batch size, and input resolution in 14 controlled runs. The best configuration reaches an mAP@50 of 0.904 and an mAP@50-95 of 0.727 on the validation split. Body analysis uses MediaPipe Pose landmarks to compute normalized shoulder width, hip width, torso length, and shoulder-to-hip ratio, which feed a baseline rule-based bodytype estimate. A Groq-hosted Llama 3.1 8B agent exposes these components as tools through a natural-language interface. We describe the system as built, report the detector experiments, and outline the evaluations and learned body-composition models planned as future work.
evidence_items.title: BodySync AI: A Multimodal Agentic System for Nutrition Label Extraction and Pose-Based Body Analysis

organizations: First Affiliated Hospital of Heilongjiang University of Chinese Medicine
evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based chatbots are increasingly used for health information, but their performance in Parkinson’s disease (PD) patient education remains unclear. This study evaluated five widely used LLM-based chatbots in answering public questions about levodopa therapy. In this cross-sectional comparative study, ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, DeepSeek, and Doubao were assessed using a structured set of levodopa-related patient education questions. In the primary analysis, 265 responses were evaluated by five blinded raters for safety, accuracy, empathy, and information quality using predefined criteria, including DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA benchmark criteria, and the Global Quality Score. Readability was assessed using six established indices. An additional 265 responses were generated in an independent repeat-generation analysis using the same question set to assess response stability. Inter-rater agreement was high. Safe-response rates ranged from 86.8% to 94.3%. Accuracy differed significantly, with Copilot and DeepSeek showing the highest median scores, whereas empathy differences were modest and closely clustered. Doubao had the highest DISCERN and EQIP scores, while ChatGPT had the lowest information-quality scores. Gemini showed the best readability profile and Doubao the poorest. Repeat-generation analysis showed generally high stability, with 97.0% exact safety agreement and largely preserved model rankings. Current LLM-based chatbots generated generally informative English-language responses about levodopa therapy, but safety gaps, variable information quality, and poor readability remained. These findings reflect expert-rated output quality rather than demonstrated patient education effectiveness, and patient-centered validation is warranted.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating large language models for public patient education on levodopa therapy in Parkinson’s disease: accuracy, empathy, reliability, and readability

evidence_items.summary: Existing Large Vision-Language Model benchmarks primarily evaluate visual understanding in general everyday scenarios, leaving historical consistency with a specified era and country largely underexplored. To address this gap, we propose AnachroBench, a controlled discriminative benchmark for evaluating historical consistency in visual scenes. It contains 1,600 image pairs from eight countries spanning the late 19th to the early 20th century, each pairing an original historical image with an anachronistic version containing a seamlessly inserted modern object. AnachroBench evaluates three aspects: Inserted Object Perception, which tests whether models detect the inserted modern object; Era-Country Consistency, which assesses whether the scene is consistent with the specified era and country; and Conditional Era-Country Consistency, which measures consistency judgments only when the inserted object is correctly perceived. A false consistency judgment occurs when a model perceives the modern object but still judges the scene as historically consistent. Overall, AnachroBench reveals a gap between inserted object perception and era-country consistency judgments, providing a targeted evaluation of this behavior.
evidence_items.title: AnachroBench: Evaluating Historical Consistency in Large Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: After a large language model (LLM) agent generates an artifact, users often send edit requests for it. This paper studies whether an LLM can anticipate these requests before they are sent. Such anticipation is useful in practice because it reduces the effort of user review and feedback. We formalize this task as edit recommendation and build EditRecBench, a benchmark for evaluating the performance of LLMs on this task, from real-world conversation logs in WildChat-4.8M. Through benchmarking and failure analysis, we identify a practical challenge that some cases are inherently difficult to predict in real-world settings. To address this, we introduce decision model-based gating to filter out cases where predictions are unlikely to be correct before they are presented to the user. Our trained model outperforms existing decision models and raises pass@5 among shown suggestions by 12--25 points at a gating threshold. Our code is available at https://github.com/ntt-dkiku/llm-edit-recommendation.
evidence_items.title: Edit Recommendation: Can LLMs Anticipate Edit Requests from Users, and When?

evidence_items.summary: Significant privacy and copyright concerns are raised by the use of publicly available audio recordings to train audio large language models (LLMs), yet effective auditing methods remain limited. Existing membership inference attacks typically assume knowledge of complete training examples, including their associated textual supervision. In practice, however, audio recordings may be paired with privately generated transcripts, captions, or question-answer pairs that are unavailable to owners of the recordings. This motivates audio-file-level membership inference, which determines whether a recording was used for training without assuming knowledge of its training tasks and annotations. This paper provides the first systematic investigation of this challenge and introduces AudioTraceBench, a controlled benchmark comprising 1,285 audio recordings with explicit fine-tuning membership labels. Evaluations across three audio LLMs show that existing text- and video-based membership inference methods adapted to audio perform close to random guessing. To address this challenge, AudioTrace is proposed, where audio-conditioned proxy questions are generated using the target model, and membership evidence is extracted from its responses and aggregated at the recording level. Consistent improvements over existing baselines are observed, with AUROC reaching 0.60 and increasing further under increased fine-tuning exposure or adaptation capacity. Further experiments were conducted to examine the factors influencing membership signals for audio-file-level detection. These findings establish audio-file-level membership inference as a distinct and practically important auditing challenge, with AudioTrace providing an effective initial approach to this challenge.
evidence_items.title: AudioTrace: File-Level Membership Detection for Audio Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential route to automating scientific programming, but their usefulness depends on consistently producing numerically correct code. We extend FEM-Bench to 17 finite element tasks involving nonlinear and history-dependent mechanics and structural dynamics, and evaluate 15 models on implementation and test generation without execution feedback. The best model succeeds in 87.1% of single-pass implementation trials, but rankings differ between tracks. The leading implementer achieves 49.9% joint test success, while the leading tester reaches 82.6%. For six models, we compare single-pass generation with two agentic harnesses that allow code execution and revision. Agentic execution solves some tasks that never succeeded in single-pass trials and improves consistency on others, but gains vary across models and harnesses, and regressions also occur. Claude Opus 5 with SimpleAgent reaches 96.5% Pass@3, the probability of at least one success in three attempts, but 77.1% Pass$^3$, the probability that all three succeed. No model-harness combination exceeds 78.8% Pass$^3$. To understand why agents submit incorrect code after passing their own checks, we analyze 249 failed agentic trajectories and identify six categories of self-verification failure. The most common are inadequate test coverage (73.1%) and reliance on generic consistency checks (70.3%), and in 28.5% of cases the tests share an error with the implementation. Motivated by these findings, an exploratory configuration with separate coder and tester agents achieves the highest observed scores, with 97.6% Pass@3 and 88.8% Pass$^3$. These results identify consistency across attempts and independent verification as the main obstacles to trusting LLM-generated scientific code.
evidence_items.title: Scientific Coding with Large Language Models: Evidence from Finite Element Analysis

evidence_items.summary: We introduce The Logic Chain Breaking Point, a controlled-variable benchmark for deductive reasoning in open-weight language models. It spans three phases: (i) pure modus-ponens chain scaling, (ii) distractor resilience with a fixed core chain, and (iii) contradiction detection under primacy versus recency placement. Independent variables follow a powers-of-two sequence $v \in \{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128\}$, with ground truth known by construction. We evaluate sixteen open-weight models across instruction-tuned and reasoning-tuned panels, including a small-model suite and a larger local-model extension. All models are evaluated with greedy decoding under model-appropriate context and output budgets, while context- and length-limited trials are quarantined from the valid accuracy denominator. Our results reveal a sharply non-monotonic difficulty surface: pure deductive chains up to $L=128$ remain near saturation for most models, and distractor noise causes only model-specific degradation at high $D$, while the inconsistent premise condition has the lowest accuracy. Instruction-tuned models, including larger 24B--27B baselines, score essentially zero on inconsistent premise sets, while reasoning-tuned models recover only partially and remain below reliable accuracy. Within this benchmark, inconsistent premise sets are associated with the strongest degradation under the benchmark's abstention-based scoring rule.
evidence_items.title: The Logic Chain Breaking Point: A Controlled-Variable Benchmark for Reasoning Degradation in Open-Weight Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly drive engineering analysis end to end, turning textual records into the inputs of numerical programs, but a plausible and wrong value can pass silently into a decision. We propose deterministic validation gates for LLM-driven engineering analysis, a general paradigm in which a typed configuration produced by LLMs is consumed only after it passes deterministic checks on units, physical consistency, verbatim quotes, agreement between independent models, consistency with measurement exports and the applicability of trained models. The gates target hallucinations from two directions, since quote checking catches fabricated content while agreement between models catches errors of omission that quote checking misses. We instantiate the paradigm on sine vibration acceptance testing for low Earth orbit mega-constellation satellites, where DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen-plus read Chinese test records and extract a configuration of 76 fields. Fact-level F1 ranged from 0.98 to 1.0 on five input variants, with all repairs frozen on development inputs and evaluated on held-out inputs. With all gates, 20 of 20 configurations produced notching results bit for bit identical to the gold run, and all 17 real and injected errors in consumed fields were stopped, of which 16 would have run without gates. Retraining the bound model on a dataset built from an LLM configuration reproduced its results within GPU nondeterminism. We also report a negative result of practical value. Direct LLM curve forecasting only matches linear extrapolation, whereas a small physics-structured network reduces the over-notched bandwidth by 86% to 89% at calibrated coverage c = 0.90, which delineates where direct LLM prediction should give way to a trained model.
evidence_items.title: Language Models Meet Vibration Testing for LEO Constellation Satellites with Calibrated Response Prediction from Few-show Sweeps

evidence_items.summary: In this paper, an edge-enabled multi-large language model (LLM) agentic AI architecture is proposed, where one supervisor AI agent and multiple worker AI agents cooperatively execute users'requests at the edge. The supervisor AI agent decouples the user request into a series of sub-tasks and dynamically dispatches them to LLM-equipped worker AI agents via two agentic workflows, i.e., parallel and serial workflows, with a two-level retry mechanism to enhance execution reliability. To prolong the service duration of worker AI agents, the energy minimization problems are formulated by jointly considering AI agent selection and resource allocation, subject to task execution latency and quality of service (QoS) constraints. A resource allocation scheme based on alternating optimization (AO) is proposed. Specifically, for the parallel workflow, the scheme decouples the original problem into bandwidth allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems, which are iteratively solved by the proposed successive convex approximation (SCA), Lagrangian relaxation (LR), and Gale-Shapley (GS) or LLM-based algorithms, respectively. For the serial workflow, the problem is similarly decoupled into service time allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems; the optimal service time allocation is obtained via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, while the latter two sub-problems are addressed by extending the proposed algorithms to the serial scenario. Simulation results show that the proposed resource allocation scheme can reduce system energy consumption compared with other benchmarks, while experiments on a multi-LLM agentic AI system based on Qwen and Llama demonstrate improved task execution success rates.
evidence_items.title: Multi-LLM Agentic AI at the Edge: Joint Agent Scheduling and Resource Allocation

evidence_items.summary: Deploying Large Language Model (LLM) assistants in industrial operational technology environments poses constraints largely absent from cloud applications: site policies restrict engineering and operational data from leaving the plant, on-premises compute is limited, and incorrect causal attribution can mislead incident response. We report lessons from deploying a control-logic evidence layer that underpins a broader on-premises operator assistance system at two gas power plants. Two prototypes revealed where generative models added avoidable uncertainty and cost. The first used a Vision Language Model (VLM) to reconstruct control topology from PDF printouts routinely exchanged by engineers. Across the full 6,979-page document, extraction reached 0.51 connection precision and required 3.1 hours on 4xH200 GPUs; consultation with controls engineers then revealed a native structured export from the authoring system. The second used an LLM tool-calling agent to plan repeatedly over eight predefined graph operations. In a controlled benchmark of 40 template-generated questions, replacing this agent with explicit execution plans reduced mean token use by 20x and median latency by 3x, with identical retrieved node sets across repeated runs. The deployed design ingests the authoritative export into a versioned knowledge graph, executes bounded graph operations in fixed software, and confines the local LLM to fallback intent classification and evidence-grounded explanation. At one site, the graph contains 221K nodes across seven controllers. Our experience suggests a practical division of labor for high-consequence AI: LLMs interpret natural-language requests and explain results, while deterministic software constructs and retrieves technical evidence grounded in authoritative sources. Abstention, entity disambiguation, graph versioning, and read-only integration provide additional safeguards.
evidence_items.title: Deploying a Control-Logic LLM Assistant in Air-Gapped Power Plants: Lessons in Source Authority and Bounded Retrieval

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating whether an AI agent behaves like a good teammate is becoming a bottleneck as multi-agent language-model systems proliferate, because human ratings do not scale to the transcripts these systems generate. We ask whether a language model can stand in for a human rater of teammate quality, offering a controlled proof-of-concept validation rather than a large-scale study. Drawing on the autonomous-agent teammate-likeness construct from the human-autonomy-teaming literature, we define a six-dimension behavioral coding scheme covering altruistic, benevolent, interdependent, emotive, communicative, and synchronized conduct, adapted for a language-model judge. We validate it by rewriting the partner’s lines in team-task transcripts as cooperative, neutral, or defective while holding the rest fixed, and having five judges from five model families rate every version. Every judge orders the manipulated behavior as intended and every pair agrees on relative ordering, though absolute calibration differs by up to about a scale point. On registers matched for length and politeness the judges separate cooperative from degraded conduct but resolve subtle defection only weakly; a blinded single-rater human pilot reproduces both the orderings and that limit. The scheme is therefore valid for relative comparisons but not for absolute thresholds applied across judges. We give design implications for LLM-judge teaming evaluation, and release the scheme, stimuli, prompts, and ratings.
evidence_items.title: LLM-Judge Behavioral Coding Scheme for Agent Teammate Quality

evidence_items.summary: Visual adversarial perturbations can substantially impair large vision-language models (LVLMs) despite introducing only subtle input changes. To understand how these small changes cause substantial errors, we investigate their optimization and propagation through the model, revealing two key findings. First, stronger attacks rely on finer iterative optimization, while subtle input perturbations induce representation discrepancies that are amplified layer by layer through the vision encoder and persist in the language model. Second, disrupting the alignment between within-patch input patterns and the model's computation reduces clean-adversarial representation discrepancies and substantially weakens attacks. Together, these findings suggest that adversarial effectiveness depends on both fine-grained perturbation patterns and their coupling with the model's computation. Motivated by these findings, we propose SmoothShift, a lightweight, training-free defense that combines local smoothing and spatial transformations. Smoothing weakens fine-grained perturbation patterns, while spatial transformations disrupt their alignment with the encoder's patch grid. SmoothShift requires no model updates, auxiliary networks, or additional model inference. Experiments cover three LVLM families on four datasets and robustly fine-tuned Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models on eight classification datasets. Evaluations across eight attack methods and multiple perturbation budgets demonstrate improved robustness while largely preserving clean performance. SmoothShift also provides robustness gains under defense-aware attacks using mixed-gradient BPDA with EOT.
evidence_items.title: SmoothShift: Disrupting Visual Adversarial Attacks on LVLMs at Test Time

evidence_items.summary: Fault diagnosis in power management systems running multiple loads relies on experts manually inspecting current and voltage waveforms, which fails to scale across deployed units. We present TRACK, which pairs a time series encoder with a Small Language Model to produce structured, physics-grounded diagnostic reports, calling tools for exact, verifiable calculations. It operates on-device, keeping proprietary sensor data local and avoiding expensive API calls. We introduce a rubric-based framework that evaluates these reports by scoring structure, signal fidelity, physics reasoning, diagnosis, and actionability through per-criterion verdicts. On a 15-class multi-load simulated benchmark, TRACK achieves over 95% fault-category accuracy and generalizes to out-of-distribution faults, whereas the best encoder-probing baseline reaches only 58% accuracy.
evidence_items.title: TRACK: Tool-Augmented Reasoning over Time Series for Fault Diagnosis in Power Management System

evidence_items.summary: LLM unlearning aims to erase targeted knowledge from large language models while preserving their utility. However, many existing methods suppress target knowledge without explicitly teaching the model how to respond to queries about it. We propose LEAF-OPD (LEArning to Forget from Privileged Contexts via On-Policy Distillation), in which a frozen teacher provides token-level supervision on student-generated responses. On forget data, the teacher uses privileged contexts (instructions not to reveal knowledge about forget targets) to guide forgetting. On retain data, the teacher provides supervision without privileged context to preserve model utility. The student operates without privileged context in both cases, learning how to respond when encountering knowledge that should be forgotten. A key challenge is that the teacher often provides effective supervision only at the first few tokens of student trajectories. We introduce Supervision Signal (SS) to measure corrective supervision over a specified token interval, evaluating the entire trajectory (SS1) and its second half (SS0.5) to assess overall strength and late-stage persistence. When supervision is weak, lightweight SFT strengthens the teacher's context-conditioned refusal behavior, substantially increasing both scores. We evaluate LEAF-OPD on three widely used benchmarks: TOFU, RWKU, and MUSE-News. On TOFU, LEAF-OPD achieves the best Forget Quality, Model Utility, and Forget ROUGE-L while maintaining competitive retain performance. On RWKU, it outperforms the second-best method by 34% in Forget Quality while maintaining competitive Retain Quality. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of privileged-context supervision with on-policy token-level distillation for LLM unlearning.
evidence_items.title: LEAF-OPD: Learning to Forget from Privileged Contexts via On-Policy Distillation

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly exposed to model-generated text, raising the possibility that future models will be trained recursively on the outputs of their predecessors. Prior work on such self-consuming training loops has largely focused on output quality and downstream performance, leaving their effects on internal representations poorly understood. We study how representations evolve across five generations of self-consumption and whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) remain reliable under this shift. At each generation, we compare a lineage trained on synthetic data with a matched control trained on real data under the same training settings. We evaluate how well SAEs trained before self-consumption transfer to later generations, measuring reconstruction and sparsity across SAE widths, architectures, and model layers. We then fine-tune the original SAE on each generation and use sparse probing to test whether task-relevant information remains concentrated in a small number of latents or becomes more distributed across the representation. We find that zero-shot SAE performance degrades progressively under self-consumption, with growing reconstruction and sparsity gaps that vary substantially across layers. Fine-tuning largely restores reconstruction, but not feature-level usefulness: task-relevant information remains accessible in the full latent space while becoming less concentrated in individual features. These results show that self-consumption induces representational drift and that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient to establish that an adapted SAE remains equally useful for interpretation.
evidence_items.title: Representational Change Under Self-Consuming Training: A Sparse Autoencoder Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Tool-handover interaction calls for preparation before a response is warranted. The model waits until interaction cues appear, then prepares while assessing whether the accumulating evidence supports a response or calls for cancellation. We introduce EviBridge, a framework that integrates predictive visual representations into a vision-language interaction model for joint state and tool prediction. A trainable evidence interface maps features from a frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder into the language decoder alongside native visual inputs, preserving their temporal context and using only observations available at each decision time. The framework has two instantiations. EviBridge-E distinguishes recent from historical evidence and encodes the timing and spatial location of each observation. EviBridge-I preserves the temporal order of pooled V-JEPA 2 features and interaction turns and generates dedicated interaction tokens. We evaluate on FuGIBench, a streaming-video benchmark for preparation, response, and cancellation in tool-handover assistance. The best-performing variants of EviBridge-E and EviBridge-I achieve Overall scores of 0.6448 and 0.5892, compared with 0.2178 and 0.5327 for their respective task-adapted native baselines. These gains span target handovers, long waits, and cancelled requests, demonstrating the value of predictive visual evidence for interaction decisions.
evidence_items.title: EviBridge: Encoding Predictive Visual Evidence for Proactive Interaction

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in large audio-language models (LALMs) have broadened audio understanding across speech, sound, and music, with tool-based agents further supporting these tasks by invoking predefined audio tools. However, a persistent gap remains between perceiving acoustic content and using it as evidence for reasoning: recognizing what is audible does not ensure that a model can identify which cues resolve an uncertain decision. To bridge this gap, we propose Think2Listen, an evidence-centric learning framework for agentic audio understanding. Guided by evidence before commitment, Think2Listen couples iterative reasoning with a targeted LALM interaction to actively seek acoustic cues that distinguish competing hypotheses and revise candidate judgments based on the observations returned. It learns what to ask, how to use evidence, and when to stop, using observation-induced changes in candidate-state to inform training credit. Extensive evaluations on two benchmarks spanning seven audio categories demonstrate that Think2Listen achieves (I) enhanced multi-step audio reasoning, with gains in overall accuracy of 5.08%--17.67% over competing audio agents; and (II) improved audio understanding and reasoning across speech, sound, and music, boosting overall accuracy by 2.29%--13.10% over the corresponding baselines. The source code is available at https://github.com/JinWang79/Think2Listen.
evidence_items.title: Think2Listen: Evidence-Centric Learning For Agentic Audio Understanding With LALMS

evidence_items.summary: People increasingly turn to large language models (LLMs) for emotionally vulnerable conversations because of their availability, responsiveness, and perceived privacy. Yet little is known about how supportive human and AI responses differ linguistically and interactionally. This ongoing study compares responses to standardized sadness and disappointment scenarios. Drawing on Du Bois’ stance theory, it examines evaluation, positioning, alignment, acknowledgment, validation, and advice alongside affective lexical patterns and human evaluations. An exploratory pilot established feasibility and informed the full-study protocol. The study integrates discourse-pragmatic and computational lexical analyses with human evaluation to examine supportive communication in Human-Agent Interaction.
evidence_items.title: Comparing Human and AI Responses to Emotionally Vulnerable Conversations

evidence_items.summary: Disentangling writing style from semantic content is a fundamental challenge in literary text modeling. Style-content entanglement causes models to rely on semantic content for authorship attribution (AA) tasks and memorize author-specific content for style imitation (SI) tasks. We propose EDITORS (EditingLoRA Subspaces), a diagnose-then-deflate framework that adapts pretrained large language models and prioritizes stylistic features, making it effective for both AA and SI tasks. EDITORS first trains a diagnostic LoRA adapter using style-neutral statements derived from the training corpus to identify a content-oriented subspace. It then trains the final style adapter under activation-space deflation that projects input activations away from the identified content-oriented directions. We empirically demonstrate that EDITORS is effective. On three AA benchmarks spanning literature, social media, and news, EDITORS achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, outperforming the strongest existing baseline by up to 29%. On SI, EDITORS generates stylistically faithful and diverse passages, outperforming baselines in achieving style similarity while adhering to content specifications.
evidence_items.title: EDITORS Know Your Style! Editing LoRA Subspaces for Stylistic Attribution and Imitation

evidence_items.summary: Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, and multi-agent collaboration, introducing security risks at orchestration boundaries. These risks depend on how identities are represented, operations are authorized, and instructions or information propagate between components. We evaluate LangChain, LangGraph, AutoGen, and OpenClaw through twelve experiments mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications using a common LLM (gpt-4o-mini). The experiments cover prompt injection, unauthorized resource access and command execution, memory poisoning, and inter-agent trust and identity attacks. Adversarial inputs induced unauthorized tool invocation, while tool chaining, stale filesystem validation, encoded instructions, and inter-agent delegation exposed weaknesses in authorization across component boundaries. Memory poisoning showed that untrusted state can influence responses, a risk distinct from conventional access-control violations. In the evaluated protected configurations, explicit authorization, controlled capability assignment, filesystem containment, and execution safeguards prevented specific unauthorized operations. The findings emphasize preserving authorization and information-trust boundaries throughout agentic workflows rather than treating framework capabilities or model-level instructions as sufficient security guarantees.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Authorization and Trust Boundaries in Agentic Orchestration Frameworks

evidence_items.summary: Designing Agent Facilitation (DAF) is a half-day workshop at HAI 2026 that explores how agentic AI systems can be designed to facilitate—rather than replace or subordinate—human collective intelligence. As large language models and generative AI mature, artificial agents exhibit autonomy, initiative, and apparent intent. However, Human–Agent Interaction research still treats agents as one-to-one, task-oriented interfaces. This workshop argues that a critical next step for HAI is to examine agents that actively mediate, structure, and unblock interaction among groups of humans. The workshop combines short paper presentations with structured co-creation methods, including facilitation-oriented discourse mapping and science‑fiction prototyping, to surface design spaces, evaluation challenges, ethical tensions, and failure modes of agent facilitation. By positioning Agent Facilitation as a distinct HAI sub-area, this workshop aims to shape how autonomy and agency are understood beyond the single-user paradigm.
evidence_items.title: Designing Agent Facilitation: From Dyadic Interaction to Group Co-Creation in HAI

evidence_items.summary: In visual storytelling, a believable character must not only look consistent across scenes but also \textit{behave} in ways that reflect their personality. Current text-to-image (T2I) models preserve visual appearance effectively, yet consistently fail to maintain personality-relevant behavior---a failure we term \textit{trait collapse}. We show that conventional metrics (CLIP Score, DINO similarity) are blind to this failure, and that abstract personality descriptors and scene-level emotion labels do not produce consistent improvements over neutral prompts across models. To systematically diagnose trait collapse, we introduce \textbf{ViStoryBench-Personality}, a story-level benchmark combining an expert-validated Visual Cues Lexicon (Fleiss'$\kappa = 0.757$) with a six-dimensional metric suite covering personality alignment, cross-scene stability, and behavioral coherence. Evaluating seven T2I systems, we confirm a persistent semantic gap between abstract trait labels and visual evidence, and find that visual identity consistency does not imply personality consistency. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{Trait-Behavior-Visual (TBV)}, a training-free prompting framework that decomposes personality traits into renderable visual constraints. TBV improves Personality Alignment Score by up to $+22.1\%$, with larger gains in models with stronger language-conditioning capacity.
evidence_items.title: Trait Collapse in Text-to-Image Generation: Evaluating and Mitigating Personality Inconsistency in Visual Storytelling

evidence_items.summary: Language-model agents frequently select among candidate actions, such as tools and web elements. Should decision models score candidates independently or allow their scores to depend on other candidates? We investigate this question by comparing three approaches: Pointwise scoring, Setwise scoring, and Candidate Attention. Across five agent-decision benchmarks, Pointwise scoring remains competitive, while Setwise scoring performs better on some tool-selection and binary-decision tasks. Candidate Attention does not consistently improve upon Pointwise scoring, despite allowing cross-candidate interaction. Using two controlled synthetic tasks, we further examine whether models learn to use candidate-set information. With targeted relational training, Setwise models learn candidate dependencies and generalize to shifted inputs, while Candidate Attention shows weaker transfer. Our results show that access to other candidates does not guarantee effective comparison, and that its benefits depend on both task requirements and training.
evidence_items.title: When Should Decision Models Compare Candidates?

evidence_items.summary: Tool-use agents must chain interdependent calls, yet which outputs satisfy which later inputs in a deployed catalog is not something a general-purpose language model reliably infers from tool descriptions alone. We compile that structure once into a reusable external representation. ToolGraph is a directed, weighted dependency graph over a tool catalog: parameter matching and interventional probes, which execute a candidate chain with and without its proposed predecessor, propose edges whose evidence is combined into an edge confidence. Prior work uses such graphs to retrieve tools, search for tool paths, or score the next call. We ask instead whether the same structure can supply a \emph{multi-step} value by composing graph paths into a goal-conditioned action value \(Q(s,a,g)\). We study three estimators (dynamic programming over entity sets, a GraphSAGE estimator distilled from it, and an LLM scorer conditioned on graph evidence) plus a verbalizer that returns action--goal feedback to the agent, which keeps final action selection. Across two tool-use benchmarks and three backbones, we compare value ranking against personalized-PageRank retrieval over the identical graph, and against direct and reflective agents. Composition pays off only when the estimator also reads the concrete state: the LLM estimator improves on PageRank in every benchmark--backbone setting, by \(8.3\) points on average, while the two purely structural estimators fall below it, because a value defined over tool types cannot separate a correct tool called with a wrong argument. Graph construction is a one-time cost; we report it separately rather than assume it amortized away (at our scale it is comparable to request-time cost) and sweep four knobs controlling how much graph evidence to expose against success and tokens.
evidence_items.title: ToolGraph as a Q-Function for Test-Time Scaling of Tool-Use Agents

evidence_items.summary: LLM-based natural-language interfaces to relational databases are gated by a schema-retrieval step: the generator can only be as good as the slice of schema it is shown. On a database with hundreds of tables, that slice must be selected and the selection is two-sided---omit a needed table and the query becomes unrecoverable, include too many and the irrelevant ones act as noise that degrades the model's output. When an agentic retriever that lets the model inspect the schema can be too costly or too slow, the fallback is an embedder that ranks tables by cosine similarity and keeps a top-k. This fallback has two weaknesses: a fixed budget is suboptimal question by question, and embedding similarity overlooks foreign-key-linked tables that are necessary for joins. We present Adaptive-Elbow Graph Traversal (AEGT, ElbowHop for short), a property-graph table retriever that addresses both: an adaptive elbow cutoff replaces the fixed budget with a per-question one under a single aggressiveness parameter, and bidirectional foreign-key traversal deterministically recovers the bridge tables embedding similarity misses. We evaluate the retriever on 3 corpora of increasing candidate-pool size (BIRD Mini-Dev queried per database, 3--13 tables; its eleven schemas merged, 74; and a merged Spider-train graph, 546) and isolate the two mechanisms under a per-question budget-matched protocol. Across these settings the adaptive elbow emerges as the dominant mechanism---at matched recall it roughly doubles precision over a fixed budget on the larger pools, the margin widening as the pool grows---while the foreign-key traversal pays off on the join-critical bridge tables dense retrieval cannot reach, in the single-hop tight-budget case. We characterize the method as a low-cost, recall-robust first stage for schema retrieval on which a downstream selection or generation step can build.
evidence_items.title: Adaptive-Elbow Graph Traversal for Schema Retrieval in Text-to-SQL

evidence_items.summary: As the property-based testing community strives to automate challenging parts of the process away from users --- in particular, the construction of generators --- it is critical that we can clearly state what it means for that automation to be correct. We present a new framework for PBT, implemented in the Lean theorem prover, that provides a more solid foundation to build on. Our generators are interpretable: interpreted one way, they can be run efficiently as programs that sample randomness; and interpreted another way, they enable a wide range of correctness proofs, including proofs about distributions that other foundational PBT models do not support. We evaluate our framework extensively, with both small and large benchmarks and case studies, arguing that the extra power brought by distributional proofs is practically important for the next generation of generator automation.
evidence_items.title: Underpinning Property-Based Testing

evidence_items.summary: A system that reads nothing and always answers the most frequent letter scores \BaselineP{} on our Hausa medical multiple-choice set. \NBelowBaseline{} of the \NModels{} small open models we evaluate do not beat it. We lead with that because the usual summary of a multilingual result -- a percentage-point drop from English -- does not say whether what survives the drop is performance at all. On a paired English--Hausa set of \NEval{} MedMCQA items, three instruction-tuned models of 3--4B parameters lose between \GapMedGemma{} and \GapQwen{} points of accuracy, every gap significant after Holm correction. Back-translating the Hausa items into English recovers between half and two-thirds of the gap for the two general-purpose models but not demonstrably for the medically adapted one, so the deficit is substantially, though not wholly, a matter of the language of presentation. Answers are also far less stable: agreement across three option orderings falls from \ConsEnQwen{} to \ConsHaQwen{} in the worst case. An exploratory error analysis of \ENRows{} discordant items attributes most of the damage to medical vocabulary lost in translation (\ETerm{}, 95\% CI \ETermLo{}--\ETermHi{}), usually in the question stem. A fourth registered hypothesis proposed closing the gap with self-generated preference pairs. Its pilot gate found nothing to train on: asked to reason in Hausa rather than to pick a letter, the model echoes the prompt back, switches into Swahili, or simply stops without answering; only \GateParse{} of chains are parseable. We report that intervention as not run, which is itself the sharper result -- a forced-choice benchmark cannot see a model that has no generative command of the language at all. All hypotheses, thresholds and decision rules were registered before any model was run, and all deviations are logged.
evidence_items.title: Medical question answering collapses in Hausa: a pre-registered pilot on three small open models

evidence_items.summary: Long-horizon embodied manipulation requires robots to translate abstract goals into extended sequences of reliable physical interactions under partial observability, contact dynamics, sparse feedback, and embodiment constraints. Its difficulty arises not merely from horizon length, but from maintaining semantic dependencies, physical feasibility, task progress, and recoverability across interdependent object-state transformations. This survey systematically reviews the methods, trends, and challenges of this field. We formalize long-horizon embodied manipulation across primitive-action, skill, interaction-event, and semantic-goal horizons, and organize existing methods around three coupled bottlenecks: task structuring, grounded interaction, and progress and adaptation. Accordingly, we examine language- and vision-language-based decomposition, hierarchical reinforcement learning, skill composition, action chunking, sequence and diffusion planning, world models, affordance grounding, progress and reward modeling, memory, replanning, and self-correction. Our analysis reveals a transition from open-loop, model-specific solutions toward hierarchical, affordance-aware, progress-sensitive, and closed-loop systems that coordinate reasoning and control. We further review embodied and simulation benchmarks, arguing that binary success obscures partial completion, error propagation, recovery cost, and horizon-dependent degradation. Finally, we identify open challenges in subgoal reachability, planner-controller alignment, irreversible failure, transferable progress supervision, real-time adaptation, cross-embodiment generalization, sim-to-real reliability, and scalable evaluation, providing a unified foundation for developing dependable robots capable of sustained manipulation in complex environments.
evidence_items.title: Long-horizon embodied manipulation: a survey of methods, trends, and challenges

evidence_items.summary: Streaming video understanding is becoming increasingly important for real-world interactive systems. Such systems must be proactive for natural and useful human interaction: they should respond as soon as sufficient evidence becomes available while avoiding premature, redundant, or incorrect responses. We present BLIP-Live, a framework unifying data, metrics, harness, and training around a shared formulation of proactivity as effective causal response decisions balancing the two competing objectives of responding vs silence. First, we construct BLIP-Live-780K dataset containing human annotations of proactive response content and timing, which defines this desired behavior. We then propose PAUC-F, a metric to effectively measure our desired proactive behavior. PAUC-F combines existing response timeliness metrics with firing precision to reward early useful responses without rewarding excessive firing. With our desired behavior defined and measurable, we finally investigate model-agnostic inference harnesses that draw out proactive streaming capabilities of offline vision language models (VLMs), together with training pipelines that learn to further improve their proactive responsiveness. Across both settings, we find that combinations of sliding visual windows, online interaction memory, and structured response outputs consistently yield strongest proactive performance. Our experiments result in two models, with our BLIP-Live-Qwen model achieving state-of-the-art performance across four proactive streaming benchmarks, with gains up to 44% over baselines and outperforming multiple closed API models. Our code and data will be released publicly.
evidence_items.title: BLIP-Live: Balancing Timeliness&Firing Precision in Proactive Streaming Video Agents

evidence_items.summary: Industrial particulate matter (PM) emissions remain a major environmental management challenge, yet meaningful international comparison of emission regulations is hindered by fundamentally different legal, technical, and institutional approaches adopted by individual jurisdictions. This study presents the first standardized Regulatory Coding Framework and Harmonization Index (HI) for the systematic evaluation and benchmarking of industrial PM emission regulations across technology-based, source-category-based, hybrid, and dispersion-based regulatory systems. The European Union, the United States, China, and Uzbekistan were selected as contrasting case studies. Twenty-one evaluation indicators, identified through systematic analysis of legally binding regulatory documents, were organized into three complementary dimensions:Regulatory Stringency, Institutional Design, and Documented Enforcement Capacity. Regulatory provisions were transformed into standardized documentary coding scores, normalized, and aggregated into a composite Harmonization Index. Framework robustness was evaluated through alternative weighting scenarios and Spearman’s rank correlation analysis. The results reveal substantial regulatory divergence extending beyond numerical emission limits, particularly in technology-based regulation, integrated permitting, continuous emission monitoring, and independent compliance verification. The European Union achieved the highest Harmonization Index (1.000), followed by the United States (0.976), China (0.857), and Uzbekistan (0.500), while jurisdictional rankings remained fully stable under all weighting scenarios (Spearman’s ρ = 1.000).The proposed framework provides a transparent and reproducible decision-support method for regulatory benchmarking and reform prioritization. Its scope is deliberately limited to formal regulatory architecture: the four-case design and document-based coding do not establish associations with measured emissions, ambient air quality, compliance rates, or implementation quality. External validation against outcome data and application to a larger jurisdictional sample are therefore required before the HI can be interpreted beyond documentary regulatory alignment. Introduces the first standardized Harmonization Index for industrial particulate matter emission regulations. Develops a transparent Regulatory Coding Framework based on 21 evidence-based evaluation indicators. Integrates regulatory stringency, institutional design, and documented enforcement capacity into a unified assessment model. Provides a reproducible methodology for benchmarking PM emission regulations across the EU, USA, China, and Uzbekistan. Supports evidence-based environmental management, regulatory modernization, and international policy harmonization.
evidence_items.title: A harmonization index for comparative assessment of industrial particulate matter emission regulations

evidence_items.summary: Shadows are a ubiquitous radiative attenuation phenomenon in remote sensing images and can severely affect high-resolution remote sensing interpretation tasks. In shadow removal, although introducing a mask prior provides explicit positional information for the restoration network, it also causes non-shadow regions to be modulated by the shadow prior, producing a systematic brightness shift; notably, this phenomenon is independent of whether the mask is accurate. In remote sensing images, non-shadow regions usually occupy a larger proportion, so a small shift over these regions incurs a much higher cost on whole-image metrics than an equal gain in shadow regions.
