Adopting a task-decoupling perspective, we therefore decompose shadow removal into two tasks, shadow-region restoration and non-shadow-region identity, within a cascaded architecture, and handle them sequentially. Based on this insight, we propose STARS, a cascaded shadow removal framework that separates regional responsibilities across stages. The method retains the advantages of the shadow mask while resolving the degradation of non-shadow regions, without requiring a complex parallel dual-branch structure. Meanwhile, to introduce large-model prior knowledge into remote sensing tasks, we further design a Feature Selection and Fusion Adapter (FSFA). We conduct extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets, UAV-SC+, ISTD+ and WSRD+ 2026, demonstrating the superiority of STARS. The framework shows that decoupling regional responsibilities can resolve the intrinsic contradiction of mask priors, providing a new direction for image restoration with region heterogeneity.
evidence_items.title: STARS: Stage-Adaptive Responsibility Separation for Shadow Removal in Remote Sensing Images

evidence_items.summary: Open-vocabulary segmenters accept class names at inference. Conformal risk control can bound how often their prediction sets miss the true label, but we show that this bound breaks when names are added after calibration. On ADE20K, a threshold calibrated for 10% risk at 150 names reaches up to 15.4% risk at 845 names in released CAT-Seg models. The risk exceeds the target on every calibration split, yet the prediction sets grow far less than the target requires. In SED they instead grow larger than needed. The cause is that pruning, cross-label attention and vocabulary normalisation make each label's score depend on the other requested labels. Scores can move either way, so a threshold recalibrated at a larger vocabulary need not hold at smaller ones. We remove this dependence without training by scoring each label against a fixed reference bank of names. A label's score then stays the same when names are added, so one calibration keeps its guarantee as the vocabulary grows. The guarantee holds whatever names are added, even ones chosen per image after seeing it. On three benchmarks and five segmenters, the converted models meet the target at every vocabulary size we evaluate. For CAT-Seg and SED at alpha=10%, they use at most one more label per pixel than the released models recalibrated at the grown vocabulary. Treating names instead of images as calibration samples also bounds the miss rate of added names. If the annotated names are a random sample of the names in the calibration images, an added name's expected miss rate on those images is at most the target. For harder added names, the excess is at most their gap in mean miss rate. Applied to Grounding DINO, which splits large vocabularies into chunks, the conversion also makes inference about six times faster.
evidence_items.title: Calibrate Once, Grow the Vocabulary: Candidate-Independent Scores for Conformal Risk Control in Open-Vocabulary Segmentation

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
Flat pigmented basal cell carcinoma (BCC) of the face is an underrecognized diagnostic pitfall that may mimic other facial pigmented lesions dermatoscopically.


OBJECTIVE
To characterize perifollicular crescentic pigmentation (PCP) as a novel dermatoscopic criterion of flat facial pigmented BCC, assess its educational impact, and compare its diagnostic utility with contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) models.


METHODS
A retrospective dataset of 120 flat facial pigmented lesions (60 BCCs, 20 lentigo maligna, 20 pigmented actinic keratoses, and 20 solar lentigines/seborrheic keratoses) was assembled. Twenty-six dermatology residents completed a diagnostic test before and one week after a structured educational session on PCP recognition. ADAE, ResNet34, PanDerm, and MedSigLIP were evaluated on the same dataset.


RESULTS
PCP was identified in 63.3% of flat facial BCCs. Interobserver agreement was substantial (κ=0.780; 95% CI: 0.706-0.857). Following education, resident sensitivity increased from 73.7% to 88.0% (P < .001), and overall accuracy from 85.8% to 90.4% (P = .001). AI sensitivities ranged from 26.7% to 70.0%. PanDerm sensitivity increased to 96.7% after linear probing on the study dataset.


LIMITATIONS
Retrospective single-center design and potential recall bias.


CONCLUSION
PCP is a reproducible and readily teachable dermatoscopic criterion that significantly improves the recognition of flat pigmented facial BCC.
evidence_items.title: Perifollicular Crescentic Pigmentation Improves Recognition of Flat Pigmented Facial Basal Cell Carcinoma: A Dermatoscopic Training and Artificial Intelligence Study.

evidence_items.summary: Lateral cephalometric analysis is necessary for proper orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning. Classically it depends upon manual landmark identification on radiographs, which is time consuming, relies on expert skills. Accordingly, this study aimed to create and evaluate a deep learning model for automated cephalometric assessment using lateral profile photographs as a radiation free alternative. A total of 1,350 dataset was used to train a dual task model using HRNetV2 combined with an Adaptive Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) to predict 19 landmark coordinates. The model was tested using 150 unseen photographs to evaluate the Mean Radial Error (MRE), Successful Detection Rate (SDR), Mean Absolute Error of the angular and linear measurements and classification accuracy. The HRNetV2 + MLP model combination achieved a mean radial error of 2.317 ± 1.80 mm, with SDRs at the 2 mm and 4 mm thresholds were 53.8% and 84.5%, respectively. The ANB angle demonstrated Mean absolute error of 1.46º. Bland-Altman analysis revealed minimal systematic bias between AI and Dolphin measurements across most cephalometric variables. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of automated landmark detection and analysis from lateral facial photographs and support further investigation of the photographic-based approaches thus eliminating radiographic exposures.
evidence_items.title: Assessment of an artificial intelligence model designed for prediction of lateral cephalometric measurements from lateral photographs

evidence_items.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) holds unprecedented potential to transform the entire Alzheimer's Disease and related dementias (ADRD) research and care continuum. During the 2025 Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease (CTAD) conference, the CTAD Task Force reviewed recent advances in the field, highlighting the emerging role of agentic AI, and discussed priorities to guide future AI-driven innovation in ADRD. Agentic AI co-scientists are emerging as transformative tools to accelerate scientific discovery by autonomously integrating multimodal data, generating and evaluating new hypotheses, and connecting previously siloed knowledge into actionable insights. Operationalized through end-to-end translational pipelines, such platforms can also link mechanistic insights to therapeutic design by automating molecular docking and drug repurposing. Complementary initiatives are creating digital wet labs for in silico experimentation. At the same time, agentic AI is increasingly being used to address pre-discovery bottlenecks by automating data harmonization and inferring missing information through digital twins and synthetic data. AI is also reshaping next-generation ADRD clinical trials, through automated assessment of clinical outcomes, precision participant stratification, individualized disease trajectory modeling and prediction of treatment response. These approaches could substantially improve trial efficiency through responder enrichment. Importantly, AI applications are expanding beyond discovery and clinical trials to support diagnosis, care navigation, and personalized disease management. To translate the momentum surrounding AI innovation into meaningful and sustainable impact across the ADRD continuum, the Task Force identified priorities including the development of AI-ready ecosystems, closer collaboration between clinicians, researchers and computer scientists, AI-enabled optimization of clinical trials and robust ethical and governance frameworks for responsible AI adoption.
evidence_items.title: Advancing the Alzheimer's disease research and care pipeline with agentic artificial intelligence: Opportunities, challenges, and priorities from the international clinical trials on Alzheimer's disease (CTAD) task force.

evidence_items.summary: Patient-positioning errors can distort panoramic radiographs and lead to repeat examinations. This study investigated artificial intelligence for correcting these errors in existing images. A physics-based simulator generated paired correctly positioned and mispositioned panoramics from cone-beam computed tomography volumes, with controlled individual and combined positioning errors. Five approaches were compared: U-Net, pix2pix, conditional diffusion, an error-conditioned model, and a mixture of error-specific specialists. Evaluation used image similarity and geometric metrics across three test sets. All approaches improved mean image similarity and reduced geometric errors, with U-Net and the two error-aware approaches outperforming pix2pix and conditional diffusion.
evidence_items.title: Fix, Don't Retake: Physics-Simulated Training for Correcting Patient Positioning Errors in Dental Panoramic Radiographs

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence is entering the home. Cloud-based assistants face governance limitations in data transmission, continuous availability, and the reliability of physical actions, which are especially salient in households where devices remain online, data accumulate over time, and commands trigger real-world actions. Using the home local server as a unifying organizing axis, this article develops a design-oriented review framework. Sources from arXiv, CNKI, ACL Anthology, and official documentation were searched through November 2026 and coded into five evidence categories: reviews, system prototypes, benchmarks, HCI and eldercare studies, and official documentation. System designs were mapped onto shared architectural modules, identifying nine recurrent responsibilities of the home local server. Generative models support perceptual interpretation, intent understanding, and candidate planning, while deterministic validation, knowledge-graph constraints, and authorization leases confine candidate actions to an inspectable space. Home control, emotional companionship, and intelligent guarding can be compared within a common framework: they share state and memory but differ in latency, false positive and negative rates, proactivity, and permissions. Existing benchmarks rely on virtual environments and cannot substitute for real-deployment evaluation. Local deployment is not inherently safer, and technical continuity alone does not establish the social or medical effects of companionship and guarding. The article proposes a five-dimensional evaluation framework covering architectural capability, system resources, privacy, safety and reliability, and human experience, together with six design principles and a future research agenda for local-first intelligent home systems.
evidence_items.title: A Generative AI-Driven Architecture for Whole-Home Intelligent Services: Edge Models, Memory Management, and Household Applications

evidence_items.summary: Research on artificial intelligence–based computer-aided diagnosis and clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) is expanding, but integrated evidence on publication patterns, keyword trajectories, online search activity, and methodological characteristics remains limited. To characterize AI-CDSS research by integrating bibliometric analysis, Google Trends comparison, and structured content analysis of citation-ranked publications. Scholarly interest was assessed using bibliometric analysis of Web of Science records from 2016 through August 2026, including author-keyword co-occurrence, bibliographic coupling, and reference co-citation, whereas Google Trends was used to characterize online search activity. A structured content analysis of citation-ranked publications was conducted to examine applications, methodological characteristics, and reported limitations. We analyzed 19,809 included publications from 2016 through August 2026. Output rose approximately 21-fold, from 193 records in 2016 to 4,082 in 2025. Output was geographically concentrated within the included corpus, with a Gini coefficient of 0.869. Among records with identifiable corresponding-author country or territory, China, the United States, and India accounted for 61.33%. Scientific Reports was the most frequent source (n = 916). Frequent artificial intelligence– and diagnosis-related keywords included machine learning (n = 5,666), deep learning (n = 4,022), and computer-aided diagnosis (n = 1,512). Bibliographic coupling identified 15 publication communities, and reference co-citation identified seven reference communities. In the monthly level-series comparison, 9 of 10 keyword concepts exhibited significant associations with Google Trends relative search interest, but none of the 10 first-difference associations remained significant after Bonferroni adjustment. Content analysis of 215 citation-ranked publications, including 191 empirical publications, showed frequent use of convolutional neural networks in diagnostic and radiology applications. Common limitations included limited external validation, infrequent calibration reporting, and sparse workflow-level or impact evaluation. AI-CDSS research has rapidly expanded around machine learning, deep learning, and diagnostic applications, but the analyzed citation-ranked publications provide more evidence of methodological development than of clinical deployment. Integrating bibliometric, search-activity, and content-based perspectives shows limited short-term correspondence between online search activity and scholarly keyword use and highlights the need to move beyond model development toward independent external validation, prospective workflow and patient-outcome evaluation, calibration, fairness, and postdeployment monitoring.
evidence_items.title: Mapping Research on AI-Based Computer-Aided Diagnosis and Clinical Decision Support Systems: a Bibliometric Study Integrating Google Trends and Content Analysis

evidence_items.summary:
OBJECTIVES
This study aims to improve the efficiency of title and abstract screening in systematic literature reviews (SLRs) supporting European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) recommendations and points to consider, by developing and validating stopping criteria for active learning-assisted screening that achieve ≥95% recall (ie, sensitivity).


METHODS
Simulation studies analysed 40 development and 5 validation datasets (202,177 records) from completed and ongoing EULAR SLRs, using active learning models (h3, u3, and u4) in ASReview. Time-to-event analyses estimated the proportion of records that required screening to reach 95% recall and the minimum safe streak length (longest sequence of irrelevant records before reaching 95% recall). Empirical stopping criteria were derived, tested on independent datasets and evaluated for workload reduction and time savings.


RESULTS
Datasets averaged 4493 records (SD, 2851), with a mean of 67 (SD, 46) records included. The u4 model was optimal for balancing screening efficacy and computational efficiency. Target recall was achieved after screening 35% of records or reaching sequences of 15% nonrelevant records. A combined criterion (26% screened plus 10% irrelevant streak) provided an alternative stopping criterion. Validation met target recall. Screening workload was reduced by 67.1%.


CONCLUSIONS
Empirically derived stopping criteria using an active learning tool can substantially accelerate SLR screening while maintaining high recall (≥95%), allowing reviewers to skip about two-thirds of records during title and abstract screening. Artificial intelligence-assisted screening can substantially reduce evidence synthesis workload, thus supporting more efficient development of EULAR recommendations and points to consider.
evidence_items.title: AI-supported screening for systematic literature reviews informing EULAR recommendations and points to consider.

evidence_items.summary: Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) adapts a model trained on a labelled source domain to an unlabelled target domain without access to the source data. Almost the entire SFDA literature assumes mutually exclusive classes, yet many deployed settings are multi-label. This paper formulates SFDA for multi-label classification and establishes the first benchmark for it: five adaptation tasks over six datasets spanning remote sensing, natural, clipart-style and driving imagery, with four single-label SFDA methods extended to provide the first baselines and a published multi-label method run alongside them, over three seeds. The benchmark shows that extending a single-label method is unreliable rather than merely suboptimal: half of the extended baselines fail to improve on the unadapted source model at all, and on two of the five tasks none of them does. The failures are not incidental. Nearest-centroid pseudo-labelling, softmax-based confidence, the diversity term of information maximization and confidence-weighted prototype construction each rely on mutual exclusivity, and each fails differently without it, so replacing the softmax with per-class sigmoids is a valid but insufficient extension. Multi-label Prototype Alignment with Contrastive Teaching (MPACT) is proposed in response, a mean-teacher framework whose objective, prototype construction and alignment term are each reconsidered for overlapping label sets. It attains the best average on every reported metric and is the only method that improves on the unadapted source model on all five tasks. The analysis further introduces a prototype-agreement diagnostic separating feature-space alignment from self-reinforcing agreement with the classifier, and reports a negative result for confidence-based pseudo-label filtering.
evidence_items.title: Source-Free Domain Adaptation for Multi-Label Image Classification: A Framework, Baselines, and Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: A robot's actions change the thermal conditions of its next interaction: heat retained after release, carried with objects or stored beneath the surface can change a later contact's outcome despite similar current temperatures. Training trajectories must capture how these effects connect earlier actions to later observations and task outcomes. We present TRR, a \emph{Thermal Robot Renderer} that attaches spatial and depth-resolved thermal state to both contact partners, updates local heat exchange through contact, transport and separation, and generates synchronized RGB--thermal (RGBT) observations and event-local task checks on one execution clock. Controlled interventions show why retained heat, spatial transport and internal storage matter for subsequent contact outcomes. From the same state, TRR produces a paired six-task benchmark of 2,224 static--dynamic pairs, that is, 4,448 trajectories with synchronized dual-view observations, states and actions. Visible thermal history raises safe contact-site selection from 75.0\% to 91.7\% on a dedicated learning corpus, and training on dynamic histories raises simulated transfer completion by 50 percentage points under a new heating procedure with shared feedback execution. We demonstrate RGBT observation adapters on MuJoCo and Isaac Sim, report an engineering inventory of ten prepared robot configurations and six demonstrated camera viewpoints, and describe a developer workflow that carries an existing robot scene to exported RGBT records. The benchmark, the workflow and the platform resources described in Section 6 form the first items of a planned public release. Demonstrations and resource updates are available on the project page.
evidence_items.title: TRR: A Thermal Interaction Engine for Robot Simulation and RGBT Data Generation

evidence_items.summary: This paper focuses on identifying useful indicators for nowcasting GDP in Sweden. We analyze 36 monthly indicators and their nowcast performance for the period 2003Q1 to 2025Q4 in a pseudo real-time setting. Additionally, we examine two distinct periods: from 2003Q1 to 2018Q4 (pre-pandemic) and from 2019Q1 to 2025Q4 (pandemic and post-pandemic). The analysis is conducted using mixed-data sampling (MIDAS) and mixed-frequency VAR models and we evaluate the pooled predictions from the model for each indicator to robustify against model misspecification. For nowcasting we identify 24 indicators that improve on the AR-benchmark and 11 that are particularly useful. Splitting the evaluation sample in the pre-pandemic and pandemic and post-pandemic periods we find that the results differ substantially with more indicators improving on the benchmark in the pandemic and post-pandemic period than in the pre-pandemic period. In addition, the set of highly informative indicators is quite different in the two periods.
evidence_items.title: Identifying Useful Indicators for Nowcasting GDP in Sweden

evidence_items.summary:
MOTIVATION
Accurate molecular property prediction (MPP) remains a central challenge in drug discovery. Given the limited availability of labeled molecular data, multimodal molecular representation learning offers a promising means of integrating complementary structural information for MPP. Existing multimodal models still face two limitations: (i) common fusion strategies, particularly direct concatenation, can introduce redundant information or signals that are weakly relevant to the target property; and (ii) the effective incorporation of complementary physicochemical priors into multimodal representations remains insufficiently explored.


RESULTS
Here, we proposed ReMoD-Mol, a reliability-aware multimodal framework that integrated molecular graphs, SMILES sequences and two-dimensional molecular images. Task-adaptive modality calibration learned one set of weights per benchmark from downstream supervision to regulate the relative contributions of the three molecular views. Descriptor- and fingerprint-based teachers further provided task-conditioned chemical priors through train-only, five-fold out-of-fold knowledge distillation. Prototype-guided embedding shaping together with graph-view and SMILES-view consistency objectives regularized the fused representation space. Across nine MoleculeNet benchmark datasets spanning regression and classification, ReMoD-Mol achieved the best mean performance on seven datasets and the second-best on the other two in a scaffold-split comparison with 14 baselines. Representation analyses revealed smoother property-related manifolds and more discriminative class structures, while learned modality coefficients exhibited distinct task-dependent fusion patterns. Teacher-prior and ablation analyses further supported the complementary roles of chemical-prior transfer and multi-view representation regularization.


AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION
Source code, processed datasets and implementation details are publicly available at https://github.com/27167199/ReMoD-Mol.
evidence_items.title: ReMoD-Mol: Reliability-Aware Multimodal Learning with Descriptor-Guided Knowledge Distillation for Molecular Property Prediction.

evidence_items.summary:
OBJECTIVE
To assess whether minimally invasive surgical therapies (MISTs) for benign prostatic obstruction (BPO) provide objective relief of bladder outlet obstruction beyond symptomatic improvement.


METHODS
We conducted a narrative review of the literature using PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase and the Cochrane Library to identify studies evaluating medical therapy, conventional surgery, and MISTs for BPO. Evidence was assessed across three complementary levels: conventional functional outcomes, including maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax) and post-void residual volume; direct urodynamic evidence from pressure-flow studies and the bladder outlet obstruction index (BOOI); and restoration of spontaneous voiding in catheter-dependent patients.


RESULTS
Medical therapy produced clinically meaningful symptom improvement but relatively modest urodynamic deobstruction, with a pooled BOOI reduction of approximately 14 points for alpha-blockers. Conventional tissue-removing surgery represented the upper benchmark, with BOOI reductions exceeding 70 points reported after holmium laser enucleation of the prostate. Among established MISTs, prostatic artery embolization and prostatic urethral lift demonstrated improvement in pressure-flow parameters, although deobstruction was frequently incomplete. Rezūm currently has the most consistent paired pressure-flow data, with BOOI reductions of approximately 49-54 points in two studies. In contrast, no paired pre- and post-treatment pressure-flow data were identified for iTind, transperineal laser ablation, or Optilume BPH. In catheter-dependent patients, reported catheter-free rates ranged from 66% to 100% across MIST studies, compared with rates approaching 99% after HoLEP, although substantial heterogeneity precludes direct comparisons.


CONCLUSION
Symptomatic efficacy of MISTs should not be considered synonymous with physiological deobstruction. Available evidence suggests a continuum of deobstructive efficacy, while direct pressure-flow evidence remains limited for most technologies. Incorporating urodynamic assessment in selected patients in future trials could better characterize the physiological effects of MISTs and inform treatment selection.
evidence_items.title: Minimally invasive surgical therapies for benign prostatic obstruction: truly deobstructive? A narrative review from the French LUTS Committee (CTMH).

evidence_items.summary: Revoking the authority of a delegated agent is not the same as proving that no consequential effect can still be committed under that authority. A revocation cut applied at one resource sink is not evidence of enforcement at another sink, and a software acknowledgement from a sink is only as trustworthy as the software that produced it. This document defines the Attested Fence Receipt (AFR), an Entity Attestation Token (EAT) profile emitted by the hardware-rooted Attesting Environment of a consequential sink after the sink has durably applied an authority-epoch fence. It further defines a verification procedure for individual receipts, a closure- evaluation procedure over a declared sink set that yields CLOSED, PARTIAL, FAILED, or UNKNOWN, and a hardware fence profile that binds the fence to measured state: an extend-only authority register, a monotonic counter, counter-gated derivation of per-epoch effect- attestation keys, and PCR-bound key release. The mechanism supplies the per-sink evidence that revocation-closure determinations require, and it is designed so that the absence of evidence can never be read as closure. evidence_items.summary: The assessment of tourism and recreational resources constitutes an essential methodological foundation for territorial development planning, enhancing tourism competitiveness, and ensuring environmental sustainability. A central research challenge lies in integrating natural, historical-cultural, socioeconomic, and infrastructural resources into a coherent assessment framework while preserving their qualitative distinctions and avoiding the overestimation of territorial development potential. This study aims to refine the conceptual and mathematical foundations of integrated tourism and recreational resource assessment and to develop an evaluation model adapted to the requirements of sustainable management. The methodological approach incorporates indicator-based assessment, normalization, weighted aggregation, comparative analysis of tourism pressure and carrying capacity, seasonality assessment, and the measurement of value added generated within the local economy. The study proposes a three-level analytical framework that distinguishes resource potential, constraints on sustainable utilization, and management effectiveness. The proposed model represents a methodological construct rather than an empirically validated universal assessment instrument. Its practical validation requires territorial data, theoretically justified indicator selection, and sensitivity analysis.
evidence_items.title: INTEGRATED ASSESSMENT AND SUSTAINABLE MANAGEMENT OF TOURISM AND RECREATIONAL RESOURCES IN A REGION: METHODOLOGICAL FOUNDATIONS, CONSTRAINTS, AND DEVELOPMENT PROSPECTS

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence is expanding the technological capabilities available to law-enforcement organizations, including investigative analysis, facial recognition, automated documentation, surveillance, and decision support. These developments offer potential operational benefits while introducing concerns involving accuracy, evidentiary reliability, algorithmic bias, privacy, constitutional protections, professional accountability, and public trust. This white paper examines the responsible adoption and governance of artificial intelligence in law enforcement through an evidence-informed analysis of technical research, governmental oversight findings, legal principles, and institutional risk-management guidance. Particular attention is given to meaningful human oversight, organizational leadership, procedural justice, community perceptions, and the experiences of historically underserved populations. Drawing upon established governance principles, the paper proposes thirteen policy recommendations and an original six-phase implementation framework: Define, Assess, Govern, Pilot, Monitor, and Reassess. The framework is presented as a proposed organizational synthesis rather than an empirically validated intervention. The analysis identifies limitations in existing research and priorities for future investigation, including the relationship between AI-assisted policing, institutional legitimacy, and willingness to seek law-enforcement assistance. The paper concludes that technological innovation should be evaluated according to demonstrated public value, lawful authority, evidentiary integrity, professional judgment, and continuing organizational accountability.
evidence_items.title: AI Is Entering the Police Department: Where Should Law Enforcement Draw the Line?

evidence_items.summary: This article examines automated DOCX formatting subject to the preservation of document content and internal structure. The capabilities of word processor styles, document conversion tools and the python-docx library are reviewed. Analysis of an earlier Word formatter implementation identifies risks associated with overwriting paragraph content and insufficient input file validation. An approach is proposed that combines a separate formatting profile, structure-based scope selection, element-specific rules and output verification. Requirements for content preservation and repeated rule application are formalized. Opportunities to reduce redundant operations are identified, and a methodology is developed for comparing manual formatting, the baseline application and an improved version. Evaluation covers total task time, profile conformity and subsequent manual corrections. The research yields a process model and verification requirements. Quantitative performance gains remain to be established in a subsequent experiment.
evidence_items.title: OPTIMIZING PROGRAMMATIC DOCX FORMATTING WHILE PRESERVING DOCUMENT STRUCTURE

evidence_items.summary: Digital twins have become a central paradigm for cultural heritage documentation, monitoring, and preventive preservation. Yet, when cultural heritage systems promise prediction, simulation, intervention planning, and decision support, a more explicit account is needed of the computational commitments behind such claims. This position paper proposes the notion of the heritage world model as a conceptual and architectural abstraction that uses the semantic digital twin as its representational layer and extends it toward prediction, memory, uncertainty-aware reasoning, and intervention evaluation. We define a heritage world model as a structured, temporally updated, semantically grounded, and action-aware model of a heritage asset and its preservation environment, capable of integrating observations, estimating latent risk states, predicting plausible future trajectories, and evaluating interventions under uncertainty. The paper does not present a validated deployed system. Rather, it clarifies the architectural conditions under which a decision-support digital twin infrastructure could support the kind of world-model-like preservation system proposed here. It further argues that such a model becomes operationally meaningful only when it includes a human-supervised controller layer that maps semantic state, predicted risk trajectories, uncertainty, memory, and institutional constraints into preservation-relevant actions, alerts, monitoring adaptations, or requests for expert review. Sensor data, remote sensing, computational models, risk assessments, policies, and conservation actions are interpreted as possible observational, dynamic, and intervention layers of a heritage world model. The paper reviews adjacent work in heritage digital twins, semantic and reactive ontologies, risk-aware preservation, agentic AI, and modern AI world models, and proposes a research agenda for moving toward predictive, memory-bearing, and intervention-aware preservation intelligence.
evidence_items.title: Towards Heritage World Models

evidence_items.summary: This record contains the analysis code and supporting metadata for a study assessing the feasibility of reintroducing Sitatunga ( Tragelaphus spekii ) to Rugezi Marsh, Rwanda. The R code reproduces all analyses reported in the associated manuscript: the cover-weighted range-condition index, ecological grazing- and carrying-capacity estimates, a composite habitat-suitability index, a stochastic stage-structured population viability analysis (PVA), and the full suite of statistical tests (Shapiro-Wilk, Levene/Brown-Forsythe, Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn, Mann-Whitney, chi-square, and Moran's I). Also included are the complete species list of 130 plant taxa, with family, taxonomic authority, ITIS Taxonomic Serial Numbers, and GBIF backbone keys, and the taxonomic-matching script. The primary vegetation dataset, which contains plot coordinates within the Rugezi Marsh Ramsar site and is owned by the Rwanda Wildlife Conservation Association (RWCA), is deposited separately under controlled access.
evidence_items.title: Data and code for an integrated habitat-suitability and population-viability framework for Sitatunga reintroduction, Rugezi Marsh, Rwanda

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The systematics of the Eurasian Late Pliocene – Early Pleistocene monkey Paradolichopithecus is a long-debated topic in primate paleontology. This taxon’s phylogenetic position has implications for our understanding of cercopithecid evolution: while it is often regarded as a baboon-like Macacina, an alternative taxonomic attribution to the Papionina subtribe has been proposed. This would challenge the commonly accepted hypothesis that baboons constitute an endemic African clade. Here, we reconstructed the face of the subadult female DFN3-150 Paradolichopithecus aff. arvernensis cranium from the Lower Pleistocene site Dafnero (Greece), using novel virtual techniques and following alternative protocols. We performed a geometric morphometrics investigation of its morphological affinities with two extant papionin genera. Our results allow for a critical evaluation of the two applied retrodeformation protocols and support stronger facial morphological similarities with Papio spp. than macaques. This is in agreement with recent studies evaluating its phenotypic and ecological traits. Nevertheless, direct inferences on phylogenetic affinities require a larger and more diverse papionin sample.
evidence_items.title: Virtual reconstruction and analysis of the face of DFN3-150 Paradolichopithecus aff. arvernensis specimen from Dafnero, Greece

evidence_items.summary: Two-channel triboelectric nanogenerator (TENG) tactile signals recorded with the TTS-Grip two-jaw robotic gripper during repeated grasping of objects from six material classes (ceramic, glass, metal, organic, paper, plastic; three objects per class). The two single-electrode TENG sensors (silicone contact layer with an embedded carbon-cloth electrode) are integrated in the gripper fingers; signals were RC-filtered and read as raw 10-bit ADC values by an Arduino Mega 2560. The record contains: (1) raw continuous recordings per object (18 CSV files) and per class (6 CSV files); (2) 900 grayscale 2D tactile images (150 per class) built from segmented, min-max normalized grasp windows, as used to train the 2D CNN; and (3) 14 recordings at 50-55%, 65-70%, and 80-85% relative humidity with four materials. See README.md inside TTS-Grip TENG signals.zip for the file structure and label definitions. This dataset supports the article "TTS-Grip: A triboelectric tactile smart gripper with self-powered sensing for visuo-tactile material recognition" (S. Oralkhan, M. Zabirova, S. Liu, Z. Kappassov, G. Kalimuldina, A. Yeshmukhametov, Z. Wen), submitted to Sensors and Actuators A: Physical.
evidence_items.title: TTS-Grip triboelectric tactile dataset: two-channel TENG grasp signals, 2D tactile images, and humidity recordings for six material classes

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains the data, trained model and Python code supporting the satellite TSS retrieval in “Flood scale shifts in suspended-solids anomalies and signal transmission through a gated weir cascade.” The study reconstructs total suspended solids (TSS) along Korea’s Nakdong River using Harmonized Landsat–Sentinel-2 (HLS) imagery and hydrologic and spatial predictors. The calibration dataset contains 5,567 observations from 31 main-stem stations and six reservoir stations. The deposit includes: Satellite–in situ matchups, the predictor matrix and observation metadata. One trained production model and Python scripts for model fitting and scene-level TSS retrieval. River centerlines, a long-term water-voting raster and 487 fixed sampling points. Nested five-fold cross-validation and leave-one-flood-event-out validation records, including outer and inner splits, the hyperparameter search specification, selected configurations and held-out predictions. Fixed-setting leave-one-station-out results and final SHAP and RFECV summaries. Standalone checking utilities and SHAP/RFECV intermediate outputs are omitted. The included analysis scripts can regenerate these intermediate outputs locally. Extract code.zip and data.zip into the same directory. README.txt provides execution instructions, data sources and methodological details, including the distinction between nested validation and the final reconstruction model. This deposit covers model training, validation and satellite retrieval. Raw HLS imagery, complete agency hydrologic records and the full downstream flood-analysis workflow are not included. Author-written code is distributed under the MIT License, and author-created data products under CC BY 4.0. Third-party data remain subject to their respective source terms.
evidence_items.title: Data and code for "Flood scale shifts in suspended-solids anomalies and signal transmission through a gated weir cascade"

evidence_items.summary: Cultural heritage assets are exposed to diverse environmental, structural, geological, biological, and anthropogenic threats, yet IoT monitoring strategies remain largely site-specific. This study presents and evaluates the ARGUS framework, a threat-oriented methodology that defines monitoring requirements according to deterioration mechanisms rather than monument typology. The framework integrates heritage characterization, risk assessment, threat-to-sensor mapping, and IoT deployment and was evaluated across five contrasting European heritage sites. Priority threats identified through preliminary risk assessment were compared with evidence obtained from environmental, structural, and operational monitoring. Most prioritized threats were observed during monitoring, whereas some were less significant than anticipated or could not be evaluated within the available monitoring windows. Cross-site comparison revealed recurring temporal associations between environmental forcing and material or structural responses and showed that heritage assets affected by similar deterioration mechanisms were monitored with comparable sensor configurations despite differences in typology, materials, and geographical setting. These recurring configurations were consolidated into candidate monitoring packages addressing moisture, climatic exposure, structural stability, pollution, and operational pressures, whose transferability to independent sites remains to be tested. The results provide preliminary evidence supporting the feasibility of a threat-oriented approach for translating conservation risks into targeted monitoring strategies, supporting risk-informed preventive conservation across heterogeneous cultural heritage contexts.
evidence_items.title: Advanced IoT Monitoring for Cultural Heritage: Evaluation of a Threat-Oriented Monitoring Framework Across Five European Heritage Sites

evidence_items.summary: Importance Hospital discharge summaries are essential for continuity of care, but fragmented electronic health record (EHR) data can compromise their quality and safety. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for clinical documentation tasks despite limited evidence regarding their performance in health care settings compared with the current standard of care. Objective To evaluate clinician acceptability of LLM-generated discharge summaries derived from EHRs compared with routine clinician-written summaries. Design, Setting, and Participants In this retrospective comparative effectiveness study using a prespecified noninferiority framework, acceptability of LLM-generated discharge summaries was compared with clinician-authored discharge summaries. Admission records from 5 London hospitals for September 1, 2022, to September 30, 2023, were evaluated against the full admission record by practicing physicians. Admissions were eligible only if the clinician-authored discharge summary contained identifiable clinical summary, plan and requested actions, and information given sections. Data analysis was conducted from July 2025 to February 2026. Intervention LLM-generated summaries were produced using GPT-4o mini (July 18, 2024 release; OpenAI) and a clinician-codesigned prompt. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was clinician signoff with no or minor edits, derived from 2 sequential questions: (1) whether the reviewer would sign the summary and (2) whether no, minor, or major edits were required. A 5–percentage-point noninferiority margin was prespecified. Secondary outcomes assessed accuracy, completeness, tone, and clarity (using a 5-point Likert scale: 1, poor; 2, fair; 3, good; 4, very good; and 5, excellent) and potential harmfulness of missing or incorrect information (using a 5-point Likert scale: 1, no harm; 2, minor harm; 3, moderate harm; 4, high harm; and 5, extremely high harm).
evidence_items.title: Clinician Acceptance of Large Language Model–Generated Discharge Summaries

evidence_items.summary: Software issue resolution task aims to address real-world issues in software repositories based on natural language descriptions provided by users, representing a key aspect of software maintenance. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs) in reasoning and generative capabilities, LLM-based approaches have made significant progress in automated software issue resolution. However, real-world software issue resolution is inherently complex and requires long-horizon reasoning, iterative exploration, and feedback-driven decision-making that demand agentic capabilities beyond conventional single-step approaches. Recently, LLM-based agentic systems have become a promising research direction for software issue resolution, since the related literature has experienced explosive growth. Advancements in agentic software issue resolution not only greatly enhance software maintenance efficiency and quality but also provide a realistic environment for validating agentic systems’ reasoning, planning, and execution capabilities, bridging AI and software engineering. This work presents a systematic survey of 242 recent studies at the forefront of LLM-based agentic software issue resolution research. It outlines the general workflow of the task and establishes a taxonomy across three dimensions: benchmarks, techniques, and empirical studies. Furthermore, it highlights how reinforcement learning has become an increasingly important training paradigm for agentic systems in software engineering. Finally, it summarizes key challenges and outlines promising directions for future research. The artifacts’ page accompanying this survey is at https://github.com/ZhonghaoJiang/Awesome-Issue-Solving.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Software Issue Resolution with Large Language Models: A Survey

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal agents can now control robot arms by calling tools and writing code. Existing benchmarks fall short in three ways: most test one or two arms on short tasks, many pause the world while the agent thinks, and many give it ground-truth object positions. We present RoboTeam, a simulated benchmark where agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone. Its 36 tasks are long jobs that the arms must do together, such as passing timbers or building a picture from hundreds of cubes. We start from the most flexible agent system, the adaptive system, where one agent decides when to fork delegates. With it, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 tasks, and four other models at most 3. But at a high price: a typical task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. We then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized. All four complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. Even so, no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. RoboTeam measures these limits where earlier benchmarks cannot: long multi-arm jobs, camera images only, and a world that never pauses.
evidence_items.title: RoboTeam: Benchmarking Vision-Based Multi-Agent Control of Many Robot Arms in Real Time

evidence_items.summary: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.
evidence_items.title: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.
evidence_items.title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?

evidence_items.summary: Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop a multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. At the high level, we train a vision-language planner and design a speech-based leader-follower coordination mechanism to synchronize decentralized execution without network communication. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-Bench, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that Heave-Ho consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks.
evidence_items.title: Heave-Ho: Decentralized Long-Horizon Multi-Humanoid Collaboration

evidence_items.summary: π^4 is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild---a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence---it recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. It couples a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch, which predicts image-space correspondences that are lifted into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry. Across diverse benchmarks, π^4 achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation, alongside competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation. With a shared backbone, the full geometry-and-motion system contains approximately 0.5B parameters---less than half the size of most baselines. It produces joint reconstructions and tracks in one forward pass, including large-scale scenes with thousands of input images despite training with contexts of at most 64 views. We further present the data and training recipe underlying these capabilities, together with empirical studies of key design choices. Code and models are available at https://github.com/yyfz/Pi4.
evidence_items.title: π^4: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion

evidence_items.summary: Tasks, specifications, references, test sets, mutants, sandbox harness, generation and analysis code, and summary data of the benchmark Time and money in LLM-generated code, behind the paper Passing Tests Is Not Enough: An Empirical Study of Hidden Date, Time and Money Failures in LLM-Generated Code. evidence_items.summary: Parsons problems have been widely recognised to support novice learners by reducing the cognitive demands of writing code from scratch through rearrangement of provided code blocks. A common variation includes distractors – erroneous blocks of code which do not belong to the correct solution. While Parsons problems have been widely studied for introductory programming, they remain underexplored in various domains including in data science education, where students may possess statistical knowledge but limited programming experience. Developing distractors is also time-consuming for educators. This study investigated the feasibility of using a large language model (LLM) to generate semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems. A set of distractors was generated for 315 Python-based data science Parsons problems and was evaluated for pedagogical plausibility, compilability, and output divergence. Validated distractors were then incorporated as exemplars in a refined prompt to generate a second set of distractors, which were evaluated using the same criteria. The findings demonstrate that LLMs can be used to develop semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems and refining the prompts using validated exemplars further improved the quality. This study contributes to the limited literature on data science Parsons problems, distractor design and LLM-supported development of these problems.
evidence_items.title: Large language model generation of plausible semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background AI is increasingly impacting health care. Large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, have shown potential in supporting clinical decision-making. However, their application in dermatology, particularly in allergen avoidance counseling for contact dermatitis, remains underexplored. Objective This study aimed to demonstrate a potential use case for LLM responses in recommending allergen-free products for the management of contact allergies. Methods A total of 30 allergen groups included in the international standard patch test were assessed. ChatGPT (GPT-4) was used in this study from September 2023 to January 2024. For each allergen, ChatGPT was tasked with recommending 5 allergen-free products using 3 question formats of varying complexity. Responses were included if they specified a product and were manually classified by dermatologists into 5 categories: valid, invalid, cross-reaction, unknown, and unresponsive. Results ChatGPT provided 79.20% (1782/2250) valid responses, with 1.78% (40/2250) classified as invalid, 2% (45/2550) classified as cross-reactions, 8.67% (195/2250) classified as unknown, and 8.36% (188/2250) classified as unresponsive. The simplest question format yielded the highest proportion of valid recommendations (640/750, 85.33%). ChatGPT performed best when recommending cosmetics (1233/1365, 90.33%) and medications (198/240, 82.5%). However, lower validity rates were observed for recommendations involving certain sensitive allergens, including fragrance mixes and para-phenylenediamine (PPD), with frequent cross-reactive recommendations related to Peru balsam. Conclusions The version of ChatGPT evaluated in this study showed potential as a supplementary tool for allergen avoidance counseling. However, its recommendations require verification and should not replace clinician guidance or established allergen avoidance resources.
evidence_items.title: Using a Large Language Model Chatbot for Allergen Avoidance Counseling in Contact Dermatitis: Quantitative Evaluation Study

evidence_items.summary: Narratives are a universal part of natural human experience. As experimental stimuli, narratives allow scientists to study complex mental processes with direct relevance to everyday experience. These analyses typically require manual labeling of key event features. Such characterization of narrative stimuli are extremely labor-intensive and prone to subjectivity. Automated tools could reduce these difficulties and enable scaling to longer, varied stimuli by exposing the exact quantities computed. We address this by introducing a metric that uses open-weight LLMs to compute contextual information gain. Our metric correlates with human ratings of event importance and causal centrality, critically distinguishing the latter from semantic centrality, thus overcoming limitations of existing automated tools. The metric similarly captures shared coactivation in the default mode network, a network implicated in narrative comprehension. Taken together, these results validate an automated, empirically-grounded tool that researchers can use to identify behaviorally- and neurally-relevant computational quantities in naturalistic stimuli.
evidence_items.title: Scaling up naturalistic narrative research: A reproducible large language model-based tool for evaluating contextual information gain

evidence_items.summary: We evaluated Jev, a non-generative decision model, for title and abstract screening using 4527 records from two systematic reviews of bipolar disorder treatments previously used in our 2024 Journal of Medical Internet Research study. Human decisions to retain records for full-text assessment served as the reference. In the primary analysis, Jev answered yes-or-no questions (Noul); at a prespecified 50% cutoff, sensitivity and specificity were 99.6% and 98.9% for light therapy and 93.2% and 93.5% for adjunctive pharmacotherapy. For direct model comparison, Jev used explicit include/exclude options (Choice) and the same prompts as GPT-5 mini and GPT-6 Astra. Jev Choice achieved sensitivity and specificity similar to or higher than those of GPT-5 mini and GPT-6 Astra, while API charges per 1000 records were US$0.043 for Jev, US$0.57 for GPT-5 mini, and US$7.39 for GPT-6 Astra. Jev retained all reports ultimately included in both reviews across all tested conditions and runs. Although these findings do not establish that decision models can replace human reviewers, they support Jev as a promising, low-cost alternative to the tested generative LLM configurations for assisting human title and abstract screening. Independent validation across diverse review topics is needed to assess Jev’s generalizability and utility in human-supervised screening workflows.
evidence_items.title: Title and Abstract Screening for Systematic Reviews with Jev, a Decision Model: Comparison with Generative Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Mobile manipulators can move between storage locations and handle goods, but transferring the semantic capabilities of foundation models to dependable warehouse operations remains constrained by execution interfaces, data coverage, and operating conditions. This thematic critical review examines perception, reasoning, planning and execution, and data and generalization. It compares hierarchical approaches with vision-language-action models and assesses their relevance to warehouse tasks using representative studies. Its distinctive value lies in relating model interfaces and transfer limits to warehouse order fulfillment, where stock-keeping unit (SKU) verification, shelf access, and onboard resource limits must be considered together. The evidence indicates that foundation models reorganize selected interfaces between observations, task descriptions, and actions; they do not remove the need for geometric feasibility checks, low-level control, or failure recovery. Open-vocabulary recognition must be connected to item-level verification, while semantic generalization should be distinguished from the acquisition of new motor skills. Reported transfer gains also depend on the task, embodiment, and adaptation budget. The review identifies order completion, coordinated base-arm motion, and measurable adaptation costs as priorities for research and evaluation. These conclusions support method selection and experimental design rather than a claim of validated warehouse deployment.
evidence_items.title: Warehouse Mobile Manipulation with Large Language Models and Foundation Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Medical students often struggle transitioning from preclinical coursework to clinical environments. Simulation-based training can bridge this gap but can be resource intensive. Large language models (LLMs) provide a scalable resource that can augment traditional training. However, their effects on learning outcomes and student perceptions are currently not understood. This study aims to evaluate medical student knowledge acquisition and perception of the utility of simplified LLM-based clinical simulation. Methods Using the RISE framework, a structured simulation was designed to assess medical student knowledge of acute asthma exacerbation management. ZotGPT, an institutional GPT-4 based platform was utilized. Medical students completed pre- and post-simulation assessments assessing knowledge, confidence, and perceptions of simulation utility. Subgroup analysis was stratified by time spent completing the simulation. Statistical analyses included Wilcoxon signal-rank and McNemar tests. Results A total of 155 students participated. The simulation significantly improved perceived understanding of key treatment steps, including initial bronchodilator and steroid therapy (p = 0.001), magnesium sulfate escalation (p = 0.002), refractory management (p = 0.021), and discharge planning (p = 0.005). Students rated the simulation as more useful than non-simulation learning tools (p = 0.017) and noninferior to in-person simulation (p = 0.226). Confidence in asthma management increased (p < 0.001), but objective knowledge gains were not observed, with balanced correct-to-incorrect and incorrect-to-correct responses for intermediate steps. Longer engagement (> 600 seconds) was associated with greater perceived benefit. Simulations were deemed helpful for learning (94.7%), and most students preferred immediate feedback (68.4%).
evidence_items.title: Assessing the Learning Gains and User Experience of Large Language Model Simulations for Clinical Medical Education: A Pilot Observational Study

organizations: Sichuan Academy of Environmental Policy and Planning
evidence_items.summary: Abstract As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to gather, process and disseminate scientific information, concerns have grown about their identity-related biases. However, national-background biases in scientific evaluation remain insufficiently understood. Existing studies are limited to a narrow range of countries, abbreviated materials and/or simplified evaluation criteria, and have reported inconsistent findings. Moreover, differences in the textual evaluations generated by LLMs have seldom been quantified. Here, we used four popular LLMs to evaluate 292 full-text manuscripts from 28 journals across 8 research fields under 12 assigned national backgrounds, yielding 14,016 manuscript assessments, each covering 28 evaluative dimensions. Further comment-based rescoring tests were conducted to quantify differences in their textual evaluations. The results showed systematic differences in both scores and comments despite unchanged scientific content, with the magnitude and statistical significance these differences varying across national backgrounds. Under different national backgrounds, LLMs could offer different views on the same issue, and give different scores alongside similar textual evaluation. Researchers and decision-makers should be aware of these biases associated with source identity, including national background, when using LLMs for information gathering and processing.
evidence_items.title: National-background bias in scientific evaluation based on large language models
Benchmark for self-organized criticality

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being considered as tools for computational social science, yet their implications for survey and public-opinion research remain insufficiently understood. This study examines whether and how they can serve as methodological instruments for estimating aggregate public opinion under out-of-sample conditions. Across three studies, commercial and open-source LLMs are evaluated against recent Pew Research Centre surveys. Study 1 shows that GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 can approximate national-level response distributions more accurately than uniform, normal-distribution, and historical-average baselines, with GPT-4 achieving mean absolute errors of approximately 4–8.5%. However, the models also exhibit important threats to validity, including underrepresentation of Republican viewpoints, underestimation of uncertainty, and, in some cases, overly homogeneous response distributions. Study 2 extends the analysis to GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, and Llama 3.3, showing that aggregate predictive accuracy generalises across models but that partisan alignment and distributional fidelity are model- and topic-dependent. Study 3 demonstrates that collective-level estimation is more valid than aggregating persona-based individual simulations, which produce substantially higher error and stronger homogeneity bias. Ablation tests further indicate that predictions are relatively robust to role prompts and temperature settings but sensitive to survey-item context. These findings suggest that LLMs may be useful as exploratory and supplementary tools in public-opinion research. However, the responsible use of LLMs requires explicit validation against human data, attention to bias and uncertainty, and careful integration with established principles of survey design.
evidence_items.title: Public opinion surveys with large language models: methodological opportunities and validity risks

organizations: Surgery, David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, Los Angeles, CA
evidence_items.summary: In December 2025, the Food and Drug Administration assessed and qualified the first artificial intelligence (AI)-powered tool for use in drug development trials; this AI system evaluates digital liver biopsies for steatohepatitis and fibrosis. However, AI is still being investigated before it can be applied directly to patient care in the field of Hepatology. Current patient-facing applications at most institutions are limited to assistive tools such as computer-aided polyp detection and large language model documentation tools that draft clinic notes and patient communications, although there exist radiographic and pathologic liver AI tools that could function at and may even exceed human capabilities. This review provides a broad introduction to AI and highlights clinical research that use AI to enhance the diagnosis, prognostication, and management of liver diseases. It will also discuss the challenges that will need to be overcome before AI can be adopted to clinical practice.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Hepatology

organizations: The University of Western Australia, School of Physics, Mathematics and Computing A , , , .
evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML) and, more recently, generative AI (GenAI) models are becoming increasingly prevalent in the healthcare setting. For microbiology professionals, these technologies create opportunities to improve diagnostic workflows, analyse complex laboratory data, support education and professional development, summarise evidence, and assist with quality improvement. They also introduce risks, including automation bias, data leakage, poor generalisability, hallucinated or unverifiable outputs, privacy breaches, and unclear accountability. This article proposes a practical curriculum framework for microbiology professionals that treats GenAI as a distinct educational priority rather than a minor extension of conventional data, statistics or ML training. The curriculum framework is organised around six domains: (1) foundations of AI, ML and GenAI; (2) microbiology data and knowledge literacy; (3) critical appraisal, validation and evaluation; (4) responsible use of GenAI in microbiology practice and education; (5) implementation, governance, regulation and professional accountability; and (6) communication, collaboration and lifelong learning. The goal is not to train every microbiology professional as a data scientist. The aim is to develop AI-literate practitioners who can critically evaluate tools, use GenAI safely, participate in governance, communicate uncertainty, and ensure that AI-enabled practice remains grounded in microbiological expertise and patient safety.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence literacy for microbiology professionals

organizations: Department of Hospital Therapeutic Dentistry, Tashkent State Medical University, Tashkent, Uzbekistan
evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most influential technological developments in modern healthcare, creating new opportunities for improving diagnosis, treatment, patient monitoring, clinical decisionmaking, and healthcare management. The increasing availability of electronic health records, medical imaging, genomic information, wearable devices, and other forms of digital health data has created an environment in which AI-based systems can identify complex patterns that may be difficult to recognize through conventional approaches. Machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and generative AI are currently being investigated and implemented across multiple medical specialties. In clinical practice, AI can support radiological image interpretation, early disease detection, risk prediction, personalized treatment selection, drug development, clinical documentation, and remote patient monitoring. These applications may contribute to earlier diagnosis, improved clinical efficiency, reduced workload, and more individualized patient care. AI-enabled medical devices have also increasingly entered clinical practice, particularly in radiology and cardiology. However, the successful integration of AI into healthcare requires careful attention to data quality, algorithmic bias, patient privacy, transparency, cybersecurity, clinical validation, and professional accountability. AI should therefore be regarded as a clinical support technology rather than a replacement for healthcare professionals. This review examines the major clinical applications and potential benefits of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare and discusses the principal challenges that must be addressed to ensure safe, ethical, effective, and patient-centered implementation.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Modern Healthcare: Clinical Applications and Benefits

evidence_items.summary: Environmental contamination is increasingly recognised as a human rights issue engaging State obligations under the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). In Cannavacciuolo and Others v Italy , the European Court of Human Rights held that prolonged environmental exposure may trigger positive obligations under Article 2 ECHR, requiring public authorities to identify, monitor and mitigate foreseeable risks to life. Implementing these obligations depends on the integration of environmental, clinical and epidemiological evidence. This paper argues that legal medicine can provide the methodological bridge between legal principles and scientific assessment. We propose an Integrated Environmental Medico-Legal Assessment Framework (I-EMAF), a conceptual model supporting transparent, multidisciplinary and evidence-based evaluation of environmental contamination. Rather than introducing new investigative methods, I-EMAF organises established scientific approaches within a coherent medico-legal structure to assist courts, public authorities and healthcare systems to implement their Article 2 obligations.
evidence_items.title: Environmental contamination, human rights and medico-legal responsibility after Cannavacciuolo and Others v Italy (ECtHR)

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) is widely used to identify genomic regions associated with a protein of interest, including transcription factors and other chromatin-associated proteins. However, the reliability of ChIP-seq experiments is questionable, because they often do not recover expected transcription factor-DNA binding sites. A robust workflow is essential for reliably detecting protein-associated genomic regions, particularly in plant tissues. Results Here we present a complete and robust plant ChIP-seq workflow from tissue harvest to annotated peaks, generating high signal-to-noise ratio, developed for approximately 2–3 g of 7-day-old Arabidopsis thaliana seedlings expressing a tagged protein of interest. The wet-lab procedure comprises formaldehyde crosslinking under vacuum infiltration, isolation of nuclei, detergent-assisted chromatin extraction, sonication, and affinity enrichment using RFP-Trap Magnetic Agarose beads. A particularly critical, yet often overlooked, parameter for achieving a reproducible high signal-to-noise ratio is the optimization of the balance between the amount of input chromatin containing the tagged protein and the volume of affinity beads used for immunoprecipitation. Then, affinity enrichment is followed by stringent sequential washing, reversal of crosslinks and column-based purification of ChIP DNA, with input chromatin and mock IP samples processed in parallel as controls. Purified DNA is converted into dual-indexed Illumina libraries using the TruSeq DNA Nano kit, quantified by qPCR and sequenced in paired-end mode (2×151 bp) on an Illumina NovaSeq X Plus. Reads are then quality-trimmed with fastp, aligned to the TAIR10 reference genome with Bowtie2, and peaks are called against matched input controls with MACS3 and annotated with ChIPseeker (https://github.com/mhajheidari/FLC-ChIP-seq-analysis).
evidence_items.title: FLC genomic occupancy as a biological benchmark for plant ChIP-seq: a complete workflow from crosslinking to motif validation

organizations: Castle Shield Holdings LLC, Scottsville, VA 24590, USA
evidence_items.summary: Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) authenticate a device by its manufacturing variation, but cryptographic verification cannot tell whether a live, honest device produced a reading, letting replays, clones, and faults pass. We benchmarked our deployed detector, UnifiedPUFNet, against six baselines on 24 static random-access memory (SRAM) PUF tokens, holding out each attack family in turn. Test clones were real readings from other chips; replays and faults were simulated. Most detectors scored known attacks near-perfectly (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUC, at least 0.999), yet five degraded on unseen families, UnifiedPUFNet included. We traced this to its input normalization, which removes each reading’s scale, where most of the attack signal lies. Our dual-signal variant restores it with a raw-magnitude input, holding AUC above 0.99 on unseen families and 1.000 on unseen chips, and rejecting clones and faults rebuilt from real readings. Two baselines and a training-free score ranked attacks as well, but the score collapsed under session drift, and the best baseline rejected more genuine readings on unseen chips; our variant did neither. Exact replays of older readings passed every detector, leaving replay to the protocol layer. Detectors should preserve each reading’s scale and be validated on unseen families.
evidence_items.title: A Leave-One-Attack-Out Benchmark and a Dual-Signal Architecture for Liveness Detection in SRAM Physical Unclonable Functions

evidence_items.summary: As artificial intelligence systems evolve beyond conversational interfaces into multi-step workflows capable of retrieving information, maintaining state, invoking tools, delegating tasks, and acting across external systems, electronic discovery faces increasingly complex evidentiary questions. A user-facing transcript or current system configuration may not establish what information an AI system received, what instructions and controls governed its behavior, what actions it was authorized to perform, or what consequences resulted from a disputed historical execution.This white paper examines the application of United States federal civil discovery and evidence law to AI and agentic systems. Drawing on emerging judicial decisions and established electronic discovery principles, it analyzes relevance, proportionality, preservation, possession, custody or control, privilege, production, authentication, and expert proof. It identifies potential evidentiary sources across system and developer instructions, model configurations, retrieval-augmented generation, tool and API schemas, Model Context Protocol (MCP) interactions, agent memory, orchestration, delegated authority, execution traces, configuration histories, and downstream business records.The paper advances reconstructable execution state as a proposition-centered analytical framework for identifying the minimum historically accurate evidence necessary to evaluate a disputed AI execution. It distinguishes technical capability from authorization, attempted actions from completed effects, present-day configurations from historical conditions, and contemporaneous records from inference or later reconstruction.Integrating recent AI-related discovery developments with practical preservation, collection, and evidentiary methods, the paper proposes an execution-centered approach to identifying relevant sources, reconstructing historical system behavior, and evaluating evidentiary reliability.
evidence_items.title: Discovering Agentic AI: Discovery, Preservation, and Proof in AI and Agentic Systems
