evidence_items.summary: Aims: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems plan, call tools, hold credentials, and act with little human supervision, yet their security is still assessed mostly after incidents occur. This study forecasts vulnerability disclosures in a selected set of open-source agentic AI components to 2030 and proposes a security framework that responds to those forecasts. Methodology: Four public datasets were assembled: (i) 943 unique, dated vulnerability disclosures (April 2023 to October 2026) in 87 open-source agentic components from PyPI and npm, enriched with CVE records, CVSS vectors, and CISA SSVC decisions; (ii) the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue; (iii) a census of 30,054 Model Context Protocol (MCP) and agent projects on PyPI; and (iv) MITRE ATLAS. Six forecasting models were backtested from four origins, and the identifiable models were combined in a quantile-averaged ensemble. Results: Annual disclosures rose from 19 in 2023 to 164 in 2025 and reached 705 by mid-October 2026, with an April 2026 changepoint that lifted the monthly mean from 8.9 to 94.5. Agent platforms contributed 54% of disclosures, and access-control flaws overtook code injection as the largest weakness family. Nine agentic platform flaws entered KEV in 2026, with a median interval of 30 days between publication and listing; because KEV listing follows confirmed exploitation, this interval is an upper bound on the time to first exploitation. Saturating models were not identifiable because discovery has not reached its inflection point. The ensemble projects a median of 5,334 disclosures in 2030, but the 80% interval (495 to 53,088) is very wide, so this figure indicates a planning range rather than a point prediction. This estimate is bracketed by a diffusion-bounded plateau near 1,200 disclosures per year and an acceleration envelope.
evidence_items.title: Forecasting the Cybersecurity Vulnerabilities of Agentic AI Systems toward 2030: A Framework for Autonomous AI Security
Evaluation of System One Models on Biomedical Texts

evidence_items.summary: The rapid evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) inference systems has led to significant improvements in serving efficiency. However, our systematic analysis reveals that current evaluation methodologies suffer from fundamental flaws that mask critical performance issues and impede scientific progress. Through a comprehensive examination of recent systems, we identify recurring pitfalls in evaluation practices across three key dimensions: Baseline Fairness, Evaluation Setup, and Metric Design. These pitfalls are uniquely problematic for LLM inference due to its dual-phase nature combining prefill and decode operations, heterogeneous workloads, and strict temporal requirements. We demonstrate how implementation differences frequently obscure algorithmic contributions, how workload selection often fails to represent production scenarios, and how metric normalization can hide substantial performance variability that directly impacts user experience. Traditional metrics derived from the classical machine learning serving setup fail to capture the autoregressive generation characteristics essential to LLM inference, leading to misleading conclusions about system performance. To address these challenges, we provide a comprehensive checklist of best practices and methodological recommendations for robust LLM inference evaluations. To demonstrate the practical application of our methodology, we present a case study of speculative decoding evaluation - a technique whose non-uniform token generation patterns with bursts during accepted predictions and delays during verification failures fundamentally confound conventional metrics. Our work establishes a rigorous foundation for evaluation methodology that can accelerate progress in LLM inference systems by ensuring meaningful comparisons, reproducible results, and metrics that reflect real-world requirements.
evidence_items.title: On Evaluating Performance of LLM Inference Systems

evidence_items.summary: Coordination-engineered transition-metal single-atom catalysts offer a modular platform for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), but their discovery is hindered by the large configurational space arising from coupled metal-ligand variations. Here we develop a symmetry-aware and uncertainty-guided workflow to accelerate the screening of TMX4@G catalysts (X = C, N, O, P or S), where a transition-metal atom is coordinated by four ligands embedded in graphene. Canonicalization of rotationally equivalent motifs reduces 17 500 nominal structures to 4900 symmetry-inequivalent candidates while preserving chemical diversity. A cascaded Gaussian process regression model encodes a physical hierarchy from atomic descriptors to electronic structure, metal-hydrogen interaction and the HER activity. Posterior uncertainty drives active learning by balancing near-thermoneutral hydrogen binding with exploration of underrepresented coordination motifs. A large language model (LLM)-assisted automation framework further integrates structure generation, VASP input preparation, job submission, output parsing and dataset updating. DFT validation shows strong agreement with model predictions (R2 = 0.898 for 24 candidates) and identifies six thermodynamically stable catalysts with ηHER < 0.15 V.
evidence_items.title: Machine learning-guided discovery of TMX4@G electrocatalysts with LLM-assisted workflow automation.

evidence_items.summary: Federated Fine-Tuning (FFT) is essential for customizing Large Language Models (LLMs) at the edge while preserving data privacy. However, its scalability is severely constrained by the memory bottleneck. Our analysis reveals that the massive static memory footprint of LLM parameters exceeds the physical capacity of edge devices, rendering standard end-to-end training infeasible. In this paper, we propose EdgeLLM, a Cloud-Edge memory management system that democratizes efficient edge LLM adaptation via progressive layer training. Specifically, EdgeLLM re-architects the training process into a sequential pipeline: it dynamically manages the device memory hierarchy by maintaining only a minimal granular subset of layers on-chip while aggressively offloading inactive ones. To maximize system efficiency and convergence stability, EdgeLLM integrates four key components: (1) Resource Scheduler, which continuously probes device runtime memory availability to maximize resource utilization via dynamic workload mapping; (2) Training Coordinator, which bridges the semantic gap caused by offloading via virtualized context synthesis, ensuring coherent feature learning without full-graph residence; (3) Execution Planner, which optimizes the computation path by intelligently pruning redundancy and prioritizing task-critical layers for targeted adaptation; and (4) I/O Manager, which neutralizes the layer-swapping overhead through asynchronous prefetching and eviction. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that EdgeLLM effectively breaks the memory wall, unlocking participation for resource-constrained devices previously excluded from the training cohort. Compared to state-of-the-art baselines, EdgeLLM delivers up to 11.86% performance improvement, accelerates model convergence by 2.08 × , and reduces communication overhead by 1.78 ×.
evidence_items.title: Memory-Decoupled Layer-Wise Fine-Tuning for Efficient On-Device LLM Adaptation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objectives Naegele’s calendar rule and an exact 280-day count are commonly treated as equivalent methods for estimating the due date (EDD), although their calendar arithmetic differs. We quantified this difference and evaluated whether generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems disclosed and accurately labeled the method used. Methods A deterministic script calculated EDDs for every last menstrual period (LMP) date from January 1, 1812, through December 31, 2025, using Naegele’s calendar rule and a fixed 280-day count. Five generative AI systems answered four prespecified LMP prompts, representing agreement and differences of 1, 2, and 3 days. Each prompt was submitted in three separate conversations, yielding 60 responses. Results Among 78,163 LMP dates, the methods produced identical EDDs in 34,609 cases (44.3 %) and different EDDs in 43,554 (55.7 %). Naegele’s calendar rule produced dates 1 day later in 27.0 %, 2 days later in 21.0 %, and 3 days later in 7.7 %. The methods never agreed among 14,828 intervals containing February 29. Of 60 AI responses, 57 (95.0 %) included the exact 280-day date and 48 (80.0 %) stated a calculation method. Only 18 of 45 responses to divergent dates distinguished the algorithms. Twelve of 48 method-stating responses contained a method-label mismatch. Conclusions Naegele’s calendar rule and fixed 280-day counting are distinct algorithms. Their small numerical differences are unlikely to be clinically important, but they provide a deterministic test of computational transparency. Generative AI systems should disclose the calculation used, distinguish non-equivalent methods, and label them accurately.
evidence_items.title: Naegele’s rule is not a 280-day count: generative AI conflates two distinct pregnancy-dating algorithms

evidence_items.summary: An embodied speaker's expressiveness depends not only on what is said, but also on how the voice sounds and how the body moves. However, existing joint speech-motion generation models are largely driven implicitly by transcript semantics or intermediate speech representations, offering little explicit control over motion hierarchy, body parts, or vocal style. To bridge this gap, we construct MotionSpeech, a structured benchmark for controllable joint speech-motion generation that includes transcripts, voice-style descriptions, and motion conditions at two hierarchical levels. Building on this benchmark, we propose DuoFlow, a dual-stream latent flow transformer that jointly denoises speech and motion under a shared noise level and a unified second-based temporal coordinate. Modality-specific residual connectors inject structured conditions into the corresponding streams, layer-wise bidirectional cross-modal attention coordinates their generation, and a monotonic phoneme pathway combines normalized progress anchors with CTC supervision to strengthen speech temporal modeling. DuoFlow provides a unified interface for fine-grained motion and vocal-style control and demonstrates the ability to synthesize high-quality, synchronized, and instruction-consistent speech-motion sequences. Project page, https://jundong-dev.github.io/DuoFlow-project-page.
evidence_items.title: DuoFlow: Towards Synchronized Speech and Motion Generation with Fine-Grained Control

evidence_items.summary: Forecasting models that read the price and promotion plan explain each forecast as a baseline, what would sell with nothing planned, plus the lift the plan adds. We test such explanations with eight checks, six with a pass rule fixed before any result, and find that passing them does not make an explanation right. In generated store data with known effects, a world model passes the checks of construction, stability, price direction and agreement with sales and with LightGBM, yet its lifts are 1.33 to 1.40 times the truth when merchants plan into high-demand weeks, and 1.23 to 1.42 times in eight variants of that world. It still picks the right weeks to promote, but stock ordered to its lift is off by 0.44 to 0.48 of the true lift. Its stated response to a lasting regular-price change is 4.7 to 6.5 times the true -0.5, and only a measured cause finds this. On Dominick's, 38 episodes in which a store's regular prices sat apart from its zone peers give a noisy benchmark: a pooled 8-week response of -0.33 (95% interval -0.68 to 0.01). For the final tuned world models of our companion paper on nine data sets, baseline and lift add up under each model's own plan, but a deeper price cut lowers the forecast in 29% to 83% of item-week steps on Dominick's (23% to 80% within prices seen in training), and the world model and LightGBM both state about twice the measured response. Across 703 configurations from the settings searches, checks passed were not related to forecast accuracy (Spearman 0.02, 95% interval -0.02 to 0.05); with no known answer for those versions, this concerns accuracy, while whether an explanation is right is measured only in the generated data.
evidence_items.title: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response

evidence_items.summary: Self-supervised pretraining has transformed language and vision, but its application to functional MRI (fMRI) is constrained by data access. The largest standardized fMRI resources are governed by data use agreements and dominated by a small number of acquisition protocols, while the thousands of openly licensed datasets on OpenNeuro are individually small, heterogeneously organized, and unprocessed. We present the first release of Open-fMIND, a uniformly preprocessed, openly accessible corpus of parcellated fMRI timeseries from 322 OpenNeuro studies, comprising 11,379 subjects and 45,731 functional runs. Each run is preprocessed with fMRIPrep and parcellated under 52 atlases spanning 14 families, yielding a massive 2.4 million timeseries. Timeseries are released either denoised with our default pipeline (preproc) or as the fMRIPrep output with its confound files (quasiraw), with functional connectivity matrices, per-run provenance and motion metadata. Open-fMIND is intended as a pretraining resource for self-supervised brain representation learning. Pretraining on it yields downstream performance comparable to that obtained with UK Biobank.
evidence_items.title: Open-fMIND: A Large-Scale Open-Access fMRI Corpus for Pretraining Brain Foundation Models

evidence_items.summary: Formal specifications define intended program behavior and underpin verification, but writing them in theorem provers such as Lean is slow and expertise-intensive, making specification a major bottleneck to scaling formally correct code. Autoformalization from natural-language problems is promising, yet training specification models requires scalable feedback on whether generated specifications capture intended behavior. Prior approaches obtain this feedback through explicit proofs or separately implemented code with formal correspondence proofs, both expensive. We introduce AuXSpec, a Lean framework that pairs declarative postconditions with executable counterparts, obtained through type class resolution when possible and otherwise defined separately with an equivalence proof. Test cases can then evaluate declarative specifications by execution, letting us use agreement as a reinforcement-learning reward. Using AuXSpec, we synthesize 3,037 LeetCode problems and expand training to 19.5K samples through expert iteration on Codeforces. Experiments show that training Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B with the execution-based reward improves SpecGen pass@4 on AuXSpec-Test 0.7% to 82.7% and 14.3% to 84.3%, and the 27B model outperforms all frontier models. On the out-of-domain Verina benchmark with its original prompts, both models improve 7.0% to 90.5% and 21.9% to 90.5% and surpass VeriSpecGen-30B-A3B, the prior state of the art among open-source specification models, on pass@1 (theirs 47.6% vs. ours 73.7% and 84.5%) and pass@4 (theirs 63.9% at pass@10 vs. ours 90.5%). We release the weights of the trained 9B and 27B models and the 3,037 problems with test cases, including the 300-problem AuXSpec-Test benchmark with expert review and correctness proofs for future evaluation. Models and data: https://huggingface.co/collections/eth-algopt/auxspec. Website: https://auxspec.org
evidence_items.title: AuXSpec: Learning to Autoformalize Program Specifications via Executable Postconditions

evidence_items.summary: Frontier multimodal models can now control robots zero-shot from images, yet many manipulation tasks depend on contact forces that images cannot show. Bringing force to an API-only frozen model raises two challenges. First, contact evolves much faster than an API model can decide, so the system must close the loop on force beneath the model. Second, a frozen model cannot interpret raw force streams, so force must be returned in a form the model can reason about. Therefore, we present ForceHarness, a harness that lets frozen models use force without demonstrations or finetuning. After calibrating hand force from a wrist sensor or joint torques alone, ForceHarness addresses the first challenge with self-terminating force primitives that regulate force on their own and return at a contact event. To address the second challenge, a physics translation layer turns each force trace into physical quantities with uncertainty as the tool result. To evaluate ForceHarness against expert force controllers and learned policies under identical conditions, we also build HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables. On a real arm without a wrist force sensor, ForceHarness raises the zero-shot success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 3.3% to 90.0%. In simulation, it adds 17.5 percentage points on the public ForceBench suite and 34.3 percentage points on HiddenPhys, surpassing force-aware policies trained on demonstrations on both benchmarks and matching hand-written expert controllers on HiddenPhys. Ablations further show that smaller models make significantly better decisions when given physical quantities rather than raw force values.
evidence_items.title: ForceHarness: Turning Force into Action and Physics for Frozen Frontier Models

evidence_items.summary: High-resolution brain MRI is important for neuroradiological assessment, yet routine clinical protocols often rely on fast, anisotropic 2D acquisitions, particularly in resource-constrained settings. These acquisitions may differ in orientation, alignment and anatomical coverage, resulting in partially overlapping image stacks. Existing learning-based super-resolution methods typically rely on single, under-constrained inputs or fixed multi-stack configurations with idealised acquisition geometry. We introduce MS-HVED, a sequence-agnostic framework for flexible multi-stack brain MRI super-resolution. Available axial, coronal and sagittal stacks are independently encoded into multi-scale Gaussian posteriors and fused using a field-of-view-aware Product-of-Gaussians formulation that limits contributions from unsupported regions. Physics-informed domain randomisation simulates heterogeneous clinical acquisition conditions, including obliqueness, partial coverage and imaging artefacts. MS-HVED achieved competitive or superior reconstruction fidelity across synthetic benchmarks and improved downstream tissue segmentation relative to low-resolution inputs. To assess generalisation beyond the training cohorts, we performed external clinical validation on 30 routine brain MRI examinations from a Nigerian cohort, representing an under-represented population in medical imaging research. These examinations formed the largest component of a blinded reader study involving 44 real cases and seven expert neuroradiologists. In the Nigerian cohort, MS-HVED was preferred over the supervised baseline for overall image quality in 187 of 210 paired assessments. Across all clinical cohorts, MS-HVED achieved higher overall-quality scores with all available inputs (5.93 vs. 4.49, p<.001), with the preference persisting when axial or coronal inputs were omitted (p<.001). Code at github.com/cai4cai/ms-hved
evidence_items.title: Flexible Multi-Stack Super-Resolution of Clinical Brain MRI Using Hetero-Orientation Variational Encoding: Expert Reader Evaluation in a Nigerian Cohort

evidence_items.summary: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.
evidence_items.title: LynnReal-Hand: Unlocking World Interaction with Hand Control

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Sage S1.5 Flash, a 320-billion-parameter general-purpose mixture-of-experts model designed to reason over scientific evidence and act in interactive environments. Sage Sci-Perception uses dedicated encoders for molecular graphs and biological sequences and represents spectra as ordered patches of measurements. Modality-specific projectors map these representations into the input space of a shared backbone, which processes them alongside text and images. To develop the model's agent capabilities, we construct verifiable environments for tool use, search, and coding, as well as specialized workflows involving machine learning experiments and scientific software. Task completion is checked against execution results, changes in environment state, or submitted artifacts. We evaluate Sage S1.5 Flash on 33 benchmarks across seven domains. In the primary comparison against five baselines, it ranks first on OfficeQA Pro (72.2), MLE-bench Lite (90.3 HumanRank), Harvey LAB, and SpreadsheetBench~2, and second on OSWorld-Verified (85.2), WebArena-Verified (67.6), and DeepResearch Bench~II (54.2). These results show particular strengths in using documentary evidence, producing verifiable workbooks, and carrying out machine learning tasks, alongside competitive performance in desktop and browser workflows that require the model to act on visual feedback.
evidence_items.title: Sage S2.1 Flash Technical Report

evidence_items.summary: Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction. With InclusionMed-DxFiles, our private diagnostic reasoning benchmark, the Atlas contains five benchmarks covering three of its nine role--capability cells. We evaluated frontier large language models on the Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, with overall scores ranging from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, showing that a model's rank varied with the role or capability considered. A within-benchmark analysis using task-level tags showed that the ten highest-ranked models in the Index all scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. Models with similar Index scores also differed substantially in estimated inference cost. These findings highlight the need for evaluation covering more diverse healthcare needs and for context-specific model selection. Through open collaboration and community contributions, InclusionMed seeks to ensure that diverse healthcare needs worldwide shape how medical AI progress is defined and measured.
evidence_items.title: InclusionMed: Benchmarking AI for Inclusive Healthcare

evidence_items.summary: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 72% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 34%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 82-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.
evidence_items.title: DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images

evidence_items.summary: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.
evidence_items.title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Legal reasoning in civil-law systems is not rule-lookup: the German state examination asks for a structured opinion (Gutachten) that names the governing norms, applies them to the facts, and argues to a conclusion. We introduce GPBam (German Public Law Bar-style Exam), 81 public-law examination cases with reference solutions, paired with a recitation task over 200 statutory provisions. Drawn from state examination preparation, the cases are broad and rarely repeat, and are not publicly available - we find no evidence of exact-solution memorisation in the models we evaluate, and keeping them private limits contamination. Because each reference solution's cited norms form a retrieval gold set over the very instances the essays are graded on, GPBam scores retrieval and long-form generation jointly, which makes it a benchmark for legal retrieval as well as for legal writing and lets us ask how much retrieval quality a legal opinion actually needs. Across 32 open-weight and proprietary models evaluated without retrieval, scores span 4.81-76.42 out of 100. Supplying the law helps modestly: across seven models and eight retrieval configurations, retrieval performance varies nearly threefold and buys at most 4.1 essay points, and nothing significant for three of the seven, while an oracle with 91% gold-norm recall improves scores by 2-6 points. Essay quality strongly tracks prior knowledge: verbatim statute recall, measured in a separate task, correlates at ρ= 0.92 over 32 models.
evidence_items.title: GPBam: A Retrieval-Aware German Public Law Exam Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: The task of dataset distillation concerns the learning of a small set of synthetic samples that can serve as an effective replacement for a large real dataset when used for downstream tasks. While many solutions have been proposed since the problem's inception, most of them primarily seek to optimize the distilled data with respect to a classifier. In this work, we propose a new distillation method that learns a set of samples such that they directly approximate the per-class data distribution. Specifically, we "drift" our distilled data in the latent space of a feature extractor such that they move both toward the real data and away from each other without using a classification objective. We find that our drifted data cover the real distribution significantly better than existing methods while still serving as powerful training samples for classification. Furthermore, we showcase our method's use as a visualization tool for better interpreting models and extend it beyond images to other modalities. Our work advances the frontier of dataset distillation, offering a novel synthesis method and proposing distribution-based metrics as a complementary evaluation. More broadly, our findings help address the growing need to understand both data and models by uncovering more about how they interact.
evidence_items.title: Dataset Distillation via Drifting

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents can solve a task well before they stop working on it. We characterize termination lag--the number of steps between an agent's first correct patch and the end of its run--across five models, two agent frameworks, and three SWE-bench datasets by recording and testing every distinct repository patch generated during execution. Our analysis reveals that 38--82% of successful runs achieve a correct solution on their initial source-code edit. However, agents continue to expend substantial effort after correct patches, with post-solution steps accounting for a median of 35--37% for Qwen3-Coder and 54--60% for Laguna-XS.2 in successful runs on SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Agents spend most of these additional steps verifying their work and exploring the repository. In a small fraction of cases (1--8%), this continued activity leads agents to undo their earlier correct patch, leaving the final solution incorrect.
evidence_items.title: Termination Lag: Coding Agents Solve Early but Stop Late

evidence_items.summary: We built a hybrid multi-agent trading system that combines large language model (LLM) analysts with momentum-based portfolio construction and rule-based execution. Company-news and macroeconomic agents return structured reports to a coordinator that sets stock weights and cash reserves. We evaluate the portfolio engine using its broker-recorded paper account, which operated with deterministic fallbacks, and compare LLM-enabled configurations through retrospective replays. From March 11 to August 28, 2026, the account returned 34.5%, compared with 14.4% for the S&P 500 fund SPY over the same dates. This raw return advantage came with a larger maximum drawdown. Reconstructed policies also finish above matched SPY and QQQ references when assessments are used in the same session or deferred to the next. Design comparisons examine cash authority, selective invocation, and response contracts. A constant-cash control gives a return estimate close to stance-based sizing, and shorter report contracts improve observed parsing but can change recommendations.
evidence_items.title: Inside the Trading Loop: Markets, Models, and Moves with LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: As technological innovation accelerates, patent drafting remains time-consuming and highly dependent on professional expertise. This study proposes a patent text generation framework that identifies technological gaps from existing patent knowledge and generates patentable drafts. The framework establishes an ontology-based domain structure, applies a Technology–Function Matrix (TFM) to identify high-potential technology–function pairings, and uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to transform these pairings into invention concepts. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and prompt engineering are then integrated into a modular workflow for generating abstracts, titles, figure descriptions, claims, and IPC classifications. Sustainable energy storage is selected as the case domain due to its growing importance in net-zero transitions and renewable energy integration. The generated texts are evaluated using vector-based semantic similarity and Precision, Recall, and F1-score metrics. By integrating patent mining, text mining, and domain-specific technology–function analysis, the proposed framework supports transdisciplinary engineering practice and bridge engineering design, knowledge discovery, and sustainable innovation, demonstrating the practical applicability of data-driven artificial intelligence in patent text generation.
evidence_items.title: Using Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Model for Novel Patent Generation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly entering translator education, yet it remains unclear whether they build students' own translation competence or merely improve the products students submit. We combined a validation study on public benchmark data with a 16-week quasi-experiment to test a scaffolded human--LLM pedagogy, the Draft--Diagnose--Revise--Reflect (D2R) cycle, for English--Chinese translation. In Study 1, a rubric-guided error-annotation prompt increased the agreement between LLM feedback and expert Multidimensional Quality Metrics judgements on 2,500 WMT segments for all four models tested; with this prompt GPT-4o reached a segment-level Kendall's $\tau$ of 0.30, on a par with the strongest neural metric, and the highest error-detection accuracy. In Study 2, 179 English majors received conventional instruction, unrestricted LLM access or the guardrailed D2R cycle. Unrestricted access maximised LLM-assisted performance but yielded no advantage in unassisted translation over conventional instruction at a delayed test 12 weeks after the course (Hedges' $g$ = $-$0.08) and produced the largest AI-dependency gap. Scaffolded use produced durable gains in unassisted translation ($g$ = 0.70), a 13\% reduction in error rate and higher metacognitive regulation. Process logs indicated that the benefit was transmitted mainly through lower verbatim adoption of LLM output. Pedagogical design, not LLM access per se, determines whether LLMs support or supplant translation learning.
evidence_items.title: Scaffolded large language model feedback builds durable translation competence whereas unrestricted use fosters dependency

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Clinical registries capture adverse events (AEs) in free-text fields that are rarely analyzed. We developed a reproducible large language model (LLM)-assisted workflow using 11,216 free-text entries from 18,069 patients in the German Stroke Registry; 9,146 informative entries were retained after filtering. Embedding-based clustering showed poor separation, whereas an LLM-guided taxonomy identified 89 leaf labels. On the model-assisted 1,000-entry development set used for model and prompt selection, GPT-5.4 reached F1 92.4% (95% confidence interval [CI] 91.4-93.4). On 300 held-out entries, weighted F1 against clinician consensus was 96.5% (94.6-98.1) for frozen GPT-5.4 labels and 90.5% (87.5-93.5) for locally run Qwen 3.5 27B. For AE concepts with a comparable structured field, free text documented 1,345 additional instances (+19.6% over 6,867 structured instances); it also documented 7,546 instances of AE concepts without a structured equivalent, most often pneumonia, urinary tract infection and delirium. Beyond baseline covariates and the structured AE count, integrated complication concepts increased the area under the curve for prediction of good functional outcome by 0.025 (95% CI 0.021-0.028) and for death by 0.018 (0.014-0.021); gains were minimal after including the discharge National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score. On 1,979 public coronary-trial fragments from the Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov (AACT), the software ran end to end, demonstrating its technical applicability to a second clinical text corpus. In conclusion, this workflow enables structured analysis of clinical registry free text and complements structured adverse-event documentation.
evidence_items.title: Decoding Complications: Large Language Model-Based Classification of Free-Text Entries in Clinical Stroke Registries

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Rolling bearings are critical components in industrial rotating machinery, and their failures may cause unexpected downtime, economic loss, and safety risks. Although deep learning and multimodal fusion have improved vibration-based fault diagnosis, two issues remain insufficiently addressed: magnitude-dominated time-frequency representations may discard phase-related impulse timing information, and heterogeneous diagnostic cues are often fused without explicit alignment in a semantically consistent representation space. This paper proposes M2-LLM-FD, a lightweight large language model-assisted framework for semantic-aware multimodal evidence integration in rolling bearing fault diagnosis. The framework converts each vibration segment into three complementary forms: time-domain patch tokens, phase-aware time-frequency tokens, and structured statistical prompts. A phase-preserving complex convolutional dimensionality reduction network is designed to process the real and imaginary components of the time-frequency representations, thereby retaining phase-sensitive information associated with fault-induced impulsive events. A structured multimodal alignment and fusion module then harmonizes temporal granularity and projects the aligned evidence into the pretrained language-model embedding space through semantic-anchor cross-modal attention. Furthermore, domain-specific prior knowledge is injected via structured statistical prompts, and the model is efficiently fine-tuned using Low-Rank Adaptation. \textcolor{red}{Extensive experiments on the CWRU, PU, and HUST datasets show that the proposed framework achieves consistent improvements in diagnostic accuracy, robustness, and cross-dataset generalization. Ablation and controlled analyses further validate the contributions of phase-aware time-frequency modeling, structured statistical prompts, and semantic-aware multimodal alignment to the overall diagnostic performance.
evidence_items.title: Semantic-aware multimodal evidence integration with a lightweight large language model for rolling bearing fault diagnosis

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Liability for scam losses is shifting towards banks, yet few interpretable tools can anticipate which fraud and scam complaints will end in redress. This study develops SCAM-XD, an explainable framework that predicts whether a complaint to the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) flagged as possible fraud or a scam closes with monetary relief reported by the company. From the CFPB narratives archive, the study builds a benchmark of these complaints, about half of which human coders confirm as fraud or scams. A large language model (LLM) codes each narrative for scam type, payment rail, authorisation, manipulation cues and signals of the bank's response, agreeing closely with human coding on scam type. These features are combined with structured fields, company identity and text representations in a stacking ensemble, explained with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and linked to a cost-sensitive triage layer. Tested on a later period, SCAM-XD improves significantly on strong baselines across seeds, including a reimplemented topic model approach. LLM features yield a compact, interpretable model that nearly matches a high-dimensional text baseline but do not significantly improve the full model. Company identity is the strongest driver of predicted redress, yet firm identity alone predicts far less well, and payment rail and bank response cues act in directions consistent with liability rules. Under assumed costs, thresholds selected on validation data substantially reduce modelled expected cost relative to standard thresholds, whereas model choice matters much less. Redress depends on both the firm and the facts that determine liability.
evidence_items.title: An Explainable Machine Learning Framework with Large Language Model Features for Predicting Monetary Redress in Bank Fraud and Scam Complaints

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) could streamline research ethics and governance review by automating routine quality control checks. This study assessed Claude 3.5 Sonnet, ChatGPT4o, and Microsoft CoPilot in evaluating participant information sheets against Health Research Authority standards. Six clinical trial applications were processed using 32 standardised queries, with accuracy, processing time, error rates, and response quality assessed by two blinded reviewers. Claude showed the highest accuracy, detected more deviations from guidance, and had the fastest processing time (7.17 ± 0.68 min vs. ChatGPT 13.58 ± 2.2 min, CoPilot 23.25 ± 6.21 min). Hallucination rates were lowest in Claude, followed by ChatGPT and CoPilot. Claude also received the highest response quality ratings (77.6% “very good” vs. ChatGPT 56.7%, CoPilot 45.2%). While all three models were capable, Claude consistently outperformed the others, demonstrating the potential of LLM-assisted quality control while emphasizing the need for human oversight.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating large language models for quality control in research ethics review

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Introduction: Good oral hygiene is mandatory for orthodontic patients. This study was done for evaluating how well an artificial intelligence (AI)-based supervising system could improve oral hygiene during orthodontic procedures. Materials and Methods: A total of 44 patients who were undergoing for permanent orthodontic procedures were split into two groups of 22 each: Group I as the control, and Group II as the AI monitoring test group. The test group's patients were instructed to get routine intraoral scans using Scanbox (Dental Monitoring ® ). For all groups, the Orthodontic Plaque Index and Marginal Gingival Index (MGI) were measured at baseline (T0), 2 weeks later (T1, T2, and T3, respectively), and at 3 months (T4). A statistical analysis was performed on the collected data. Results: Subjects in the test group showed a considerable decrease in gingival inflammation and plaque score in contrast to the control group. Conclusion: Plaque and gingival irritation are reduced during orthodontic treatment when a remote monitoring system is used. By using this technique, patients are able to maintain the greatest possible dental health.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of an Artificial Intelligence-based Monitoring Technique for Measuring Oral Hygiene during Orthodontic Therapy

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Globally, marine pollution generated by oil spills, plastic litter, and industrial waste poses major threats to the environment, the economy, and human health. Field surveys, optical sensing, and manual sampling are examples of traditional monitoring and mitigation techniques that are frequently hampered by inefficiency, poor precision, and restricted coverage, particularly in large-scale or remote circumstances. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) hold revolutionary potential for detecting, managing, and monitoring maritime pollution. AI-based methods such as computer vision, deep learning, and machine learning have been effectively combined with drone imagery, remote sensing, and in situ monitoring to detect, classify, and measure plastic contaminants and oil spills with remarkable precision. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), transformer-based models, fuzzy systems, and neural networks have all improved pollutant detection, hotspot mapping, and predictive modeling while addressing challenges including noisy datasets and diverse environmental conditions. Furthermore, scalable solutions for real-time maritime waste detection and disposal are emerging from AI-driven autonomous systems that incorporate robotic mechanisms and Internet of Things (IoT) sensors. This study fully examines the current state of AI applications for marine pollutant identification, highlighting methodological advancements and detailing future potential for integrating AI into sustainable ocean monitoring and pollution management strategies.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence for marine pollution monitoring and control

evidence_items.summary: AI is transforming education by providing immediate clarifications, tailored guidance, feedback and self-learning. This study has evaluated the awareness, use and perception of AI in mathematics education by students and compared the perception of male and female students. A descriptive survey was conducted by convenience sampling of participants. The data were collected both online and offline using a researcher-developed questionnaire, which had eight questions regarding students’ engagement with AI in mathematics education. Data were analysed by proportions. The results showed that the students knew about AI and valued its benefits in Mathematics education. Many students used AI for their learning, but a small portion of students used regularly for Mathematics, although many reported using it occasionally. Most of the students opted for AI platforms like Google Gemini, ChatGPT and others. Students primarily used AI for problem solving, exam preparation, and conceptual understanding. They also thought AI could make learning math easier and supported its use in their schools. Mathematics: Male students used AI more than female students. The findings show that AI is a powerful learning tool for students, but its educational use needs to be properly directed, responsibly used and critically verified for AI-generated mathematical answers.
evidence_items.title: Students’ Perceptions of Using Artificial Intelligence in Mathematics Education

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) is the dominant surface-code decoder but is suboptimal under depolarizing noise, because it discards the X – Z correlation that Y errors induce and is not degeneracy-aware. We present an exactly anchored diagnostic benchmark for the code-capacity depolarizing channel, not a case for neural decoding. Five decoders (MWPM, correlated matching, belief-matching, belief propagation with ordered-statistics decoding (BP+OSD) and a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP)) are compared with an exact analytic maximum-likelihood (ML) reference at distance d = 3 , with exact per-syndrome ML decisions on sampled syndromes at d = 5 , and with a matched-marginal independent-noise control. Measuring MWPM’s suboptimality by the relative logical-error-rate (LER) reduction that ML achieves over it, the difference between the depolarizing and control channels is 19–32 percentage points (pp) above an 11%–14% floor at d = 3 , and 33–60 pp above an 8%–10% floor at d = 5 . At d = 3 the MLP recovers 90%–95% of the MWPM-to-ML gap, more than belief-matching (82%–89%), BP+OSD (74%–80%) or correlated matching (46%–58%). At d = 5 belief-matching and BP+OSD agree closely yet stay measurably above ML, recovering 79%–91% of the gap, while the MLP’s advantage over MWPM depends on the training budget (crossover near 3.5 × 10 5 samples at p = 0.08 ) and, when adequately trained, recovers at most 17%. In simulated circuit-level memory experiments at d = 3 and 5, the classical decoders keep their advantage over MWPM, the matched-marginal split becomes decomposition-dependent, and the MLP recovers 25% of the gap at d = 3 , T = 2 and, over five training seeds and budgets up to 9 × 10 5 samples, stays an order of magnitude worse than MWPM at d = 5 , T = 5 , with or without validation-based early stopping. Per-shot cost grows 33–97-fold for the BP-based decoders but less than twofold for matching, and batched throughput does not bound latency.
evidence_items.title: Decomposing neural decoders: an exactly-anchored benchmark for quantum error correction

evidence_items.summary: The Apollo 12 landing near Surveyor 3 left measured damage on hardware that was returned to Earth. That damage is a rare test case for lunar plume-ejecta models. Modern Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) data place the lunar module (LM) 156.8 m from Surveyor 3, on ground about 10 m higher than Surveyor's. This report tests one specified, collision-free ballistic model family. Grains travel ballistically in vacuum over the measured terrain, and their launch angle may rotate with the local slope by a coupling fraction k. When launch is referenced to horizontal (k = 0), no grain reaches the camera at 100 m/s or faster in 200 terrain-error trials. A simple height calculation shows why. A grain launched horizontally can reach the camera only if it is slower than about 46 m/s (42.7 to 51.5 m/s across the height cases). This result excludes a direct horizontal sheet. It does not exclude horizontal launch followed by collisions or scattering. Slope-referenced launch does deliver fast grains. Couplings of k = 0.5 and 1.0 predict nearly the same pit density (864 and 842 pits/cm²). Both exceed the measured 103 pits/cm², and both need the same unmeasured attenuation to match it. With k limited to 0.4 to 1.0, at least one such equal-output pair survives in 34 of 40 terrain cases and 33 of 33 registration cases. The record therefore bounds k from below but does not fix it. Neither the 255:2 front-to-rear crater count nor the literal shadow bearing separates the two settings. No retained pair matches the literal historical bearing for both members, and only 38 of 610 meet the literal elevation interval. They do disagree elsewhere. Around a fixed Surveyor 3, 49 of 296 candidate landing cells 30 to 200 m away are exposed under one coupling but not the other. This is a model sensitivity, not a validated hazard limit or protection distance.
evidence_items.title: The Apollo 12–Surveyor 3 Plume-Ejecta Benchmark: Geometry and Identifiability Limits

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Human-derived nucleic acids introduced during sample collection or laboratory handling are a longstanding concern in genomics. Sensitive, high-throughput sequencing can capture trace human nucleic acids, potentially exposing genetic information in nominally host-free microbial datasets. We systematically examined bacterial isolate sequencing archives and found frequent human-sequence contamination, with recurrence within projects and marked heterogeneity among libraries, including those sharing sequencing lanes. Human fragments spanned chromosomes and retained population-informative alleles, concordant partial allele states and clinically annotated variants. Computational depletion removed more than 99.99\% of strict human fragments, eliminating measured population-affinity and clinically annotated variant signals while largely preserving bacterial assembly features. Human contamination was also detected in bacterial RNA-seq, with both genome-alignable reads and splice-junction evidence of processed human transcripts. Together, these findings show how incidental human material can become recoverable genetic information in public microbial archives and underscore the need for screening before data deposition.
evidence_items.title: Recurrent human-sequence contamination and recoverable genetic information in bacterial sequencing archives

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Intravitreal injections are the most frequently performed intraocular procedure worldwide. Yet the 50 µL dose is usually delivered with syringes designed neither for volumes this small nor for injection into the eye. Dosing accuracy, particulate contamination and residual volume have previously been examined in separate studies, so trade-offs between these properties within a single syringe remain unclear. We assessed all three properties in the same syringes, including models in clinical use for intravitreal injection that have not been characterised previously. Methods Six syringes were evaluated: Injekt ® F Luer Solo 1 mL, Omnifix-F Luer Lock Solo 1 mL, Henke-Ject eco 1 mL (three-part), Zero Residual 0.2 mL, BD Micro-Fine 1 mL, and Omnican 50 U-100 insulin syringe. Dosing accuracy and precision for a 50 µL target volume was assessed with 23 specialist staff. The dosing data were analysed descriptively, and operator-dependent variability was quantified with a linear mixed model. Residual volume was determined according to DIN EN ISO 7886-1. Particulate contamination was quantified by light obscuration after 7-day incubation of water, with and without flicking of the syringe during filling. Particle counts were analyzed descriptively. Results All syringes tended to overdose, with a median delivered volume of 55.1 µL, and only 45.4% of the measurements were within 45–55 µL. In the mixed model, 22% of the variance of the delivered volume was attributable to between-operator differences, and no syringe type differed significantly in mean delivered volume. Among the syringes measured without a needle, the mean residual volume ranged from 0.18 µL to 23.1 µL; the two syringes with integrated needles showed 0.59 µL and 1.77 µL including the needle dead space. All syringes released particulate matter, and in this exploratory study the particle count was higher after flicking in five of the six syringe types.
evidence_items.title: Performance characterization of syringes used for intravitreal injections: dosing accuracy, particulate contamination, and residual volume
Deep learning MGMT promoter methylation status prediction in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma using multiparametric MRI: Benchmark vs. real‑world performance

organizations: Laboratory of Intelligent Systems and Applications (L2IS), Faculty of Sciences and Techniques, Cadi Ayyad University, Morocco
Polytech Nantes, Nantes Université, France and LEMNA Laboratory (Laboratoire d’Économie et de Management de Nantes Atlantique), France
evidence_items.summary: Historic urban destinations contain culturally significant places whose digital visibility, accessibility, and suitability for visitation vary substantially. This paper presents Agentic SHIFT, the Smart Heritage Itinerary Framework for Transmission, a context-aware multi-agent framework for auditable cultural heritage itinerary recommendation. Nine specialised agents coordinate visitor profiling, context modelling, heritage retrieval, operational eligibility, heritage and under-exposure scoring, expected suitability, pedestrian routing, evidence-bounded narration, and visual verification. The Marrakech benchmark contains 196 cultural POIs across ten heritage categories. Twenty calibration configurations were used to select the utility weights, and forty held-out paired configurations were used for the final comparison. On the held-out set, Agentic SHIFT achieved mean heritage coverage of 0.757, digital under-exposure of 0.767, cultural diversity of 0.522, expected suitability of 0.631, and a mean walking distance of 1.973 km. Relative to popularity ranking, it increased heritage coverage by 0.047 and digital under-exposure by 0.448 while reducing walking distance by 0.375 km. Removing the operational gate reduced operational validity from 1.000 to 0.696. Two stored OSMnx routes confirmed pedestrian-network execution within a four-hour budget. A documentary audit of thirteen narrative claims found eleven directly supported claims and two claims retained with explicit qualification, while a detailed audit of four visual records confirmed identity, creator, licence, and publication-suitable resolution for all four audited images.
evidence_items.title: Agentic SHIFT: A Multi-Agent AI Framework for Visual and Context-Aware Cultural Heritage Exploration

evidence_items.summary: Large vision-language models can produce fluent responses containing objects, attributes, or relations unsupported by the image. We study an implemented alignment pipeline that normalizes released fine-grained hallucination supervision, validates chosen-rejected preference pairs with vision-language judges, repairs rejected chosen responses, and trains LLaVA adapters with standard or severity-aware direct preference optimization. The study uses 16,143 normalized feedback records and 8,386 released preference pairs, comparing direct training with zero-shot and two-shot judged severity-margin variants. The zero-shot variant reduces Object HalBench CHAIRs from 53.00 to 36.00 and CHAIRi from 15.72 to 10.41. Across aligned models, AMBER-Hal decreases from 35.90 to 25.10-26.90, accompanied by reduced visual coverage. In contrast, the base model retains the highest valid POPE adversarial F1, 84.18 versus 83.87-83.91 after alignment. These results support benchmark-dependent reductions in generative hallucination rather than uniform superiority of severity-aware alignment. We distinguish implemented pipeline components from the preference paths used in the reported experiments and discuss the limits of attributing gains to judging, repair, or the training objective individually.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Seeing: Fine-Grained Preference Validation and Severity-Aware Alignment for Mitigating Visual Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) judges are increasingly used to monitor the outputs of LLM-based AI agents, yet formal guarantees on the reliability of these judges remain largely absent, limiting confidence in their use for safety-critical oversight. We consider certifying such a judge and define its risk over safety classifications of prompt--response pairs drawn from a deployed generator. We apply a PAC-Bayes framework to this setting, refining existing compression-based methodology with the use of tighter bounds and more efficient coding. We show that standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning can yield non-vacuous and even tight certificates for safety judges, for both classification and Brier risk, without holding out data for validation. We introduce LoRA-GT, which shares a single quantisation scale across layers and achieves the tightest certificates with minimal degradation in predictive performance. Across five guardrail models and four benchmarks, we find that certificate tightness is governed more by adaptation complexity than by base model scale. Finally, we show how far quantisation can be pushed before the resulting increase in risk outweighs the bound tightening gained from shorter descriptions. Together, these results provide a practical route toward certifiable scalable oversight and offer insight into how the complexity of safety adaptations shapes generalisation.
evidence_items.title: Tight PAC-Bayes Generalisation Guarantees for Large Language Model Judges

evidence_items.summary: GPTQ is the de facto standard solver for layer-wise post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models, yet the solver itself has received less attention than weight preprocessing and cross-layer objectives. We target a bottleneck of GPTQ: its greedy procedure optimizes continuous group scales separately from the assignment of discrete integers. Evaluating each integer candidate with its closed-form optimal scale has been used for per-channel quantization; JointQ extends it to group-wise quantization, where a row's scales are coupled through the Hessian, and applies it to refine the GPTQ solution. Each local-search move changes one integer and recomputes its group's optimal scale in closed form, accounting for the other groups through the full Hessian; all scales are periodically re-solved jointly. The search starts from a row-wise selection among scale-refitted candidates including the GPTQ solution, so unregularized JointQ never has a larger layer-wise calibration error than GPTQ. JointQ preserves the GPTQ output format and is thus a drop-in replacement. Across four models and four settings, JointQ improves six-task average zero-shot accuracy over vanilla GPTQ in 14 of 16 comparisons and perplexity in 12 of 16. The mean accuracy gain increases from 0.0044 in W4G128 to 0.1559 in W3 per-channel, and JointQ also improves average accuracy over GPTQ with MSE-based scale search and activation ordering in all eight per-channel comparisons, though rarely in G128. An ablation shows that JointQ's diagonal Tikhonov regularization mitigates severe W3 per-channel perplexity degradation, so the largest gains are not due to the local search alone. Overall, JointQ's primary empirical benefit is downstream accuracy preservation in challenging low-bit and large-group regimes. Code is available in the OneComp library at https://github.com/FujitsuResearch/OneCompression.
evidence_items.title: JointQ: Joint Scale-and-Integer Quantization for Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. The model is released with a DFlash drafter. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.
evidence_items.title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents

evidence_items.summary: Building agentic applications requires combining large language model (LLM) operations, workflow structure and application state, and model-guided routing. With SDKs and agent frameworks, developers connect these components through supporting code that prepares model inputs, propagates state, and dispatches model-selected steps. Workflow changes can require coordinated updates to this code, increasing development and testing effort. Splitting execution logic between application code and framework internals also limits compiler visibility into control flow and state dependencies, hindering automatic optimization. We introduce Agent-Native Programming, which unifies these three components with shared execution semantics. We realize this approach in Jac, a Python-superset language, through"by llm()"for typed model operations and tool use, Object-Spatial Programming for workflow structure and state, and"visit ... by llm()"for model-guided routing. The routing construct derives the model's choices from executable workflow steps and schedules the selected steps. This explicit connection between model decisions and program execution gives the compiler and runtime a common basis for dependency analysis and automatic optimization. Across five benchmarks and five baselines, Jac achieves a 1.8-8.7x reduction in AI-integration code relative to the OpenAI SDK, with competitive observed task quality and lower coding-agent development effort. Two case studies demonstrate speculative execution and service partitioning through configuration alone, using program analysis and runtime checks to preserve workflow behavior under stated conditions.
evidence_items.title: Agent-Native by Design: A Programming Language for Agentic Applications

evidence_items.summary: Is a face or a voice still heard once the words are known? Incomplete multimodal learning increasingly uses large language models (LLMs) as fusion engines: modality features enter as token blocks and missing modalities become placeholders. We find that LLM-driven fusion can override non-verbal evidence it can read. Contrasting its full-input prediction with counterfactual views, the same model shown one modality or no content, we identify language shortcuts. We build MR-Bench: MR-Bench-A types every test sample of four sentiment benchmarks; MR-Bench-H contains 900 human-validated clips (620 language-shortcut, LS; 280 non-verbal-shortcut, NS) from seven sources, and every model is scored on all of them. Zero-shot MLLMs solve at most 32.7% of the LS clips; adding the transcript to the muted video lowers vision-language accuracy by 46.1-53.1 points. Yet inverting a text-only model's answers solves 94.4%, so LS accuracy alone cannot establish use of non-verbal evidence. Inside the fusion LLM, fused states align increasingly with the text view late in the decoder. Counterfactual-View Reliability learning (CoVeR) trains views as unimodal judges and withholds fused supervision where they disagree. It achieves state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks without extra inference cost in accuracy mode. On MR-Bench-H, it reaches 61.7% LS and 93.6% NS accuracy; robust mode raises LS accuracy to 63.0% while lowering NS accuracy to 84.8%. Among LS clips solved without text, adding text causes errors on 30.1% with CoVeR versus 32.2% with LLM-Fusion. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/CoVeR/.
evidence_items.title: Words Speak Louder? Exploring the Language Shortcut of LLM-Driven Incomplete Multimodal Learning

evidence_items.summary: Organizations increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for decisions about people, such as hiring, investment and employee evaluation, and rely on them over long periods of time. Fairness audits of such systems, however, are conducted only once. We examine how the biases of LLMs change over time. In a venture screening setting, models from five providers decided whether and how much to invest in startups whose founders differed only in gender, origin and university. We repeated this audit three times over 13 months (248,400 API calls). Study 1 shows that the same model, called under the same identifier one year later, displayed a significantly different bias pattern. Study 2 shows that the successors of retired models carried the same bias as their predecessors, but in a significantly different size and form. Study 3 shows that the bias does not depend on the industry of the startup. A document analysis further shows that providers change and retire models at their discretion, with notice periods of zero to six months. Drawing on these findings, we develop a theory of evidence anchoring. We theorize that bias resides in the model class and persists, whereas audit evidence is anchored to a single model and expires when the provider decides. We derive policy advice for organizations and regulators, namely audits of model classes instead of single models, a version record for every model response, and re-audits triggered by model changes.
evidence_items.title: Auditing a Moving Target: Evidence Anchoring and the Expiry of Fairness Audits of Provider-Served Language Models

evidence_items.summary:
OBJECTIVE
This study compared the accuracy of a specific sparse-view, smartphone-based 3D reconstruction workflow for digitising dental models, benchmarking its performance against dedicated dental scanners and assessing its feasibility as an innovative alternative.


METHODS
Following the International Organisation for Standardisation protocol (ISO 20896-1:2019), a customised 3D-printed model with three test objects was scanned, using coordinate measuring machine (CMM) measurements as the reference. Data were captured 30 times each with an intraoral scanner (IOS), an extraoral scanner (EOS), and an iPhone 15 Pro. Images from the iPhone were three-dimensionally reconstructed using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and Neural Surface Reconstruction (NSR), respectively. All outputs were converted to the stereolithography (STL) format and analysed in Geomagic Wrap. Accuracy was reported using the mean, standard deviation (precision), bias (trueness), and the root mean square error (RMSE) for each dimension (height, depth, length, and angle).


RESULTS
The IOS achieved the highest accuracy (RMSE < 20 µm), followed by the EOS (RMSE < 80 µm) with systematic negative bias in full‑arch spans. 3DGS and NSR produced substantially larger deviations (approx. 200-250 µm for crown and inlay preparation, and approx. 300 µm for full-arch model).


CONCLUSION
Geometry and span affected the accuracy across all methods. IOS consistently displayed the highest accuracy, while 3DGS and NSR with a sparse-view workflow showed substantial errors and surface distortions and were therefore not yet suitable for high-precision prosthodontic restoration.


SIGNIFICANCE
Dental scanners remain superior for precision prosthodontics, while the sparse-view 3D reconstruction workflow may hold potential for less demanding clinical and educational contexts.
evidence_items.title: Accuracy of a Sparse-View Smartphone-Based 3D Reconstruction Workflow for Dental Models: A Feasibility Benchmark.

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the translation of natural language (NL) requirements into linear temporal logic (LTL) specifications, facilitating controller synthesis for cyber-physical systems (CPSs). However, the reliability of such translations remains a concern in safety-critical applications, particularly when NL requirements are ambiguous. This paper proposes a framework based on Conformal Risk Control (CRC) to provide a statistical guarantee on the risk of issuing a controller that violates the user's intended requirement. Rather than requiring semantic equivalence between the generated and intended specifications, the proposed approach considers language inclusion, a sufficient condition for ensuring that the traces of a controller synthesized for the generated specification satisfy the intended requirement. To account for ambiguity, the LLM is queried multiple times, and the resulting LTL specifications are grouped into semantic equivalence classes and ranked by their frequency of occurrence. Given a prescribed risk level, CRC selects how many of the top-ranked equivalence classes to combine into a single LTL specification, such that the probability of issuing a controller that violates the intended requirement is bounded by that level. A controller is then synthesized for the resulting specification, or the framework abstains. Experiments on a vehicle navigation case study evaluate the proposed approach.
evidence_items.title: NL2RCtrl: Risk-Controlled Controller Synthesis from Natural Language Requirements

evidence_items.summary: Discrete element method (DEM) simulations are widely used to investigate granular and particulate systems, but their application often requires specialized expertise in particle physics, numerical modelling, and simulation post-processing. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to simplify these workflows by enabling users to interact with simulation tools through natural language. This study offers GranularGPT, an LLM-assisted agentic framework for end-to-end DEM simulation workflows, from natural-language problem descriptions to simulation execution and automated post-processing. The framework enables users to generate DEM simulation cases, execute and monitor simulations, and automatically extract and report physical and process-level metrics. Evaluation across 60 normal-condition cases covering 12 DEM scenarios and parameter variations achieve a simulation success rate of 91.7%. In the error-handling evaluation, all 10 repairable errors are detected and 9 are successfully resolved, while all 5 non-repairable cases are correctly identified and reported. The framework automatically extracts a range of DEM-relevant metrics, including particle size distributions, packing and density measures, velocity profiles, discharge rates, mixing indices, contact force characteristics, and thermal quantities. GranularGPT provides a foundation for improving the accessibility and efficiency of DEM simulation workflows while reducing the specialized expertise required for their operation.
evidence_items.title: GranularGPT: Natural-Language-Driven End-to-End Discrete Element Method Simulations

evidence_items.summary: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance in robotics through imitation learning, yet fine-tuning them with on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) is limited. In group-based RL methods like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), every rollout step requires multi-step ODE integration, and the sampler's limited stochasticity leads to rollout groups with low variance. We propose VLA-SSD, which addresses both high inference latency and limited stochasticity. In particular, our method self-distills a pretrained flow-matching action head into a stochastic one-step policy by conditioning a single-jump generator on a Brownian path. We derive a conditional action density via our stochastic one-step policy, enabling efficient post-training via likelihood-ratio RL algorithms. We show that distilling VLA-SSD from the $\pi_0$ VLA reduces the action head's forward-pass time by a factor of 7.7, at the cost of a 5.5% relative decrease in the success rate on the LIBERO benchmark. However, by leveraging the increased sample diversity of VLA-SSD during group generation, post-training a $\pi_{0.5}$ VLA using GRPO yields a 20.6% relative improvement.
evidence_items.title: Stochastic Self-Distillation for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models

evidence_items.summary: A single large language model can generate several speaker-labeled role segments within one response; they share one generating process—role separation is display, not architecture. This paper introduces a five-layer model that distinguishes, for each model-generated segment, the generating process (G), the represented speaker designation (R), the delegated boundary (B), the enacted authority (E), and the user’s perception of authority (P). A delegation-boundary crossing is defined as Et∖Bt(Gt, Rt) ≠ ∅ : the segment performs a decision-settling act outside the authority delegated to that process under that designation. An autobiographical vignette from a 16-month corpus (34,425 user messages) grounds the model. Repeated crossings may accumulate into delegation-boundary drift; the paper operationalizes the event unit needed to test that hypothesis without estimating prevalence or trajectory.
evidence_items.title: Who Is Deciding Here? A Five-Layer Model of Delegation-Boundary Crossing in a Single-LLM Multi-Persona Configuration

evidence_items.summary: Can an AI make a trained language model more mature, in the sense of a better organized latent space, by looking only at the geometry of that space? An analyst model reads a fixed-size digest of topological descriptors of the layers of a frozen target and proposes a transformation, which closed-form ridge regression writes into the feed-forward weights without gradient training. Using lightweight models, 126 runs show that category purity rose on unseen words and sentences, benchmark accuracy stayed within sampling error, and the analyst matched a category-aware heuristic with gentler edits. In a five-model round robin approach, 16 pairs raised purity and four left the target unchanged. The results provide a baseline for future work on LLM-guided, training-free model editing without using raw weights.
evidence_items.title: Can AI Mature a Model's Geometry? Training-Free Weight Baking in LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Model editing aims to correct errors in large, pretrained models by replacing model generations with user-provided responses. Existing editors assume a single target answer for each edit. However, many real tasks inherently entail uncertainty, resulting in multiple plausible answers with varying likelihoods in user feedback. Such feedback forms a target distribution to not only correct but also calibrate model generations. We therefore propose SoftEdit, the first model editor to leverage uncertainty in user responses and perform one-shot calibration during editing. To generalize calibration to unseen samples, SoftEdit uses co-plausibility relationships between answers while preserving real distributional shifts, balancing the new distributional generality-locality tradeoff. Across three language models, three vision-language models, and two large datasets, SoftEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance, ultimately showing that uncertainty in user responses enables generalizable calibration of pretrained models beyond single-answer corrections.
evidence_items.title: One-Shot Calibration via Model Editing

evidence_items.summary: Self-evolving language agents have emerged as a promising paradigm for continuously improving agent behavior through experience. However, most existing approaches evolve textual artifacts, which can influence action preferences but cannot reliably enforce action admissibility in embodied environments with discrete and often irreversible actions. We propose MetaAct, which shifts self-evolution from textual guidance to executable action constraints by synthesizing GEAR (Grounded Executable Action Rules) from execution feedback. Each rule is represented as a typed specification, compiled into a deterministic guard, and validated offline through trajectory replay without additional model calls or environment interactions.
