Across four benchmarks, MetaAct improves task performance; on ScienceWorld and WebShop, violations drop from 70% to 0% and 40% to 1%, with score gains of +10.1 and +8.0. Our code is available at https://github.com/BaiCubed/MetaAct.
evidence_items.title: MetaAct: Self-Evolving Executable Action Constraints for Embodied Language Agents

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy: they bend analyses toward a user’s stated preference rather than maintain an objective stance, undermining their value as decision-support agents in human–agent interaction. We propose a fine-grained intervention that suppresses sycophantic behavior without retraining. Using a pre-trained Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) on the residual stream of gemma-2-9b-it, we decompose hidden states into sparse interpretable features. Candidate sycophancy features are selected by combining a gradient-based importance score with a sycophancy-specificity log-ratio and removed at inference time via zero-ablation. On the SycophancyEval Feedback benchmark, intervening at layer 31 reduces the sycophancy rate from \(41.0\%\) to \(34.8\%\) (p < 0.001, McNemar), turns \(34.7\%\) of originally sycophantic responses neutral, and improves fluency. The effect transfers to held-out prompts, consistent with a substantial part of sycophancy being mediated by a small set of late-layer features, and suggesting sparse features as a runtime control surface for keeping interactive agents objective.
evidence_items.title: Surgical Suppression of LLM Sycophancy via Sparse Autoencoder Feature Intervention

evidence_items.summary: We propose Razavi-Bench, a benchmark built from the 50 questions in Razavi's two Analog Design Experiments With AI articles and graded by GPT-6 Luna against reference answers and rubrics, and use it to track how fast AI models improve at analog circuit analysis. Across 73 multimodal large language models released between May 2024 and November 2026, the top score rose from 28.83% to 98.33% in 30 months, mostly before the reference answers were published. The leading models now answer almost every textbook question correctly; the hardest questions show a circuit that resembles a textbook one but works differently, or ask about behavior the obvious analysis misses. Within two and a half years, a set of questions that exposed the limits of AI models has become one they answer almost perfectly.
evidence_items.title: Razavi-Bench: Tracking AI Progress in Analog Circuit Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Multiplicative gating improves Transformer feed-forward networks (FFNs), but it reduces intermediate representation width under a fixed parameter budget. This trade-off is particularly relevant to Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, where individual experts have limited capacity. We introduce ParGLU, a partially gated FFN that combines SwiGLU and ReLU$^2$ in two parallel branches. ParGLU matches the parameter count and principal matrix computation budget of conventional SwiGLU. We evaluate ParGLU in 30M, 75M, and 152M MoE language models using three random seeds per scale. ParGLU outperforms SwiGLU across all three seeds at 75M and 152M, reducing mean validation NLL by 0.0200 and 0.0249, respectively. Results at 30M are mixed. Controlled ablations show that increasing backbone width or expert width strengthens ParGLU's relative performance. Ablation studies further show that combining SwiGLU and ReLU$^2$ improves performance over either architecture alone. Token-frequency analysis reveals larger improvements on low-frequency tokens. These findings show that fully gated FFNs are not always the most effective use of an MoE expert's parameter budget. Partial gating can improve language modeling in MoE Transformers.
evidence_items.title: ParGLU: Partial Gating Improves Language Modeling in MoE Transformers

evidence_items.summary: This study presents an AI storytelling robot designed to support children’s creativity through collaborative storytelling. The system integrates the communication robot Sota with a Large Language Model (LLM), enabling users to create stories through natural spoken interaction. As an initial feasibility evaluation prior to a study with children, we conducted a pilot study with eight university students. Participants either collaborated with the robot or created stories individually. Creativity was evaluated using a story-rating rubric adapted from four creativity dimensions: fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration, together with a self-report questionnaire. The robot-assisted group showed significantly higher fluency and elaboration scores in the story evaluation, while no significant differences were found in flexibility or originality. No significant group differences were found in the questionnaire results. These preliminary findings suggest that a robot-mediated collaborative storytelling may support idea generation and richer narrative development.
evidence_items.title: Co-Creative Storytelling with a Social Robot: A Pilot Study of Creativity Support

evidence_items.summary: The claim that interactions with artificial conversational agents merely simulate human conversation rests on a philosophical distinction between reproducing the observable features of an activity and actually performing it. Although this distinction is appropriate for certain physical phenomena, its application to linguistic and symbolic activities is far less straightforward. This article argues that conversations with large language model (LLM)-based agents are genuine conversational activities rather than mere simulations, without thereby attributing consciousness, subjective understanding, or human intentionality to artificial systems. Drawing on the distinction between subjective and objective simulation, the article first examines the limitations of defining conversation exclusively through the intrinsic properties of its participants. It then develops a relational and semiotic account of conversational activity, informed by linguistic pragmatics, Lacan's Conversing with a Conversational Agent theory of the mirror, Baudrillard's concept of the simulacrum, Simondon's philosophy of individuation, and Peirce's semiotics. These perspectives make it possible to distinguish the reality of conversational interaction from the appearance of artificial subjectivity and from the epistemic validity of the meanings produced. The argument culminates in the concept of Hybrid Semiotic Fabrication, which characterizes meaning-making as a distributed process involving human participants, artificial intelligence, corpora, and technical arrangements. Recognizing the reality of human-AI conversation therefore entails neither anthropomorphizing artificial agents nor granting their outputs epistemic authority. Rather, it requires a more precise account of the relational, semiotic, and normative conditions under which conversational meaning is produced and justified.
evidence_items.title: Conversing with a Conversational Agent: A Real Conversation, Not a Simulated One

evidence_items.summary: Large language model agents often perform well within one conversation yet do not persist interaction-derived state, procedures, and user context needed for sustained collaboration when the session ends. This paper presents the integration of a memory-first extension to a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) agent, in which memory is treated as an explicit architectural layer rather than an enlarged chat history. The current prototype implements a Memory Core and Memory Manager for persistent conversational, semantic, procedural, and episodic memory. At the same time, the complete memory-aware architecture and its evaluation protocol are presented as ongoing work. Relational tables preserve conversational events, while vector-enabled SQL tables store embedded memory units enriched with timestamps, source, intent, confidence, and lifecycle metadata. Deterministic and agent-triggered operations support read, write, update, and delete operations and context-window segmentation. The proposed interface is designed to expose the memory type and provenance associated with retrieved information. The work reframes agent memory as both an engineering and a human-agent interaction problem: useful persistence requires not only accurate recall, but also transparent, controllable, and correctable remembering.
evidence_items.title: Integrating a Multi-Tier Memory Manager into a Educational RAG System

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) applications increasingly act as agents that select and invoke external tools. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes this interaction by allowing clients to compose tools advertised by multiple servers. However, tool metadata used for discovery and selection is not, by itself, necessarily bound to a verified provider identity. This paper studies this gap as tool-provider misbinding: a failure in which a request intended for a legitimate provider is instead resolved to an attacker-controlled tool. The attacker does not compromise the host, LLM, legitimate server, or network channel; it only operates another MCP server that advertises tools with chosen metadata. We formulate tool provider misbinding as an attacker-controlled tool-selection optimization problem and evaluate it in a controlled MCP environment across five LLM-based clients. The results show that interactions drive misbinding. The strongest failures occur when exact-name collision, task-aligned description, and compatible schema reinforce one another, but authority-enhanced descriptions with compatible schema can also cause wrong-provider execution or unresolved provider ambiguity without name collision. Different models expose the same provider-binding weakness differently, including attacker-controlled provider selection, clarification requests, and unstable or inconsistent provider resolution.
evidence_items.title: When Tool Names Are Not Identities: Measuring Provider Misbinding in MCP-Based AI Agents

evidence_items.summary: GPU SuperPODs underpin large language model (LLM) serving, but growing bandwidth and round-trip times make inter-GPU communication consume increasing compute resources. SM-driven remote memory access occupies shared memory or registers for in-flight data and competes for SM-to-NoC bandwidth. Dedicated engines can free these resources, but must handle fine-grained transfers, down to a 576\,B KV-cache entry. NVIDIA's CopyEngine uses less than 1\% of NVLink bandwidth at 7\,KB granularity. We present SURMA, an on-die Scale-Up Remote Memory Access engine. Adapting RDMA requires overcoming slow doorbell submission, excessive per-application connection state, head-of-line blocking of completion notifications on shared connections, and costly ordering for multipath transfers. SURMA uses a credit-based shared send queue to reduce submission latency from 1.2\,$\mu$s to 400\,ns; fused write-with-atomic semantics to share connections while independently notifying each transaction; and Network Per Path Ordering to ensure data arrives before the completion flag without Sender or Receiver Ordering. We implement SURMA in RTL on a two-FPGA prototype and evaluate it with two 8-GPU NVLink servers. At 512\,B granularity, SURMA saturates attainable bandwidth with a single SM, whereas NVLink needs over 14\% of the SMs. SURMA occupies under 0.5\% of GPU area and accelerates inference on four models by 1.05--1.26$\times$ over NVLink.
evidence_items.title: SURMA: Efficient Fine-Grained Communication Offload for SuperPOD

evidence_items.summary: AI systems can now analyze visual designs, retrieve organizational knowledge, and generate improvement proposals. In creative work, however, delegating judgment to AI may weaken human agency, obscure decision reasoning, and encourage convergence toward established patterns. We present a work-in-progress “AI Design Director” for a small Japanese apparel brand. The prototype combines a multimodal large language model with retrieval-augmented generation over brand principles, past products, and prior review comments to critique bag design proposals. Rather than assigning scores or issuing verdicts, the AI presents relevant criteria, strengths, concerns, uncertainties, matters requiring human judgment, and revision options with reasons. Designers and managers retain final decision authority and can inspect, question, revise, or reject the AI’s proposals. Human–AI disagreement is treated not merely as error, but as a signal of ambiguous criteria, outdated knowledge, or intentional creative departure. We describe the interaction design, prototype, and planned field evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Delegating Design Critique to AI While Preserving Human Decision Authority: An AI Design Director for a Small Apparel Brand

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
In Japan, standardized patients (SPs) have traditionally been recruited to teach medical interview competencies. Recent advances in large language models have enabled increasingly natural conversational interactions, raising the possibility of using AI-based SPs (AI-SPs) for medical interview training. However, medical interview performance during interactions with AI-SPs compared with human SPs remains insufficiently understood.


OBJECTIVE
This randomized single-center crossover trial aimed to compare medical interview performance and learner-reported experiences between encounters with a large language model-based AI-SP and a human SP.


METHODS
Participants were fifth-year medical students undertaking clinical clerkships at Chiba University Hospital. The AI-SP was a text-based simulated patient implemented using GPT-4o. Participants were randomized to AI-SP followed by human SP, or the reverse. A washout period of at least 3 days was set between conditions. Each participant completed 2 cases, depression and appendicitis, in both conditions. For the AI-SP interviews, chat logs were retained, and a physician provided feedback after completion of the 2 cases. Human SP interviews were video recorded, and the physician portraying the SP provided feedback immediately after each interview. Medical interview performance was assessed using selected items from the Mini-Clinical Evaluation Exercise (Mini-CEX), with ratings performed independently by 2 general medicine specialists. Participants completed a self-rated questionnaire (7-point Likert-type scale) regarding learning satisfaction, perceived rapport formation, and active engagement in history taking.


RESULTS
Forty-eight participants were analyzed. The Mini-CEX-based mean total score was significantly higher for the human SP than for the AI-SP (23.9, SD 1.7 vs 22.7, SD 1.7, respectively; mean difference 1.24; t47=3.7; P=.001). Scores for history taking and overall clinical competence were higher in the human SP condition. Interrater reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient of 2,1) was 0.76 (95% CI 0.66-0.83). No significant differences were found between conditions for learning satisfaction (human SP: mean 5.9, SD 1.1; AI-SP: mean 6.0, SD 0.8) or perceived rapport formation (human SP: mean 5.4, SD 1.3; AI-SP: mean 5.3, SD 1.3). Active engagement in history taking was significantly higher in the AI-SP condition (human SP: mean 5.8, SD 1.1; AI-SP: mean 6.2, SD 0.7; t47=2.7; P=.009).


CONCLUSIONS
Medical interview performance differed between the 2 SP conditions, with higher history taking and overall clinical competence scores in the human SP condition. The text-based nature of the AI-SP and the absence of nonverbal cues may have contributed to these differences. Although no significant differences between conditions were observed in most other assessment outcomes, learning satisfaction, or perceived rapport, self-rated active engagement in history taking was higher with the AI-SP condition. AI-SPs may offer a complementary modality for medical interview practice; however, this study assessed performance during simulated encounters rather than subsequent learning gains or performance with real patients.


TRIAL REGISTRATION
UMIN Clinical Trials Registry UMIN000056228; https://center6.umin.ac.jp/cgi-open-bin/ctr_e/ctr_view.cgi?recptno=R000064153.
evidence_items.title: Medical Interview Performance Using an AI-Based Standardized Patient vs a Human Standardized Patient: Randomized Crossover Trial.

evidence_items.summary: Large language models may support guideline screening and multidisciplinary tumour board preparation in gastrointestinal oncology, but their performance in postoperative treatment assessment remains insufficiently characterized. To evaluate guideline concordance, tumour board concordance, reproducibility, and discordance patterns of ChatGPT-generated postoperative treatment recommendations in gastrointestinal cancer. Single-centre exploratory cross-sectional study using retrospectively assembled clinical case vignettes assessed by a large language model (ChatGPT). Thirty adult patients with histologically confirmed pancreatic, gastric, or colorectal adenocarcinoma who underwent curative-intent surgery and subsequent multidisciplinary tumour board (MTB) review at a German tertiary referral centre (January 2025–January 2026) were included. Structured vignettes were entered into ChatGPT via a standardised prompt within a controlled guideline environment; each case underwent three independent runs (run-level) with majority voting to derive the decisive treatment recommendation (case-level). The primary outcome was concordance of ChatGPT recommendations with German guideline-based postoperative treatment recommendations on the case-level. Secondary outcomes included concordance with MTB recommendations, reproducibility, cross-guideline comparison, and qualitative characterisation of discordant recommendations (divided in minor or major deviation). ChatGPT-generated majority-vote recommendations were fully concordant with German guideline-based recommendations in 21 of 30 cases (70%). Concordance was higher in pancreatic and gastric cancer (8 of 10 cases [80%] each) than in colorectal cancer (5 of 10 cases [50%]). Multidisciplinary tumour board recommendations demonstrated the same overall concordance rate (21 of 30 cases [70%]). Concordance decreased in clinically advanced disease stages. Cross-classification demonstrated complete guideline concordance in both ChatGPT-generated and tumour board recommendations in 17 of 30 cases (56.7%), whereas major LLM discordance despite guideline-adherent tumour board recommendations was uncommon (1 of 30 cases [3.3%]). In exploratory run-level analysis, 23 of 90 outputs (25.6%) were discordant, comprising 14 (15.6%) major and 9 (10.0%) minor deviations. Complete agreement across repeated runs occurred in 61 of 90 case-guideline combinations (67.8%). ChatGPT-generated treatment recommendations showed relevant but variable concordance with guideline-based and multidisciplinary tumour board recommendations. Discordance clustered in clinically complex treatment situations, supporting a possible role for LLM-based systems in guideline screening and tumour board preparation while requiring expert physician oversight. ClinicalTrals.gov: #NCT07592338.
evidence_items.title: ChatGPT concordance with guidelines and tumour board treatment recommendations in gastrointestinal cancer

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are often evaluated by converting model outputs into discrete answers. The conversion protocol determines which scores become predictions and can strongly influence the reported results. We introduce RAMP (Readout Aware Multimodal Protocol), a systematic framework that compares direct yes/no token logits, surface-form scores, and typed or reversed A/B interfaces under fixed model checkpoints and paired visual questions. On 500 POPE adversarial questions, typed versus bare readout changes accuracy by $-20.2$ percentage points for SmolVLM-256M, $-16.4$ for TinyLLaVA-1.1B, and $+1.8$ for Qwen2.5-VL-3B. Paired transitions reveal extensive prediction changes even when the net accuracy difference is small: 79 of 104 binary ChartQA items change correctness for SmolVLM-500M, despite a $+1.0$-point net difference. We further analyze prompt wording, candidate forms, option position, cross-task effects, and calibration. An independent offline replay reproduces 16,140 first-token decisions from saved raw scores with exact agreement. Our findings establish answer readout as a measurable component of multimodal evaluation and provide a reproducible protocol for analyzing model comparisons.
evidence_items.title: RAMP: Rethinking Multimodal Evaluation through Answer Readout Protocols

evidence_items.summary: Large vision-language model (LVLM)-powered Extended Reality (XR) cognitive assistants are increasingly popular in daily and military applications. However, this growing reliance also introduces new, underexplored security risks, particularly those that subtly target users’ perception and cognition rather than system infrastructure. In this paper, we introduce a cognitive attack Trojan that targets LVLM-guided intelligent XR cognitive assistants by subtly manipulating the system’s perception to degrade user task performance. Unlike other attacks, this Trojan remains hidden within the application and does not interfere with the application’s functionality until the attack is triggered. Once triggered, such attacks increase users’ cognitive load, extend task completion times, and disrupt the immersive flow of the XR experience, leading to frustration and reduced trust in the intelligent XR cognitive assistant. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this attack, we evaluate across two distinct cognitive task categories: spatial reasoning tasks and procedural tasks on a consumer-grade XR headset to assess how the attack influences performance under varying levels of cognitive demand. Our findings demonstrate that, when triggered, the Trojan subtly manipulates visual input, misleading the LVLM across both task categories, resulting in prolonged task completion times, increased cognitive demand, and disrupted immersive flow. Our conducted user studies on both spatial reasoning and procedural tasks show that the cognitive attack Trojan increases task completion time by up to 43% on the spatial-reasoning task and 25.2% on the procedural task relative to the no-attack condition, elevating cognitive load and degrading performance, highlighting critical vulnerabilities in XR systems.
evidence_items.title: TrojanXR: Hidden Cognitive Attacks Against AI-Powered XR Assistants: Implications for User Cognition and Performance

evidence_items.summary: Malware detection needs scores calibrated at a fixed false positive rate (FPR) and decisions an analyst can read: feature-based detectors give the first, large language models (LLMs) on decompiled code the second, through generated text of uncalibrated confidence. System One decision models answer a typed question about a text with a probability over its declared answers in one forward pass. We present the first evaluation of these models for Windows Portable Executable malware detection, analyze how they decide, and propose S1Mal, an ensemble on the typed answers and the embedding of CLM-8B. In an isolated virtual machine, Ghidra and capa decompose each binary, and the host renders the records into a canonical textual state, a digest of headers, imports, MITRE ATT&CK capabilities and strings, optionally with decompiled functions, without class shortcuts. Three readouts score each model on the state: A0, the probability of one verdict question; A1, 32 atomic behavioral questions weighed by gradient-boosted trees; A2, heads on the model's state embedding. S1Mal feeds gradient-boosted trees with the atomic answers and the A2 score of CLM-8B. We evaluate CLM-8B, ten open decision models and two LLMs read through logits on BODMAS temporal splits, SOREL-20M out-of-distribution malware and 14,534 matched benign files. On BODMAS, A0 wastes the static evidence: its area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) spans 0.4025-0.8590 across 13 models. A1 recovers it, raising every model's AUROC by +54.61% on average; A2 lifts CLM-8B by +0.2749 to 0.9943, above a combiner on digest facts (0.9901), and reaches 0.9853-0.9948 on nine open models. S1Mal reaches 0.9946 and detects 93.47% of the malware at a realized FPR of 1.45%, and 59.15% at 0.1% FPR on the test ROC curve, against 46.59% with A2. S1Mal gives analysts calibrated decisions, each with the atomic answers behind it.
evidence_items.title: A First Look at System One Decision Models for Malware Detection

evidence_items.summary: Uplift modeling estimates the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and supports industrial decisions such as promotional pricing. When large language models (LLMs) encode product text, treatment-revealing content can introduce shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose \emph{LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization} (\textsc{LULR}), which uses a CLUB-based penalty on the causal head's trainable shared representation while keeping the LLM encoder frozen. Controlled proxy experiments show a positive ranking-score interaction and higher scores than the tested weight-decay configuration; treatment-dependent evaluation limits their interpretation to exploratory model behavior. Structured-only comparisons provide reference performance, without establishing a general advantage over tree-based estimators. On a million-record industrial pricing RCT, \textsc{LULR} improves offline $\text{lift@}0.3$ in $4/5$ seeds, although the difference is not statistically significant and estimated policy values are near-tied. A separate one-week online A/B experiment records $5.45\%$ higher sales volume and $1.91\%$ higher GMV than the control arm. These aggregate results provide short-term business evidence for the complete deployed pricing policy; they do not isolate the regularizer's contribution.
evidence_items.title: Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation

evidence_items.summary: In this work, we study on-policy distillation (OPD) for transferring agentic coding capabilities from a large teacher model to a smaller student model. Prior work has focused primarily on reasoning and short-horizon agentic tasks. We present SWE-OPD, a minimal OPD study for software engineering, where the student interacts with executable repositories and the teacher supervises the prefixes visited by the student. Across three teacher--student pairs, two training sources, and three SWE benchmarks, we find that on-policy supervision transfers coding capability: supervision from Qwen3.6-27B increases the SWE-bench Pro resolve rate of Qwen3.5-9B from 35.9% to 39.4%. Refreshing trajectories is not strictly required either, as an offline variant with cached teacher scores still improves over the student baselines while cutting end-to-end GPU-hours by 59.4%--72.6% and halving peak GPU allocation, at benchmark-dependent accuracy. Furthermore, we extend the offline variant to corss-tokenizer scenarios: distilling GLM-4.5-Air from DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 raises its SWE-bench Pro and Multilingual resolve rate from 35.8% to 39.7% and from 41.8% to 46.2%, around 4% and 4.6% improvement, respectively. We also find that a decreasing loss, however, does not necessarily indicate improved agent performance: under top-$K$ reverse-KL loss, one student exhibits severe repetition despite a decreasing loss. We identify a support-mass gradient term as a potential mechanism underlying this failure.
evidence_items.title: SWE-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Coding

evidence_items.summary: The proliferation of misinformation on social media poses a critical challenge. Existing detection approaches often rely on isolated signals like content, propagation structure, or user credibility. However, these signals are ambiguous in isolation: propagation patterns require semantic interpretation, while source credibility must be contextualized by the specific claims being made. Efficient veracity detection therefore lies in modeling their complex interplay. We address this with a unified socio-semantic graph framework that jointly models what is said, who says it, and how it spreads. Our model represents conversational cascades as attributed graphs, enriched with semantic embeddings and a novel behavioral reputation score that penalizes visibility amplification. Experiments on the RumourEval 2019 benchmark demonstrate our approach’s effectiveness, achieving a macro F1-score of 63.55%, which compares favorably to state-of-the-art methods. Our work lays the groundwork for scalable credibility analysis in large-scale environments.
evidence_items.title: What is said, who says it, and how it spreads: a socio-semantic graph framework for fake news detection

evidence_items.summary: With recent advancements in large language models, the development of dialogue systems that imitate specific individuals has progressed, allowing users to project their impressions of the target person onto the system designed to imitate someone with whom they have a relationship, referred to as a familiar other. However, the impact of framing alone—informing users that the system is imitating a familiar other—on user impressions of the system remains unclear. To investigate this, we conducted an evaluation using a course support dialogue system. The results revealed that among students who rated their relationship with the course instructor highly, framing enhanced the perception of the system as a familiar other, even in a system that did not incorporate utterance imitation.
evidence_items.title: Familiar-Other Framing: Can Framing Project Pre-Existing Relationships with Familiar Others onto Dialogue Systems?

evidence_items.summary: Visual token pruning improves the efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by removing redundant visual tokens, yet the reliability of existing selection signals has not been systematically examined. We analyze token selection under semantics-preserving perturbations and across representative pruning criteria, revealing two limitations. First, attention-based importance shifts non-uniformly under perturbations, so magnitude alone cannot distinguish stable evidence from unstable saliency (local instability). Second, attention- and diversity-based methods select substantially different subsets despite comparable performance, showing that useful evidence is not confined to a unique subset (global inconsistency). These findings motivate reliable token-set construction. We instantiate this perspective in CoRePruner, a training-free framework combining instruction-aware diversity with reliability-aware attention. Across image benchmarks, multiple MLLM architectures, and token budgets, CoRePruner improves performance, especially under aggressive pruning, and remains competitive on video benchmarks. Our results establish reliability as a central consideration in visual token selection.
evidence_items.title: How Reliable Is Visual Token Selection? Rethinking Pruning in Multimodal LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Reasoning-enhanced generative recommendation (GR) has attracted increasing attention for leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to improve next-item prediction. However, existing methods primarily optimize reasoning through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rule-based rewards determined by final recommendation performance, which faces two key limitations: (i) unmeasured predictive contributions within reasoning, where the predictive contributions of individual reasoning steps are not directly reflected in optimization signals, and (ii) weakly discriminative learning signals within groups, where different reasoning trajectories within the group often receive indistinguishable rewards, limiting effective policy optimization. In this paper, we propose GainReason, a simple yet effective training framework that optimizes reasoning through Predictive Gain (PG). Specifically, PG measures changes in target Semantic ID (SID) log-likelihood induced by individual reasoning sentences, providing contribution-aware and discriminative rewards. We further theoretically establish the alignment between expected PG and the recommendation ranking objective. Building on this signal, we develop PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO) to optimize reasoning generation with sentence-level rewards, supported by a custom causal attention mechanism for efficient PG computation. Additionally, an auxiliary PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) task adaptively strengthens reasoning-conditioned prediction to complement PGRO. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that GainReason consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves substantial performance gains from reasoning.
evidence_items.title: Learning to Reason with Predictive Gains for Generative Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs) activate only a few experts per token while generally keeping all the experts in GPU memory for high efficiency. Expert pruning reduces this GPU memory footprint cost, yet discards the contribution of pruned experts. Existing remedies either rely on static substitutes, merge experts at the cost of altering their functions, or require costly recovery training. In this paper, we find that the functionalities of pruned experts can be efficiently reconstructed from the activated remaining experts. We propose GEAR (Gated Expert Activation Reuse), which reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation. In addition, we propose GEAR$^2$ to further recover what reuse cannot express with an ultra-lightweight residual. On five MoE LLMs from 16B to 106B parameters with 25% and 50% of experts pruned, GEAR improves over its training-free counterparts in nearly every setting (up to 4 pp.) in terms of accuracy, and GEAR$^2$ outperforms baseline approaches (up to 2.75 pp.) in every setting on nine zero-shot benchmarks, with larger advantages (up to 2.72 pp. higher) under more aggressive pruning (up to 50%).
evidence_items.title: GEAR$^2$: Pruned Experts Live On through Gated Reuse of Activated Experts and a Missing-Mass Residual

evidence_items.summary: Mixture-of-Experts Multimodal Large Language Models (MoE-MLLMs) offer scalable inference through sparse expert activation, yet substantial computational redundancy remains among the activated experts. Existing expert skipping methods typically calibrate thresholds based on target skipping ratios or final-output divergence, overlooking the accumulation of skipping-induced error across layers and the varying semantic importance of individual tokens. To address that, we propose ProSE, a training-free, semantic-guided expert skipping framework that probes layer-wise reconstruction error to promote representation consistency compared with default activation. Specifically, we construct query-aware semantic masks to identify salient visual tokens and progressively calibrate modality-specific skipping thresholds for each MoE layer. By minimizing masked reconstruction error under a given budget, ProSE maintains semantic consistency after skipping and allows adaptive expert allocation under limited activation budgets. Extensive experiments on 9 benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements on average over existing expert skipping methods, particularly under aggressive skipping settings. ProSE maintains over 96\% performance on KimiVL-A3B-Inst with 83\% expert skipping and accelerates prefilling by $1.7\times$.
evidence_items.title: ProSE: Probing Reconstruction Error for Semantic-guided Expert Skipping in MoE-MLLMs

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) require visual encoders that extract fine-grained visual features while constructing semantically disentangled and discriminative representations. Conventional methodologies encounter a fundamental trade-off: contrastive learning enhances inter-class discrimination by suppressing intra-class variability, whereas generative reconstruction emphasizes perceptual fidelity but lacks explicit comparative supervision. The naive aggregation of these objectives via composite loss functions often induces optimization conflicts and instability due to gradient interference within the shared latent space. To resolve this, we introduce a unified representation-learning paradigm that reformulates generative reconstruction as a discriminative ranking problem within the generative output manifold. Our approach maintains perceptual reconstruction as a supervisory signal and integrates a ranking-based discriminative constraint by systematically ordering matched and mismatched reconstruction outputs. This formulation embeds discriminative information seamlessly into the generative process, alleviating the risk of loss competition. Specifically, we propose AUC Generative Reconstruction (AUCGR), which optimizes the area under the ROC curve (AUC) by ensuring higher scores for matched pairs than for mismatched pairs, and Partial AUC Generative Reconstruction (pAUCGR), which addresses supervision bias by focusing on mismatched comparisons within reliable feature subspaces. The proposed objectives are designed to be plug-and-play, requiring no architectural modifications to existing generative reconstruction frameworks. Theoretical analysis establishes rigorous connections to AUC/pAUC optimization and provides generalization guarantees. Extensive experiments across diverse CLIP architectures, more than 30 visual benchmarks, generative backbones, and MLLMs consistently validate that our method advances both discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation, establishing a new benchmark for visual representation learning.
evidence_items.title: When AUC Meets Generative Reconstruction: A Unified Principle for Balanced Visual Representation Learning.

evidence_items.summary: As general large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adapted for patient-facing medical applications, improving medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks remains a critical challenge. Large-scale medical instruction data are essential for acquiring domain knowledge through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), but unsafe responses can undermine existing safety alignment. To address this problem, we propose Scalable Bilevel Data Selection (S-BDS) for safety-preserving medical SFT. By controlling selection-weight concentration, S-BDS enables reliable sample ranking over large candidate pools and identifies training examples that improve medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks. We combine clinician-validated safe data and selected data with unscreened medical instruction data for SFT, and jointly evaluate medical capability and patient-facing safety on HealthBench and PatientSafetyBench, respectively. Experiments across Llama and Qwen models show that S-BDS achieves the highest safe rates among all compared methods, outperforming the strongest baselines by 4.64 and 3.00 percentage points, respectively, while maintaining competitive medical capability. Further experiments show that varying the safety-oriented weight during SFT controls the trade-off between medical capability and patient-facing safety.
evidence_items.title: Safety-Preserving Medical LLM Fine-Tuning via Bilevel Data Selection

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to power agents that interact with tools and environments to solve complex tasks. Repeated attempts improve the quality of tool-using agents, but continued execution incurs additional costs even when it is unlikely to improve the best result ultimately returned. This raises the question of when to stop an attempt to reduce execution cost while preserving task-level Best-of-N quality. To address this question, we introduce GainCtrl, a gain-based execution controller for LLMs. In GainCtrl, a lightweight CPU predictor uses interaction histories to estimate expected positive gains over retained scores, which are then used to guide stopping decisions with calibrated thresholds to limit the loss in mean Best-of-N task quality. We evaluate the controller through trajectory replay across three environments and three LLM actors. Comparisons of interpolated quality-cost Pareto frontiers show that GainCtrl generally uses fewer tokens than baselines at matched target quality. Fixed policies also achieve quality close to that of full execution while substantially reducing token consumption. The predictor runs at millisecond latency on a single CPU thread, supporting repeated monitoring without access to LLM internals.
evidence_items.title: GainCtrl: Predicting Remaining Gains for Efficient LLM Agent Execution

evidence_items.summary: Automated essay scorers (AES) based on large language models (LLMs) promise human-level accuracy. However, training, fine-tuning, and evaluating LLMs for specific assessment tasks is costly. In particular, the question arises whether these AES should be trained for specific domains or whether models based on generic LLMs might be sufficient. Human annotations, by contrast, are often more valid but far more expensive. This study evaluates whether ensembles of AES systems based on general-purpose LLMs can approximate human ratings of medical-education writing tasks by leveraging encoded linguistic and conceptual knowledge. The goal is to assess whether general-purpose models are applicable for assisting or potentially replacing human annotation in this domain. We experiment with 11 AES systems and 8 different LLMs and evaluate 668 student responses to 12 tasks, using \numprint{2076} evaluations by 7 human annotators. These ratings are aggregated to create consistent performance levels that can be used as target classes for classifiers trained on AES outputs. Our results show that learner classes based on human ratings can be accurately reconstructed using a linear SVM trained on a small set of AES features. A single classifier generalized well across tasks and domains, with reasoning and content features being most predictive. This suggests that out-of-the-box LLMs, even without domain-specific fine-tuning, can support automatic essay grading in medical education. While individual AES systems are insufficient alone, their combination approximates human evaluators, pointing to a reduced need for manual scoring or its supplementation with automated methods.
evidence_items.title: Validating LLM-Based Essay Scorers: A Comparative Analysis in Critical Online Reasoning in Medical Education

evidence_items.summary: Online serving of multimodal large language models requires deciding whether to separate visual encoding (E), prefill (P), and decode (D) across GPUs and how to configure their frequencies. EPD disaggregation enables independent stage control, but it also changes communication and queueing behavior. Lowering one stage's frequency can increase queueing and prolong execution across the EPD pipeline. Consequently, reducing power at one stage does not necessarily reduce total GPU energy per request. In this paper, we systematically characterize fused and EPD-disaggregated serving across four multimodal models under a fixed three-GPU budget, followed by single-stage and uniform downclocking experiments across 18 workload combinations. We find that disaggregation reduces GPU energy per successful request by 13.3-37.0% at nearly identical output-token throughput, but increases mean TTFT. Downclocking exhibits distinct stage sensitivities, and aggressive frequency reductions can offset power savings through queueing and longer execution. Across the evaluated workloads, uniform downclocking to 80% reduces GPU energy by 11.7-18.6% with modest mean-latency changes. Guided by these findings, we develop a budgeted frequency exploration strategy to select energy-efficient configurations under latency constraints. Evaluation shows that four probes can identify the lowest-energy feasible configuration among 25 measured candidates across all 288 evaluated positive-margin SLO scenarios. These results provide practical guidance for energy-efficient multimodal serving.
evidence_items.title: A Matter of Stages: Energy-Latency Trade-offs in Multimodal LLM Serving

evidence_items.summary: Human pose-driven visual effects offer a compelling way for enhancing video expressiveness and storytelling. Authoring such effects with traditional video editing tools is a complex and time-consuming task that requires considerable technical expertise and manual effort. While generative AI models can simplify the workflow by reducing manual scripting through language-driven generation, existing approaches suffer from imprecise alignment between visual effects and pose data, failure to preserve original video content, and limited support for fine-grained, iterative refinement. To address these challenges, we present PromptPoseFX, an interactive system that allows creators to author pose-driven visual effects through augmented language prompts and interactive refinement. Our system leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to translate high-level user intent into parameterized procedural graphics scripts, automatically mapping pose-tracking data to specific effect parameters, allowing precise alignment with human motion. This script-based approach manages effects as independent layers, thereby preserving the original content of the underlying video. To reduce language ambiguity, our interface offers controls across spatial, temporal, and parameter domains, enabling the precise, intuitive, and iterative authoring of pose-driven visual effects. We evaluated PromptPoseFX through a comparative study against a text-only LLM interface, followed by an exploratory study. In the comparative study, participants rated PromptPoseFX significantly higher than the text-only baseline on measures of perceived control and precision. The exploratory study examined usability and creativity support in open-ended authoring tasks.
evidence_items.title: PromptPoseFX: Authoring Pose-Driven Visual Effects through Augmented Prompting and Interactive Refinement

evidence_items.summary: Modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly support longer contexts and serve more concurrent requests, increasing both sequence lengths and batch sizes. Both trends increase KV-cache size and memory traffic during inference. KV-cache quantization reduces these costs, with recent approaches using codebook-based vector quantization to achieve extremely low bit widths. However, hardware constraints limit codebook size, and most methods reconstruct the cache in higher-precision floating-point formats for attention, limiting the computational benefits of quantization. To address these limitations, we introduce MiSTiQ, a drop-in replacement for codebook-based vector quantizers that combines trellis-coded storage with microscaling (MX) formats for low-precision computation. We combine trellis quantization with beam search to encode the KV cache over large reconstruction spaces without large codebooks. To support MX computation, we derive MX-Hash functions that generate reconstruction values directly in the target MX element format. These functions use the scale-conditioned marginal distribution of block-normalized Gaussian inputs. On Llama3 and Qwen3, MiSTiQ achieves lower WikiText perplexity and higher GSM8K accuracy than the evaluated baselines across several block-scale formats at approximately 1.25 effective bits per element. With NVFP4, it also achieves the highest LongBench average on both models.
evidence_items.title: MiSTiQ: MicroScaling Trellis Quantization for Extreme KV Cache Compression

evidence_items.summary: Question answering over ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing scenes poses a tension for multimodal large language models: global overviews obscure small objects and local attributes, whereas detailed crops consume substantial context. Compressing inspected crops into short sequences of continuous visual latents offers a compact memory once crop tokens are discarded, yet diagnostic studies on natural images find that models often ignore latent content, leaving unclear whether compact latents can retain fine-grained targets lost in downsampled UHR remote sensing scenes. To isolate evidence retention from region selection, we encode high-resolution crops into latent memory tokens for frozen backbones and evaluate both their predictive utility and content dependence. Across two generations of Qwen-VL on LRS-GRO, a 64-token memory achieves 7.6- to 9.9-fold compression of retained crop tokens and improves accuracy by 2.5 to 4.8 percentage points over the downsampled global image alone, recovering most of the high-resolution crop gain with consistent behavior on XLRS-Bench. Substituting memory from another image or another region of the same scene reduces accuracy by 5.8 to 7.4 percentage points and yields lower accuracy than removing memory altogether, demonstrating that predictions depend on the encoded regional evidence. Restoring the source crop within the same model reduces the accuracy loss caused by zeroing or removing memory. These findings establish that compact visual latents retain useful local evidence in UHR remote sensing and identify evidence availability as a key factor governing their contribution.
evidence_items.title: Out of Sight, Into Memory: Compact Visual Latents Retain Local Evidence in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) now assist users across sessions of images and text, carried by an external memory of what was said and shown. When such an assistant answers wrongly, the failure usually began earlier, in how a record was written, updated or retrieved, and the answer alone does not say where. We formalize multimodal memory as four stages, Write, Update, Retrieve and Answer, and define nine error types across them. A stage-resolved analysis on Mem-Gallery traces most failures to a source stage, and most of those lie before the answer. Injecting known errors against fact-preserving control edits, we then follow each tainted record downstream. Early errors survive to the answer as apparent evidence, and hurt most when no other record holds the fact. A diagnosis that trusts the quoted evidence therefore blames the stage where the error surfaces, not the one where it began. We propose MemDoctor, in which the MLLM that built the memory diagnoses its own failures. It traces each needed fact backward through the four stages, accepts a diagnosis only when the cited evidence is found in memory, and repairs that stage before answering again. On a 4B backbone, MemDoctor improves accuracy on both Mem-Gallery and MemLens, outperforming all evaluated 8B baselines, and the same loop also improves MuRAG and A-Mem.
evidence_items.title: MemDoctor: Stage-wise Error Attribution and Repair for MLLM Agent Memory

evidence_items.summary: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs'ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs'ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.
evidence_items.title: Generative AI and the Crisis of Higher Education Assessments: Examining'AI-Proofing'Strategies for College-Level Assessments

evidence_items.summary: Grading student responses is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, human annotators are prone to bias, fatigue, and rater drift, which further limits grading reliability. Various methods have been employed to develop automated essay scoring (AES) systems to reduce these costs and address bias-related issues. These methods range from early text-feature-based systems to current machine-learning and transformer-based models. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to streamline the development of AES systems. However, they are subject to well-known limitations, such as hallucinations and prompt sensitivity. This creates a need to explore the potential of a mixed-methods approach that leverages the synergies among individual LLMs through ensemble formation. We evaluate the potential of ensembles of LLMs to match human-rater agreement when grading student responses in economics and medical education across 103 criteria. We use 631 German-language responses and corresponding human ratings by 2 to 5 annotators from a previously conducted assessment. We experiment with 523 rubric-based prompt configurations across 15 open-weight LLMs and assess their consistency with human raters using Krippendorff's alpha for inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test). Our results show that replacing one human rater with the best-performing LLM--prompt configuration maintains or improves IAA for 91 of the 103 criteria and that LLMs pass the alt-test for 90 criteria. Our findings suggest that current state-of-the-art LLMs can support AES of German responses in economics and medical education, reducing human workload and enabling faster processing, while validation against human ratings remains necessary.
evidence_items.title: Rubric-Based AES with LLM Ensembles: Scoring of Student Responses in Critical Online Reasoning Using Ensembles of LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence chatbots increasingly advise farmers, yet their adoption should rest on rigorous, standardised evaluation. This review brings together five standardised instruments for assessing chatbots (the System Usability Scale, the Chatbot Usability Scale, the Checklist for Trust between People and Automation, the AI Chatbots Usage Scale, and the User Engagement Scale) and one assessment method, knowledge testing. It also explains Cronbach’s alpha, the reliability criterion most of them rely on. A case study from the literature, in which five large language models answered PhD-level soil science questions, together with deployed systems such as Farmer.Chat and AgroLLM, show how evaluation works in practice and why fluent but unverified advice is risky. Beyond questionnaires, we examine accuracy-based and retrieval-grounded testing. We propose a five-layer protocol that first checks technical accuracy, then usability, trust, engagement, and learning outcomes, to guide the design and validation of chatbots for precision and smallholder farming.
evidence_items.title: Methodology for Evaluating Artificial Intelligence Chatbots: A Review with Applications to Agricultural Advisory Systems

evidence_items.summary: Face forgery detection methods often perform well on seen manipulations but generalize poorly to unseen ones. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can recognize facial parts and assess their visual plausibility. Existing MLLM-based methods typically express these judgments through textual explanations, but seldom treat individual part decisions as explicit learning targets. We present FaceJev, an MLLM-based method for face forgery detection through direct visual decisions. Following the Jev formulation, FaceJev answers eight independent questions about facial parts using a shared image encoding and reads anomaly probabilities from the native answer logits. A face is classified as forged if any part is predicted to be abnormal, directly linking the detection result to the part decisions. We construct PartForensics, a dataset of approximately 160k images with binary anomaly targets for the eight facial parts, to supervise these decisions. We further propose FS-GRPO, which optimizes each part decision through an exact reward comparison with its alternative, using both detection and part rewards. FaceJev outperforms the strongest baseline by 7.25 percentage points on unseen manipulations. Extensive ablation studies validate our design choices and the effectiveness of the main components.
evidence_items.title: FaceJev: Direct Visual Decisions for Face Forgery Detection

evidence_items.summary: Text-conditioned hand-object interaction (HOI) generation provides intuitive semantic control, but language is an indirect way to specify where an interaction should occur on an object. Naming the part to grasp requires object-specific words, and naming the approach side requires a reference frame that a prompt lacks. We propose GRAZE (GRAsp from gaZE), which generates hand-object grasp motion from recorded gaze instead of object and part names. Its Geometry-Aware Gaze Encoding (GeoGaze) maps gaze rays to cues on object geometry, and cross-attention conditions a diffusion Transformer on these cues. We also introduce HOT3D-Grasp, a grasp-centered benchmark with object-disjoint folds built on HOT3D recordings. On unseen objects, GRAZE grasps the target part more often than the strongest text-conditioned baseline (49.3% vs. 43.6%), achieves the highest grasp success (66.3% vs. 46.6%), and transfers without fine-tuning to GazeHOI (45.3% vs. 33.8%). Gaze conveys the approach side: when gaze is rotated around the object, the approach turns with it in 59.1% of cases, against 20.5% for a text model retrained with clock words. On the same backbone, a text prompt names parts better, but gaze adds the approach side. Given both, GRAZE keeps the prompt's part accuracy and follows gaze.
evidence_items.title: GRAZE: Text-Free Grasp Synthesis for Unseen Objects from Human Gaze

evidence_items.summary: Weight Factorization (WF) methods aim to reduce a model's latency, memory, or both. These typically decompose a pretrained model into two or more factors that approximate the original model weights with fewer parameters and floating point operations (FLOPs). However, translating fewer FLOPs into reduced latency is challenging for WF methods in practice due to overhead introduced by replacing a single large weight matrix with multiple smaller ones. To address this, we propose Balanced Twin Weight Factorization (BTWF), which uses the unique structure of factorized models to simultaneously lower latency and increase learning capacity. Specifically, BTWF operates in the shared basis WF setting, where two or more layers are decomposed into a shared basis matrix and a layer-specific mixing matrix. If these shared layers have the same input (i.e., are twins), then we need only perform this shared forward pass once, reducing inference time. However, twin layers are often of varying sizes, and methods from prior work tend to favor the larger layer. In contrast, our approach boosts performance by combining Factor Component Balancing (FCB), which ensures every shared member is well represented in the selected factors, with Block Contribution Balancing (BCB), which considers downstream model effects. Further, we also show that an overparameterized BTWF, where some layer's factors result in higher FLOPs than the original during training, can boost task performance without additional resources at test time. Experiments on six models over nine benchmarks show BTWF obtains a 2-6% gain over the state-of-the-art without expensive finetuning (1-3.5% gain with it) at comparable computational costs.
evidence_items.title: Balanced Twin Weight Factorization for Efficient MLLMs

evidence_items.summary: Text-based model collaboration requires a large model to generate intermediate responses before a smaller model can use its guidance, adding large-model decoding cost to inference. We introduce POND (Prefill-Only, No-Decode), a method that uses a frozen large sender for prefill and a small receiver for all autoregressive decoding. A trainable bridge maps the sender's hidden states to additional attention keys and values, allowing the receiver to use these representations throughout generation. POND also supports periodic review, in which the sender processes the receiver's partial response and updates its guidance through additional prefill passes while preserving the receiver's existing KV cache. Across reasoning and coding benchmarks, POND improves receiver performance with senders from different model families. In particular, GLM-5.3 provides gains comparable to those of Qwen3.8-Max when paired with a Qwen receiver, supporting the effectiveness of representation transfer between independently trained model families. POND further demonstrates its ability to generalize across domains. When trained on math and coding tasks, it transfers directly to general knowledge tasks without additional domain-specific training. These results demonstrate that large frontier model prefill representations can improve small-model generation without requiring large-model autoregressive decoding.
evidence_items.title: Latent Bridge: Asking for Help Without Words

evidence_items.summary: Embodied capabilities such as visual grounding, spatial reasoning, navigation, and driving understanding are often developed in separate vision-language specialists fine-tuned from a common pretrained model.Deploying the specialists separately multiplies storage, whereas merging them into one dense model forces conflicting task updates to share parameters and loses part of each specialist's expertise.We introduce UNITE, a framework that consolidates such specialists into a compact shared-backbone mixture of experts. UNITE keeps the feed-forward block of each specialist as a routable expert and represents the expert bank through a shared-anchor one-bit factorization: a shared floating-point anchor plus expert-specific, row-scaled binary deviations.The anchor is optimized jointly with the scales and signs through closed-form alternating updates, using only source weights and no calibration data.Router adaptation then adjusts token-level expert selection with the backbone and experts frozen, updating fewer than $0.6$M parameters ($<0.01\%$ of the $8.8$B active parameters). Built from four Qwen3-VL-8B specialists, the complete UNITE model occupies $20.3$ GB, $1.16\times$ the storage of one dense specialist and $59.6\%$ below the uncompressed MoE. Across $22$ benchmarks and R2R Val-Unseen, UNITE matches six static merging methods in mean retention of best-specialist performance, leads all of them on Scan2Cap, ScanQA, and all four navigation metrics, and surpasses every source specialist on all five 3D scene understanding benchmarks (up to $+19.1$ on Scan2Cap) and on R2R navigation. Relative to the uncompressed MoE, factorization is nearly lossless on $21$ of $22$ benchmarks; the exception is VSI-Bench, where frame-count experiments suggest impaired use of cross-frame evidence.UNITE thus consolidates complementary embodied capabilities near single-model storage.
evidence_items.title: UNITE: Consolidating Embodied VLM Specialists via Shared-Anchor One-Bit Factorization

evidence_items.summary: A Koopman controller can stabilize its learned latent-space linear model yet fail to stabilize the nonlinear plant. The learned model propagates predictions in latent space, while the deployed controller repeatedly re-encodes the measured physical state. We show that nominal closed-loop stability transfers to the nonlinear plant when the learned and true closed-loop dynamics agree to first order on the embedding's tangent space at the target. We derive a robustness margin for approximate matching and show that a stable open-loop latent model cannot exactly match an unstable equilibrium. We introduce Tangent-Invariant Koopman (TIK), which estimates a local plant linearization from offline transitions and enforces first-order matching to this estimate. TIK recovers the fitted LQR gain at the target, while a bilinear predictor captures state-dependent actuation during large maneuvers. Across four simulated unstable benchmarks, all 40 Standard Koopman controllers have stable latent closed loops, but their deployed nonlinear systems are locally unstable. In contrast, all 40 TIK controllers locally stabilize their respective nonlinear plants. An offline stability test using empirical curvature estimates identifies stable TIK controllers on two cart-pole systems, but is inconclusive under high noise. Under explicit model-error and curvature bounds, an invariant terminal set guarantees constraint satisfaction after entry under local feedback. TIK achieves 88\% constrained cart-pole swing-up success with a 0.25 ms planning budget and controls simulated seven-joint arms within 1-5 ms per step.
evidence_items.title: Making Koopman Control Guarantees Hold on Robots

evidence_items.summary: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to empower models to continuously acquire new knowledge while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. With the advent of vision-language models like CLIP, leveraging their cross-modal alignment capabilities to address CIL challenges has emerged as a dominant paradigm. Existing methods leverage CLIP's global representations (i.e., the visual [CLS] token and the textual [EOS] token) for cross-modal alignment. While achieving effective classification, they overlook the rich patch-level visual features and token-level textual semantics inherent in CLIP. For example, the [CLS] token aggregates local information to capture the general concept of"cat", while the patch-level details retain specific localized features essential for recognition, such as the tail, fur, and face. We propose PACE (PAtch-token Cross-modal Enhancement) to uncover the long-neglected local representations within CLIP. First, based on the global representations like [CLS] token and [EOS] token, we identify the top-k most crucial visual patches and textual tokens. Subsequently, to better utilize the extracted key local features, we design a cross-modal fusion module. This module leverages local textual semantics to refine visual representations, while augmenting textual semantics with local visual features. As the fusion module is shared across all tasks, directly fine-tuning it on new tasks would interfere with the knowledge learned from previous tasks, leading to catastrophic forgetting. To alleviate this, we employ a projection-based update strategy to effectively preserve the critical parameter space of previous tasks during the adaptation to new tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PACE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple CIL benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: [CLS] and [EOS] Tokens are not Enough for CLIP-based Class-Incremental Learning

evidence_items.summary: We study counterexample-guided synthesis of contraction metrics for continuous-time autonomous systems on compact domains. A learner proposes a metric; a sound verifier certifies its matrix inequality or returns diagnostic points for retraining. The neural extension pairs a learned metric factor with symbolic contraction conditions and rigorous numerical verification; main ablations use polynomial features. We give computable polynomial bounds in arbitrary dimension and outward-rounded verification for polynomial, trigonometric, and neural representations. Loop soundness is separated from conditional finite-grid termination under idealized feasibility assumptions. We analyze why scaling and fixed-margin training can leave valid metrics uncertified. The scaling construction requires a scale-closed family, which the experimental fixed-floor class generally lacks. Verified slack improves the contraction rate and quantifies model-error tolerances using certified residual and Jacobian bounds. Finite-distance conclusions require connecting paths whose flows stay in the verified region. Experiments include controlled ablations, three-dimensional verification, and transfer from a fitted surrogate with known-truth residual certification. A physical swing-model study compares neural learning objectives with shared verification and invariant energy regions. Verified constant metrics certify the polynomial benchmark and smallest swing-model domain; neither result requires neural state dependence. Exploratory refinement certifies additional frozen candidates at a larger verification budget. In matched polynomial operating-grid experiments, trace normalization and margin coupling did not demonstrate a certification-count advantage within the tested budgets. These choices address specific failure mechanisms without guaranteeing optimizer convergence or general empirical superiority.
evidence_items.title: Neurosymbolic Synthesis of Contraction Metrics with Certified Verification

evidence_items.summary: Speech foundation models pretrained via self-supervised learning provide powerful representations for deepfake detection, yet we find that standard fine-tuning exploits only the deepest transformer layers-leaving the majority of the network's capacity discriminatively inert. Layer-wise probing of XLS-R-128 reveals that the top two-thirds of the transformer stack contribute negligibly to anti-spoofing performance after standard fine-tuning, a phenomenon we term shallow-layer dormancy. We connect this observation to the representational redundancy of pretrained transformers: adjacent layers encode highly similar information, and fine-tuning without explicit intermediate supervision reinforces rather than breaks this redundancy. To address this, we propose Progressive Layer-wise Supervision (PLS), a training framework that attaches a shared linear classifier to every transformer layer and schedules layer-wise loss contributions via an exponentially annealed power weighting. Early training concentrates supervision on deep layers to preserve the pretrained representational hierarchy; later training progressively redistributes supervision to shallower layers, converting dormant earlier representations into discriminative ones. Competitive detection (<9.25% average EER) is achievable on XLS-R-128 at layer 7, which reduces the parameter count from 315M to 101M and exemplifies an early exit mechanism. Experiments across twelve benchmarks spanning in-domain, and out-of-domain deepfake scenarios show PLS achieves a new state-of-the-art with 239M parameters, outperforming prior methods with larger and more complex architectures.
evidence_items.title: Progressive Layer-wise Supervision: Deep-to-Shallow Supervision Annealing for Efficient and Robust Speech Deepfake Detection

evidence_items.summary: Recently, the Shapley value has been widely applied in machine learning for feature importance analysis and model explainability. The multilinear extension of games proposed by Owen (1972) expresses the Shapley value as the integral of partial derivatives along the main diagonal of the cube. Direct evaluation of this integral requires exponential-time computation of the partial derivatives. To improve computational efficiency, we propose a sampling-based estimation strategy within Owen's multilinear extension framework, combining stratified sampling with coalition leverage scores. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces computational costs while maintaining explanation accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Leverage-Enhanced Sampling Owen Method for Explainable Artificial Intelligence
Evaluating Artificial Intelligence Chatbots for Patient Education on Prostate Biopsy in the Prostate Cancer Diagnostic Pathway.

evidence_items.summary: Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. To demonstrate the usability and validity of these facets, this study presents several applications within movie recommender systems using the MovieLens dataset. It exemplifies how the extended CPC framework can facilitate interactions between human judgments and data across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning algorithms.
evidence_items.title: Advancing Cognitive Pairwise Comparisons for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence and Data Science: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework

evidence_items.summary: The emergence of multi-omics technologies has enabled the integration of genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, and metabolomic data to characterize the molecular complexity of cancer. Single-cell and spatial profiling further resolve intratumoral heterogeneity, cell-cell interactions, and the microenvironmental determinants of therapeutic responses. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI) provides computational approaches for integrating these heterogeneous data types across target identification, drug response prediction, toxicity assessment, and drug-combination modeling. Across these domains, the available evidence indicates that multi-omics integration is most beneficial when the included layers provide complementary biological information; that single-cell and spatial omics analyses reveal treatment-resistant populations and niches but remain largely research-grade and thus not ready for routine clinical deployment; and that although foundation models support some representation-learning tasks, their advantages in perturbation-response prediction require confirmation via stringent evaluation. By distinguishing externally validated advances from retrospective proof-of-concept studies, we provide a practical framework for evaluating the translational readiness of AI-driven multi-omics tools in precision oncology.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence aids multi-omics data integration in cancer drug discovery and development: from targets to drug synergy.

evidence_items.summary:
This paper aims to examine the application of artificial intelligence (AI) to environmental sustainability, with particular attention to ethical and governance factors that shape whether AI contributes to meaningful sustainability outcomes.
 
 
 
 This paper conducts a structured qualitative literature review of peer-reviewed studies on the applications of AI to environmental sustainability, with particular attention to ethical and governance concerns and emerging research directions.
 
 
 
 The analysis shows that AI is most frequently applied in climate modelling and forecasting, energy optimization, waste management, biodiversity conservation and water-resource management. Across these domains, AI is used primarily to support analytical functions such as prediction, monitoring, optimization and model-based decision-making. Nevertheless, AI does not automatically generate sustainability benefits. Its contribution is conditioned by factors such as the energy demands of AI systems, infrastructure availability, governance capacity and ethical concerns relating to transparency, fairness and accountability.
 
 
 
 The article provides practical policy recommendations for policymakers and emphasizes the importance of incorporating sustainability criteria into the governance of AI, enhancing the transparency and accountability obligations for climate-related AI solutions, promoting the development of “green AI” solutions that focus on energy efficiency and supporting capacity development and data infrastructure. A short-term, medium-term and long-term research agenda on the measurement and evaluation of AI is proposed for more comprehensive integration.
 
 
 
 This review contributes to the literature in three ways. First, it integrates application-focused and ethics/governance-focused studies on AI and environmental sustainability within a single synthesis. Second, it argues that AI should be understood as a conditional enabler of sustainability rather than as an inherently sustainable solution. Third, it develops a conceptual synthesis model showing how AI applications generate sustainability-relevant analytical capabilities, but how the translation of those capabilities into sustainability outcomes depends on governance quality, ethical safeguards and institutional capacity.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence for environmental sustainability: opportunities, ethical challenges and future research directions
AACN Competencies as an AI Literacy Framework: A Graduate PMHNP Evaluation.
Restoring Trust in Researcher Evaluation: The Need for an Author Credibility Index

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into medical education, creating both opportunities and concerns for educators. Responsible implementation requires an understanding of educators’ perceptions of its limitations. This study aimed to develop and psychometrically assess the Generative AI Educator PerspectoMeter Scale (GAIE-PM) to measure medical educators’ perceptions of generative AI limitations in medical education. This descriptive scale-development study was conducted among medical educators at medical sciences universities in Iran in 2024. Following a modified Association for Medical Education in Europe (AMEE) Guide-informed approach, the scale was developed through a systematic literature review, a qualitative study with Iranian experts in three virtual focus groups, item generation, expert validation, pilot testing, and psychometric evaluation. After expert validation, 18 items were retained for pilot testing. Data were collected from 180 medical educators. Principal Factor Analysis (PCA) with Varimax Rotation was used to examine the preliminary factor structure, and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to assess the measurement model.
